News.title: Moment boy, 6, shouts ‘I CAN’T’ to laughing mum after getting stuck in railing he tried to slide down in shopping centre
News.content:
THIS is the hilarious moment a six-year-old boy shouts in frustration at his giggling mum after getting his head stuck in a railing.

Little Jason Duxbury got his noggin caught after sliding down the metal rails at Accrington Arndale Centre in Lancashire.



The youngster had been out shopping with his family for clothes and toys last Wednesday ahead of their camping trip to Newquay, Cornwall.

Jason was desperate to slide down instead of taking the stairs, despite his mum’s hesitation to let him slide down.



But as he reached the bottom of the railings, he fell through the gap, managing to get himself stuck and unable to free himself.

And Jason’s mum, Toni Millen, 38, admitted the sight of her lad with his cranium trapped between bars left her in fits of giggles.



She can be heard laughing at her son before asking him to “get out”, to which Jason then replies in frustration, “I can’t”.

Recalling the moment, she said: “Jason had climbed on top of a set of hand rails on a ramp and was saying to me ‘Mum please can I slide down’.



“I told him ‘no’ but he kept asking so I agreed as it was the end of a long day.

“When he got to the bottom he slipped through the middle and managed to get himself stuck the poor thing.

“He then couldn’t pull himself back out. I couldn’t stop laughing when I realised.

“I only recording the video to show his dad what he had done.”

The stay at home mum said after a couple of moments she told him to put his arms in the air so she could lift him out.



Toni said: “He lost a shoe in the process of me getting him out.

“I’m sure he won’t be sliding down a railing again anytime soon.”

Despite his cries for help, Jason was eventually “laughing about it” when he got home, his mum added.

He then asked her to post it on TikTok to see if it would go viral.

Toni said Jason now “thinks he is famous” after the hilarious eight second clip has since been seen by over 6 million people.



Viewers joked that the shopping centre was offering “child parking” aftet watching the video.

One said: “I’d leave him there if he shouted at me like that.”

Another added: “How did he get in there then.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A third said said: “Didn’t know there was child parking so you could shop in peace, that idea will definitely catch on.”

While another commenter said: “Look, just tell him your off to Maccies, he’ll free himself.”

News.title: Law student, 25, charged over intercepted Semtex bomb near Irish border appears in court after ‘manipulated’ claim
News.content:
OUT ON BAIL Law student, 25, charged over intercepted Semtex bomb near Irish border appears in court after ‘manipulated’ claim

A LAW student charged in relation to a bomb intercepted in a car near the Irish border has appeared in court.

Isobella Perrie Sullivan, 25, of Abbeylands Park, Clane, Co Kildare, had previously been granted bail after being charged with possession of explosives.



Ms Perrie Sullivan attended a brief hearing at Monaghan District Court today.

She stood when her case was called. The matter was adjourned until September 28 after a garda officer said the DPP is waiting for updates.



At a previous hearing, her defence solicitor said she had been asked to take a bag to the north and had not been aware what was in it, adding that she had been “manipulated”.

The car was stopped on the N2 at Aclint, Carrickmacross, Co Monaghan, in July.



During a search of the vehicle, a bag was discovered in the rear seat that contained an amount of Semtex military grade explosive and a detonator.

In court previously, Ms Perrie Sullivan was granted bail with conditions, including that she not have any contact with anyone in Saoradh or the New IRA.



Also charged in relation to the bomb interception is Simon O’Donovan, an employee at a Dublin museum.

The 44-year-old is charged with possession of an explosive substance at St Laurence’s Road in Chapelizod in the city on Wednesday July 22.

He has been remanded in custody until October 5.

News.title: OAP, 75, admits assaulting her neighbour who has late-stage cancer after ‘poisoning him with ant killer’ in driveway row
News.content:
A PENSIONER has admitted assaulting her neighbour after she allegedly poisoned him with ant killer.

Sally Beaney assaulted her neighbour Matthew Perry – who has late-stage cancer – in a row over their shared driveway.



The 75-year-old pensioner was previously charged with poisoning him with ant killer.

Beaney appeared at Southampton Crown Court and admitted to causing assault occasioning actual bodily harm to Matthew.



They share a driveway in Southampton, Hampshire, and the OAP assaulted him on October 13, 2025.

Matthew, who has “late stage cancer”, was left with swelling on his eye and a “mild corneal injury”, the court heard.



Defending Beaney, Annabel Hazlitt said the assault was caught on camera.

The pensioner kept her not guilty plea of maliciously using ant killer to poison him on October 13, 2025, “with intent to injure, aggrieve, or annoy”.



She will not be sentenced for the ant killer charge but it will lie on the file in case a similar incident happens in the future.

A charge of harassment has been dropped.

Prosecutor Gaylene Coles said: “[Matthew] is certainly at late-stage cancer, so he is still with us if I can put it in those terms.”

Talking about the damage to his eye, Ms Hazlitt said: “In terms of his eye in relation to this offence, it says there seems to be a mild reaction in the right eye, there is a little bit of swelling in the left eye.

“There is relatively mild corneal injury.”



A previous hearing was told Beaney allegedly accused her neighbour of trespassing and wrongdoing.

The homeowner is said to have repeatedly parked her car to block access to his home and placed plant pots, wooden structures and other obstacles across their shared driveway.

Ms Hazlitt said: “Ms Beaney is now 75. She has got no previous convictions.”

She said that prior to sentencing she will be assessed for a mental health treatment requirement.

Judge Nigel Peters KC said: “I think this should be dealt with at sentencing hearing. It is a neighbour dispute that has gone very badly wrong for this defendant.”



Beaney remains on unconditional bail and will be sentenced on September 18.

News.title: Mum, 25, and dad, 26, charged after death of baby boy, 1, from ‘severe malnutrition’ and ‘neglect’ of second child
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

BABY TRAGEDY Mum, 25, and dad, 26, charged after death of baby boy, 1, from ‘severe malnutrition’ and ‘neglect’ of second child

A MUM and dad have been charged after their one-year-old baby died from “severe malnutrition”.

Another child in the care of Adam Johnson, 26, and Kylie Smith, 25, was found to be “neglected and underdeveloped”.

Little Maero Johnson was rushed to hospital but, despite the best efforts of medical teams, tragically died in August 2023.

The one-year-old was later found to have been suffering from ketonic hypoglycaemia – low blood sugar – and severe malnutrition.





Merseyside Police launched a probe after another child at the home was found to be neglected and underdeveloped.

Johnson, of Hempstead Close, and Smith, of Holly Bank Street in St Helens, have now been charged with causing/allowing the death of a child.

The pair also face charges of child neglect and possession of a controlled Class B drug, cannabis.

They are set to appear at Liverpool Magistrates Court next week.

The force said: “Two parents have been charged following the death of their child three years ago in St Helens.

“Just after midnight on 23 August 2023, we received a report that a one-year-old boy, Maero Johnson, had been taken to hospital.

“But despite medical staff’s best efforts he sadly passed away.

“A Home Officer postmortem confirmed Maero died of ketonic hypoglycaemia and severe malnutrition.



“A second child was found to be neglected and underdeveloped.

“Adam Johnson, 26 years, of Hempstead Close in St Helens, and Kylie Smith, 25 years, of Holly Bank Street in St Helens, have been charged with causing/allowing the death of a child, child neglect and possession of a controlled Class B drug, cannabis.

“They will appear at Liverpool Magistrates Court on Thursday 13 August.”

News.title: Terrifying moment surgeons cling to patient on operating table as violent earthquake strikes sending equipment flying
News.content:
THIS is the horrifying moment surgeons cling onto a patient on the operating table after a destructive earthquake hits Japan.

Shocking CCTV footage shows Kumamoto hospital and its operating theatre swaying from the sheer force of the 7.1-magnitude quake that hit the country on July 28.



Two people can be seen pinning down the table and protecting the patient from danger as objects are flung across the room.

Other staff were tossed onto the floor while trying to hold down the hospital’s equipment.



The room almost descends into complete darkness as the lights flicker on and off.

The surgery resumed after the quake subsided, according to Japanese media.

The hospital’s operations returned to normal on Aug 5.

The Japanese quake hit the southern region of the island of Kyushu at6 at 4:26pm local time (7:27 am GMT), and reeled off more than 100 aftershocks.



There are reports that the tremors could be felt as far away as South Korea.

It has been reported that 34 people have died, injuring at least 100 people.

Among those who died were two workers after their boss had ordered them back into an earthquake-stricken mall to retrieve cash.



The retail company Habita and their sales manager Goji Yuse had admitted instructing the two workers to rush back into the Aeon shopping mall and put sales proceeds into a safe.

The store collapsed following an explosion due to a gas leak, according to the mall’s operator, taking the life of the two employees.

Kurumi Otake, 22, was named as one of the employees who lost his life.



Their bosses have apologised for the fatal instruction that led to their sacrifice.

They added: “Looking back now it was not worth a life.”

The quake crumbled buildings and power was cut for thousands of homes, with damaged railways leaving trains stranded and roads ruptured.

At least 79,000 people were without water in the punishing 35 degree Celsius heat for days, including no electricity for air conditioners for around 3,500.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The most severely damaged part of Kumamoto was the town of Hikawa.



Officials have said that more than 800 of the town’s 4,500 homes were left in ruins, forcing residents to sleep in their vehicles in their local car parks.

News.title: Russia could attack Nato within WEEKS, US intelligence warns as Putin ‘aims to test alliance amid weapons shortage’
News.content:
RUSSIA could attack Nato within weeks, according to new US intelligence reports.

US officials fear Vladimir Putin is plotting a small-scale land incursion to test the alliance as he faces daily humiliating attacks on his doorstep.



Until now, US intelligence believed Putin would not risk provoking Nato while fighting in Ukraine.

But the assessment has changed this year, The Wall Street Journal reports.





Possible threats include a cyberattack on a Nato country, sending armed groups to occupy territory or a limited incursion on the alliance’s eastern flank.

Putin could test Nato with a possible attack at any point between autumn this year and 2029, the report said.

One theory is Putin could grab a city in Poland, or one of the three Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, all Nato nations which have strongly backed Ukraine during the war.

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda warned recently: “I cannot deny that we have such information and that it concerns kinetic operations.



“Not on a large scale, but targeted kinetic operations that are very likely to be directed against critical infrastructure.”

And on Thursday, Lithuania’s defence minister said Russia is planning to use Ukrainian-made drones to attack the Baltics in a “false flag” hit.

Russian opposition politician Garry Kasparov believes Putin will launch a “small incursion” into Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania or Poland.



He added: “I think the chances are growing because Putin needs a winning narrative and Ukraine doesn’t offer it.”

Putin might try to grab limited Nato territory in the Baltics to claim he has scored a victory against the West.

All three Baltic states have strengthened their border defences against Russia and close ally Belarus.

Nato spokesman Colonel Martin O’Donnell said: “We are always thinking through and preparing for any number of scenarios.

“Nato is watching and we are ready to deter and defend as necessary.”



A land incursion has previously been considered highly unlikely as it would trigger Nato’s Article 5 – meaning an attack against one ally is considered an attack against all members.

Nato members believe Putin is already conducting probing attacks to test the alliance.



This includes Russian drones flying into Romania.

The Nato member has faced dozens of incursions by unmanned aerial vehicles since the outbreak of Russia‘s war in Ukraine.

Recently, Western fighter jets have been scrambled three times to shoot down drones.

Fighter jets were scrambled 250 per cent more in July compared with a year ago as Russia probes the West’s defences.



“The numbers do not lie,” NATO’s Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum said.

And just days ago, an explosives-laden drone was found beside a Ukrainian Antonov An-124 cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany in a possible Russian provocation.

Police deployed a bomb disposal robot to inspect the drone and found it had been equipped with professional explosives and a detonator.

If it had exploded then the blast could have not only injured those nearby but also set light to the aircraft, its fuel and the ammo inside.



In Lithuania, air raid alerts were issued earlier this year after a drone flew close to the border in neighbouring Belarus.

The US intelligence assessment comes amid US concern about a shortfall of munitions after supplies to Ukraine and use in the Middle East conflict.

But Trump hit back at reports of weapons shortages, saying: “The US has massive amounts of ‘munitions,’ especially of certain types.

“Additionally, large amounts are being manufactured and shipped to the US as needed.”



Wes Streeting this week warned that Russian provocations against the UK were just the “tip of the iceberg”.

On his first day as Defence Secretary a Russian warship opened fire as it steamed towards the Channel.

The frigate Neustrashimy spent 30 minutes blasting shells as big as traffic bollards into waters off the coast of Plymouth.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He told The Sun: “Incidents like the shooting in the Channel are performative, irresponsible and designed to provoke.

“It does at least provide the British with a visible manifestation of the provocations we see from Russia every day.”

News.title: Moment hero cafe owner plunges into sea fully clothed to save three screaming children from choppy waves at UK beach
News.content:
A CAFE owner has been hailed a hero after plunging into the rough sea fully clothed to save three children.

The chef rescued screaming kids from choppy waves off the Kent Coast on Wednesday.



Former Royal Marine Steven Doorey-Williams, 56, was working in the kitchen at Bayside Cafe at Dumpton Gap beach near Broadstairs when he heard screams coming from the water.

He ran outside and saw two boys and a girl struggling in the sea.



Steven immediately grabbed a buoyancy ring and waded into the water fully clothed, before bringing the children back to safety one by one.

The footage shows the hero dragging the kids through the choppy water into the shore.



Local resident Jo Drake, who witnessed the rescue outside the café, said Steven had been cooking when the incident unfolded.

She said: “I walked past his kitchen and saw him cooking then as I walked on it became apparent these children were in trouble.

“He didn’t hesitate when he heard the screaming. He just waded in fully clothed and rescued the children.

“He’s a hero.”



Fellow witness Andy Milnes also saw the incident and praised Steven for his quick response.

He said: “I saw the whole incident. Steve was there immediately and assisted all three kids ashore.”

Steven, who is also a retired firefighter, was praised by other locals following the dramatic rescue.

Amanda Rooke said: “Well done Steve, fantastic response and bravery.”

Another witness, Michelle Hallissey, added: “What a hero. Well done for saving these children, amazing.”

News.title: From Thames Water to South West Water, full list of hosepipe bans in the UK – and if there’s one in your area
News.content:
MILLIONS of Brits are facing water restrictions this weekend as another hosepipe ban comes into force.

Half of England is in drought conditions following a prolonged spell of dry, hot weather, and many water companies have now taken measures in response.



From Saturday August 8, South West Water is introducing a hosepipe ban that will impact around 1.8million people.

It means all domestic customers across Devon, Cornwall, parts of Dorset and Somerset, and the Isles of Scilly will be banned from using a hose.



South West Water already had a ban in place for Mid and East Devon, but this new measure will see almost the entire South West region face restrictions from 12.01am on Saturday.

Nine water companies have now introduced bans across the UK, affecting over 23million customers in total – here’s everything you need to know.

Which suppliers have put hosepipe bans in place?

If you live in any of the following regions, you are currently subject to a hosepipe ban:

Affinity Water: The Central region, covering Bedfordshire, Berkshire, Buckinghamshire, Hertfordshire, Surrey, and parts of London and Essex.

The Central region, covering Bedfordshire, Berkshire, Buckinghamshire, Hertfordshire, Surrey, and parts of London and Essex. Anglian Water: The whole supply region.

The whole supply region. Cambridge Water: The whole supply region.

The whole supply region. Dwr Cymru Welsh Water: Mid and South Ceredigion, North Pembrokeshire, and North Carmarthenshire.

Mid and South Ceredigion, North Pembrokeshire, and North Carmarthenshire. Essex and Suffolk Water: All household customers across the supply area.

All household customers across the supply area. South East Water: Kent, Sussex, Surrey, Hampshire, and Berkshire.

Kent, Sussex, Surrey, Hampshire, and Berkshire. South West Water: Devon, Cornwall, parts of Dorset and Somerset, and the Isles of Scilly (from Saturday August 8). Mid and East Devon are already under restrictions.

Devon, Cornwall, parts of Dorset and Somerset, and the Isles of Scilly (from Saturday August 8). Mid and East Devon are already under restrictions. Southern Water: Hampshire and the Isle of Wight.

Hampshire and the Isle of Wight. Thames Water: The entire supply area, including Greater London, the Thames Valley, Surrey, Gloucestershire, and North Wiltshire.

Is there a hosepipe ban in my area?

If you’re unsure who your water supplier is, or whether your specific street is included in the ban, the easiest way to check is online.

Visit your water supplier’s website and enter your postcode into their designated hosepipe ban checker to find out if a hosepipe ban applies to your home.

What are the rules of a hosepipe ban?

Under a Temporary Use Ban (TUB), you cannot use a hosepipe, sprinkler, or pressure washer for a variety of domestic tasks. This includes:



Watering your garden, plants, or lawn.

Cleaning your car, patio, or driveway.

Filling up a paddling pool, swimming pool, or hot tub.

Cleaning external walls or windows.

You can still carry out most of these activities if you use tap water from a bucket or watering can.

You can also use water not sourced from the mains, such as grey water (leftover bath or sink water) or rainwater collected in a water butt.

Anyone caught breaking these temporary rules can face a hefty £1,000 fine, unless they have an approved exemption or loophole in place.

Who is exempt?

Most water companies offer exemptions for some vulnerable customers.

Those on the Priority Services Register, disabled people, and Blue Badge holders who may struggle to carry heavy buckets or watering cans are generally permitted to continue using a hose for essential tasks.



To check if you’re exempt from hosepipe ban restrictions, visit your water supplier’s website to view their exemption criteria or contact their customer service team.

Why are bans being introduced?

Half of England and the entirety of Wales are currently under official drought conditions.

Sam Bottomley of South West Water explained that “exceptionally low rainfall” and “high demand during warmer weather” had provoked the decision to roll out the new restrictions.

He said: “Introducing a hosepipe ban is never a decision we take lightly, and we fully appreciate the inconvenience it will cause.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“However, these temporary restrictions are an important step in helping to protect our rivers and essential water supplies for homes, businesses and critical services across the region.”



Customers are also being urged to use less water by taking shorter showers, turning off the tap when brushing their teeth, and ensuring washing machines and dishwashers are only run on full loads.

News.title: Academics call for independent inquiry into Jason Arday's Cambridge appointment
News.content:
A group of academics is calling for an independent investigation into the appointment of Prof Jason Arday, who resigned from his University of Cambridge roles following allegations of plagiarism.

The former chair of the education faculty has also faced accusations of fabricating or exaggerating elements of his CV. He has defended himself and his work.

Attention has now turned to Cambridge's handling of concerns about Arday, who became its youngest-ever black professor in 2023.

Priyamvada Gopal, professor of postcolonial studies at Cambridge and among those calling for an independent inquiry, said the university was facing "massive reputational damage" over the affair.

"This is reputational damage that has upset colleagues across disciplines, across the political spectrum," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday.

"I've been quite struck by the number of people who are very upset by what has happened. So I don't think it is an option for Cambridge to just sweep this under the carpet and not take any action at all."

Cambridge announced on Thursday that it had begun an investigation into "new information" about Arday's academic qualifications and appointments, having already said it was looking into allegations of plagiarism.

But Gopal said the university should not be "marking its own homework", adding that the group of academics of which she is a part had suggested a mix of senior academics at Cambridge and elsewhere to conduct an investigation.

Accusations of plagiarism in Arday's work were first voiced by Nathan Cofnas - a US researcher whose role at a Cambridge college was terminated after backlash against his view that under a true meritocracy black people would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment".

He highlighted that plagiarism detection software had found several tracts of Arday's PhD dissertation to be copied verbatim or lightly rephrased from prior academic works by other authors.

Liverpool John Moores University (LJMU), which awarded Arday's PhD, has said it investigated the allegations of plagiarism last year and dismissed them, saying they were likely the result of "honest and reasonable error".

Cofnas also noted that a retired professor had previously raised concerns about Arday's subsequent academic articles, which led to two journals issuing correction notes, and raised questions about some of his claimed achievements, including extensive marathon running and raising millions for charity.

Several universities at which Arday claimed on his CV to have had academic roles have since denied him having those roles.

The controversy has attracted a range of opinions, including within academia, about whether he had been scrutinised unfairly because of his race.

Arday has admitted errors in his work but denied plagiarism, saying his autism and a lack of adequate supervision early in his academic career may have contributed to those mistakes. He also denied lying about his achievements.

He said his decision to step down should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me", which he has previously said were "racially motivated".

Gopal said universities were "being targeted in particular by a lazy and false division between academic excellence and diversity and equality on campus" which was "really part of culture wars rather than any part of university life".

She and her colleagues found it "unusual" that Arday had been appointed to a "very senior, very prestigious" post early in his career - and that he had been put forward in the media with "frankly a bit of a target on his back".

Gopal also said any investigation should review "whether the university was involved in any way or any level with efforts to deter journalists from reporting on the allegations".

This came after it emerged the Metropolitan Police investigated Times Higher Education (THE) reporter Jack Grove over a complaint of harassment after he contacted Arday concerning allegations of plagiarism last year.

The Telegraph also reported that Arday hired law firm Carter-Ruck to send a letter to THE which implied that the "apparent attack" on Arday might be "racially motivated".

The Met closed the case and Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley apologised for the investigation, telling LBC on Thursday that the complaint should have been "screened out earlier on as not requiring investigation".

The BBC has approached the University of Cambridge and LJMU for comment.

News.title: Officer who led PC Harper investigation 'appalled' killers could be released early
News.content:
Speaking to BBC Breakfast on Friday, former Det Sup Blaik, who led the Thames Valley Police investigation, pointed to remarks by the judge who sentenced PC Harper's killers. Mr Justice Edis referred to their case of manslaughter as being "very close to a case of murder in its seriousness".

The former officer called for prisoners who were judged to have had a high level of culpability for a manslaughter offence to be excluded from the scheme.

Allowing them to walk free would "undermine" the judicial process and impact police morale, Blaik said, before urging the government to have a "long, hard think" about the case.

The former Det Sup left Thames Valley Police in 2023. This is the first time he has publicly shared his views on the issue.

In an earlier statement given exclusively to BBC Breakfast, he said "like many people across the country" he was "deeply concerned and appalled" by the prospect of Bowers and Cole being considered for early release.

He said that because the "death of Andrew was such a serious and tragic case", Bowers and Coles should "not be afforded the opportunity" to be released early.

"Neither of them showed any remorse during their time in police custody or during their subsequent trial.

"I hope the Government takes account of the strength of public feeling on this issue, which has been both clear and widespread," he added.

Under revised plans announced by the government on Monday, prisoners who have committed rape, grooming, and serious child sex offences will be excluded from an early release scheme for England and Wales.

But those guilty of manslaughter may still be eligible.

Bowers and Cole were sentenced to 13 years for the manslaughter of PC Harper.

They will become eligible for release from prison after serving half of their sentences under the plans, instead of two-thirds.

The driver of the getaway car, Henry Long, was jailed for 16 years for the same offence. But Long will not be eligible.

News.title: England footballer Ivan Toney charged with assault at Soho nightclub
News.content:
England footballer Ivan Toney has been charged with assault at a nightclub in central London.

The 30-year-old, who plays for Saudi Pro League club Al-Ahli, was charged on 31 July following an incident on Wardour Street in Soho on 6 December.

The former Brentford striker, who started England's 6-4 win over France in the "bronze final" of the World Cup last month, has been charged with assault causing actual bodily harm and is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on 24 September.

A spokesperson for Toney said: "Ivan acknowledges the charge and although he is naturally shocked, he looks forward to being given the opportunity to clear his name in court."

After starting his career at Northampton Town, the striker had permanent spells at Newcastle, Peterborough and Brentford before moving to Saudi Arabia in 2024.

He was a surprise selection for England's World Cup squad but apart from the France game, his only other appearance was as a late substitute in the 2-1 semi-final defeat to Argentina.

News.title: How a 90-second power outage sparked  chaos for rail commuters
News.content:
The power failure which hit a Network Rail operations centre in Manchester was a rare incident.

But after commuters were left facing chaos, it has raised questions about how a short outage at one operating centre could have a widespread impact.

Network Rail will face scrutiny for how its systems coped and responded to the outage.

That's the publicly-owned body whose job it is to operate and maintain Britain's railway infrastructure. That means the tracks, signals, embankments and major stations.

It was at Network Rail's operating centre in Manchester that the problem started. Its operating centres are where crucial controls are housed that let trains run safely across the country, with Manchester's centre responsible for large parts of the North West.

It was hit by a power cut in the area, which was resolved within 90 seconds. And despite having a backup supply, given the centre's importance, this failed to kick in as quickly as expected.

Because signalling was affected - think of that as the traffic lights of the railway - trains had to stop.

Systems had to be rebooted. But there was some damage to the systems controlling signalling, and that took time to fix because of the need to replace certain parts.

Thinking about how busy parts of the rail network are, and how many trains and crews were left out of position across the North West of England and beyond, helps explain why the impact was so big.

Network Rail has apologised to customers and opened an investigation.

Bosses say engineers have been working hard to "build additional resilience into our signalling systems to ensure that this doesn't happen again".

News.title: Data breach investigation into Minnie Merriman's medical records
News.content:
NHS Tayside is investigating an alleged data breach into the medical records of a nine-year-old girl at the centre of a murder probe in Arbroath.

Minnie Merriman, from West Yorkshire, died at Ninewells Hospital in Dundee after being found seriously injured at an industrial estate in the town.

A 35-year-old man, who was known to the girl, has appeared in court charged with her murder.

NHS Tayside said it was "investigating the circumstances" of the alleged breach that happened in a clinical area where staff access patient information.

A spokesperson added : "As a matter of governance, any data protection breach would be recorded and investigated by NHS Tayside and, where appropriate, reported to the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO).

"It would not be appropriate for us to comment further on individual staffing matters."

News.title: Norway call for Infantino to resign as Mexico and Argentina back president
News.content:
Norway have called on Fifa president Gianni Infantino to resign following his aborted attempt to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors, but Mexico and Argentina have voiced their support for the 56-year-old.

Norway have gone a step further than the football associations of England, Wales, Croatia and Albania, all of whom have withdrawn support for Infantino without explicitly calling for him to resign.

"He [Infantino] does not have the institutional trust required to govern Fifa stably in the times we are in," Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) president Lise Klaveness said on Friday.

"There is no going back for Gianni Infantino. The international football cooperation is very much in trouble, and we must have a reason to get together now, and we want to ask the Fifa president to resign now.

"We will see which other countries eventually join in, if that becomes the strategy from the Uefa board. We are not going to ask for an extraordinary [Uefa board] meeting, we will ask him to resign in our dialogue with Fifa."

Klaveness, who is a qualified lawyer, went through a list of concerns that the Norwegian FA has expressed to Fifa during her four-year tenure.

Among them were questions around the awarding of tournaments, the inaugural Fifa peace prize that was awarded to US President âDonald Trump in December, and the overturning of a ban for American forward Folarin Balogun during the recent World Cup following a phone call from Trump.

Fifa has been approached for comment.

Meanwhile, earlier on Friday the Mexican Football Federation broke ranks with its regional governing body Concacaf to come out in support of Infantino.

Concacaf, which runs football in North and Central America and the Caribbean, called for a "comprehensive reckoning" of Infantino's presidency after he aborted plans to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

However, 2026 World Cup co-hosts Mexico have backed Infantino's leadership amid widespread calls for him to resign.

"The FMF [Mexican FA] supports president Infantino's leadership in continuing to promote the development of football through institutional strengthening," a statement read.

It echoed a statement from Conmebol - South America's governing body - in saying it would reject any attempt to remove Infantino without a vote involving all 211 Fifa members.

News.title: Arrests in Norfolk town as disorder continues for third night
News.content:
The Labour MP for South West Norfolk, Terry Jermy, said the unrest had "put Thetford back decades" after years of trying to improve the town's reputation.

Speaking to the BBC on Friday, he said: "It's been awful the last few nights, it's been terrifying for many Thetford residents."

He said he had been made aware of properties being "pelted with eggs" on Thursday and said the town was "on edge".

He said the violence was "scaring and terrifying people who live in Thetford, particularly people from minority ethnic communities who are contacting me terrified that they are going to be misidentified as an asylum seeker and attacked".

He urged fellow politicians to "call out" the violent protests and assaults of police officers.

Jermy has previously called on the Home Office to end "secrecy and confusion" around plans to house more asylum seekers in former military barracks â including at RAF Barnham, near Thetford.

The town's mayor, Vic Peters, said he supported peaceful protests but condemned "willful disregard of the law".

Commenting as an individual and not on behalf of the town council, he said council staff had been subjected to abuse and intimidation and councillors have been verbally abused in the past week.

Scott Hussey, a Reform councillor for the nearby Brecks division on Norfolk County Council, said a "peaceful protest" had started at the town's police station on Wednesday night before it moved to Clover Way.

He described the protest as "spirited" and said there had been "some skirmishes" but said he saw no violence.

He accused the Home Office of "opening a number of these HMOs across Thetford" and "trying to rush through the site for asylum seekers at Barnham".

A Home Office spokesperson condemned the behaviour, warning that "anyone taking part in this criminal activity will face the full force of the law".

They acknowledged concerns about immigration in Thetford but condemned the violence of some protesters.

A spokesperson said: "The right to protest is fundamental to our democracy and the concerns of communities are central to our immigration reforms."

News.title: How a diary entry solved the murder of a missing man
News.content:
When Det Con Tom Ryan came across a diary entry about an old cattle trailer in July 2025, he knew he had finally solved the murder of a man who had disappeared six years earlier.

Richard Dyson vanished without trace in November 2019. He was last seen alive on 17 November that year and was reported missing eight days later when he failed to meet his daughter, Bethany.

"He was by all accounts a very good father, and he was regularly in contact with his daughter Bethany who was, I believe, 19 at the time of his disappearance. It was totally out of character," Ryan recalled.

"It was clear that he had disappeared off the face of the Earth."

Richard, who was 55 at the time, had been living in his car at Parkside Cottage on Christopher Wright's farm on Sheffield Road in Barnsley, helping with small jobs around the farm.

The farm was searched, but other than a collection of illegal weapons belonging to Wright, nothing more unusual was found and there was no sign of Richard.

His phone, however, showed it had never left the farm.

Police believed from the outset that Richard had been killed and that Wright and his childhood friend, Karl Schwalbe, were responsible, according to Ryan.

"We very much suspected their involvement, but without a body it's very difficult to prove murder," he said.

On 28 July, Wright, 73, and Schwalbe, 72, were convicted for their roles in Richard's disappearance and murder, ending a six-year wait for answers for Richard's family.

At a sentencing hearing at Sheffield Crown Court on Thursday, Wright was jailed for 35 years for murder and Schwalbe was given a three-year sentence for perverting the course of justice.

But how did police finally catch them?

News.title: Conservatives pledge to ban foreign nationals from social housing
News.content:
The Conservatives have said they would end the provision of social housing for foreign nationals in England if they win power at the next election.

The party said ending new tenancies for all foreign nationals, as well as current tenancies for couples where neither person is a UK, Irish or EU citizen, would free up an estimated 228,144 homes for British families.

The Conservatives said Labour had "lost control of immigration" and British families had been left sitting on housing waiting lists as a result.

But Labour said the policy was an "unserious, unworkable proposal, copied from Reform, that does nothing to tackle the housing crisis the Tories themselves created".

In June, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said he would make it a requirement for foreign national tenants to find private accommodation within three months or face possible deportation if his party won power.

Under the Tory proposals, ineligible tenants would be expected to move out of their homes within six months.

Any single person currently living in social housing who is not a UK, Irish or EU citizen would lose their social home. This includes those with or without children.

Couples, where neither of them are UK or EU citizens, and they do not have EU settled status, will also lose their entitlement.

Anyone with EU settled status would not be evicted.

For future tenancies, UK nationals and those with EU settled status would be eligible but any new EU citizens without settled status would not be.

Foreign nationals with settled status, refugee status, or specific humanitarian protections can currently qualify for social housing.

Asylum seekers are not eligible for social housing, unless in exceptional circumstances such as domestic abuse cases.

Social housing, usually provided by housing associations or local councils, is typically cheaper and more secure than privately rented homes.

When they were last in government in 2024, the Conservatives were considering plans to make it a requirement for foreign nationals to have to live in the UK for 10 years before qualifying for social housing.

There are 1.34 million households on social housing waiting lists, as of March 2025, the latest government figures.

The vast majority of social housing lettings are given to single people.

In 2024-25, most lead tenants of new social lettings, the person in whose name the social home is rented, were UK nationals - 89% or 233,000 tenants.

In the same period, 2.3% of new lettings were given to refugees - 800 refugees were UK nationals, while the remaining 3,900 were non-UK nationals.

The most common nationality of refugees in a new social letting was Afghanistan with the second most common being Ukraine.

News.title: Girl, 11, found dead after search at Midlothian beauty spot
News.content:
An 11-year-old girl has died after being found in the water at a beauty spot in Midlothian.

A major search was launched over reports of concern for the girl in Gore Glen Woodland Park, near Gorebridge, at about 12:40 on Thursday.

The girl's body was found in the park's Gore Water, near Shank Bridge, at about 16:25. She was pronounced dead at the scene.

A Police Scotland spokesperson said: "Her death is being treated as unexplained and inquiries are ongoing to establish the full circumstances."

The force said the girl's family was aware.

News.title: Assistant referee Massey-Ellis retires to take FA role
News.content:
Assistant referee Sian MasseyâEllis has announced her retirement from officiating to take up a position with the Football Association.

MasseyâEllis, who officiated in more than 150 Premier League matches, will start a senior manager role focused on supporting and developing female officials.

Since rising to the Premier League as an assistant referee in 2010 - becoming only the second woman to do so - MasseyâEllis became the first Englishwoman to officiate in a men's European fixture and first woman to officiate in a men's FA Cup final, as well as being involved in five Women's FA Cup finals.

After announcing her retirement, Massey-Ellis said: "Although I am stepping away from the touchline, I am not stepping away from football.

"If my journey has helped change perceptions, open doors or inspire even one young person to believe they belong in the game, then I will consider that one of my greatest achievements."

News.title: London launches bid to host WorldPride in 2032
News.content:
London has launched a bid to host WorldPride 2032, which would coincide with the 60th anniversary of the UK's first Pride march in the capital in 1972.

The bid for the 10-day festival is led by Pride in London, entertainment hub Outernet London and UK Black Pride, with backing from City Hall.

Organisers have started a global campaign inviting LGBTQ+ creatives to design the official logo outline for the bid.

The winning design - which carries a Â£3,000 prize - will be filled with thousands of photographs submitted by LGBTQ+ individuals and allies worldwide, "creating one living symbol of Pride", organisers said.

Rebecca Paisis, chief executive of Pride in London, said the initiative aims to let the community shape the bid's future from day one.

"As we approach the 60th anniversary of London's first Pride march, this project gives every generation an opportunity to leave their mark on what could become one of the defining moments in our movement's history," she said.

WorldPride is a major international event featuring marches, human rights conferences and cultural festivals.

Held every two to three years, the festival aims to promote LGBTQ+ visibility and rights internationally.

Since the inaugural event in Rome in 2000, host cities have included Toronto, Madrid, New York, Copenhagen and Sydney.

London previously hosted the event in 2012 and unsuccessfully bid to stage it again in 2030, while the 2026 event is currently taking place in Amsterdam and Cape Town is set to become the first African host city in 2028.

News.title: Sullivan set to attend West Ham tie against advice
News.content:
West Ham are expecting David Sullivan to attend Saturday's Carabao Cup first-round tie against Portsmouth despite him being advised to stay away from home matches at London Stadium.

Sullivan, 77, resigned from his position as co-chair of West Ham in June after a joint investigation by BBC Panorama and The Times revealed that seven women have accused Sullivan of sexually exploitative and predatory behaviour.

He has categorically denied the allegations.

On Monday, a spokesperson for London Stadium told BBC News it had "recommended" to West Ham that Sullivan does not attend matches because of concerns about fan unrest.

London Stadium has asked for advance notice of any planned visits by major shareholder Sullivan - who retains a 38.8% stake in the club - in order to implement additional safety and operational measures.

The match against Portsmouth will be the first the club has played since the allegations against Sullivan were first reported.

The Panorama and Times joint investigation also revealed that Sullivan has been banned from contact with West Ham's women's and youth teams for the past three years because of safeguarding concerns.

London Stadium was unaware of the restrictions until the BBC's report.

Sullivan was banned after a historical allegation about his conduct was raised with the Football Association in 2023. He has previously said the allegation was false.

Sullivan had already been the subject of intense fan abuse for his running of the club, who were relegated to the Championship last season for the first time since 2011.

Although West Ham have stabilised on the pitch, with key figures, including manager Nuno Espirito Santo and skipper Jarrod Bowen committing their future to the club, there remains huge uncertainty off it.

Vanessa Gold, daughter of Sullivan's late business partner and former West Ham co-chair David, backed out of a deal to sell part of her stake in the club to Czech billionaire Daniel Kretinsky, and instead reached an agreement with Amanda Staveley, the public face of the Saudi Arabia-backed takeover at Newcastle, to sell her entire 25.1% stake.

However, Kretinsky has since sold a small part of his own stake, bringing him under 25%.

That would allow him to buy Gold's shares under West Ham's pre-emption rights rules - which allow existing shareholders first choice to buy shares when they become available.

If he did so he would become West Ham's biggest shareholder, without triggering another clause that would force him to then buy the rest of the club.

It is anticipated Saturday's match against fellow Championship side Portsmouth (15:00 BST) will set an attendance record for an EFL Cup first-round tie, with the Hammers having sold 55,000 season tickets for the new campaign.

News.title: Man 'humiliated' after being told mobility scooter too big for train
News.content:
A man with osteoarthritis and learning difficulties has said he feels "humiliated" after being told he cannot take his new mobility scooter on Translink's train services because it has been deemed to be too big.

Stephen Magee had been using his previous scooter for about five years without any problems.

But he said after Translink assessed his new scooter he was told it is 10cm too large.

A Translink spokesperson said the company was committed to providing accessible services for everyone and that all mobility scooters were assessed through an independent process to make sure they could be accommodated and taken on and off its vehicles safely.

Magee, who lives in Coleraine, said he bought the new scooter as the previous one had begun to show its age.

He originally contacted the Nolan Show to share his story.

He said he deliberately bought a scooter that was the same size as his old one, thinking it would be suitable to take onto trains, but after it was assessed he got a letter from Translink saying it was too big.

"I felt disheartened, I felt humiliated in so many ways," he said.

"I'm left not being able to go on any trains and I can't use the buses because it will not fit on any of their buses.

"It seems like we're [mobility scooter users] an inconvenience to people.

"I don't like the fact that I use a mobility scooter but unfortunately I've been left with no choice."

News.title: Police to end review into siblings who died in farmhouse 'bloodbath'
News.content:
A forensic review into the deaths of a brother and sister 50 years ago will end almost four years after it began, despite not delivering any new conclusions.

The bodies of Martha and Griff Thomas were found at a farmhouse in Llangolman, Pembrokeshire in 1976, originally prompting a double murder investigation.

Family member Huw Gibby, 79, said he was left "shell-shocked" that the investigation had failed to find any new answers, and described crime scene photos as a "bloodbath".

Dyfed-Powys Police said a "significant amount of complex work" had been undertaken, and "the family has been updated on the limitations faced in reviewing an incident that took place 50 years ago".

On a chilly Saturday morning in December 1976, postman Nigel Rossiter pulled up outside the isolated Ffynon Samson farmhouse in west Wales.

It was his first week in the job, and he spotted a couple of letters still lying on the floor of the porch where he had delivered them days before.

Smelling burning inside, he raised the alarm. This led to the discovery of two bodies, Griff, 73, who was badly burnt, and Martha, 70, who had severe injuries.

Police were called and found Martha, known as Patti, lying slumped on a magazine rack in the corner of the living room, with severe head injuries.

Chairs had been knocked over, and an overturned television lay at her feet. It was still switched on, with the sound of static filling the room.

News.title: Why is Amanda Knox's upcoming Edinburgh Fringe comedy show causing controversy?
News.content:
Amanda Knox, a woman involved in one of the world's most famous murder cases, is set to perform a comedy show at The Edinburgh Festival Fringe.

Knox was convicted and later acquitted of murdering her British roommate, Meredith Kercher, in Italy in 2007.

Knox's show, Cartwheel, is about motherhood and how she will explain her experiences to her daughter, according to the festival's website.

"I don't joke about Meredith's death. I joke a lot about how I was vilified, but I don't joke about her murder," she had told the Telegraph newspaper, external.

Kercher's sister, Stephanie told BBC Breakfast her sibling "wouldn't find these topics of any comedy value".

A petition against the show, set up by a friend of Meredith, has been signed by just over 2,400 people, and says the show disrespects her memory and also risks normalising violence against women.

A spokesperson for Knox said the show, set to run over 11 days from Friday, honours Kercher's memory.

Find out more about what Stephanie Kercher told the BBC.

News.title: The careers with the lowest alzheimer’s death rates — and what we can learn from them
News.content:

Taxi and ambulance drivers are less likely than workers in almost any other job to die of Alzheimer’s disease. That was the surprising result of a 2024 study examining the death certificates of nearly 9 million people in the U.S.

These findings stopped me in my tracks because those two jobs rely on the same thing as my own work: maps.

I have spent more than two decades staring at maps. Not paper maps on a wall, but digital ones with multiple layers: flood boundaries draped over census blocks, car crash hot spots plotted against road geometry, and satellite readings of rainfall stitched across river basins. Much of my work as a civil and environmental engineer is done through GIS – that is, geographic information systems. Engineers like me hold several spatial relationships in their minds at once, reasoning about where things sit relative to one another across scales ranging from a city block to a whole watershed.

I always assumed that spatial reasoning across map layers was purely professional. But that study on taxi and ambulance drivers made me wonder whether all that mental work might be doing something good to the brain.

But that study on taxi and ambulance drivers made me wonder whether all that mental work might be doing something good to the brain ( Getty/iStock )

Taxi driver brains

Of the 9 million death certificates from January 2020 to December 2022 that researchers examined, taxi and ambulance drivers had the lowest risk of dying from Alzheimer’s disease out of 443 occupations. After adjusting for age, sex, race, ethnicity and education, roughly 1 in 100 taxi and ambulance drivers died of Alzheimer’s, compared with 1 in 60 people overall.

This pattern did not extend to other driving jobs. The researchers concluded that the key to reducing the risk of Alzheimer’s was not driving itself but continuous real-time navigation: the constant work of locating yourself in space, tracking a destination and updating a mental map as conditions change. Drivers whose jobs relied on fixed or predetermined routes, like bus drivers and aircraft pilots, didn’t seem to experience a similar advantage.

Researchers believe the association between navigation-heavy work and lower Alzheimer’s risk centers on the hippocampus, a part of the brain that governs memory and spatial navigation. It’s one of the first brain regions that Alzheimer’s damages: Problems with spatial navigation and orientation are among the earliest signs of the disease, sometimes surfacing before obvious memory loss.

In one landmark 2000 study, neuroscientists compared the brains of licensed London taxi drivers with those of people who did not drive cabs. Their findings provided the first evidence via structural imaging that regions of the adult brain can measurably change under sustained navigational demand. To earn a license, London cabbies must memorize more than 25,000 streets within a 6-mile radius of Charing Cross, a challenge known as “The Knowledge” that takes three to four years.

The researchers found that London taxi drivers had measurably more gray matter in the posterior hippocampus, a brain area tied to storing large-scale spatial maps. That volume tracked with experience: The longer someone had driven, the larger that part of the brain. The change was built through practice, not inherited. While people who are good at navigation might gravitate to this kind of job, the job itself does have an impact on the brain.

Together, these two studies make a coherent case: Work that intensively exercises the hippocampus may reshape it, and that reshaping may protect against one of the most feared diseases of aging.

Where map specialists fit in

Cartographers, urban planners and geospatial analysts spend their working days in sustained spatial reasoning. A geographic information system specialist might use a computer to overlap population data on flood exposure maps to find who is at risk, or read satellite imagery to map land cover after a wildfire. Researchers juggle several layers of data, coordinate systems and scales at once.

Does spatial reasoning through a screen engage the hippocampus the way moving through a real city does?

While a taxi driver navigates from inside the scene at street level, GIS researchers picture space from above as a map – what cognitive scientists call allocentric reasoning. But these two perspectives overlap in the brain: The hippocampus also builds maps from outside viewpoints, not just from a navigator’s own position.

Research on cognitive maps points toward the same conclusion as the study on taxi drivers. In 2023, researchers ran a machine learning model on more than 22,500 people in a national dataset and were able to predict which ZIP codes had higher rates of Alzheimer’s with 84% accuracy based on how complex the environment was. Those living in spatially complex surroundings – the kind that force active map building, such as dense street networks with numerous intersections, diverse points of interest and landmarks, and multiple path options – were less likely to develop Alzheimer’s.

A follow-up study tied geospatial complexity in one’s environment to greater volume in the brain’s spatial navigation regions. The researchers hypothesized that routinely building cognitive maps exercises the very circuitry that Alzheimer’s attacks first. Repeatedly engaging the cognitive systems involved in spatial navigation could help delay symptoms of disease.

However, these two studies focus on where people live, not the work people do. Whether spatial reasoning through a screen exercises the same circuitry as real-life city navigation remains untested.

Protecting your brain

The implications of whether sustained spatial reasoning protects the brain reach beyond mapmakers and cab drivers. Studies have repeatedly found a link between mentally complex occupations and delayed cognitive decline and lower dementia risk, even after accounting for education.

About the author Hatim Sharif is a Professor of Civil and Environmental Engineering, The University of Texas at San Antonio. This article was first published by The Conversation and is republished under a Creative Commons licence. Read the original article .

Research on cognitive reserve – the brain’s capacity to continue functioning despite disease – can help explain why two people with a similar disease burden can show markedly different levels of cognitive impairment. If demanding spatial thinking protects the brain, then how societies design schooling, professional training and retirement all become questions of brain health.

Spatial reasoning can be trained, and training opportunities are already widespread. GIS and remote sensing instruction are available through geography, engineering, public health and environmental science programs worldwide.

If sustained engagement with spatial reasoning can help the brain strengthen the circuitry that Alzheimer’s attacks first, its value reaches well beyond the technical skills it builds.

Former safeguarding minister Jess Phillips has said she "hated" being in Keir Starmer’s government as she described the battle she faced to persuade other departments to take action on violence against women.

Ms Phillips, who managed domestic abuse refuges for Women's Aid before she became an MP, also also said she would not return to a similar role to “just start knocking heads together again”.

“I hated it. I hated being a government minister actually, I hated it,” she said.

open image in gallery Jess Phillips (L) and Sir Keir Starmer (R) both stood for the Labour leadership following Jeremy Corbyn’s resignation ( PA )

Speaking to Sky's Electoral Dysfunction podcast, she said that she was "deeply unhappy throughout most" of her time in the post.

Ms Phillips quit as a minister in May in a bid to force Sir Keir from No 10, and said that he lacked “the drive to get anything done with gusto".

She warned the government was "nowhere near the level of will and commitment it will actually take to halve" violence against women and girls, the policy Labour set out in in the 2024 general election manifesto.

"The Violence Against Women and Girls strategy, if you were to do everything in it, you would probably drop [VAWG] by about 25 per cent,” she said.

She added that she used to give "gold stars" to ministers in other departments who took the pledge seriously – but expressed frustration at some departments.

open image in gallery Labour MP Jess Phillips said she would not return to a similar role ( Getty )

"I understand other government departments have other priorities, but it's not my job to be flexible," she said. "I have one job, and it is to stop women having to be flexible about their safety."

Asked if she would return to government, she said: "I won't go back and be a junior minister who – whilst having an awful lot of gumption and kudos in the field – I won't go back and just start knocking heads together again."

She added: "I don't think I'm suited to it, …is the actual answer... I won't go back in and do more of the same. So no is the answer," she said.

Sir Keir survived the attempt to force him from office earlier this year but bowed to growing frustration within his party at the start of the summer when he announced he was standing down, clearing the way for Andy Burnham to become prime minister.

Texas Republican Rep. Dan Crenshaw has found himself at the centre of a social media storm after belittling voters’ concerns about the affordability crisis.

Crenshaw, who was primaried for his seat and lost to GOP state Rep. Steve Toth in March, weighed in on a debate on X about soaring grocery prices after Turning Point USA spokesman Andrew Kolvert said he had recently been told by a college student: “A burrito shouldn’t cost $20.”

“A lot of this is a hangover from Covid and Biden-era inflation, but the lived experience is the same: It just feels like basic things cost too much,” Kolvert observed.

The outgoing congressman and former Navy SEAL said: “Just hearing about this dumb $20 burrito debate so just thought I’d make the losers on social media angry before going to bed.

“Stop whining, get a job, eat Ramen like the rest of us did in college, on a budget with 4 roommates.

open image in gallery Texas Republican Rep. Dan Crenshaw provoked an uproar on X by belittling concerns about the cost of living ( Getty )

“The market doesn’t care what you think something ‘should’ cost. Only communists care (they set prices remember? Then everyone starves, remember?) Are you a communist? Or are you an American adult male capable of handling his own s***?”

The “ragebait” response provoked a storm of anger and derision, notably from Crenshaw’s fellow conservatives, with one characteristic comment pointing out that the price of 10lbs of hamburger meat had tripled between 2020 and 2026.

Several people pointed to the Republican’s own contradictory past output on the same subject, including one tweet from September 2021 in which he had written: “America: our food prices are too high what are you doing about inflation? Biden admin: just be vegan and stop complaining you bunch of rubes.”

Forced into a climbdown, Crenshaw said: “Okay, I am SORRY for triggering the comment section. Of course the world is objectively harder than EVER, and while a $20 burrito is rare, the fact that it exists anywhere is obviously proof that capitalism has FAILED.

open image in gallery Vice President JD Vance also found himself caught up in the exchange of insults ( Getty )

“lol no just kidding. Remember when the right had principles and made fun of leftists for elevating victimhood as a virtue? Want to tell people the truth? Or just bribe them for their vote in the next election?”

He was not the only conservative to get caught up in the storm.

Right-leaning columnist Marc Thiessen responded equally unsympathetically to Kolvert, writing: “Cry me a river. The burritos in the college cafeteria are included in your meal plan.”

That drew a response from Vice President JD Vance, who, rather than offering anything more constructive, replied by fat-shaming Thiessen: “I’m surprised to hear Mark [sic] say this. If you’ve ever met him in person, it’s quite obvious the man has never missed a burrito.”

Vance in turn was hit with a series of unflattering photographs of himself as a portly, beardless younger man, as well as an AI image in which he was portrayed devouring a corndog.

Voters have consistently told pollsters they believe the Trump administration – which Vance aspires to inherit – is not doing enough to address the inflated cost of living, which threatens to cause major problems for Republican candidates come November’s midterms.
