Sports.title: Mexico and Argentina line up behind Infantino to deepen football’s civil war
Sports.content:
The Mexican football federations have broken ranks with the rest of Concacaf by issuing their public backing for beleaguered Fifa president Gianni Infantino in a move that has deepened world football’s civil war.

Concacaf has called for a thorough review of Fifa’s governance in the light of the World Cup sell-off debacle, and is backing Uefa’s demands for meaningful change, although has yet to follow their European counterparts by threatening to boycott tournaments if they do not achieve their objectives.

A statement issued on Thursday night by the Mexico federation (FMF) went some way towards explaining Concacaf’s reticence, as their second biggest member after the United States was unequivocal in their support for Infantino.

In a Fifa statement released under Infantino’s name on Wednesday, the world governing body had called for its institutional practices to be respected, a coded way of condemning any leadership challenge before next March’s scheduled presidential election, which the FMF endorsed.

“The Mexican Football Federation is convinced that football is its fundamental value and that its best defence lies in institutional integrity and respect for the governance and processes that safeguard it,” the FMF said.

“Therefore, the FMF will not recognise or approve any process convened outside of this institutional framework, and it embraces the call issued by President Infantino on August 5, 2026, to collectively continue developing football for the benefit of its 211 member associations. The FMF supports President Infantino’s leadership in continuing to promote the development of football through institutional strengthening.”

The Argentina Football Association (AFA) followed Mexico’s lead by backing Infantino in a gushing tribute and expressing support for his leadership over the past decade.

Unlike Concacaf, South America’s Conmebol appears united behind Infantino, while in an intriguing subplot there is growing speculation that Mexico would like to switch confederations to join the latter.

“In relation to the recent events that are public knowledge, we must recognise the decision of the administration to withdraw a project that generated, within the football family and from its inception, many more uncertainties than certainties,” the AFA statement read.

“That is why it is worth highlighting the acceptance of the errors made in this process and the apology expressed in the heartfelt message displayed to the 211 member associations of Fifa. Prioritising governance standards is a fundamental pillar for strengthening good relations between Fifa, its member associations and the confederations.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“In the same way, and as we have already expressed, you are leading a management that led to a profound transformation of Fifa, which opened the doors of the organisation to all member associations and confederations, so that with a frank and direct dialogue, we can, together, continue to promote football at all levels and disciplines.

“From our point of view, this transformation was based on a model of transparent governance, respect for statutory structures and the monitoring of democratic procedures, essential principles for the football family to be united, firm and working to continue generating improvements in sports and institutions, which have an impact on a better quality of life for millions of human beings who practice our beloved sport.

“Accordingly, with the upcoming Fifa Congress approaching, the association that we proudly preside over firmly believes and reaffirms that the way forward is to continue to work under your leadership, so that we can continue to develop better and even more inclusive football.”

Earlier on Thursday the Confederation of African Football had reaffirmed its support for Infantino, providing him with further allies as he fights to extend his 10-year reign.

Sports.title: Norway’s Klaveness tells Fifa president Infantino to resign: ‘There is no trust now’
Sports.content:
The Norwegian FA will ask Gianni Infantino to resign with immediate effect after his doomed attempt to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors. Norway is the first federation to call directly for the Fifa president to step down after a series of controversies that came to a head with the current crisis surrounding his Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme.

The decision was made at a meeting of the Norwegian Football Federation board (NFF) on Thursday night. Norway has consistently taken a lead in efforts to scrutinise Fifa’s governance and recent events have taken any faith in its leadership beyond the point of no return.

“We decided that there is no trust in Infantino now,” the NFF president, Lise Klaveness, told the Guardian. “We have been worried consistently and there has been one more step in worrying direction every year, every part of the year. The trust is now gone for us, there is no way back for Infantino.

“We’re left in a very polarised cooperation globally and, I would say, chaos. So we will ask him to resign immediately so that the global football community can look ahead and cooperate going into the future.”

The NFF is expected to formally write a letter requesting Infantino’s resignation in the coming week. Norway was among a handful of countries not to back his re-election as president next March, although several European federations have withdrawn their endorsement in the past week.

“We understand that we’re one country, but it’s our position,” Klaveness said. “It’s just one step further for us. We did not vote for him in 2023 but we hoped we would support him, he was elected and the reason why we were so clear in our statements was to really give the signal that we wanted him to implement the good reforms he was part of. But he didn’t, and now we will ask him to resign.”

The NFF agreed to demand a full review into the package of reforms passed upon Infantino’s ascent to the presidency in 2016, which were intended to extricate Fifa from the corruption crisis that had previously dogged the governing body. Klaveness said the investigation should ask “what was implemented, what was not, what should have been implemented and what we should also implement to make this a functioning organisation.”

Norway will also formalise a fresh complaint to Fifa’s ethics committee on three fronts, taking in the FFE scandal, the award of Fifa’s “peace prize” to Donald Trump and the Folarin Balogun affair at the recent World Cup. It will attempt to bring a number of major European federations on board for its submission in a bid to further increase the pressure on Infantino.

“We want the ethics committee to show their work transparently because this is a very big part of the issue,” Klaveness said. “There are all kinds of control mechanisms in place but they are not really holding the council and president accountable.”

In June, the NFF wrote to the ethics committee supporting a complaint by the advocacy group FairSquare, which centred on alleged breaches of political neutrality by Infantino. It will now make a new submission that asks for the three situations to be considered individually.

“We will join them in one letter but they are very different cases and we want the ethical committee to treat them separately,” Klaveness said.

The NFF is understood to have particular concerns that the timing of Infantino’s FFE offer, which promised federations significant financial gains if accepted, may constitute an abuse of position at this proximity to a presidential election. It has also been observed that the FFE scheme, had it been passed, would have locked in commitments extending well beyond Infantino’s term of office.

Similarly to its call for Infantino to step down, Norway is the first federation to adopt a public stance regarding the peace prize or Balogun case. Fifa’s decision to suspend the US striker’s red card during the World Cup, meaning he was free to face Belgium in the last 16, came after Trump had called Infantino to discuss the ban.

Uefa’s federations have stood together in backing a potential boycott of Fifa competitions, a stance it reasserted on Thursday despite Infantino’s shelving of FFE. Klaveness said the move is not merely symbolic and is intended to bring swift results.

“There’s no point in Uefa standing in a war position for half a year,” she said. “That would not be good at all. Now it’s crucial that we do it because global football cooperation is at stake. It’s very good to see we have strong leadership in Uefa that knows now is crunch time for this case. We cannot sell out this core of football.”

The first competition in line for a boycott would be the under-20 Women’s World Cup, which is due to start in Poland on 5 September, but Klaveness expects the continued turmoil to have been resolved by then.

“I hope and think it will not come to that,” she said. “A lot of water will go under the bridge before that. But this is why we ask Infantino to resign. It’s so unstable now that it’s a matter of time. He cannot recover this and we cannot put the sport on the spot. The biggest priority is to be together with Uefa and have this strong position.”

Klaveness and the NFF have held a consistent line in calling for scrutiny of Fifa’s operations since she assumed her current position in March 2022. She has been vocal on human rights issues and governance standards within Fifa, criticising failings surrounding the Qatar World Cup and questioning the process that awarded Saudi Arabia the 2034 edition of the tournament.

Sports.title: Tottenham and Atlético in talks over Romero with Van de Ven set to sign new deal
Sports.content:
Tottenham are in talks with Atlético Madrid over the sale of Cristian Romero after categorically rejecting Arsenal’s approach for the Argentina defender and are expected to agree a new five-year deal with Micky van de Ven.

Romero has made no secret of his desire to leave Spurs despite signing a new four-year contract at the start of last season and had looked set to join Internazionale for a fee of around £35m. But Atlético are long-term suitors of the 27-year-old and are thought to be his preferred destination, with Diego Simeone’s side understood to be prepared to match Inter’s bid.

Reports in Spain on Friday suggested that personal terms have already been agreed with Romero, although his move may have to wait for Atlético to free up space in their squad before they can complete the transfer. Nahuel Molina, Romero’s Argentina teammate, is expected to join Roma while Aston Villa are hoping to sign Matteo Ruggeri.

Arsenal had also made their interest known as they search for a replacement for William Saliba, with the Frenchman out for an extended period due to a back issue. But Tottenham – who have signed defenders Jan Paul van Hecke and Marcos Senesi this summer – insisted that they did not want to sell to another Premier League club, least of all their north London rivals. Arsenal are also interested in Aston Villa’s Ezri Konsa.

It is understood that Van de Ven had been considering his future in north London at the start of the summer after Tottenham narrowly avoided relegation last season. But the impact of the new manager, Roberto De Zerbi, has persuaded the Netherlands international to commit his future to the club after talks with his representatives.

Tottenham have already spent more than £200m on six new players this summer and are still in the market for a new attacker. Last week, De Zerbi said that they had “completed 60% of our project in the transfer market”.

Sports.title: England striker Ivan Toney charged with assault after Soho nightclub incident
Sports.content:
The England footballer Ivan Toney has been charged with assault after an incident at a nightclub in Soho in December last year.

Scotland Yard said the striker had been charged on 31 July with assault causing actual bodily harm. Toney, who plays for the Saudi Pro League club Al-Ahli, is due to appear at Westminster magistrates court on 24 September.

The Sun newspaper reported in December that Toney had been arrested after an alleged head-butt. It claimed a fan recognised the footballer and grabbed at him while seeking a photograph with him before the incident.

On Friday the Metropolitan police said the charges related to an incident on 6 December at a nightclub on Wardour Street in central London, reportedly the now-closed 100 Wardour Street.

A spokesperson for Toney said: “Ivan acknowledges the charge and although he is naturally shocked, he looks forward to being given the opportunity to clear his name in court.”

Toney was at the centre of one of the most curious transfers on deadline day in August 2024 when he completed a late move from Brentford to Al-Ahli worth a reported £40m. He has also played for Newcastle United and his home town club Northampton Town, as well as several others on loan as he looked to establish himself.

Seen as a late bloomer in football terms, he had made only two Premier League appearances before his 25th birthday, but went on to score 67 goals in 128 appearances over the next three seasons at the top level.

He has played 10 times for England, scoring once in a friendly match against Belgium in 2024, and was part of the 2026 World Cup squad, making appearances against Argentina in the semi-final and in the win over France as England finished third.

Sports.title: Afcon’s biennial switch cost African governing body deal worth more than $1bn
Sports.content:
A deal worth at least $1bn in secured income over eight years was abandoned by the Confederation of African Football (Caf) because the governing body decided to switch the Africa Cup of Nations from a biennial to a four-yearly event, the Guardian can reveal.

On 5 July 2025, the eve of the delayed Women’s Africa Cup of Nations in Morocco, the Caf president, Patrice Motsepe, told the Guardian in Rabat, after a prolonged discussion of the bidding process at an executive committee meeting, that a decision on a winning bid would be made “in due course”.

“We announced in Addis Ababa this $1bn partnership that we are looking at over the next eight years. There is a lot of good progress that has been made,” he said.

On 23 July, four days after the World Cup final in New York, Caf opened a fresh tender for the marketing and commercial rights of the 2028, 2032 and 2036 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) tournaments, with bidders given until 24 August to hand in their bid books.

The tender is in complete contrast to the 2025 bidding round, in which the entirety of Caf’s competition portfolio was bundled for sale.

Luxolo September, Caf’s head of communications, confirmed that the change in Afcon frequency is wholly responsible for the abandonment of the 2025 bidding round that was on the verge of completion.

“As foreshadowed by the president in his comments last year, following the receipt and evaluation of bids and presentations from the bidders, in the second half of 2025, Caf entered into detailed discussions with shortlisted bidders regarding the precise terms and conditions of their proposals.

“However, at its meeting on 20 December 2025, the Caf executive committee took a unanimous decision – in the interest of African football – to move the Afcon to a four-year cycle, bringing the competition into alignment with the international match calendar,” September said. “This was a significant decision for African football. That executive committee decision materially changed the scope of the commercial rights available for tender, with the result that the 2025 ITT (Invitation To Tender) process could no longer proceed in its existing form.”

View image in fullscreen Patrice Motsepe (left) said in 2025 that ‘good progress’ was being made over a $1bn deal for Caf. Photograph: Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty Images

It has been seven years since Caf has had a long-term deal to secure its financial future. The 2016-2028 billion-dollar “minimum guarantee” revenue contract that it signed with the French company Lagardère during the tenure of Issa Hayatou, the late Cameroonian president of Caf, was the first of its kind for the organisation.

“The Memorandum of Understanding with Lagardère was agreed by a team I led with Hicham [El Amrani, then Caf general secretary] in May 2015, in Zurich,” Suketu Patel, then chair of Caf’s finance committee, said in 2019.

“On that same day, we met with Infront. Their indicative offer on the table was a $450m minimum guarantee for eight years, as opposed to the $1bn, for 12 years, from Lagardère.

“If you look at our earlier contract of 2009, we had a minimum guarantee of $150m, but our income for the period was actually around $350m. We anticipated that the 12-year contract would have yielded about $1.3bn.

“I can tell you that whilst President Hayatou and I had differences on political matters, we never had one on the management of Caf finances. He did not interfere with the processes established for good governance.”

But that agreement was unilaterally terminated in December 2019 during the tenure of Ahmad Ahmad, Hayatou’s successor as Caf president.

A protracted legal dispute at the International Chamber of Commerce led to Caf, just over a year into the presidency of Motsepe, paying Lagardère a final settlement of $50m, as compensation for the breach of contract, just before the 2022 World Cup in Qatar.

“There is no way that any sponsor will be prepared to pay the same amount of money for a deal in which you would normally have four Afcons over an eight-year period, when you will now only have two. That is certainly a no-brainer,” said a former FA president with expertise in financial matters.

Sports.title: Behind Milburn’s magic: Wor Jackie was a pit village hero and ‘everybody’s friend’ in Newcastle
Sports.content:
Of all the footballers who have worn the black and white, that possessive geordie pronoun “Wor” (our) was unique to Jackie Milburn; for he was a man of the people as much as he was a great sportsman. In that respect, his birthplace of Ashington in Northumberland only added to the mythology.

“The biggest pit village in the world,” as it was known, was the north-east in microcosm – a one-horse coal town where miles of identical terraced houses spread out from the pitheads and the menfolk were obsessed by whippets, leeks, association football and pints in the club. Nevertheless, he had a self-discipline that saw the pitfalls of alcohol: “Certainly it prevented my dad, Alec Milburn, from making the big time,” Jackie recalled. “He could have gone to Tottenham but preferred to stay home and drink his ale.”

At the St James’ Park homecoming following the 1951 FA Cup final, “Wor Jackie” (by which epithet his skipper Joe Harvey introduced him) was invited to address the throng. “At first I tried to ‘talk posh,” Jackie later recalled, “then there was a roar of laughter when a voice shouted, ‘Taak tiv us in your own language, Jackie!’” The dialect of Ashington is one of the most melodious varieties of the ‘pitmatic’ geordie of the coalfields, and still the butt of numerous jokes to this day (when an electrician asked a barmaid where the mains were, the answer came, “Tha just doon there, past the ladies.”)

View image in fullscreen A statue by Tom Maley of Jackie Milburn at Woodhorn Colliery Museum, near Ashington in Northumberland. Photograph: John Angerson/Alamy

Jackie’s lineage was important, for Ashington was an unusually fertile footballing hotbed. His great-grandfather, “Warhorse” Milburn, had kept goal for Northumberland in the 1880s, and young Jackie grew up reading about the Football League exploits of his four Milburn cousins who played professionally, while another cousin, Cissie Charlton, née Milburn, was later almost equally famous as the mother of World Cup winners Jack and Bobby.

Although the coalmines of Ashington demanded their human tribute, professional football was a feasible way out for many – and Milburn once counted 47 local boys he knew of who had played in the First Division. In his 1957 autobiography Golden Goals, he recalled waking early one Christmas morning to find a new pair of football boots at the end of the bed. He slipped them on straight away and headed out into the back lane at half past three in the morning only to find “most of my friends, wearing their new boots, playing football by torchlight in the middle of the street”.

View image in fullscreen Jackie Milburn’s second cousin Bobby Charlton thought that ‘his ball control at speed was as good as anyone I’ve seen’. Photograph: Colorsport/Shutterstock

The prevailing work ethic in pit villages throughout the coalfield helped to mould such formidable players. Miners were famed for their stamina, and with generations of pitmen in his family tree Milburn’s genetics shaped the way he played. In Ashington folklore it was told that Jackie kicked the same stone to school and back for three years, and his one-time teammate Len Shackleton was always impressed by his tenacity and “never-say-die spirit”. This was exemplified by tireless high pressing, and a trademark sliding tackle that hooked the ball from any defender unwise enough to prevaricate on the ball. In his early life he had made money as a sprinter, competing at Edinburgh in the famous Powderhall Handicap and running 100 yards in around 10 seconds.

With his pace, allied to phenomenal shooting power with either foot Milburn rightly takes his place in the Newcastle pantheon. His record of 200 goals in 401 appearances is second only to that of Alan Shearer.

Until 1948 Milburn combined football with work at local collieries, and as he didn’t then have a car, with almost too-perfect symbolism he would take the bus from Ashington into Newcastle with the same supporters who would pay to watch him. “The size of the crowd meant that it sometimes took us up to three-quarters of an hour to walk up the bank and round to the players’ entrance,” Milburn recalled. “But what could we do? Our supporters were a marvellous warm-hearted lot. They even flooded the club with clothing coupons to help kit out the side.” That cosy, close-knit and deeply sociable world of the postwar north-east suited Jackie down to the ground.

View image in fullscreen Newcastle United captain Joe Harvey (centre) introduces Prime Minister Winston Churchill (left) to Jackie Milburn before the 1952 FA Cup final. Photograph: PA Images/Alamy

“He was everybody’s friend!” wrote his famous second cousin Jack Charlton. “If you ever walked through Newcastle with him, you got stopped every two minutes; everybody said hello to him.”

Yet he never sought this fame, and it’s telling that whenever he went to the pictures in Ashington, he always waited until the lights were down before he entered the auditorium. Here was a modest and even shy man, who shared the small-c conservatism that characterised the otherwise Labour-voting north-east. He was thrilled to meet Winston Churchill at Wembley in 1952 – “the greatest hero of my life whose bust has occupied pride of place in our house since 1948” – as well as the ailing King George VI, whose courage he admired.

View image in fullscreen Newcastle centre forward Jackie Milburn with his wife Laura and daughters Linda (3) and Betty (2) in front of a picture on the wall of Milburn shaking hands with King George VI at the 1951 Cup Final, when his goal won the Cup for Newcastle. Photograph: Mirrorpix/Getty Images

In Golden Goals Milburn presents an image to the world of domestic bliss with his wife, Laura, admitting his aversion to gardening and patterned socks, and his enjoyment of watching TV, reading thrillers and going to the dog track most Wednesdays (greyhounds were always a miners’ passion).

Due to the dominance of a handful of dangerous, heavy industries it was a truism to say that communities across the north-east thrived on being in it together. This may have been one of the reasons why Jackie never quite made a consistent mark on the international stage, despite his 13 caps and 10 goals for England. In later life he confessed that many of his international teammates were too self-obsessed to play as a team and even suggested that “one or two of them were outright snobs”.

View image in fullscreen The Manchester City defenders can only stop and stare as Newcastle United’s Jackie Milburn (left) heads home to score his first-minute goal in the 1955 FA Cup final. Photograph: Popperfoto/Getty Images

Milburn became talismanic for Newcastle. When United’s new manager Dugald Livingstone took the probably rational decision to drop the ageing Milburn for the 1955 FA Cup final against Manchester City on form and fitness grounds, the wily former manager Stan Seymour – by then back upstairs in the boardroom – stepped in to overrule him. Milburn was duly reinstated and would score what was then the fastest Cup final goal – with a rare bullet header from a corner after only 45 seconds.

The people of the area saw in Jackie Milburn the image of their favourite son. He was modest, witty, warm and honest. He was effortlessly, unaffectedly dashing and handsome. He was hard when necessary, but always ready with a grin and a conciliatory word. He was a canny lad with a passion for his homeland.

He was never cautioned in his 14-year career, and the noted First Division whistler Arthur Ellis concluded that: “If there were 22 players on the field like Jackie you wouldn’t need a referee!” His teammate Joe Harvey noted that Jackie was “gentle and generous in victory, always first with the handshake in defeat”, and Milburn himself conceded that his innate courtesy, and tendency to play in colleagues when he had a chance to shoot himself, was a drawback. “I had a lack of devil.”

It’s amazing to think how much more lethal a ruthless Jackie Milburn would have been. But then he probably wouldn’t have been so endearing.

Sports.title: Arsenal hopes dashed after Vinícius Júnior extends Real Madrid contract to 2032
Sports.content:
Vinícius Júnior has ended summer speculation over his future by agreeing a new six-year contract with Real Madrid. Arsenal had been heavily linked with a move for the Brazil international, who had entered the final 12 months of his deal at the Bernabéu.

A tumultuous 2025-26 campaign in which Real failed to win a trophy and initial uncertainty after the arrival of José Mourinho in Madrid alerted the Premier League champions, but Vinícius has now committed his long-term future to the Spanish club.

“Real Madrid and Vinícius Júnior have agreed on the extension of our player’s contract, which links him to the club until 30 June 2032,” a club statement read.

“Vinícius Júnior joined Real Madrid in July 2018 at the age of 18. In his eight seasons wearing our jersey, he has played 375 matches, scored 128 goals, and won 14 titles: two Champions Leagues, three Club World Cups, two Uefa Super Cups, three La Liga titles, one Copa del Rey, and three Spanish Super Cups.

“His contribution to all these titles has been pivotal due to his gameplay, assists, and goals.”

Vinícius wrote on Instagram: “Eight years at the Bernabéu are too few … six more years, and for ever!”

The 26-year-old had hinted at extending his association with Real during an in-house interview on Tuesday where he spoke about Mourinho wanting him to be “happy” and “joyful” after a difficult spell.

A shock last-16 World Cup exit in America with Brazil also added to a frustrating 12-month period for Vinícius, but with his future settled the former Flamengo prospect will aim to help Real get back to competing for major honours again under Mourinho.

Tying down ‌Vinícius represents another significant ​step in an ​active summer for Real. The club have also strengthened their squad with the arrivals of winger Yan Diomande, midfielder Bernardo Silva, centre-back Ibrahima Konaté, left-back Marc Cucurella and wing-back Denzel Dumfries.

Sports.title: Kerolin failed to report for pre-season at Manchester City before Barcelona switch
Sports.content:
The Brazil forward Kerolin failed to report back for pre-season training at Manchester City in July before her transfer to Barcelona had been agreed.

Barcelona announced their signing of the 26-year-old on Tuesday but it was not until Thursday evening when Manchester City first made any reference to the transfer, eventually confirming they had received a WSL record fee for a sale more than 48 hours later.

Several staff and players at Manchester City were disappointed at what were perceived to be efforts by Kerolin to force a transfer to Barcelona and that her time at the club ended on a surprisingly sour note. She did not join pre-season with the Women’s Super League champions, which began in late July, despite previously having been felt to have been on good terms with the squad.

The deal, worth an initial €1.2m (£1m), represents the largest transfer fee received by a WSL club, and it could rise with add-ons to approximately £1.25m, although this has not been officially confirmed. It is one of the largest transfer fees in women’s football.

City said of Kerolin: “She grabbed 14 goals and six assists during that time, helping City to a WSL and FA Cup double in her solitary full season in England. And upon her transfer to Barça, City have received a WSL-club record transfer fee of €1.2m.

“Everyone at Manchester City would like to thank Kerolin for all her efforts at the club and wish her the very best in her future career.”

Kerolin was part of the City side that lifted their first WSL title in a decade last season and also helped them win the Women’s FA Cup. But within weeks of those celebrations many of her City colleagues have been stunned after she did not say goodbye in-person. Kerolin’s representatives have been contacted for a response.

High-profile examples of such transfer standoffs have been seen in men’s football, but incidents in the women’s game have been comparatively rare.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

City have no objections to the transfer in principle but sources have said the team were taken aback by the former North Carolina Courage star’s absence from pre-season fitness testing. For Kerolin, it is a dream move to the European champions, who beat OL Lyonnes in last season’s Women’s Champions League final.

City and Barcelona will meet in a friendly at the Joie Stadium on 15 August as the reigning champions of England and Spain step up their pre-season preparations.

Sports.title: Inside the new-look Birmingham City: How Blues' recruitment has been supercharged, their transfer wishlist, the coaching talents taking centre stage and why Chris Davies is shaking things up at rebranded HQ
Sports.content:
For the first time in many years, there is a welcome air of calm around Birmingham City on the eve of a new campaign.

Life has rarely been dull for Blues supporters in recent seasons. They have watched their club wobble on the edge of oblivion. They have witnessed Jude Bellingham, Wayne Rooney and Tom Brady at close quarters and marvelled at US owners’ Knighthead’s £2-3billion investment plans, including a 62,000-seat stadium.

Blues’ American owners have developed a rivalry with their counterparts at Wrexham that brought David Beckham to St Andrew’s when the teams met in September 2024.

They bought Jay Stansfield for £15million in League One and showcased a six-part Amazon Prime documentary a year ago.

This summer has allowed Blues finally to pause for breath. Although there will be more signings, so far they have spent less than £5million. The training ground looks different, so too the style of play. The approach to recruitment feels more measured.

Ahead of Saturday’s Carabao Cup tie at Swansea, Daily Mail Sport visited Blues’ base in rural Warwickshire to see how they are shaping up.

After a rollercoaster few seasons at St Andrew's, Birmingham City look set for a year of stability and solid progression

But ambitions remain high under the stewardship of Tom Wagner (left) and Tom Brady

What are the goals?

Promotion to the top flight remains the focus – but perhaps with a little more realism attached. When boss Chris Davies pointed out a year ago how few teams were able to bounce straight from League One to the Premier League in consecutive seasons, it did not fit the script.

When Birmingham won promotion from the third tier, there was a two-year plan to reach the summit – and ideally, it would happen instantly.

Though nobody will say it publicly, Daily Mail Sport understands that senior figures at Blues realise that it might not be quite that easy. There is an acceptance that promotion might take longer than the initial two-year forecast, though the expanded six-team play-offs should play into the hands of clubs like Blues.

Last season Davies stuck to his high-possession game and though it yielded excellent home form, Birmingham struggled on the road, winning only five times in the league and losing 13. Expect a more flexible style this term with Blues playing a more direct game, especially away from St Andrew’s.

This switch dates back to New Year’s Day, when Birmingham lost 3-0 at Watford and Davies saw a lack of strength – in body and mind. Like the Premier League, the Championship’s athletic demands have grown dramatically and, in some fixtures, Blues felt they were being physically outmatched.

In came Jhon Solis, August Priske, Carlos Vicente and Ibrahim Osman in January. The first three are expected to be key figures this term after having six months to adapt while Blues remain key to re-sign Osman from Brighton.

Blues have added set-piece coach Scott Fry, whose input helped Lincoln score 30 set-piece goals in League One in 2024-25. After a spell at Rangers, he was snapped up by Blues and in the recent friendly against Barcelona, Fry took centre stage in the technical area at every restart.

Blues are keen to re-sign Ibrahim Osman after taking him on loan from Brighton last season

‘It seems to be calmer than it was last year,’ says Davies. ‘That’s not to say we lack ambition, but I think that calmness bodes well.

‘We know what we’re walking into – the players do, I do. We’ve got that continuity and it’s the best way to approach it.

‘There was a lot there last year, because of winning League One the previous season and I felt we deserved to finish higher than 10th – but it was a creditable finish. We went through the ups and downs and emerged stronger, so I’m hopeful and excited.’

What could happen before the window closes?

Davies feels Blues are well set at the back and in goal but the club are keen to improve the squad in midfield and attacking positions.

Following Craig Gardner’s departure as director of football in June, Blues are a little more methodical in their approach to recruitment and will rely heavily on data. Joe Carnall and Micky Moore are running the department as Blues consider a long-term replacement for Gardner. Keep an eye on the experienced Mike Rigg, currently working as technical director in the Blues academy and another who follows data closely.

Here, though, Davies sounds a note of caution. He has watched with interest as Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck have joined Chelsea this summer, while James Milner retired at the end of last season aged 40.

‘Football has gone "data, data, data" but it doesn’t measure character, personality type or leadership skills,’ said Davies. ‘There’s a very human side to it.

‘I worked with Jordan Henderson at Liverpool – he’s 36 now but he’s gone to a massive club like Chelsea and went to the World Cup. That’s because of his personality and leadership skills.

‘I am happy with what we have here,' says boss Chris Davies. 'We don’t have a team of mercenaries here for the money'

‘You have your ups and downs in the Championship. Someone could be outstanding on the data and you think, "Wow, he’s too good for this level". But what is he like when you lose three games in a week, or he’s not starting? Will he help the team?’

‘I am happy with what we have here. We don’t have a team of mercenaries here for the money. These players want to win games for this club. I’d rather have a worse player on paper but I know he’s committed, than someone who’s a better player but you’re not quite sure (about his character).’

How might the season go?

At heart, Davies is a coach. He has never been one of those managers to watch from the sidelines and leave sessions to others.

Before becoming Blues boss, Davies was right-hand man to Brendan Rodgers and Ange Postecoglou and loves to be – as the modern football buzz phrase has it – on the grass.

In recent times, though, Davies’ assistant Ben Petty is thought to have taken a more prominent role in sessions, allowing Davies to take a wider view of life at the Elite Performance and Innovation Centre (EPIC), Blues’ base near the picturesque town of Henley-in-Arden.

Visting EPIC ahead of the Swansea fixture, the change was noticeable. Bare walls told the story of an imminent rebrand and there were fewer motivational quotations emblazoned on various surfaces.

NFL superstar Brady remains an influence behind the scenes and the logo of his performance and fitness company, TBRx, was still visible, although not as prominent as 12 months ago. Yet TBRx staff will continue to manage players’ recovery, which means reporting to EPIC the day after every game. No Sundays off for Blues players.

Much is made of the rivalry between Birmingham’s Americans and those at Wrexham – Hollywood superstar Ryan Reynolds and fellow actor Rob McElhenney. Blues leaned into that last season but this term, it may be a little different. It will be intriguing to take the temperature when the teams meet in north Wales on August 28.

Birmingham have a natural leader in defender Christoph Klarer but Davies is keen to share the responsibility around his dressing room

Davies is also keen for his players to take greater responsibility. In Christoph Klarer, they have a natural leader as skipper but he cannot do it alone. So during pre-season, Davies asked players to split into small groups to discuss certain topics – sometimes tactical, others technical or mental – and report their findings to the squad.

‘If it’s just me explaining things to them, it’s like you’re preaching all the time,’ Davies argued. ‘When the players speak, nuggets come from it that I find really useful. We did it during pre-season in Portugal. They have to have a voice.’

As well as Klarer, Blues have a natural leader at the top of the club. Chairman Tom Wagner has been absent from St Andrew’s since suffering a stroke in February. In an update last week, Knighthead wrote that they ‘expect to see (Wagner) at a match in the near future.’ That would be hugely welcome news across the club and fanbase.

Sports.title: Aston Villa transfer briefing: Players fear losing Ezri Konsa, the latest on Nicolas Jackson move and UEFA stumbling block, Matteo Ruggeri deal close and wingers on radar after Johan Manzambi injury blow
Sports.content:
Aston Villa transfer briefing: Players fear losing Ezri Konsa, the latest on Nicolas Jackson move and UEFA stumbling block, Matteo Ruggeri deal close and wingers on radar after Johan Manzambi injury blow

Unlock more from Tom Collomosse inside the Villa camp with a DailyMail+ subscription - brilliant exclusives, in-depth insight, analysis and more

Aston Villa supporters could be forgiven for feeling angry and confused. Barely two months after one of the greatest nights in their history, they have lost two of their most important players and more are expected to follow.

Under Unai Emery, the club have finished seventh, fourth, sixth and fourth in the Premier League. They have qualified for the Champions League twice, won the Europa League and will have a chance to add the UEFA Super Cup against Paris Saint-Germain in Salzburg on Wednesday.

Yet because of UEFA’s maddening financial rules that appear designed to help revenue-generating monsters like Chelsea and Manchester United and punish ambitious rivals like Villa, Emery finds himself without Youri Tielemans and Morgan Rogers heading into the new season, after they joined United and Chelsea respectively for a combined £152million.

Left back Lucas Digne is expected to join PSG and centre back Ezri Konsa – another pillar of Emery’s best teams – is a target for Arsenal, with Liverpool also monitoring the situation.

There are positives, however. Pound for pound, Emery is perhaps the best coach in the league and he is still at Villa. Champions League football will boost the balance sheet and plans to take the capacity of Villa Park to 50,000 are moving ahead. That should also deliver improved revenue and a bigger transfer warchest.

Yet football is always about the here and now and Daily Mail Sport looks at where Villa stand...

Under Unai Emery, Aston Villa have qualified for the Champions League twice, won the Europa League and will have a chance to add the UEFA Super Cup in Salzburg on Wednesday

It's been a tough transfer window for Villa fans, with Morgan Rogers and Youri Tielemans (pictured) leaving the club for a combined £152million

Could there be more outgoings?

FIRST SIX FIXTURES Weds PSG (n, Super Cup) Aug 23 Brighton (a, PL) Aug 31 Arsenal (h, PL) Sep 5 Hull (a, PL) Sep 12 N Forest (h, PL) Sep 19 Tottenham (a, PL)

The big one to watch after Digne is Konsa. At 28, the England defender is probably at the peak of his market value and heading into the summer he was one of three principal targets for Arsenal, along with Bruno Guimaraes and Vinicius Junior.

Guimaraes is due to sign for £75million this week and while Vinicius is set to stay at Real Madrid, Arsenal have not given up hope of landing Konsa, who is needed while they handle injuries to William Saliba, Jurrien Timber and Ben White.

The champions will have to do better than the original offer, though, which was believed to be little more than half of Villa’s £60million valuation. That did not go down well with co-owner Nassef Sawiris, but it is thought the Villa squad are becoming increasingly concerned about the possibility of Konsa departing.

There continues to be interest in Ollie Watkins, particularly from clubs in the Turkish top flight and the Saudi Pro League, though with so many experienced players already out of the door, it would be brave to let Watkins follow them. Though he turns 31 in December, Watkins has been Villa’s top scorer in every season since he joined the club in 2020, and is their leading all-time Premier League marksman.

It is a different matter with Tammy Abraham – another curious Villa transfer. Emery and his lieutenants pushed hard to sign Abraham for £18.2million from Besiktas in January yet it is thought that after only four starts Villa are prepared to let him go again, ideally on a permanent basis.

Earlier in the window, Villa were open to offers for Ross Barkley but with Tielemans leaving and Amadou Onana recovering from ACL damage, the former England man will not be placed on the market unless Villa can strengthen in midfield.

Arsenal are pushing to make Ezri Konsa (centre) the next big exit at Villa this summer

Tammy Abraham's £18.2million January move has not panned out and he could leave this summer

And what about incomings?

This is where it becomes tricky. Villa’s £54million club-record signing Johan Manzambi is not fit due to the knee injury he sustained playing for Switzerland at the World Cup.

Joao Gomes has made a promising start after joining for £38million from Wolves but more strength is needed in midfield, with Joao Palhinha still a target, though Bayern Munich would prefer to sell the Portugal international permanently.

Digne’s impending departure means another left back is needed, and Matteo Ruggeri could join from Atletico Madrid. The clubs have all but agreed terms on a deal worth about £15million for the Italian.

Alejandro Garnacho has joined on loan from Chelsea while Marseille winger Igor Paixao is another on Emery’s radar. Plenty of wingers have been observed this summer – from Ibrahim Mbaye to Harvey Barnes and Crysencio Summerville (who has since joined Al Hilal for £68million) – but Villa’s strong relationship with Chelsea helped get the Garnacho move over the line. Keep an eye on that for later in the window.

Then there is the striker. Ever since Emery joined the club, it feels like Villa have been looking for a forward to complement Watkins and ultimately succeed him. Jhon Duran had the talent to do so, but not the temperament. Donyell Malen did reasonably well when he played and his departure to Roma last January felt more of a financial move than a football one, given the constant pressure from UEFA rules. Quite simply, Abraham Part 2 simply has not worked.

Could Nicolas Jackson be the next one? At the moment, Villa are playing down interest in the Senegal forward. But Emery has always admired him since their days together at Villarreal and as highlighted, Villa and Chelsea have a good relationship.

But there's a hitch. UEFA rules state that permanent transfers between the same clubs within a 45-day period will be deemed ‘swaps’, which affects how profits can be recorded on balance sheets and stops any financial chicanery between teams.

The final day of the window is 41 days after Chelsea announced they had signed Rogers. Would that stop Villa signing Jackson? In such a frantic window, nothing can be ruled out – especially as players often sign for clubs some days before the official announcement.

Club-record signing Johan Manzambi is still recovering from the injury he suffered playing for Switzerland at the World Cup

Villa have all-but agreed a £15million deal with Atletico Madrid for Italian left back Matteo Ruggeri (left)

Emery's admiration for Nicolas Jackson dates back to their days together at Villarreal

How are Villa shaping up for the season?

Given the departure of Rogers, Villa need the Manzambi transfer to work and as things stand, the 20-year-old is unlikely to be fit for their Premier League opener at Brighton on August 23, and the early part of the season. Supporters are understandably alarmed at this summer's exodus while the squad are keen to see more high-level players join.

There is also a feeling, though, that Villa needed a refresh. The majority of last season’s squad had been at Villa throughout Emery’s four-year tenure and Villa knew they would have to sell this summer. Perhaps Emery would have preferred not to lose both Tielemans and Digne, who were key figures in the dressing room, but he will rarely stand in the way of a player who wishes to leave.

Roberto Olabe replaced Monchi as Villa’s transfer chief last September and this is his first summer window. Softly spoken and methodical, he is a much calmer figure than his predecessor and is a good counterbalance to the more instinctive Emery and director of football Damian Vidagany.

Villa started last season dreadfully, failing to score in any competition until September 16 and waiting until September 25 for their first win. It did not stop Emery’s men recording one of their best seasons in modern times, turning that first win into a run of 12 in 13 league matches as they roared back to finish fourth.

So a slow start is no reason to panic – but with so many changes to their team, Villa fans will struggle to stay calm if August goes awry.

Sports.title: South Korea FA 'provided "sexual entertainment" for foreign referees at massage parlours ahead of international matches including World Cup qualifier'
Sports.content:
South Korea FA 'provided "sexual entertainment" for foreign referees at massage parlours ahead of international matches including World Cup qualifier'

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

South Korea's football federation provided sexual entertainment to foreign referees before and after international matches, a government audit report revealed.

The report said the Korea Football Association (KFA) used business credit cards to pay for sexual entertainment for visiting referees at massage parlours in Seoul and other cities that hosted international matches between March 2011 and March 2012.

Those matches included qualifying games for the 2012 London Olympics and the 2014 FIFA World Cup.

Around twelve referees and match coordinators received the favours provided by the KFA across seven matches, according to the report compiled in 2016.

The officials came from Japan, the United Arab Emirates, Iran, Bahrain and Uzbekistan.

South Korea's news outlet Yonhap News Agency reported South Korea remained undefeated in the seven matches with five wins and two draws.

The report emerged this week as part of an investigation into the KFA's appointment of former coach Hong Myung-bo in 2024.

In two Olympic qualifying matches, South Korea beat Oman 2-0 on September 21, 2011. The nation then drew against Qatar, with no goals scored, on March 14, 2012.

The report said the Korea Football Association (KFA) used business credit cards to pay for sexual entertainment for visiting referees at massage parlours in Seoul and other cities that hosted international matches (Pictured: KFA HQ)

But South Korea had already secured an Olympic spot before the game.

On February 29, 2012, South Korea beat Kuwait 2-0 to progress to the next phase of the World Cup qualification.

South Korea had been the favourites in all three matches.

The KFA could also escape FIFA sanctions. The organisation's Code of Ethics bars most cases from being pursued after five years, with only bribery and corruption allegations carrying a 10-year limitation period.

There is no time limit for cases involving sexual abuse, harassment or exploitation. But paying for sexual entertainment may not be covered by those provisions.

Cho Chung-yun, who was KFA president at the time, was referred to police by South Korea's Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism following a 2016 audit that alleged he had misused federation funds.

The ministry also found that current and former KFA staff had used business credit cards at massage parlours and other inappropriate establishments.

The ministry said on Friday it had investigated claims referees had been provided sexual entertainment, but it struggled to verify all the facts.

Those KFA employees accused of improper business credit card use were not convicted and did not receive disciplinary repercussions from the football association.

South Korea's defender Lee Gi-hyuk reacted in dismay after his team lost a FIFA World Cup match to South Africa this year

Former KFA officials told local news outlet JTBC that the referees asked to visit the adult establishments and that it was 'common practice at the time' to accommodate their wishes.

While one noted the practice extends past South Korea and is more common in other countries.

A current KFA official has since said strict internal guidelines have been implemented.

The report, compiled by the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism, emerged mere hours after police raided the KFA HQ in Cheonan and the KFA House in Seoul.

The raids came as part of an investigation into the KFA's appointment of the former coach Myung-bo in 2024.

His appointment faced criticism after the KFA abandoned a months-long search involving foreign applicants and appointed him after a brief meeting.

Hong returned as national team coach after a brief time in the position from 2013 to 2014.

The investigation was sparked after South Korea's disappointing performance in the FIFA World Cup campaign, which ended in a group-stage exit.

During the raids, police seized documents believed to show whether Hong's hiring process included improper meddling and obstruction by KFA leaders, including by its former chief Chung Mong-gyu.

Both Hong and Chung stepped down after South Korea's exit from the tournament this year.

The pair also testified in parliament last month and were scrutinised over the reasons behind the disappointing performance and the operations within the KFA.

Sports.title: England footballer Ivan Toney charged with assault after 'headbutting fan who wanted selfie' in Soho nightclub
Sports.content:
England footballer Ivan Toney has been charged after allegedly headbutting a fan who was trying to get a selfie at a Soho nightclub.

The 30-year-old striker was charged with assault causing actual bodily harm last Thursday after an incident at 100 Wardour Street in London on December 6 last year.

Toney, who is originally from Northampton but currently plays for Saudi Pro League club Al-Ahli, will appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on September 24.

Reports at the time alleged that the former Brentford player, who moved to Al-Ahli for £40million two years ago, had been grabbed by a fan who had wanted a selfie.

A witness said: 'He [Toney] walked past a table of a group of lads. One of them recognised him and said, 'Oh, it's Ivan Toney' and tried to put his hands around his neck to get a photo with him. And then Toney has said, 'Get off me, get off me'.'

The witness said Toney wore a 'real nice watch' and may have been concerned he was being mugged. Toney was reportedly arrested after an alleged headbutt.

His spokesperson said: 'Ivan acknowledges the charge and although he is naturally shocked, he looks forward to being given the opportunity to clear his name in court.'

A Metropolitan Police statement said today: 'A man has been charged with assault following a Met investigation. Ivan Toney, 30, of Northampton, was charged on Thursday, July 31 with assault causing actual bodily harm.

England's Ivan Toney ahead of kick off against France at the World Cup in Miami on July 18

The alleged incident took place at 100 Wardour Street in London's Soho (file photograph)

'He will appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Thursday, September 24. The charge relates to an assault, which reportedly took place on December 6, 2025 at a nightclub on Wardour Street, W1.'

Toney has been on unconditional bail since being arrested by the Met last year, but was granted a US visa and allowed to travel to the World Cup in June.

He played twice - coming on as a substite in the final minutes of England's semi-final defeat to Argentina, then starting the third-place play off victory against France.

Toney began his career at hometown club Northampton Town in 2012, scoring 11 goals across 53 appearances before signing for Newcastle United three years later.

He only played twice for Newcastle between 2015 and 2018 but had loan spells in that period at Barnsley, Shrewsbury Town, Scunthorpe United and Wigan Athletic.

Toney then joined Peterborough United for about £350,000 in 2018, where he scored 40 goals in 76 appearances, before a big-money move to Brentford in 2020.

This was for an initial fee of £5million which later rose to £10million. He scored 67 times across 128 appearances for Brentford before leaving for Saudi Arabia in 2024.

Toney signed with Al-Ahli until 2028 and has so far scored 55 goals across 62 appearances, winning the AFC Champions League Elite title in his first season.

He has played ten times for England, with his debut coming at Wembley against Ukraine in March 2023 and his only goal being against Belgium in March 2024.

100 Wardour Street opened in 2016 but shut in January. It is on the site of the former Marquee Club, which hosted early gigs from The Rolling Stones and David Bowie.

Sports.title: Inside Leeds' blueprint to get into Europe: Daniel Farke's brutal pre-season regime borrowed from Jurgen Klopp, how they beat Champions League clubs to sign Harry Wilson and the two new faces they want now
Sports.content:
Inside Leeds' blueprint to get into Europe: Daniel Farke's brutal pre-season regime borrowed from Jurgen Klopp, how they beat Champions League clubs to sign Harry Wilson and the two new faces they want now

Unlock more from inside the Leeds camp with a DailyMail+ subscription - brilliant exclusives, in-depth insight, analysis and more

Leeds United are making a splash this summer – and not just because players had the pleasure of rubbing shoulders with Michael Phelps in the United States last week.

The minority investor was there to watch his team play Liverpool off the park in the second half of a 4-2 friendly win in Chicago, with two training-ground throw-in routines that would not have looked out of place in the NFL matches Soldier Field usually hosts.

Phelps, the greatest Olympian of all time with 23 gold medals, has brought his kids up as Leeds fans and he will be hoping Daniel Farke’s team are ready to progress after a season battling to stay afloat upon their return to the Premier League.

Leeds have had an encouraging summer window so far that saw them win races to sign Harry Wilson on a free transfer and England goalkeeper James Trafford in a club-record £45million deal from Manchester City.

New £34million Bosnia defender Tarik Muharemovic, fresh from having his ankle trodden on by Folarin Balogun at the World Cup, looks a solid buy from Sassuolo to replace Pascal Struijk. And, with a couple more signings – a left back and another attacker are on the list – Leeds could have a squad ready to challenge the top half of the Premier League after finishing 14th last time out.

Some are even mentioning the dreaded ‘E’ word and want to take inspiration from Sunderland and Nottingham Forest, two clubs who managed to get into Europe within three years of promotion back to the top flight, as well as Brighton and Bournemouth.

Leeds turned on the style in Chicago last week against Liverpool, coming from 2-0 down to win 4-2

Daniel Farke put the squad through a gruelling pre-season. Many days saw two training sessions, with double workouts to condition the body for an arduous campaign ahead

Minority investor Michael Phelps was there to watch his team play Liverpool off the park in Chicago

Farke put the squad through a gruelling pre-season. Many days saw two training sessions, with double workouts to condition the body for an arduous campaign ahead. In the morning, they would be football-focused and, in the afternoon, sessions would be strength-based.

There were two days of fitness tests to start pre-season and the footballs have been out every day but one, with players feeling a difference on the pitch after Farke’s physically demanding routines.

Farke, who asks players to call him ‘boss’ and dislikes the moniker ‘gaffer’, took inspiration from Jurgen Klopp for his workouts that involve a 1km running drill known as the lactate test, which measures how long it takes for lactic acid to build quicker than the body can clear it. The longer, the better – and it exposed who was keeping fit and who had slacked over summer.

When Leeds were promoted 12 months ago, the recruitment team were ahead of the curve in noticing a trend in the Premier League. They knew the game was switching to a more direct style and many of their transfer targets were, for want of a more diplomatic phrase, big brutes. Anton Stach is 6ft 4in, Jaka Bijol and Sebastiaan Bornauw 6ft 3in, Lukas Nmecha and Sean Longstaff 6ft 1in.

This year, they will stick by that policy and 6ft 4in Muharemovic fits into it – but Leeds are keen for a bit of flair, too. Germany winger Julian Brandt was targeted but ended up going to Ajax. Former Fulham man Wilson, then, is the star attraction.

Several clubs, including Champions League-bound Aston Villa, had made a pitch to sign Wilson when it became clear he would follow manager Marco Silva out of the door at Craven Cottage. But he chose Leeds for a number of reasons.

One was the fact Leeds made a push to sign him 12 months earlier, which proved to Wilson that they did not simply want him because he was available for nothing. With the possibility of qualifying for the World Cup with Wales, Wilson did not want the turbulence of moving at that time.

Chairman Paraag Marathe has recently stepped aside from his position at the San Francisco 49ers to focus on his football ventures, including Rangers. He sold the winger a dream on the second of many calls between player and club. Marathe made Wilson feel wanted.

New 6ft 4in, £34m signing Tarik Muharemovic (right) adds to Leeds' land of the giants

Several clubs, including Champions League-bound Aston Villa, had made a pitch to sign Harry Wilson, but he chose Leeds

Chairman Paraag Marathe has recently stepped aside from his position at the San Francisco 49ers to focus on his football ventures, and played a key role in convincing Wilson to join Leeds

He talked about the loud, proud and loyal fanbase and discussed how Leeds were in the process of redeveloping Elland Road to increase its capacity.

‘After the first call I had with Leeds, with the chairman about the direction of the club, they were my number one choice,’ Wilson told us this week. ‘I spoke to a couple of other teams and nothing changed my mind.

‘The ownership group, the plans they have for the club. They know the size of the club with the fanbase and the history and the work they're doing to the stadium already to increase the capacity, the investment they're putting into the squad. It's all just going in one direction and that's what I want to be a part of.’

Marathe and a phone call from Farke, who tried to sign Wilson at his former club Norwich City, went a long way – but nothing sweetened the deal more than the persistence of club captain Ethan Ampadu, a Wales team-mate.

‘I almost had to block Ethan!’ laughed Wilson. ‘He played a big role. I'm really close with all the Welsh boys here. DJ (Dan James), I've played with since we were 14. Joe (Rodon), similar.

Asked about his ambitions, Wilson – who had the best season of his career last term, with ten league goals and seven assists – added: ‘Clubs have shown in recent years that the first season back in the Premier League, it's all about making sure you stay up. But in the end, Leeds stayed up really comfortably last season.

‘When you look at the likes of Sunderland and Forest, who've come up in recent years and have got into Europe, that's definitely an aim that we can have.

'But I think that second season syndrome has been the case with a few teams. So this season let's try and build on what the club created last year, that strong base, making sure our home form is good, which is massive and let's see where that takes us.’

Harry Wilson (left) adds to the Welsh contingent in Leeds' squad, including Daniel James (second left), Ethan Ampadu (right) and Joe Rodon (not pictured)

Wilson believes Leeds can take inspiration from the likes of Sunderland and Nottingham Forest in qualifying for Europe soon after promotion to the Premier League

Farke is set to stick by the back-five formation that turned his fortunes around last term. The boss had been sleepwalking towards the sack as Christmas approached, with Leeds in the relegation zone with a run of six defeats in the seven games leading up to December.

But after the switch, Leeds lost only five of 25 matches and reached an FA Cup semi-final.

Farke was criticised for his negative tactics at Wembley and knows he must build on solid defensive foundations with more exciting football this time around.

Trafford is a marquee signing. Some City observers believe he should have been given the No 1 jersey ahead of Gianluigi Donnarumma and many in the England set-up expect him to be the long-term successor to Jordan Pickford.

Comfortable in possession and a strong shot-stopper, it is an excellent addition, beating Newcastle United to the punch. Business is not done yet and a versatile attacker is top of the list. Dominic Calvert-Lewin had a fine season, scoring 15 times in all competitions, but needs help in sharing the goals around, with none of his team-mates managing more than eight.

Farke believes US international Brenden Aaronson is vastly underrated but another creative outlet would be welcomed with open arms, especially after Jack Harrison departed for MLS side New England Revolution. A deputy for injured left back Gabriel Gudmundsson is also wanted.

The boss has three more friendlies to fine-tune his squad: RB Leipzig and Augsburg at home on back-to-back Saturdays, and a clash with rivals Manchester United in Dublin at Croke Park on Wednesday.

Farke fell into coaching by accident having graduated in economics and originally wanted to be a sporting director.

This is his third crack at the Premier League after two relegations with Norwich, but sources insist he is growing every week and he believes that relationships have a greater impact than tactics.

Farke believes US international Brenden Aaronson is vastly underrated but another creative outlet would be welcomed with open arms

Sources insist Farke is growing every week and he believes that relationships have a greater impact than tactics

A literature nut whose favourite author is Gabriel Garcia Marquez, he also likes 19th-century poet Walt Whitman. The American’s best-known line ‘I contain multitudes' speaks to how leaders must contradict themselves to find answers.

Farke and the hierarchy will be mulling those over in the coming weeks: how to maintain Leeds’ solid base but still take attacking strides? How to keep his trademark calm demeanour while demanding more? How to be more ambitious in the transfer market without it coming back to bite financially?

If they can get the answers right, they can be successful this season. Just maybe not quite as successful as Mr Phelps.

Sports.title: Roy Keane and Micah Richards dress up as traditional Victorian gentlemen, perform pigskin keepy-uppies and enjoy a day out at the terraces as they turn back the clock for Sky Bet's new 'Game's Back' advert
Sports.content:
See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Roy Keane and Micah Richards have embraced football's roots by dressing as Victorian gentlemen for Sky Bet's latest 'Game's Back' campaign.

Revisiting football's earliest days ahead of the new Premier League season, the popular Sky Sports punditry duo donned period costumes as they took in the action from the terraces and showed off their keepy-uppy skills with a traditional pigskin ball.

Sky Bet's new advert, which officially launched on August 7, plays on the familiar 'game's gone' phrase often used by supporters looking back nostalgically at how the sport has changed over the years, from players refusing to celebrate against former clubs to the introduction of VAR.

The advert begins with Keane and Richard sitting on the sofa watching modern-day football, before the Manchester United legend complains that the 'game's gone' over a five-minute VAR decision.

The punditry duo then take a trip through different eras of football to discover that supporters were always questioning how the game was evolving.

Transported first to 1965, the pair complained about the introduction of the substitutions law before heading further back in time to 1891 to learn how fans moaned when nets were first attached to goalposts.

Popular punditry duo Roy Keane and Micah Richards have embraced football's roots by dressing as Victorian gentlemen for Sky Bet's latest 'Game's Back' campaign

Richards and Keane also showed off their keepy-uppy skills with a traditional pigskin ball

In one light-hearted moment, Richards shushes his famously fiery punditry partner while the pair watch on from the stands, poking fun at Keane's well-known habit of questioning changes in the modern game.

Sky Bet also shared behind-the-scenes footage of Keane and Richards shooting the advert, which showed off the duo's chemistry.

Keane said: 'One thing about football history is that people have always questioned changes to the game, but it's funny looking back at some of the things we'd never want to lose now.

'We had good fun bringing those moments to life.'

Richards added: 'Football fans love a debate and that's never going to change'.

'Game's Gone is a phrase that has engrained itself in football culture and beyond,' said Harry Phillips, Sky Bet Marketing Director.

'Yet even though we all love to moan about the game, it's never been more universally popular and when push comes to shove, it's the incredible moments of football culture, both on and off the pitch that keeps us coming back.

Sky Bet's new campaign plays on the familiar 'the game's gone' phrase often used by supporters looking back nostalgically at how the sport has changed over the years

'We believe football always has and always will create moments no fan can resist. And at Sky Bet, we champion those iconic moments of football and fandom by giving our customers more ways to get in on the action.'

The new Premier League season kicks off with champions Arsenal hosting newly-promoted Coventry City on Friday, August 21.

Sports.title: Powerlifting racism row: Spotter declares 'I am racist' after sabotaging star's record attempt - admitting in astonishing social media post: 'I did it intentionally'
Sports.content:
See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

A powerlifting assistant is under police investigation in Lithuania after claiming he deliberately sabotaged a Black athlete's squat attempt because he is 'racist'.

Belgian athlete Sonita Muluh's attempt to squat 334.5kg at the World Classic Open Powerlifting Championships in Lithuania in June was disqualified after spotting assistant Ernestas Kusinas placed his knee under the barbell during the lift.

After the event, Kusinas sparked outrage by claiming in an Instagram post that he had deliberately sabotaged Muluh's lift because he is 'racist', a remark he later insisted was intended to mock those accusing him of racism.

The Lithuanian Powerlifting Federation referred the case to police, who have launched an investigation into both the Instagram post and the events at the championships, a spokesperson told Reuters.

The Instagram remark read: 'Sorry for you morons, I'm racist and I did it on purpose because I hate you pieces of s***'.

If found guilty, Kusinas could face a maximum sentence of two years in prison.

Powerlifting assistant Ernestas Kusinas (above) is under police investigation in Lithuania after claiming he deliberately sabotaged a Black athlete's squat attempt because he is 'racist'

The spotter placed his knee on the barbell during Sonita Muluh's attempt to squat 334.5kg

Kusinas later told Reuters the Instagram post was written in anger and was intended to mock social media users who had accused him of racism, rather than reflect his true views.

The spotter claimed he had unintentionally interfered with Muluh's attempt as a result of being tired from his duties at the event.

Kusinas, who has since been banned for life from all powerlifting events by the Lithuanian federation and switched his social media accounts to private, claimed he had 'thrown him the bone he wanted' in response to an unidentified Instagram user who had accused him of racism.

Muluh, 29, became world champion in 2024 and has won medals at multiple Powerlifting Championships throughout her impressive career.

The Cameroon-born powerlifter's partner Kristof De ​Coninck urged that she could have won the event in Lithuania without Kusinas' interference, insisting poor assistance risked 'very serious injuries'.

'Initially, we thought it was a mistake,' De Coninck said.

'But then, it became clear (because of the social media comment) that the person had done it ⁠deliberately, motivated ​by racial bias.'

Speaking to BBC Sport about the controversy, Muluh said: 'It's shocking to wake up five weeks later and it's all over the internet that he did it on purpose because of the colour of my skin.

'I feel unsafe and uneasy that this person is standing beside me with massive weight, with what can go wrong, with the amount of weight on your back.

'I was lucky when I realised [it hit his knee] and I could stabilise it. Not everyone could. It was the heaviest ever squat for a female.

'(Kusinas) did not reach out afterwards to apologise, but he is not obliged to. I thought it was a human mistake, that cost me a lot on the day.

In an Instagram post after the event, he claimed he did it intentionally because he is 'racist'

Muluh, pictured in 2025, admitted she feels 'unsafe and uneasy' after his Instagram comment

'But there was no hatred [from me]. I didn't lash out; didn't curse at him. There was a video of it posted afterwards and I said: "I hope he does not get hate." I believed it was an honest mistake.

'And then I find out five weeks later that he said this.'

Meanwhile, the Lithuanian Powerlifting Federation has said in a statement: 'We would like to address the situation that unfolded on social media.

'We reviewed available information relating to Ernestas Kusinas and were deeply shocked by the views and activities addressed publicly which contradict the principles we stand for.

'The federation takes full responsibility for addressing this matter.'

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"
