That has left women facing a "deadly gamble" as they go out to collect water, according to U.N. Women East Africa Director Anna Mutavati.

"Under the perception that darkness offers protection from aerial attacks, these women and girls have been harassed, raped and subjected to other forms of sexual violence — all while trying to access water," she said.

Meanwhile, a deadly cholera outbreak is spreading in parts of the city, with children the worst affected.

"Cholera is tearing through certain communities in the city, with the outbreak being compounded by incessant rains and recent drone strikes that have crippled critical medical facilities and left thousands without access to urgent treatment and life-saving medications," Plan International Sudan Director Mohamed Kamal said this week.

"The situation facing children is particularly dangerous," he said. "They are far more susceptible to disease, some face the prospect of recruitment by armed groups, and they are experiencing lasting psychological trauma."

toggle caption AFP via Getty Images/AFP

U.S. senators urge action

Since the war broke out in 2023, at least 59,000 people have been killed, according to the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project, a conflict-monitoring group. But the true toll could be much higher.

Sudan's government forces have been buoyed by recent gains against the RSF. Last week, they celebrated retaking a major highway in North Kordofan and several other key positions.

Sponsor Message

But despite those military advances, Sudan researcher Eric Reeves told NPR this week: "There is no likelihood of a military rescue of el-Obeid."

More than 100,000 displaced people there are now sheltering in camps, and some are facing extreme hunger.

"Many families are struggling to meet their basic needs in IDP camps," Esperanza Santos, Sudan emergency coordinator for Doctors Without Borders, told NPR.

Aid funding cuts and rising diesel and fertilizer costs linked to the broader disruption caused by the war in Iran are also worsening the situation, according to the World Food Programme, which is distributing food in the city.

"At a time when needs continue to grow, humanitarian resources are shrinking," Derk Segaar, special Sudan envoy for the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, told a U.N. briefing in Geneva this week.

Pressure is mounting on the international community to act. On Tuesday, a group of more than 20 U.S. senators wrote to Secretary of State Marco Rubio urging him to take steps to prevent mass atrocities in el-Obeid.

"While we welcome the State Department's expression of concern about the escalating situation in el-Obeid, words are not enough," the letter, signed by Democratic Sens. Tim Kaine, Bernie Sanders and Adam Schiff, said.

"The encirclement and systematic crippling of resources in el-Obeid increasingly parallels el-Fasher," the letter continued.

The senators also urged the administration to stop selling arms to the United Arab Emirates, which has been accused of supporting the RSF.

Reeves agreed that such action from the U.S. is critical.

"Until the United Arab Emirates is called out and dissuaded from pursuing its grotesquely destructive policy in Sudan," he told NPR, "we're going to see this war continue."

World.title: Amid cost of living stress, many parents are supporting children well into adulthood
World.content:
Amid cost of living stress, many parents are supporting children well into adulthood

toggle caption Mabel Lago

Mabel Lago and her husband are retired and in their 70s. But before they decided to move from New Jersey to South Carolina this year, they checked with their younger son. That's because he was still living with them, at age 39.

"We could not leave him behind, because he could not afford to live on his own," she said.

Her son is a hard worker, she explains, but his job helping to manage a liquor store paid low wages and no benefits. He also has Type 1 diabetes, and his Affordable Care Act insurance was nearly a thousand dollars a month. So he came with them to South Carolina, where his plan now is a lot cheaper — but he hasn't yet landed a new job.

Sponsor Message

"The young people have really been shafted, big time, with the economy, with the cost of living," Lago said.

She is among a majority of Americans who, according to polls, think it's more difficult for young adults today to achieve financial independence than it was for their parents. It's a view that's grown sharply in recent years, as prices for essentials such as housing, food and energy have shot up and inflation has stayed stubbornly elevated.

Such concerns partly explain why most parents help support their grown children in some way, many well beyond the traditional age of financial independence. The share of 25- to 34-year-olds living with parents has also nearly doubled since 2005, to about 20%, according to the Urban Institute. One analysis found a third of all those under 35 are living back at home, just shy of the record peak during the COVID-19 pandemic, even though most are employed.

Lago and her husband built their 1,500-square-foot retirement home in South Carolina a bit larger than they might have, to include a bedroom for their son. They also gave part of the land they bought to their older son, 43, who has a well-paying job but has not been able to buy a house on his single income. But he just built one next door, with money his parents gave him from their own inheritance.

Sponsor Message

toggle caption Mabel Lago

Lago is happy to help, but she and her husband have to watch their spending carefully. This year, as gas and food prices spiked, they cut back on driving and stopped eating beef. Now, they're thinking not only of their own long-term finances, but also that of their sons.

"Did we plan for that when we had our children 40 years ago? No," she said. "Do we plan for that now? Yes, we have to."

"A different economic landscape"

Some parents have long helped children — pitching in so they can buy a first home, for example. But over recent decades, as families have gotten smaller and people marry later, researchers have found more parents have done so and in larger amounts.

"Young adults are kind of coming of age in a different economic landscape than their parents did," said Rachel Minkin, a researcher at the Pew Research Center.

A Pew survey this year found a growing majority of Americans say it's harder today for young people to find a job, pay for college, buy a home and save for the future. In a new survey question, 80% even agreed that "it's harder for young adults today to cover basic expenses," Minkin said.

A 2024 Pew analysis found young adults are also more likely to have student loan debt compared to three decades ago. And while the share with mortgage debt was about the same, the median amount of that debt adjusted for inflation was larger.

This changing economic landscape has helped fuel the rise in adult children living with parents.

An AARP survey last year found 75% of parents across income levels help support adult children in some way, from paying cellphone and Wi-Fi fees, to helping with transportation and rent, or giving straight cash. On average, that amounts to $7,000 a year.

"What's striking is that so many of the people we see in our survey actually were living independently for a while and then went back in with their parents, primarily because of financial pressures," said Richard Johnson, who leads a financial security policy team at AARP.

Most give because they want to, not because children need it, according to the survey. But many lower-income families said they help even though it hurts their own finances.

Sponsor Message

"When people have to divert what little resources they have to help their children, and they can't put it toward retirement, that jeopardizes their own financial futures," Johnson said.

Advising parents to protect their own retirement

Nate Kinzinger, a wealth manager affiliated with the financial services firm Northwestern Mutual, has seen this shift during his 25-year career. He's had clients delay retirement in part to continue supporting adult children. So many have stepped in to pay student loan debt that he now advises families to consider the "return on investment" from a given field of study.

Clients also help with down payments or high rent, especially when children live in big cities where the cost of living can far exceed early-career wages. Others pay a monthly stipend.

"There's usually some degree of guilt, you know, and there's some degree of, well, the money's in my account, so I can do it,'" he said.

Some continue regular payments even after retirement, he said, not understanding they will need that money later. "And so we'll have to have those conversations of, all right, how do we close this gap for you, cause I'm not comfortable that you could continue doing this," Kinzinger said.

This year, Northwestern Mutual found in its own survey that 42% of Americans still feel financially dependent on their parents. That included a third of Gen Xers, who are now middle-aged.

"That was a bit of a shocking number," he said. The survey did not delve into the reasons why, but that cohort includes many of the parents helping struggling young adult children.

toggle caption David Zucchero

Is it coddling or the new norm?

David Zucchero and his wife are retired, living near Seattle, and have children ages 31, 32 and 34. Helping them out is "just an ongoing thing for all three kids," he said, and it's "gotten worse in the last, I'd say, five to eight years."

To be clear, he's well-off and all the children — or a spouse — make good pay. Over the years, the parents have helped with education and handed down old cars.

But Seattle area home prices are double the national median. A year ago, one daughter moved back home, with her husband and now two young kids, so she could be a stay-at-home mom. Another daughter wants to rent out her condo and move back home to cut down on expenses. And their son and his family? They live with his wife's parents.

Sponsor Message

"When I look at the salaries these kids make, I'm like, 'how can you not live on this?'" Zucchero said. "But they can't."

toggle caption David Zucchero

At least not comfortably, he added, admitting that he and his wife are guilty of coddling them. Zucchero's best friend chides him about it. But everyone else seems to be in the same boat.

"One or two of the kids are living at home," he said. "Neighbors, same thing, one right behind us. The kid's been living there probably 10 years, he's in his 40s."

For now, he and his wife are not charging rent or setting deadlines for anyone to move out. The truth is, they love having the children and grandkids around.

World.title: White supremacist meeting shakes some residents of Alberta town
World.content:
Residents of a small town outside Calgary are shocked to learn that Canada's most prominent white supremacist group held its second annual national meeting — where masked group members participated in military-style drills — at a volunteer-run community centre in early July.

"My first reaction is: that scares me," Lou Kuiack, a Millarville-area resident, told a CBC Calgary reporter. "I didn’t think that would come to our small little town, in our backyard."

Using visual clues in videos posted by the group, Second Sons Canada, CBC’s visual investigations team identified the location of the gathering roughly 70 kilometres southwest of Calgary, near the hamlet of Millarville, Alta.

Second Sons Canada was formed in 2024 and has chapters across the country.

Founded by Jeremy MacKenzie, Second Sons describes itself as a "men’s nationalist club." But it more closely resembles the " active club" -style model favoured by the global white supremacist movement. Second Sons' leaders have welcomed neo-Nazis into their ranks, called for mass deportations "at gunpoint" of non-white people from Canada and said Canadian politicians should be executed as traitors.

WATCH | Residents react to white supremacist group meetup: Locals 'shell shocked' by white supremacist group training in Alberta hamlet | Duration 2:16 Second Sons, Canada's predominant white supremacist group, held a large meeting in July where masked members participated in military-style drills. CBC's visual investigations team and CBC Calgary uncover the location of the meeting and speak to residents of the small Alberta hamlet of Millarville, shedding light on a recurring strategy for white supremacist groups: booking unsuspecting community centres.

Videos and images from the Alberta event, posted by Second Sons on its social media accounts, show more than 60 members participating in exercises including army crawls and marching with cots. MacKenzie, an Afghanistan veteran, led a military-inspired chant that referenced fighting the Taliban and included a Second Sons slogan: "Our people, our home, our future."

Group members also wore shirts with the slogan "old stock enforcer" emblazoned with crossed swords behind an old-school goalie mask.

"When they say 'old stock,' they mean white and European people," said Evan Balgord, executive director of the Canadian Anti-Hate Network.

"When they label themselves as enforcers, it’s tied to their belief that they will have to use culture, politics and violence to achieve their goal of a racist mass deportation of people who aren’t old stock Canadian."

Exposing the location

Second Sons routinely publishes visuals of its exercises but its members are often masked or digitally obscured, and the group does not publish the precise locations of its gatherings. The group did not identify the exact location of its July meetup, only saying that it took place in the "foothills of Alberta."

In a Telegram post published weeks after the gathering took place, MacKenzie praised the group's members and said they had spent the weekend in activities that included "friendly combat sports competition, organizational training, promotions, awards, excellent food and social time."

Second Sons Canada founder Jeremy MacKenzie delivers a speech to members inside Square Butte Hall. (Second Sons Canada/Telegram)

In a video posted to Telegram recapping the weekend, Second Sons members can be seen holding a banner with the traditional active club slogan "Tribe and train" over an overpass on Highway 2 near Okotoks, Alta., a town about 47 km south of Calgary.

An illustration shows matching elements between an image released by Second Sons Canada and Google Streetview imagery. (Illustration: Froilan Untalasco/CBC; Second Sons Canada/Telegram, Google Maps)

Using that clue as a lead, CBC matched the community centre used by the group that weekend with Square Butte Hall near Millarville, located approximately 43 km from Okotoks.

A distinctive welcome arch belonging to the hall can be seen in shots of Second Sons members arrayed in their ranks outdoors.

CBC News matched images from the Second Sons video, like this welcome arch, to the Square Butte Hall. (Illustration: Froilan Untalasco/CBC; Second Sons Canada/Telegram, Google Maps)

Similarly, interior details of a clip showing MacKenzie leading members in a chant related to the war in Afghanistan match photos of the hall that can be seen on the venue's Facebook page.

Square Butte Hall is a volunteer-run space that hosts community events like dances, recipe exchanges and fire prevention training.

Second Sons Canada members stand outside Square Butte Hall near Millarville, Alta. (Second Sons Canada/Telegram)

"The organization that booked the hall did not identify itself to us in any way," said Shanna Dunne, president of the hall’s board of directors, in an emailed statement to CBC.

"The Square Butte Community Association is committed to providing a respectful and inclusive community space, and our volunteers work hard to support the many positive events and activities that bring our community together."

In a phone call with a CBC Calgary reporter, Dunne said an RCMP officer contacted the hall and asked for information about the Second Sons meetup.

In a statement to CBC, the RCMP said it does not confirm or deny investigations, but that it is "aware of the Second Sons."

It emphasized it does not "investigate movements or ideologies," focusing on criminal activities by individuals or groups. But it said it is "actively monitoring the rise of hate-motivated crime and incidents across the country."

Residents shocked

Millarville residents who spoke to CBC said they didn't know the Second Sons meetup had taken place, and were concerned about the group’s presence in the community.

Leanna Bridgeman, manager of local coffee shop Miss Marple’s, said she was "absolutely shell-shocked that something like that would happen out here," calling it "completely disturbing."

Leanna Bridgeman, manager of a coffee shop in Millarville, says she was 'shell-shocked' after learning that Second Sons held a meeting in her community. (CBC News)

Tim Babey, owner of the Millarville General Store, said he was "really surprised."

"People out here are pretty accepting, but I think they'd still be quite shocked at seeing something like that going on," he said.

Tim Babey, owner of the Millarville General Store, told CBC that he was surprised to learn of Second Sons’ presence in town. (CBC News)

CBC reached out to the Foothills County reeve — a position similar to mayor — for comment.

"Foothills County recently became aware of activities that are reported to have occurred on private property," said Reeve Rob Siewert. "At this time, the county has not received any formal complaints and is not aware of any calls having been logged with staff regarding the matter."

Second Sons Canada’s use of the community hall fits a pattern CBC has observed elsewhere in Canada, where they book spaces like recreation centres without disclosing the full scope of the group’s planned activities or overall aims.

Last September, CBC News tracked a similar meeting in southern Ontario to a Lions Club in Caledonia, Ont. The hall told CBC at the time that if staff had been aware that Second Sons was behind the booking, it would not have been approved.

"Booking community spaces under false pretenses is normal for white nationalist movements, because most spaces wouldn’t agree to hold their events," said Balgord of the Canadian Anti-Hate network.

Second Sons Canada did not respond to a request for comment from CBC.

CBC News has contacted CSC and local police for more information about what happened.

World.title: 72-year-old hiker attacked by grizzly bear in B.C.
World.content:
A woman is recovering after being attacked by a grizzly bear while hiking in B.C.'s South Chilcotin.

Pemberton Search and Rescue (SAR) was notified by RCMP on Sunday around 3:45 p.m. PT that a grizzly bear attacked a hiker.

The woman, 72, was in an area east of Tyaughton Lake in a remote area near Gold Bridge, roughly 70 kilometres north of Pemberton, according to SAR president David McKenzie.

“The bear was batting them around in the altercation,” McKenzie said.

Search crews responded as quickly as possible to the area and coordinated with the B.C. Conservation Officer Service (BCCOS).

“They didn't want us to enter into the scene until they had cleared it just because of safety,” McKenzie said.

The BCCOS responded immediately by helicopter with a three-member predator attack response team.

Multiple first responder agencies collaborated on the rescue including BC EHS, Pemberton SAR, RCMP, Conservation Officer Service and B.C. Wildfire Service. (Pemberton Search and Rescue)

The individual was hiking in an area called Pearson Ridge, a remote hike accessible through forest service roads.

“There is a series of trails throughout that area,” McKenzie said.

The B.C. Wildfire Service, which was fighting a wildfire nearby, found the hiker and helped rescue her.

“They met up with our team, and we had already arranged for an air ambulance,” McKenzie said.

Paramedics were waiting at the former Gun Lake Airport near Gold Bridge to transport the hiker.

“Two ground ambulances and an air ambulance attended the scene,” said Brian Twaites with B.C. Emergency Health Services.

One person was taken to hospital by air ambulance in serious condition.

“It was quite serious. They had several lacerations of the face, arms, neck, along with an actual C1 [neck] fracture,” McKenzie said.

McKenzie said the woman is recovering.

“I understand they are doing well,” McKenzie said.

Believed to be 'defensive attack'

The Ministry of Environment said in a statement that conservation officers followed up with the woman and collecting clothing with potential "linkage" evidence.

The next day, on Aug. 3, officers returned to the site and completed an investigation and retrieved the woman's personal items.

The ministry said the investigation has led them to believe the attack was defensive in nature, from a female grizzly with at least one cub.

The bear has not been removed or killed and no capture devices are being set up.

"COS has put up signs in the area as a precaution," said the ministry.

'We just have to do our best to avoid encounters'

Bear biologist and researcher Wayne McCrory has done bear risk assessments for many national and provincial parks in the province over the last 40 years.

“Lots of people are out enjoying our beautiful province and backcountry in occupied grizzly habitat,” McCrory said.

He said the recent bear attack is tragic.

“My heart goes out to the person,” McCrory said. “It's difficult. I've had my own serious, very, very close near-death encounters.”

He said B.C.’s South Chilcoltin region is a large protected area for grizzly bears with lots of salmon streams for them to feed on.

“Also, lots of the subalpine and riparian areas are prime habitat for grizzly bears,” McCrory said. “It’s got a fairly good population, especially since the grizzly bear hunt was closed in 2017.”

More serious encounters tend to occur where there is an overlap of the trail and campsites in grizzly bear movement corridors, he said.

“Grizzly bears like to use park trails if their terrain is rough,” McCrory said.

He suggested mitigation measures such as not hiking during the early morning or late evening, carrying bear spray and knowing how to use it and making sure trails and campsites are not in prime feeding areas.

“We have these happen every year in British Columbia because we live in prime grizzly habitat,” McCrory said. “We just have to do our best to avoid encounters.”

World.title: Man accused of starting Spokane wildfire looked up best weather to ignite blaze: police
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A detective who interviewed the man accused of starting one of the wildfires near Spokane, Wash., says the man confessed, described his planning and explained how he made a device to ignite the blaze.

Det. Michael Drapeau said in a court filing Wednesday that Aaron Farinacci told him he had planned the Old Trails fire for about two weeks. He researched the weather to identify a day with "high winds, low humidity, sort of high heat."

Farinacci also researched a well-known serial arsonist and bought items to make a "time delay device" using notebook paper, matches, a cigarette and a rubber band, Drapeau said.

1 of 3 fires burning in Spokane area

The fire Farinacci was charged with starting is one of three burning near Spokane that have burned more than 850 homes and forced the evacuation of tens of thousands of people.

WATCH | Sifting through the ashes in the wake of Spokane wildfires: ‘We’re homeless’: Wildfires leave hundreds of Spokane, Wash., residents with nothing | Duration 2:34 Hundreds of Spokane, Wash., residents are sifting through what’s left of their homes after devastating wildfires tore through the community.

Drapeau said Farinacci told him that "fire is powerful, beautiful, and that things that go through fire experience a kind of rebirth."

Farinacci is due in court Thursday on an arson charge.

Drapeau said Farinacci chose Saturday, Aug. 1, to start the fire because he knew winds would reach 80 km/h.

He chose the location "because he knew it 'was gonna get bad,'" the detective said.

Farinacci told Drapeau he knew the fire would become large but didn't intend for it to grow as much as it did.

He assembled a time-delay device, placed it in the grass and ignited it with a cigarette, Drapeau said.

Farinacci told the detective he then ran from the tracks toward the street.

World.title: Canada has 'nasty leadership,' says Trump as he praises U.S. tariff policy
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump took aim at Canada on Wednesday night, calling the country — and its leadership — "nasty" during a speech in Las Vegas in which he also praised his administration's use of tariffs.

"I love tariffs, right? Because we’ve been screwed by tariffs used against us for years. By China, by Japan, by South Korea, by Germany, by everybody — by Canada," Trump said, as the crowd cheered.

"Canada’s nasty. They are. They’re nasty," he said. "I love the people, but they’re nasty. Nasty leadership."

WATCH | Trump calls Canada 'nasty' during speech: Canada has 'nasty leadership,' says Trump as he praises U.S. tariff policy | Duration 0:40 U.S. President Donald Trump, speaking from Las Vegas on Wednesday, praised his government's use of tariffs and once again mentioned Canada, saying, 'I love the people' but that the country has 'nasty leadership.'

The U.S. president used the adjective to describe Canada a total of five times.

When asked about Trump's comments during an event on Thursday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney described the situation as a "tough negotiation."

"We can change the adjective and say 'nasty,' if you will," Carney added.

Carney said he spoke with Trump on the phone last week and that there would be "other conversations" to come.

WATCH | Carney responds to Trump's comments: Carney responds to Trump's comments that Canada's leadership is 'nasty' | Duration 1:36 Responding to U.S. President Donald Trump's comments that Canada's leadership is 'nasty,' Prime Minister Mark Carney said 'whatever adjective is used, yes, we're standing up for Canadian workers, for Canadian businesses as we always have.'

Trump's Wednesday-night comments on Canada follow pointed remarks Carney made earlier in the day.

When his Teleprompter malfunctioned during a news conference on Toronto housing, ​Carney smiled and made a quip.

"I would like to inform you that the Teleprompter has ceased to function. Unlike a certain world leader, I do not view this as a conspiracy," he said.

The comment was an ​apparent reference to Trump's demands for an investigation into "triple sabotage" after ​he encountered a halted escalator, a non-functioning ⁠Teleprompter and sound issues last year at the United Nations General ​Assembly, where he delivered a speech.

Rocky relations

Relations between Canada and the U.S. have been rocky of late, as the two countries work to address trade irritants and an upcoming Aug. 19 deadline, at which point the U.S. plans to put 50 per cent tariffs on about five per cent of Canadian exports to the country. The targeted goods range from alcohol to hockey sticks to cement.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc and chief trade negotiator Janice Charette are back in Washington this week for more meetings with their U.S. counterparts. The pair will meet with U.S. Trade Representative Greer at his office in Washington, D.C., this afternoon.

On Tuesday, LeBlanc and Charette met with Jay Timmons, CEO of the National Association of Manufacturers. On Wednesday morning, LeBlanc met with North Dakota Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer and Tennessee Republican Sen. Bill Hagerty.

Carney said he's been "very involved" in those talks.

Canada has already addressed multiple trade irritants listed by the Trump administration, including killing a planned digital services tax and rolling back a Canadian content levy on streaming companies — moves that appear to have done little to move the needle with the U.S. president.

The Trump administration has also taken issue with multiple provincial bans on U.S. booze. The Distilled Spirits Council of the United States has called the bans "devastating," highlighting that exports to Canada fell 63 per cent last year.

Canada has maintained that the booze bans were a direct response to previous U.S. tariffs and would only end as part of a comprehensive trade agreement with the U.S.

Carney has not ruled out retaliation if the additional tariffs come to fruition. But last week, he said he didn't see the "value" in using Canadian energy exports as a bargaining chip in negotiations.

"We have time, and we have real constructive negotiations that are happening on a number of issues," Carney added on Wednesday.

World.title: Jalapeno-linked salmonella outbreak hits 27 U.S. states. What's the risk in Canada?
World.content:
More than 300 people across 27 U.S. states have fallen ill with salmonella infections in an outbreak that health officials say is linked to jalapeno peppers from Mexico.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) said on Wednesday that at least 345 people had gotten sick across the United States so far.

There have been 36 hospitalizations linked to the outbreak and no recorded deaths.

This is the second major outbreak of food-related illnesses in the U.S. since July, as thousands of people across the country have been infected with a diarrhea-causing parasite linked to fruits and vegetables, including lettuce.

The Public Health Agency of Canada is "not currently investigating any salmonella illnesses associated with the salmonella outbreak linked to jalapenos in the U.S.," a spokesperson for Health Canada told CBC in an email on Thursday.

The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) also told CBC it was aware of the U.S. outbreak, but there was no evidence that any affected products were distributed in Canada.

What is salmonella, and how is it transmitted?

Salmonella is a type of bacteria that makes people sick with what's called salmonellosis, an intestinal tract infection.

People most frequently get salmonella infections by ingesting food or water contaminated with feces that contains salmonella bacteria.

“The contamination usually happens at the level of the farm, but technically you can introduce a contaminant at any point,” said Isaac Bogoch, an infectious diseases specialist at the Toronto General Hospital.

Many types of foods can be affected, from nuts and produce to chicken, eggs and dairy products.

WATCH | Cyclospora, the diarrhea-causing parasite linked to earlier U.S. outbreak: What is cyclospora? A diarrhea-causing parasite | Duration 2:37 A diarrhea-causing parasite has led to a growing outbreak in the United States that has sickened more than 1,000 people and sent dozens to hospital. As of Wednesday, multiple states had reported cyclospora infections, which can cause watery diarrhea, bloating, fever and nausea. While cases are common in the spring and summer, the current outbreak has led to an unusually high number, making it one of the largest the country has seen. No deaths have been reported.

What's the source of the current U.S. salmonella outbreak?

The FDA and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said they had traced the salmonella outbreak to jalapenos from Sinaloa, a state on Mexico's west coast.

The agencies said the jalapenos were imported into the U.S. by Coast Citrus Distributors, which then delivered them to other distributors as well as to restaurants and food service companies.

"At this time, Coast Citrus Distributors does not appear to supply jalapenos directly to grocery stores," the FDA said.

Bogoch explained that salmonella bacteria can be killed off when food is cooked. But in the case of jalapenos, which are often consumed raw, "there's the risk of ingestion of the bacteria and you can get this infection."

Where in the U.S. have infections been reported?

According to data from the CDC, Minnesota and Colorado recorded the most salmonella cases so far, with 110 each.

That was followed by Illinois with 30, Kansas with 13 and Wisconsin with nine.

So far, jalapeno-linked salmonella infections have been reported in at least 27 U.S. states. (Gregory Bull/The Associated Press)

Which restaurants have been affected?

The FDA said restaurant chains Chipotle and Qdoba had received jalapenos distributed by Coast Citrus Distributors from Sinaloa.

Chipotle said it removed the affected peppers from its U.S. restaurants after the outbreak was reported while Qdoba said it removed jalapenos from all its locations "out of an abundance of caution."

"The recalled jalapeno peppers are no longer in Chipotle restaurants," Laurie Schalow, the company's chief corporate affairs and food safety officer, said in a written statement sent to CBC.

The FDA says it no longer considers the two restaurant chains to pose any health risk.

Were any outbreak-linked jalapenos distributed to Chipotle or Qdoba restaurants in Canada?

No.

A Chipotle spokesperson told CBC News the recalled jalapenos were not distributed to any restaurants in Canada. Chipotle has 86 locations across the country: 15 in Alberta, 23 in B.C. and 48 in Ontario, according to its website.

Qdoba, which has seven restaurants in Manitoba and seven in Ontario, also told CBC in an email on Thursday that none of the company's Canadian locations received jalapenos from Coast Citrus Distributors.

"Meanwhile, Qdoba has proactively removed jalapenos from all our U.S. restaurants at this time," the email said.

The FDA said it 'does not consider there to be a current ongoing risk' from Chipotle or Qdoba restaurants after they removed affected jalapenos. (Shannon Stapleton/Reuters)

Have any of the outbreak-linked jalapenos entered Canada in other ways?

Not that we know of.

A Canadian Food Inspection Agency spokesperson said in an email on Thursday that, "at this time, there is no evidence that products implicated in this outbreak were distributed in Canada."

CBC reached out to Coast Citrus Distributors by phone Thursday but could not get a comment in time for publication.

What are the symptoms of salmonella?

While some people who get salmonella infections won't have any symptoms, many develop gastrointestinal problems such as diarrhea, nausea, stomach cramps and vomiting.

People usually begin to exhibit symptoms between six hours and six days after they are infected, and the symptoms can last between four to seven days, according to the CDC.

Bogoch at the Toronto General Hospital said people who are immunocompromised, as well as children and the elderly, are at greater risk of developing more severe infections.

"The other way people can get really sick is just through dehydration" as a result of salmonella-caused diarrhea, he added.

How can you prevent salmonella from spreading?

Bogoch stressed that "impeccable hand hygiene" is key.

He also noted that because U.S. health authorities have tracked the source of the current jalapeno-linked outbreak, they can move more quickly to mitigate its spread.

"There are rarely any positives when you're talking about foodborne outbreaks," Bogoch told CBC, "but at least in this case it's been identified to a particular food source and a particular region, which means you can take steps to remove the impacted products a little faster."

World.title: Charles Darwin finally proven right about bug-eating plant after 150 years
World.content:
LISTEN | Interview with botanist Douglas Soltis: As It Happens 7:05 Charles Darwin finally proven right about bug-eating plant after 150 years

Scientists have finally proven what Charles Darwin suspected more than a century ago — that a small, innocent-looking flowering plant is, in fact, a stone-cold killer.

"I hope he'd be really excited and wanted to give us a big high five or two thumbs up," University of Florida botanist Douglas Soltis told As It Happens guest host Rebecca Zandbergen. "I'm imagining him smiling right now."

Soltis is one of the authors of a new study that identifies Saxifraga candelabrum, which grows in the rocky mountain crevices of southwestern China, as a carnivorous plant that uses its sticky little hairs to trap and devour unsuspecting insects.

The findings, published Tuesday in the journal Nature Communications , come 151 years after Darwin first theorized that predators lurked among the Saxifraga genus.

Hairy and scary

Many Saxifraga species, including the one researched in this study, are covered in millimetre-long hairs, the tips of which produce a sweet, sticky substance that lures insects in with its scent.

"You'll just see insects plastered to the leaves and stems of these plants. And so it just makes you wonder: What are they doing with all those insects?" Soltis said. "That is what fascinated Darwin."

Darwin, an English naturalist known for his contributions to evolutionary biology, first wrote his musings about Saxifraga plants in 1875 when he observed tiny insects stuck to leaves and stems of two European varieties.

Saxifraga candelabrum rarely traps larger pollinators, such as flies, that play an important role in its reproduction. (Xian-Jian Zhang/Reuters)

But he had no way to prove the plants were carnivorous. To do that, Soltis says, you have to demonstrate that the plant can digest the insects it traps, absorb their materials, and distribute those materials throughout its body.

Unfortunately for Darwin, it's not the kind of thing you can just see happening in a field in 1875. But fortunately for Soltis and his colleagues, it is something you can observe in a modern laboratory.

"You can have an insect eat a radioactively labelled substance [in] very small, tiny, tiny amounts," Soltis said. "And then you can actually — much as you would do in medicine — trace where those materials are flowing throughout the plant."

An evolutionary advantage

To determine whether it was actually feeding on insects, the researchers used fruit flies raised on food enriched with a stable form of nitrogen.

Nitrogen, says Soltis, is what the nutrient-starved mountain plants are after.

"They're not eating for the same reason that we are. They don't need carbon. They're able to make that," he said. "But they really need nitrogen."

The yellow flowering plant grows in rocky mountain crevices in nutrient-poor spoil. (Xin-Jian Zhang/Reuters)

In fact, most carnivorous plants are found in bogs and wetlands, where the watery and acidic soil is nutrient-poor, says Peter Ryser, a plant ecologist at Laurentian University in Sudbury, Ont., who was not involved in the study.

He says it's possible, from an evolutionary standpoint, that Saxifraga candelabrum and other similar plants first developed sticky hairs to keep bugs from eating their seeds, then seized on an unexpected opportunity.

"Eventually they notice, 'Hey, if there are some nice insects which get stuck, and if we exude some enzymes, then we can also get the nutrients out of them,'" he said.

But there is a conundrum. Plants need nutrients, but they also need pollinators. Saxifraga candelabrum has a solution for that.

"They trap a smaller type of insect, and then larger insects that are the pollinator are not really affected by these hairs," Soltis said.

More killers in our midst?

The researchers say this study shows there may be more carnivorous plants out there hiding in plain sight, including among Darwin's beloved Saxifraga genus.

Five years ago, researchers at the University of British Columbia discovered that a plant in B.C.'s Cypress Provincial Park uses a similar method of trapping and eating insects as Saxifraga candelabrum.

"At the time, we predicted that additional examples of carnivory would be discovered, and so it was really gratifying to read this paper and see our predictions coming true," UBC botanist Sean Graham told CBC in an email.

"I'm sure there are other examples of plant carnivory out there, waiting for discovery."

According to the U.K.'s Natural History museum , there are more than 630 known carnivorous plants in the world.

Some, like Venus flytraps, snap their jaw-like leaves shut to imprison insects. Others, like pitcher plants, lure prey with a sweet nectar, only to drown them in a digestive fluid.

Their taste for flesh can even extend beyond the bug world. One pitcher plant in Ontario has been known to snack on salamanders.

It's no wonder Darwin had a well-documented obsession with carnivorous plants, Soltis said.

"Plants have invented incredible ways to trap insects for nitrates," he said. "It's amazing to think of, you know, plants kind of turning the tables"

World.title: Canadian workers speak out against growing screen time surveillance
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Workers at some of Canada's biggest companies say increased workplace surveillance is taking a toll on their mental health as their employers ramp up the use of software that monitors their screen activity.

TD Bank told employees in its financial crimes and risk management team in June, in a call first reported by Reuters , that it will start tracking their screen time — specifically the time they spend on browsers, internal chat and meeting apps — using a tool called WorkiQ.

TD employees in other departments have raised concerns about this and other productivity tracking tools, saying they cause added stress and unease in the workplace.

"We are all very, very worried about what it's going to do," a TD employee in Edmonton told CBC News.

Companies across a range of industries are increasingly facing pushback from employees over the deployment of software that monitors screen activity. The practice has raised questions about privacy, trust, workers' rights and workplace stress.

In June, Meta paused a program that tracked employees' keystrokes and mouse movements amid concerns about data privacy and staff backlash, including a petition signed by 1,600 employees.

Worker feeling 'extreme unease'

The TD employee, who CBC News has agreed not to name because she fears she could lose her job for speaking out, said she worries the new monitoring tools will come to her workplace soon.

Her managers currently use ControliQ, she said, which is made by ActiveOps, the same U.K.-based company behind WorkiQ. ControliQ tracks time spent on tasks, but not granular details like keystrokes and mouse movements.

Introduced about two years ago, the tool is increasingly used to "shame and belittle" workers by displaying and comparing their "productivity" metrics at meetings, the employee said.

Bosses also use "Active" and "Away" status on Microsoft Teams to gauge work activity, she said, even though much of the work she does requires reading documents and other tasks not reflected by screen time.

As this type of monitoring ramps up, the employee — who has been with the company for eight years — said she and her colleagues are feeling burnout, frustration and "extreme unease."

"It's going to start impacting colleagues, because there's a lot of stuff that we do in our day that isn't recordable or isn't quote-unquote productive, but it's necessary work," she said.

"We run the risk of losing bonuses, losing raises, losing performance ratings — that sort of thing. And then we run a risk of getting written up, and eventually, possibly, losing our jobs."

TD spokesperson Mick Ramos did not answer specific questions about the software or employee concerns in an emailed statement to CBC News.

"Like many organizations, we use workflow tools in some areas of our business to better understand how work gets done and where we can make it simpler and more effective," he said. "Colleagues are informed about their use and purpose well in advance."

An ActiveOps spokesperson said in an email that the company aims to improve workplace environments by giving employers "the visibility they need to plan work and resources." He added that WorkiQ is being rebranded as Application Mining.

Using an internet archive search, CBC News found ActiveOps explicitly called WorkiQ "employee monitoring software" in 2021. It has since changed the language on its website and no longer refers to it as such.

Tracking 'degrading and humiliating': Bell employee

Surveillance and monitoring tools have become commonplace at telecom companies in Canada.

A longtime Bell employee in Toronto told CBC News that WorkiQ sounds "eerily similar" to software that's used at her work.

Bell started using Verint software to track employees' screen time and mouse movements during the COVID-19 pandemic, when everyone was working from home, she said, using "occupancy" or "effectiveness" metrics to track their active time.

A Bell Canada employee in Toronto says the company's screentime monitoring software is hard on her mental health. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

Workers can be punished for not meeting their effectiveness targets, the employee said, first with a verbal warning and then with progressive discipline, up to and including termination.

"The amount of surveillance that's done, it's very hard on your mental health," she said.

"I don't know if the company actually understands how almost degrading and humiliating it is to know that you have to have a babysitter when you're in your 50s, and you've been doing your job for 30 years, and you've been doing it well."

CBC News is also not naming the Bell employee because she fears she could lose her job for speaking out.

The employee said the effectiveness time requirements in her specific workplace have continued to increase since the pandemic, to 85 per cent from 72 per cent.

The current target is "almost impossible" to achieve, she said, and leaves no room for people to have bad days.

"When you do the math, it works out to about 23 minutes a day that you've got that you're able to use the bathroom, go grab a drink of water — or, say, you're reading," she said, adding employees are also allowed one half-hour lunch break and two 15-minute breaks.

WATCH | Benefits and concerns around monitoring tools: Should employers use productivity monitoring software? | Quick Question | Duration 7:21 Anti-surveillance advocate Matthew Mitchell and Jay Godse of Awareness Technologies, whose company develops electronic worker-monitoring software, discuss the benefits and concerns surrounding software that tracks employees while they work.

The Bell employee also worries about repetitive strain injuries from constantly moving a mouse to meet the requirements.

CBC News could not verify the 85 per cent target at the employee's specific workplace, but obtained documents from another Bell workplace showing an 80 per cent effectiveness target.

She said she's heard from managers that Verint is not only monitoring workers, but pulling their work to train AI systems and offshore workers, which she suspects has factored into recent layoffs .

"It's a weapon and it shouldn't be wielded the way it is," she said.

A Bell spokesperson told CBC News in an email that the company does not use Verint to train AI or offshore workers, but did not respond to specific questions about employee complaints or the way the software is used.

"Bell uses call-monitoring and screen-capture software to help customers get the best experience possible. This is standard industry practice for call centres," she said.

A spokesperson for New-York based Verint did not respond to CBC News's requests for comment.

Do the tools even work?

Tara Behrend, a professor at Michigan State University's School of Human Resources and Labor Relations who studies monitoring and surveillance tools, said her research has consistently found two things: these tools increase stress on workers and don't actually improve performance.

Tracking tools tend to narrow workers' focus to the metrics that are being monitored, which can then cause them to ignore other aspects of their job and also create "anti-social incentives," she said, like discouraging them from taking a screen break to help a co-worker.

"When someone starts micromanaging you and babysitting you, it breaks that contract of trust. And so then you just say, 'Fine, if you think all I am is this collection of tasks that you wrote down, then that's what you'll get from me and nothing else," Behrend said.

"It just makes work this really superficial imitation of itself. Work is not just a collection of tasks. Nobody wants to feel like that's what their contribution is."

Nevertheless, she said, these tools have proliferated with recent transitions to remote work and accelerated as part of a general societal push toward more data gathering and algorithm training.

Increased worker monitoring has led to negative physical and psychological consequences for workers in some industries, Behrend adds, citing a 2024 Oxfam report that found Amazon and Walmart warehouse workers suffered from pain and dehydration, and were afraid to take bathroom or hydration breaks because of intense surveillance.

Roch Leblanc, a national representative for Unifor, a union that represents 19,000 Bell workers across Canada, raised alarms about growing worker surveillance in telecoms when he addressed the House of Commons committee on industry and technology in April.

WATCH | Ontario employers have to disclose tracking software: Is your boss watching you work? Some Canadians are about to find out | Duration 1:56 In Ontario, employers must now disclose if they have been using productivity tracking software to keep tabs on their employees. Experts say while this may address transparency concerns, businesses should be tracking output instead.

Unifor has also raised concerns to Bell's management about Verint software specifically.

Leblanc tells CBC News the software is "invasive," has created significant stress in the workplace and does not always represent the true picture of a worker's productivity.

"The work intensification is at such a level now, there's no ups and downs in the work on a daily basis," he said. "It's constantly intense, constantly frustrating."
