One System, Two Emergency Responses

Uruguay’s National Emergency System said the extratropical cyclone could generate gusts above 120 km/h from the Pando stream eastward to Aguas Dulces. The zone covers much of the coast through Canelones, Maldonado and Rocha, including the wider Punta del Este area. Authorities also warned of a significant rise in coastal waves.

The red alert ran from 9 p.m. on August 6 until 4 a.m. on August 7. It restricted mobility and suspended risk-related public activities, while essential state services remained active. The government urged private organizations to follow the same precautionary standard. The fixed seven-hour window was not an all-day shutdown; it targeted the period of greatest expected intensity.

In Rio, the operational response was longer and more preventive. The city entered Stage 2, the second level on a five-stage scale, at 7:05 p.m. Thursday. That classification means high-impact incidents are possible, even if the city has not yet recorded a generalized emergency.

Rio Closes Schools Before the Strongest Winds

Rio’s municipal and state public-school networks canceled Friday classes, and the Faetec technical-school system also suspended activities. Paraty and Angra dos Reis made the same decision for municipal schools. Officials described the closures as a way to reduce travel by students, families and education workers during the risk period.

The state Civil Defense warned that gusts could exceed 90 km/h in metropolitan Rio. Forecasts for the Serra Fluminense, southern Rio state and the Costa Verde ranged from 91 km/h to 110 km/h. Within the capital, Alerta Rio described Friday gusts as strong, at 52–76 km/h, to very strong, above 76 km/h.

Early measurements were lower than the day’s maximum forecast. The strongest reported gust during the early morning reached 54.6 km/h, according to figures cited by Exame from city monitoring. That gap matters: a forecast ceiling is not an observed speed, and the closures were ordered before the anticipated afternoon peak.

An orange coastal-wind notice also covered sections of Rio state’s shoreline, including Cabo Frio, Arraial do Cabo, Búzios and Campos dos Goytacazes. Authorities highlighted the risk of moving dunes, falling branches and damage to exposed structures.

Uruguay Used Its Highest Alert Level

Uruguay’s decision went beyond a meteorological warning. By declaring a red alert, the executive activated emergency operations and attached legal restrictions to the forecast. The measure covered named communities in Maldonado and Rocha as well as surrounding areas along the eastern coastal strip.

Officials advised residents to remain indoors, avoid unnecessary travel and stay away from the exposed coastline. They also urged people to secure loose objects and prepare for falling trees, signs and power lines. The notice emphasized wave action as well as wind, making beaches, ports and waterfront roads especially vulnerable.

The official alert described what could occur, not a confirmed damage total. Any assessment of outages, structural losses or injuries should therefore rely on later emergency reports rather than on the forecast itself.

Why This Matters for the Southern Cone

The episode demonstrates the cross-border reach of South Atlantic cyclones. The center of the low does not need to pass directly over every affected city. Its pressure gradient, fronts and coastal circulation can produce dangerous winds hundreds of kilometers away and at different hours.

That creates a coordination problem for governments, transport operators and power companies. Uruguay used a narrow overnight restriction for its most exposed coast. Rio reduced daytime movement through school closures and raised its operational readiness. Both responses were tailored to local timing rather than to a single regional warning window.

For residents and travelers, the practical risk extends beyond rain. Strong crosswinds can disrupt bridges and airports; falling trees can block roads and cut electricity; high waves can affect ports and coastal recreation even after inland winds start to ease.

What to Watch Next

Whether observed gusts in Rio approach the 90–110 km/h forecast range outside the capital.

Official reports of power outages, fallen trees, transport interruptions or injuries in Rio state and Uruguay.

Any extension or replacement of Uruguay’s expired red-alert window.

Rio’s operational-stage decision after winds ease and the front moves through.

Coastal-wave and marine warnings through the weekend.

Connected Coverage

Frequently Asked Questions

Were winds of 110 km/h already recorded in Rio?

Not in the early-morning figures cited here. The 91–110 km/h range was a forecast for parts of Rio state; the strongest early gust reported in the capital was 54.6 km/h.

Was Punta del Este under Uruguay’s red alert?

The official alert covered the eastern coastal strip from the Pando stream to Aguas Dulces, including areas of Maldonado Department around Punta del Este.

Why were Rio’s schools closed?

Officials said the preventive closure would reduce travel and exposure for students, families and staff during the period of strongest expected winds.

What does Stage 2 mean in Rio?

It is the second level of Rio’s five-stage operating system and indicates a risk of high-impact incidents, with the possibility of a further change if conditions worsen.

When did Uruguay’s red alert end?

The declared window ended at 4 a.m. on Friday, August 7. Later conditions remain subject to fresh notices from SINAE and INUMET.

World.title: Inter&Co Hits Record US$81m Profit as Bad Loans Rise
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Earnings · Brazil

Key Facts —Record net profit Inter&Co reported net income of R$421 million (US$81 million) in Q2 2026, a company record and 34% higher than the R$315 million (US$61 million) of a year earlier. —Stronger profitability Return on equity reached 16.3% in Q2 2026, up from 15.5% in Q1 2026 and 240 basis points higher than a year earlier. —Loan book expansion Inter&Co’s gross loan portfolio reached R$51.9 billion (US$10.0 billion) at the end of June 2026, 29% larger than a year earlier. —Customer base scale The group reported 45.3 million total customers and 26.4 million active customers through its Brazilian‑rooted super‑app at the end of the second quarter of 2026. —Rising delinquency Loans more than 90 days overdue rose to 5.3% of the gross book from 5.1% in Q1 2026 and 4.6% a year earlier, with the increase concentrated in private payroll loans and credit cards. —Share price reaction Nasdaq‑listed INTR opened 5.4% lower on 6 August 2026 and fell as much as 6.8% during the morning, and ended the day at US$5.72, up 0.2%.

Inter&Co posted a record quarterly profit and its best return on equity yet, while bad loans climbed to a fresh high and the shares gave up an early slide to close little changed.

Illustrative. (Photo internet reproduction)

Key numbers behind Inter&Co’s Q2 2026

Inter&Co’s own earnings release for the quarter shows net income of R$421 million, or US$81 million, the strongest profit in the bank’s history. On the company’s own chart of quarterly earnings, profit has risen in every quarter since the start of 2023.

Return on equity reached 16.3%, up from 15.5% in the first quarter and 240 basis points higher than a year earlier. Every real figure in this article is converted at R$5.20 to US$1, the rate implied by the company’s own dollar conversion in the release.

The gross loan portfolio reached R$51.9 billion (US$10.0 billion) at the end of June, 29% higher than a year earlier, on a deliberate push into consumer and small-business credit. Total assets passed R$100 billion (US$19.2 billion) for the first time, and funding reached R$77 billion (US$14.8 billion), up 24%.

The super‑app counted 45.3 million total clients and 26.4 million active clients at the end of June. Growth is concentrated in Brazil, though the bank has been adding cross‑border users through its payments, shopping and investment tools.

The R$421 million (US$81 million) compares with R$315 million (US$61 million) in the second quarter of 2025, a rise of 34%, and with R$395 million (US$76 million) in the first quarter of 2026, a rise of 7%. The company’s press release describes the 34% as a quarter-on-quarter gain, but its own earnings release states plainly that the increase is measured against the year-earlier quarter.

Inter&Co says the quarter delivered its internal “Rule of 50”, a target it set at its Owners’ Day in May for net revenue growth plus return on equity to exceed 50. The company publishes the shortfall itself: the slide prints “Rule of 50 = 48%”, built from net revenue growth of 31.7% and a return on equity of 16.3%, and charts a path of 37.6% in 2023, 45.8% in 2024, 45.0% in 2025 and 48.0% in the second quarter of 2026 against a target of about 50% for 2026 to 2029. Nothing is hidden. What overreaches is the press release’s claim that the rule has already become a reality.

Asset quality: the sore spot in an otherwise bright quarter

Behind the record profit, the sore point is loan delinquency. Loans more than 90 days overdue reached 5.3% of the gross book in the second quarter, the highest reading in the nine quarters the bank discloses, up from 5.1% in the first quarter and 4.6% a year earlier.

Early-stage arrears, of 15 to 90 days, rose in step to 4.8% from 4.6% and from 4.1% a year earlier. The bank says the increases are concentrated in private payroll loans and credit cards.

Two qualifications matter, but they cannot simply be subtracted from the rise they qualify. The headline ratio climbed 70 basis points over the year, from 4.6% to 5.3%. Inter&Co says private payroll lending alone accounts for 53 basis points of the yearly rise, but that bridge is drawn on the expanded loan portfolio, which went from 4.4% to 5.0% — a different base from the gross-book ratio quoted above. Private payroll is a product the bank launched recently and whose collection systems it describes as not yet fully optimised.

The bank also changed its credit-card write-off policy during the quarter. It says that one-off adjustment added 30 basis points to the 90-day ratio, with no effect on provisions or the cost of risk. Because the two explanations are measured on different bases, adding them together and comparing the 83-basis-point total with the 70-basis-point rise does not work.

Provisioning still covers the problem loans comfortably. The coverage ratio stood at 134% at the end of June, down from 143% a year earlier, while the all-in cost of risk rose to 5.9% from 5.0%.

Taken together, the picture is of a franchise that has grown fast into lower‑income and small‑business lending. The level of bad loans is covered and disclosed, but it is rising in a country where credit cycles can turn quickly.

For many Latin America watchers, that tension feels familiar. Brazil has lived through long periods where credit is both the engine of inclusion and the trap door of crisis.

A super‑app bank like Inter&Co, born digital and riding the hopes of a more frictionless financial life, is now learning the old lesson: when household budgets are squeezed and informal jobs wobble, even the slickest app is still fighting the hard gravity of delinquency.

The company offers banking products and services, including checking accounts; cards; deposits; loans and advances; and other services, as well as debt collections; foreign exchange and…

How the market handled a record quarter

Inter&Co published the figures after the New York close on 5 August 2026 and held its call the following morning. Total net revenue was R$2,637 million (US$507 million), below the FactSet consensus of US$513.3 million. The company’s own release converts the same figure at a slightly stronger rate and puts it at US$509.5 million.

The first reaction was negative. INTR opened at US$5.40 on 6 August against a previous close of US$5.71, and traded as low as US$5.32 during the morning, a fall of 6.8%.

The selling did not hold. The stock ended the day at US$5.72, up 0.2%, on volume of 7.7 million shares against a recent average nearer 3 million.

For foreign investors watching from New York or London, the round trip says something about how Latin American financials trade. The first instinct on a higher bad-loan print is to sell; the second look weighs it against a record profit and a 16% return on equity.

The wider question is not one quarter’s delinquency figure. It is the bank’s expansion from a small lender into a nationwide player with R$51.9 billion (US$10.0 billion) of loans, much of it to consumers who live from pay cheque to pay cheque.

How Inter&Co compares with its own past and with peers

Inter&Co’s Q2 2026 performance marks a clear break from its early‑stage years. On the company’s own quarterly series, net income has risen from R$11 million (US$2 million) in the first quarter of 2023 to R$421 million (US$81 million), and return on equity from single digits to 16.3%.

The first quarter of 2026 brought net profit of R$395 million (US$76 million) and a 15.5% return on equity. That pace contrasts with more mature Latin American banks, which tend to deliver steadier but lower growth.

From a risk perspective, Inter&Co sits closer to other growth‑heavy regional lenders than to conservative incumbents. A 90-day bad-loan ratio of 5.3% and a cost of risk of 5.9% are not unusual among institutions pushing into underserved segments, but they sit above the levels of large universal banks.

Q2 2026’s numbers – record profit, high ROE, elevated NPLs – crystallise that dual identity and explain why the stock can swing so sharply on each new data point.

Frequently Asked Questions

What was Inter&Co’s net profit in Q2 2026?

Inter&Co reported net income of R$421 million, or US$81 million, in the second quarter of 2026. That is its highest quarterly profit to date and 34% above the R$315 million (US$61 million) reported a year earlier.

How many customers does Inter&Co serve through its super‑app?

The company’s Q2 2026 release describes Inter&Co as a super‑app providing financial and digital commerce services to more than 45 million customers, largely in Brazil. Its earnings release puts the exact figure at 45.3 million total clients and 26.4 million active clients.

What happened to Inter&Co’s share price after the Q2 2026 results?

INTR opened 5.4% lower on 6 August 2026 and fell as much as 6.8% during the morning, as investors weighed revenue below the FactSet consensus and a higher bad-loan ratio. It ended the day at US$5.72, up 0.2%.

World.title: Tenaris Q2 Profit Falls to US$477m on Hormuz Closure
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Earnings · Argentina

Key Facts —Sales Fall Tenaris posted second-quarter 2026 net sales of US$2,967 million, down 4 per cent both on the first quarter and on the same quarter of 2025. —Profit Decline Net income attributable to shareholders fell to US$477 million from US$531 million a year earlier, squeezed by logistics disruption. —EBITDA Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation was US$649 million, down from US$733 million, with the margin narrowing to 21.9 per cent from 23.7 per cent. —Hormuz Impact Management attributed weaker margins to shipment delays and higher freight costs tied to Middle East shipping disruption. —Argentina Layoffs Separately, in late June the Techint group’s Tenaris Siat unit cut 150 fixed-term contract jobs at Valentin Alsina after losing two Argentine pipeline tenders. —Volumes Tubular product shipments totalled 946,000 tonnes, down 5 per cent on the first quarter and 4 per cent on a year earlier.

Tenaris (NYSE: TS) booked net sales of US$2.97 billion in the second quarter of 2026, down 4 per cent, after the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz pushed Middle East shipments into later quarters. Weeks earlier its Argentine welded-pipe unit had cut 150 fixed-term contract jobs at Valentin Alsina.

Large-diameter line pipe under construction in Argentina. Illustrative. (Photo internet reproduction)

The Quarterly Numbers in Detail

Tenaris published its second-quarter 2026 results on 5 August 2026, reporting net sales of US$2,967 million. Sales fell 4 per cent against the first quarter and 4 per cent against the second quarter of 2025.

The top line masked a familiar strain. Net income attributable to shareholders dropped to US$477 million from US$531 million in the same quarter a year earlier.

Operating income came in at US$494 million, down 15 per cent both sequentially and year on year. Total net income, before deducting the share attributable to minority holders, was US$492 million against US$542 million.

Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation was US$649 million, delivering an EBITDA margin of 21.9 per cent against 23.7 per cent in both the first quarter and the year-earlier quarter.

Sales volumes of tubular products stood at 946,000 metric tonnes, of which seamless pipe accounted for 768,000 tonnes. Delivery, more than order intake in the Americas, held the quarter back, although demand in parts of the Middle East also weakened.

For context, net sales in the first quarter of 2026 were US$3,100 million, meaning sequential revenues slipped about 4.3 per cent. The year-earlier second quarter had net sales of US$3,086 million, so the 2026 quarter also represented a 3.9 per cent year-on-year decline.

What the Hormuz Disruption Did to Costs

Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has become Latin America’s long-distance headache. The narrow waterway carries a huge share of global oil and gas, and when tensions flare, freight rates spike and vessels reroute, adding days or weeks to delivery schedules.

Tenaris management linked the profit compression directly to Middle East disruption. Higher logistics costs and delayed tubing shipments bit into margins that would otherwise have been healthier. Because the company moves heavy steel pipe by sea to drilling basins from the Middle East to the Gulf of Mexico, any choke point immediately raises the cost of doing business.

These disruptions also warp inventory timing. When a rig in Argentina’s Vaca Muerta or Saudi Arabia’s desert waits for pipe, the dollar clock ticks louder. Tenaris cited higher unitary logistics costs, weaker absorption of fixed costs and rising raw material prices. Together these cut the EBITDA margin to 21.9 per cent from 23.7 per cent three months earlier.

For investors across Latin America, the episode confirms that geopolitics and supply-chain fragility are now permanent line items in quarterly earnings. A flare-up half a world away can cool profits from Buenos Aires to Houston.

The 150 Layoffs and What They Mean for Argentina

The 150 job cuts at Valentin Alsina were not announced in the quarterly results release, which does not mention them. Tenaris Siat, the Techint group’s Argentine welded-pipe unit, notified the redundancies in late June, effective from 1 July.

The plant sits in Lanus, in the industrial belt south of Buenos Aires, where tens of thousands of families depend on the metalworking and energy supply chain.

The cuts land at a delicate moment for Argentina’s economy. Industrial employment remains one of the few anchors of household income in the sprawling suburbs south of the capital.

When a plant of this size tightens its workforce, nearby workshops, transport contractors and neighbourhood shops feel the drag.

The 150 posts were fixed-term contract roles, not permanent staff jobs. Of roughly 200 contract workers on the site, about three-quarters were not renewed, while the plant’s roughly 150 permanent employees were left untouched. On the figures cited by the Argentine press, that is about 43 per cent of a total workforce of some 350. The plant employed some 550 people in 2023, when it rolled pipe for the gas pipeline now officially called the Gasoducto Perito Moreno.

Local reporting carried the weight of a region that remembers job losses turning into long-term social erosion.

The cause was commercial rather than geopolitical. Siat rolls large-diameter welded line pipe, and it lost two tenders to supply pipe for Vaca Muerta gas pipelines, one of them to India’s Welspun.

The Strait of Hormuz did not cause these redundancies. They belong to a separate, domestic story about who wins Argentina’s pipeline contracts.

Demand for Oil-Country Tubular Goods and the Outlook

Drilling activity is rising in the United States, Canada and Argentina, and customers worldwide are pressing ahead with cost-competitive offshore projects. In the United States, prices for oil-country tubular goods have been climbing to offset higher raw material and logistics costs.

The Middle East is the weak spot. Tenaris says drilling in Iraq, Kuwait and Qatar has been severely affected, while activity in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates has largely held up.

Management tempered enthusiasm with caution. The Strait of Hormuz disruption is not resolved, and rerouted cargoes add unpredictable lead times.

Tenaris expects second-half sales and EBITDA to stay in line with the first half. It flagged possible upside if the shipping disruption ends before the year is out.

The board approved an interim dividend of US$0.59 per share, or US$1.18 per ADS, worth about US$600 million and payable on 25 November 2026. Free cash flow was US$396 million in the quarter, and the net cash position stood at US$3.6 billion at 30 June.

Board changes were also disclosed. Jaime Serra Puche has resigned as a director and audit committee member, and German Cura has stepped down as vice chair for sustainability while remaining on the board.

Alicia Mondolo joins the board as vice chair responsible for sustainability, risk management and compliance. Paolo Rocca remains chairman of a ten-member board.

For Latin American investors who track Tenaris as a bellwether, the message is mixed. Sales held up in North America, where first-half tubes revenue rose 11 per cent, but margin sensitivity to logistics shows the premium on geographic diversification is rising.

Tenaris says first-half EBITDA was negatively affected by the cost of United States tariffs. As offshore campaigns in Brazil’s pre-salt and Guyana’s Stabroek block continue, the company should benefit from deepwater demand, but only if sea lanes stay open.

Argentine shale play Vaca Muerta offers a domestic growth pocket that partly insulates Tenaris from global shipping chaos, yet even there the economics depend on imported steel inputs that must navigate the same troubled waters. The second half of 2026 will therefore test whether the company can convert its revenue momentum back into profit growth once Hormuz tensions ease.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much did Tenaris sell in the second quarter of 2026?

Net sales were US$2,967 million, down 4 per cent against the first quarter of 2026 and 4 per cent against the second quarter of 2025.

Why did Tenaris’s profit fall in the second quarter of 2026?

Profit was squeezed by shipment delays and higher logistics costs linked to shipping disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, which weighed on margins.

How many layoffs did Tenaris announce in Argentina?

Tenaris Siat cut 150 fixed-term contract jobs at Valentin Alsina in Lanus, Buenos Aires province, notified in late June 2026 and effective from 1 July. The cuts followed the loss of two Argentine pipeline supply tenders, one of them to India’s Welspun, and were not part of the quarterly results release.

Sources: Tenaris, “Tenaris Announces 2026 Second Quarter Results”, 5 August 2026, Infobae on the 150 redundancies at Tenaris Siat, Ámbito on the Valentin Alsina notifications

World.title: Axia Energia posts US$233m profit as it exits NYSE
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Earnings · Brazil

Key Facts —Q2 net profit Axia Energia reported net income of R$1,191 million (US$233 million) in the second quarter of 2026, against a loss of R$1,325 million (US$259 million) a year earlier. —The underlying figure On the company’s own adjusted basis, which strips out one-off items, net income was R$1,608 million (US$314 million) — up just 9.5 per cent. —New York exit The company’s depositary receipts were due to trade on the New York Stock Exchange for the last time on or about 6 August 2026. Trading moves over the counter. —Transmission pipeline 288 large-scale transmission projects are under construction, carrying estimated capital spending of R$15.5 billion (US$3.03 billion). —Company name Eletrobras now trades as Axia Energia, under the ticker AXIA3, after completing its migration to B3’s Novo Mercado in June 2026. —Currency Reais are converted at R$5.12 to the US dollar throughout this article.

Axia Energia, the former Eletrobras, reported a second-quarter net profit of R$1,191 million (US$233 million), reversing a loss of R$1,325 million (US$259 million) a year earlier. On the company’s adjusted measure, however, profit rose only 9.5 per cent — and its receipts were due to leave the New York Stock Exchange on or about 6 August.

The profit, and what it does not say

Axia Energia booked a net profit of R$1,191 million (US$233 million) in the second quarter of 2026. In the same quarter of 2025 it lost R$1,325 million (US$259 million).

The reversal is real. It is also smaller than the headline suggests.

On the company’s own adjusted basis, which removes non-recurring items, net income was R$1,608 million (US$314 million). That is 9.5 per cent above the R$1,469 million (US$287 million) it earned on the same basis a year earlier.

In other words, the year-earlier quarter was dragged into loss by one-offs rather than by the operating business. Strip those out and this was a quarter of modest progress, not a transformation.

Net operating revenue reached R$11,188 million (US$2.19 billion), 9.7 per cent above the R$10,199 million (US$1.99 billion) of a year earlier. On the regulatory basis the company also reports, revenue was R$10,007 million (US$1.95 billion), up 4.3 per cent.

Reported EBITDA was R$5,925 million (US$1.16 billion), against R$1,259 million (US$246 million) a year before. Once again the base was depressed: adjusted EBITDA rose a far more sober 22.5 per cent, to R$6,307 million (US$1.23 billion).

Two operating factors did most of the work, both reported on the company’s regulatory basis rather than under IFRS. The generation contribution margin rose 17.5 per cent to R$3,653 million (US$713 million), helped by more energy available for sale after the end of the quota regime and a generation scaling factor of 99.2 per cent, while operating provisions fell 64 per cent.

Equity income, also on that regulatory basis, swung from a loss of R$205 million (US$40 million) to a gain of R$296 million (US$58 million). Transmission, the larger of the two margins and likewise a regulatory figure, was essentially flat at R$4,025 million (US$786 million) against R$3,972 million (US$776 million).

Net debt closed June at R$45,461 million (US$8.88 billion), R$585 million (US$114 million) below the March figure. The average cost of that debt fell to the interbank CDI rate minus 0.02 per cent a year, from CDI plus 0.58 per cent a year earlier.

For a foreign reader, the useful discipline here is to watch the adjusted line rather than the reported one. Brazilian utilities carry large provisions, tariff-cycle timing effects and legal contingencies that can throw a single quarter in either direction.

The last day on the New York Stock Exchange

Axia Energia filed a Form 25 with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on 27 July 2026 to withdraw its American Depositary Shares from the New York Stock Exchange. The last day of trading was expected to be on or about 6 August.

This is a voluntary exit, not an expulsion. The board approved it on 1 April 2026, and the company said the receipts represented only about 2.5 per cent of its outstanding shares.

Two classes are affected: the common receipts, which traded under the ticker AXIA, and the Class C preferred receipts, which traded as AXIA PRC.

Delisting takes legal effect ten days after the Form 25 was filed. Deregistration is a separate and later step.

Axia says it intends to file a Form 15F to deregister its securities and end its US reporting duties, a process that can take up to 90 days after filing and is subject to no objection from the regulator.

Holders of the receipts need do nothing immediately. The receipts are expected to continue trading in the United States over the counter, through a Level 1 sponsored programme with Citibank as depositary.

What genuinely changes is disclosure. On the notice’s own account, filing the Form 15F suspends Axia’s duty to file 20-F annual reports and 6-K updates immediately; only full deregistration waits up to 90 days. Either way, American holders will have to follow the company through Brazilian filings instead.

The exit ran alongside a second change at home. In June the company completed its migration to the Novo Mercado, B3’s strictest governance tier, leaving a capital structure of common shares under the ticker AXIA3 and Class C preferred shares under AXIA7.

The trade-off is straightforward. Some large US funds cannot hold a security that is not listed on an American exchange, and Axia is betting that concentrating liquidity in São Paulo, where the overwhelming majority of its shares already trade, is worth losing them.

It is a wager repeated across the region in recent years, as boards weigh the prestige of a New York listing against its cost and legal exposure. In Axia’s case the 2.5 per cent figure made the arithmetic unusually easy.

Where the transmission money is going

Axia invested R$3,117 million (US$609 million) in the quarter, 52.6 per cent more than the R$2,043 million (US$399 million) of a year earlier. Transmission took the bulk of it.

Spending on transmission expansion reached R$636 million (US$124 million), against R$85 million (US$17 million) in the same quarter of 2025. Reinforcements and improvements to the existing grid absorbed a further R$1,073 million (US$210 million).

The forward pipeline is much larger. The company reports 288 large-scale transmission projects under construction, carrying total estimated capital spending of R$15.5 billion (US$3.03 billion).

Those projects are expected to add roughly R$2.0 billion (US$391 million) of allowed annual revenue between 2026 and 2030. Allowed annual revenue, known in Brazil as RAP, is the regulated sum a transmission operator is paid each year for keeping its lines available.

Axia also won Lots 8, 9 and 10 at Brazil’s Transmission Auction 01/2026, awarded on 3 July 2026, shortly after quarter end. On the terms set out in the auction notice, those lots should generate an additional R$50.8 million (US$9.9 million) of allowed annual revenue once operating, for R$668 million (US$130 million) of investment.

Transmission is the unglamorous backbone of the Brazilian electricity system. Power is generated in northern hydro basins and in a fast-expanding north-eastern wind and solar belt, while the demand centres sit hundreds or thousands of kilometres to the south-east.

Regulated transmission offers something generation cannot: inflation-linked, long-dated revenue that does not depend on how much rain falls. For a company still proving its post-privatisation credibility, that predictability matters more than headline growth.

Brazil’s recent transmission auctions have drawn fierce competition from domestic players, Chinese state-owned groups and European infrastructure funds, compressing the returns on offer. Whether Axia can deploy this much capital and still earn an acceptable spread is the open question.

Alongside the capital spending, the board approved up to R$3.7 billion (US$723 million) of capital available for allocation to shareholders from the second-quarter result. Added to the R$4.0 billion (US$781 million) approved on the first quarter, that takes the half-year total to as much as R$7.7 billion (US$1.50 billion).

What the rebrand to Axia Energia signals

The change from Eletrobras to Axia Energia is not cosmetic. The old name carried half a century of history: a state-controlled champion created in 1962, the symbol of Brazil’s ambition to electrify a continent-sized nation, and later the subject of endless political battles over its role, its tariffs, and its eventual sale.

Axia, by contrast, suggests a leaner, more private-sector identity. The word means “value” or “worth” in Greek, a deliberate signal that this is now a corporation measuring itself by returns rather than by the number of households it connects.

Yet the legacy cannot be erased with a new logo. The company remains Brazil’s largest electricity generator and transmitter, with 74,829 kilometres of transmission lines and 44,430 megawatts of installed generating capacity.

The state has not gone away either. The Brazilian government and related entities still hold about 40 per cent of the total capital, though no shareholder may cast more than 10 per cent of the votes at a general meeting.

The rebrand therefore expresses a duality at the heart of Brazilian capitalism. It tells the financial world that the privatised entity is a normal company, subject to market discipline. At the same time, it must operate within a political ecosystem where the state never truly steps back, where affordability is a permanent demand, and where profit can quickly be recast as profiteering if the weather turns bad and bills rise.

This tension is what makes covering Brazil so compelling. Axia Energia is not just a stock ticker—it is a portrait of a country that has liberalised deeply but not completely, that welcomes foreign capital but keeps a hand on the regulatory tiller, and that wants First World energy infrastructure while still grappling with Third World inequality. Every quarterly result is a fresh snapshot of that unresolved, entirely human negotiation.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Axia Energia report for the second quarter of 2026?

Net profit of R$1,191 million (US$233 million), against a loss of R$1,325 million (US$259 million) a year earlier. On the company’s adjusted basis, which excludes one-off items, net income was R$1,608 million (US$314 million), up 9.5 per cent.

Has Axia Energia really left the New York Stock Exchange?

Yes. It filed a Form 25 on 27 July 2026 and its depositary receipts were due to trade for the last time on or about 6 August. The receipts are expected to trade over the counter instead. Separate deregistration from the US regulator has not yet been completed.

How much is Axia Energia investing in transmission?

It has 288 large-scale transmission projects under construction, with estimated capital spending of R$15.5 billion (US$3.03 billion), expected to add about R$2.0 billion (US$391 million) of allowed annual revenue between 2026 and 2030.

Note on currency: reais are converted throughout at R$5.12 to the US dollar.

World.title: Globant Launches Glob.AI With Pay-Per-Output AI Services
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Argentina · Technology

Key Facts —The launch. Argentine-founded technology group Globant introduced Glob.AI on August 6, 2026, as an online marketplace for enterprise AI services. —The pricing shift. Customers pay per expert-validated output or actual consumption, rather than per employee, seat or hour. —The delivery model. Specialized “AI Pods” combine teams of AI agents with human supervision, documented workflows and enterprise governance. —The claim. Globant says the model is at least 30% more productive than a typical engineer-plus-AI approach; the comparison has not been independently audited. —The rollout. Glob.AI is initially available through a waiting list, so broad commercial availability and a public price catalog remain pending. —The business backdrop. Globant’s first-quarter 2026 revenue slipped 0.7% year on year to US$607.1 million as the company pushed toward AI-integrated delivery.

Globant is trying to rewrite one of technology consulting’s oldest rules: that clients pay for the people and hours assigned to a project. Its new Glob.AI platform instead sells work by validated output or measured consumption, placing artificial-intelligence agents inside service units supervised by the company’s specialists.

The model could align spending more closely with delivered work, but it also transfers more execution risk to Globant. The company must define an output, validate its quality and deliver it efficiently enough for outcome-linked pricing to beat traditional time-and-materials contracts.

Globant is moving its enterprise technology-services model from labor-based billing toward AI-assisted outputs. (Photo: internal archive)

Glob.AI Replaces Hours With Validated Outputs

Glob.AI is designed as a self-service destination where enterprises can select and deploy specialized AI Pods. Globant says billing will be linked either to expert-approved outputs or to actual consumption. Clients should not be charged for hallucinations, retries or wasted token cycles, according to the company’s launch statement.

That distinction matters. “Outcome pricing” can imply payment for a business result such as higher sales, while Globant’s description is narrower: payment can be tied to a defined technical output or usage. The company has not yet published a price list, standard contract terms or the metrics it will use to settle disputes over whether an output meets the agreed specification.

Organizations can join a waiting list for early access. Globant says the catalog will cover enterprise platforms and industry-specific tasks, with offerings connected to Anthropic, Amazon Web Services, Vercel, OpenAI, Adobe, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, SAP and Salesforce.

What the AI Pods Actually Do

The underlying AI Pods are not new. Globant introduced them in June 2025 as subscription units for engineering, product definition, design and testing. Glob.AI turns that delivery model into an online catalog and changes the commercial emphasis from monthly capacity toward outputs and consumption.

Each Pod uses multiple agents, loops and deterministic workflows, while Globant experts supervise the process and validate the result. Customers can choose which models to use and where they run. The company says client data will not train external models and that token use will be recorded in a proprietary Token Vault for traceability.

Globant reports that FIFA increased throughput efficiency by 20%, YPF cut contract timelines by as much as 40%, PharmaMar generated oncology-research insights 15 times faster and a commercial bank completed a COBOL migration in two months instead of a projected 14. These are company-supplied case studies, not independently audited comparisons, and the release does not disclose project scope, cost or baseline methodology.

Rio Times · Live Ticker Intelligence Launches .AI With Pay-Per-Output AI Services Share price · live — Peers & comparators IBOV ▼ -1.23%

The Commercial Pressure Behind the Launch

Glob.AI arrives as conventional IT-services growth slows and clients demand measurable returns from artificial intelligence. Globant reported US$607.1 million in first-quarter 2026 revenue, down 0.7% from a year earlier. Its adjusted operating margin narrowed to 14.1% from 14.8%, while headcount fell to 28,510 from 31,102 a year earlier.

Management framed the lower headcount alongside record revenue per professional as evidence that AI-integrated delivery can produce more value with fewer labor inputs. Glob.AI is the commercial test of that thesis. If automation reduces delivery cost faster than output-based prices decline, the model could support margins. If projects require heavy human correction or customers contest output quality, Globant absorbs more of the downside.

The company is due to report second-quarter results on August 13. Investors will be looking for evidence that AI Pods are moving beyond selected case studies into repeatable revenue, particularly as Globant’s first-quarter customer count and million-dollar accounts were below their year-earlier levels.

Why This Matters for Latin America

Globant was founded in Buenos Aires and built a global delivery network from Latin American engineering talent. Its move away from hourly billing is therefore more than a product launch: it tests how one of the region’s most visible technology exporters can defend its position when coding and consulting labor become increasingly automated.

For Latin America’s software-services sector, the opportunity is to sell intellectual property, orchestration and measurable results rather than lower-cost hours. The risk is that productivity gains reduce entry-level work before companies create enough higher-value roles in architecture, governance, domain expertise and AI quality control.

What to Watch Next

Commercial access. Globant must move from a waiting list to a usable catalog with clear prices, service levels and acceptance criteria.

Revenue disclosure. The August 13 results may show whether AI Pods are generating material recurring sales or mainly supporting broader consulting contracts.

Margin evidence. Output pricing only strengthens the business if agent productivity exceeds the cost of expert supervision, failed runs and quality guarantees.

Workforce effects. Revenue per professional, hiring and junior-role demand will reveal how quickly Globant is replacing labor hours with AI-enabled delivery.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Glob.AI?

Glob.AI is Globant’s online platform for selecting and consuming enterprise AI services delivered through expert-supervised AI Pods.

How does Glob.AI pricing work?

Globant says customers will pay per validated output or real consumption, not per seat or hour. Detailed public pricing and standard contract terms have not yet been released.

Is Glob.AI generally available?

Not yet. Organizations can join a waiting list for early access to the catalog.

Are Globant’s productivity claims independently verified?

No independent audit was cited. The 30% productivity comparison and client case-study results come from Globant’s own release.

How does Glob.AI handle client data?

Globant says clients can choose models and deployment locations, external models will not be trained on client data, and token use will be tracked in a proprietary Token Vault.
