World.title: Pesticide Runoff Is Quietly Draining Costa Rica’s Caribbean Tourism Economy
World.content:
Costa Rica sells rainforest, biodiversity and pura vida to millions of visitors a year. It is also, by the standard international measure, among the most pesticide-intensive farming countries on the planet. Figures compiled from Food and Agriculture Organization data and reviewed in a peer-reviewed survey of Neotropical rivers put national use at 22.9 kilograms of active ingredient per hectare of cropland in 2016.

It also put it above 20 kilograms per hectare in every year since 2000 — several times the rate in Colombia, Guatemala or Brazil, and far above most of Europe. Nowhere is the distance between the brand and the balance sheet wider than on the Caribbean coast, where decades of banana and pineapple production have left a documented chemical trail through the rivers that feed Limón’s mangroves, reefs and fishing grounds.

The underlying science is not seriously contested. Researchers from the Regional Institute for Studies on Toxic Substances at the Universidad Nacional, working with Stockholm University and Wageningen University, sampled five sites along the Río Madre de Dios in Batán de Matina over two years and detected 26 different pesticides.

Modeling of those mixtures indicated a greater than 50 percent probability of clear toxic effects on algae, aquatic plants, zooplankton, macroinvertebrates and overall community metabolism, with ecological risk highest near the plantations and declining progressively downstream.

Seven substances accounted for roughly 90 percent of the modeled risk: the herbicides ametryn and diuron, the insecticides carbaryl, chlorpyrifos, diazinon and ethoprophos, and the fungicide difenoconazole. A companion assessment covering four years of sampling in the river and its coastal lagoon identified 32 pesticides in total.

The models found comparatively low acute risk to fish, but the authors were careful to note why that finding should be read narrowly: water samples were not collected during fish kill events, and several pesticides known to be applied locally — including mancozeb and pyrethroids — could not be analyzed with available laboratory capacity. Frequent fish kills have been reported in the watershed since 2004, with 18 observed events documented between 2007 and 2009 alone, and further mass mortality events have followed in recent years.

The pattern repeats at the southern end of the coast. United Nations Development Programme sampling conducted in 2019, 2022 and 2023 in the binational Sixaola watershed, shared by Costa Rica and Panama, detected a mixture of 33 pesticides contaminating the lower basin, including the Gandoca lagoon inside a protected wildlife refuge.

Thirteen of those substances were flagged as particularly concerning, either because they are classified as highly hazardous or because concentrations ran between six and 24 times the applicable international reference standard. Among them were terbufos, banned in the European Union, the United Kingdom, Canada and China, and chlorothalonil, whose use is prohibited in Costa Rica.

The mechanism is structural rather than accidental. Plantations on the Caribbean slope apply heavy volumes of active ingredient in a region that receives more than 3,000 millimeters (about 118 inches) of rain a year. That combination reliably pushes residue off the fields, through drainage canals and into the watershed.

Field research on the Río Jiménez watershed, published in Science of the Total Environment, tracked the consequence directly: the ecological quality of both riparian habitat and benthic macroinvertebrate communities deteriorated steadily from upstream reference sites down into the reaches affected by pineapple plantations, while intact riparian forest cover measurably improved those indicators.

The tourism consequences travel the length of that same chain. Rivers feed mangroves, mangroves stabilize the coastline and nurse fish populations, and healthy fish stocks support both the reef systems that draw snorkelers to Cahuita and the tarpon and snook fisheries that have anchored angling lodges at Barra del Colorado and Parismina for half a century.

Certification adds a second transmission line. Blue Flag ratings are reassessed annually against water quality and sanitation criteria, and tour operators and environmentally minded travelers screen for them, which means a downgrade functions less as a symbolic embarrassment than as a booking problem.

The economic stakes sharpen the case. The OECD’s Tourism Trends and Policies 2026 report found that direct tourism activity represented 6.3 percent of Costa Rican GDP in 2024, against an OECD average of 4.0 percent, supporting roughly 183,000 direct jobs and $5.5 billion in travel exports. The same report identified the uneven regional distribution of those benefits as a central weakness. Limón illustrates the point.

The National Institute of Statistics and Census reported in its 2025 National Household Survey that the Huetar Caribe region carries the highest poverty incidence in the country at 24.9 percent of households, and the highest extreme poverty at 8.3 percent — figures that track closely with decades of underinvestment relative to Guanacaste, which absorbed the bulk of Costa Rica’s tourism and real estate capital from the 1990s onward.

Sport and tourism fishing nationally generates an estimated $520 million a year, roughly ¢235 billion and supports around 33,000 direct and indirect jobs, according to figures from the Costa Rican Fishing Federation. That activity is concentrated on the Pacific, which is precisely the asymmetry at issue: the Caribbean’s fishing and reef assets remain comparatively undercapitalized, and water quality determines whether they can be developed at all.

That question is now live rather than theoretical. President Laura Fernández in July signed legislation clearing the way for a marina and dedicated cruise terminal in Puerto Limón, a project officials describe as a structural correction to the Pacific’s long dominance of tourism investment. Cruise passengers arriving through that terminal would head for Tortuguero’s canals, Cahuita National Park and the southern beach towns — the same coastal systems downstream of the plantation drainage.

The remedies with a track record are unglamorous. Riparian (i.e. relating to a riverbank) buffer strips already enjoy protection under Costa Rican forestry law; the gap is enforcement, since regulators in plantation zones consistently lack the staffing and laboratory resources to monitor compliance or sanction violators.

Sampling costs are one measure of that constraint: a single water sample runs around ¢120,000. Expanding wastewater treatment capacity to match Caribbean tourism growth, extending certification standards such as Rainforest Alliance beyond voluntary exporters, and funding genuine monitoring infrastructure in Limón would protect the certifications, reef health and fishing yields that determine whether the province can capture a larger share of the national tourism economy.

The same pressures are visible in the Térraba-Sierpe wetland on the Pacific side, where research traced 71 percent of detected contaminants to pineapple farming some 80 kilometers (50 miles) downstream. Anyone who witnesses pollution firsthand — discolored water, dead fish, visible runoff — can trigger a formal inspection.

Reports go to the Integrated System for Processing and Attention of Environmental Complaints, known as SITADA, at sitada.go.cr, administered by the Environmental Comptroller within the Ministry of Environment and Energy. Complaints can also be filed with the Administrative Environmental Tribunal, which has authority to investigate violations of environmental law and set damages. In either case a report is far more likely to produce an inspection if it includes a precise location, dated photographs and the time of observation.

None of this is an argument against visiting the Caribbean coast, which remains one of the most biologically rich and culturally distinct corners of Costa Rica. It is an argument that the coast’s economic future runs through its water. The reefs, the fisheries and the certifications that would let Limón compete are all downstream of the same drainage canals, and the area cannot build a premium destination on a watershed nobody is measuring.

World.title: Costa Rica Offers Panama Two-Part Plan to End Trade Block
World.content:
Costa Rica has presented Panama with a two-part proposal aimed at ending a seven-year agricultural trade dispute that has blocked meat, dairy products, fruit and other Costa Rican goods from entering the neighboring country. Foreign Trade Minister Indiana Trejos sent the proposal Wednesday to Panama’s minister of commerce and industries, Julio Moltó. The plan combines practical steps to address Panama’s export concerns with international arbitration to resolve the legal case stalled at the World Trade Organization.

The first part would establish a memorandum of understanding covering products Panama wants to export to Costa Rica. Under the proposed agreement, Costa Rica would process Panama’s export applications with the assistance of an international organization. The outside participation is intended to make the process more transparent and give Panama greater confidence that its requests will receive fair treatment.

The second part would send Panama’s appeal in the agricultural dispute to a special WTO arbitration process. Both countries would agree in advance to accept the arbitrators’ decision, providing a way around the prolonged shutdown of the WTO’s regular appeals system. The WTO Appellate Body has been unable to hear cases since December 2019 because it lacks enough appointed members. Panama appealed the ruling against its restrictions in February 2025, effectively leaving the case unresolved despite Costa Rica’s earlier victory.

The dispute began between January 2019 and June 2020, when Panama stopped allowing imports of several Costa Rican agricultural and food products. The restrictions have affected strawberries, fresh pineapples, bananas, plantains, dairy products and meat from Costa Rican cattle, pigs and poultry. Sixteen Costa Rican meat and dairy facilities lost access to the Panamanian market after their sanitary approvals were not renewed.

Panama defended the measures as necessary to protect public health, agriculture and local producers.Its concerns included pesticide residue detected in strawberry shipments, a pest associated with pineapples and the potential regional threat from a banana disease. Panama also required Costa Rican meat and dairy exporters to restart parts of the sanitary approval process.

Costa Rica argued that the restrictions were not supported by adequate scientific evidence and were more restrictive than necessary. After consultations failed, Costa Rica formally brought the case to the WTO in January 2021. A dispute panel was established later that year, although staffing shortages, the complexity of the case and translation requirements delayed the final decision.

The panel’s report was released in December 2024 and largely supported Costa Rica’s position. It found that several of Panama’s measures were not based on sufficient scientific evidence and that less restrictive alternatives were available. The panel also found that Panama had treated some Costa Rican products differently from comparable imports allowed from other countries.

The ruling recommended that Panama bring its restrictions into line with international trade rules. Panama appealed, but the inactive WTO appeals system prevented the ruling from becoming a final, enforceable resolution. The new arbitration proposal is designed to break that deadlock without requiring either government to abandon the formal trade process.

The conflict became more politically tense after President Laura Fernández took office in May. Fernández ordered Costa Rica’s foreign ministry to pursue international action over the restrictions, arguing that farmers and food producers had been harmed by years of blocked exports.

Panamanian President José Raúl Mulino responded by suspending planned electricity sales to Costa Rica and accusing the Costa Rican government of escalating the dispute publicly rather than resolving it through direct talks. The Costa Rican Electricity Institute said at the time that the country was not buying electricity from Panama and did not expect to do so during 2026.

The two governments later reopened diplomatic contact and discussed a broader agenda including trade, security, migration, customs and regional cooperation. Costa Rica’s latest proposal represents the clearest attempt so far to convert those discussions into a formal settlement.

The plan offers Panama a supervised process for its own export requests while giving Costa Rica a path toward a binding decision on the restrictions affecting its agricultural products. A settlement would reopen a nearby market for Costa Rican farmers and food companies while giving Panamanian exporters a clearer route into Costa Rica.

The proposal now depends on whether Panama accepts the two agreements or requests changes before moving forward.

World.title: Forbes Highlights Costa Rica Oxcart Painting Experience
World.content:
A hands-on workshop that allows visitors to create their own version of Costa Rica’s traditional painted oxcart designs has earned international attention as travelers increasingly look for souvenirs with a deeper connection to local culture. Forbes included the oxcart-painting experience at El Silencio Lodge & Spa in Bajos del Toro in a selection of 10 workshops around the world where visitors make their own keepsakes alongside local artists and craftspeople.

Rather than buying a mass-produced souvenir, guests learn traditional painting techniques and create a colorful wooden mandala inspired by Costa Rica’s oxcart patterns and the surrounding cloud forest. The workshop is led by Kenneth, an eco-concierge and local artist at the lodge. He guides participants through the bright geometric shapes, floral details and precise brushwork associated with one of Costa Rica’s most recognizable artistic traditions.

The completed mandala is small enough for travelers to take home and frame, providing a more practical alternative to attempting to pack an actual oxcart wheel into a suitcase. Costa Rica’s elaborately painted oxcarts began as working vehicles used to carry coffee and other agricultural products across difficult roads. By the early 20th century, owners increasingly decorated their carts with distinctive patterns, colors and symbols.

Different regions developed their own designs, allowing people to recognize where a cart came from by its painted wheels. The tradition eventually became an important expression of Costa Rican identity rather than simply a decorative addition to farm equipment. Costa Rica’s oxherding and oxcart traditions were added to UNESCO’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2008. Sarchí, northwest of San José, remains the country’s best-known center for traditional oxcart production and painting.

The Forbes recognition reflects a broader change in what many travelers expect from a vacation. Cultural workshops, cooking classes, farm visits and meetings with local artisans allow visitors to participate in traditions rather than observe them from a distance. These activities can also create income for local craftspeople and encourage hotels to preserve knowledge that could otherwise decline as younger generations move away from traditional trades.

El Silencio Lodge is in the cloud forest of Bajos del Toro, about 65 kilometers northwest of Juan Santamaría International Airport. The property offers several nature and cultural activities, including waterfall hikes, birdwatching, coffee tasting, Costa Rican cooking, tree planting and visits to nearby rural communities.

The lodge currently holds two Michelin Keys, the hotel equivalent of the restaurant guide’s Michelin Stars. The designation recognizes properties offering an exceptional stay based on their design, service, character and connection to their surroundings. Costa Rica was one of 10 destinations featured in the Forbes selection.

Other experiences included recycled-glass jewelry making in Namibia, Maasai beadwork in Kenya, basket weaving in Rwanda, volcanic-stone carving on Easter Island, Tibetan painting in China and Berber pottery in Morocco. Each workshop produces a physical object, but the larger attraction is the process behind it: spending time with a local craftsperson, learning why the tradition matters and understanding the work required to create something by hand.

For Costa Rica, the international recognition provides another example of how it can expand its tourism appeal beyond beaches, wildlife and adventure activities. Oxcart painting gives visitors a direct connection to Costa Rica’s rural and agricultural history while offering them something personal to take home. The value is not simply the painted piece, but the story of how and where it was made.

World.title: Cincinnati Open 2026 Guide: Dates, Players and What to Know
World.content:
The Cincinnati Open returns to Mason, Ohio, this August with one of the strongest combined men’s and women’s fields of the North American hard-court season. The tournament begins with public events and player practices on August 8 before qualifying starts August 11. Main-draw competition begins August 13, with the men’s and women’s singles champions scheduled to be crowned August 23.

Played at the Lindner Family Tennis Center outside Cincinnati, the tournament brings ATP and WTA competition together at the same venue. Both sides carry 1000-level status, placing Cincinnati among the most important events outside the four Grand Slam tournaments.

It also represents one of the final major tests before the US Open, giving players an opportunity to adjust to North American hard courts, earn significant ranking points and build momentum before traveling to New York.

When Does the Cincinnati Open Begin?

The 2026 Cincinnati Open officially opens with Community Weekend on August 8 and 9. The two-day program includes player practices, autograph opportunities, children’s activities, entertainment and the tournament’s inaugural 5K race. A fast-paced Red Bull BassLine exhibition is also scheduled for Saturday evening.

Fans will have another opportunity to watch open practices on Monday, August 10, before competitive matches begin. Qualifying will take place August 11 and 12. The men’s and women’s qualifying draws will each feature 48 players, with 12 men and 12 women advancing into the main tournament.

Main-draw play begins Thursday, August 13. Day sessions are scheduled to start at 11 a.m., with night sessions beginning at 7 p.m. during the early rounds. The singles finals will both be played Sunday, August 23.

Which Players Are Expected to Compete?

World No. 1 Jannik Sinner leads the men’s field and will attempt to regain the Cincinnati title he won in 2024. The Italian is joined by several of the sport’s biggest names, including Alexander Zverev, Novak Djokovic, Daniil Medvedev, Ben Shelton, Taylor Fritz, Alex de Minaur and Frances Tiafoe.

Defending champion Carlos Alcaraz will not compete. The Spaniard withdrew on August 4 as he continues to recover from a wrist injury. The withdrawal removes one of the tournament’s leading attractions, but the men’s field remains deep. Cincinnati has also awarded main-draw wild cards to Stan Wawrinka, Grigor Dimitrov, Jack Draper and Gael Monfils.

Wawrinka and Monfils are both competing in their final ATP seasons, adding another storyline to the opening rounds. Dimitrov won the Cincinnati title in 2017, while Draper has already established himself as a dangerous opponent on hard courts. The women’s tournament is led by Aryna Sabalenka, Iga Swiatek, Coco Gauff and Jessica Pegula.

Other prominent entries include Madison Keys, Elena Rybakina, Naomi Osaka, Mirra Andreeva, Linda Noskova and Jasmine Paolini.One of the tournament’s biggest attractions will come in doubles, where Serena and Venus Williams have received a wild card to compete together. It will be their first Cincinnati Open appearance as a team.

Venus Williams has also been awarded a singles wild card. Other women’s wild-card recipients include Sloane Stephens, Taylor Townsend, Caroline Dolehide and Lois Boisson. Player entries remain subject to change until the draws are finalized.

Latin American Players to Follow

The men’s field includes a sizable Latin American presence, led by Brazilian João Fonseca and Argentina’s Francisco Cerúndolo. Fonseca has quickly become one of the region’s most closely followed young players. His aggressive baseline game and growing international profile should make his matches among the most anticipated of the early rounds.

Cerúndolo arrives as Argentina’s highest-ranked entrant and one of the region’s strongest candidates to make a deep run. Argentina will also be represented by Sebastián Báez, Juan Manuel Cerúndolo, Tomás Martín Etcheverry, Mariano Navone, Román Andrés Burruchaga, Thiago Tirante and Camilo Ugo Carabelli.

Peruvian Ignacio Buse, Chilean Alejandro Tabilo and Paraguayan Adolfo Daniel Vallejo are also listed in the men’s field. On the women’s side, Colombia’s Camila Osorio will be the leading Latin American player in the main draw. Additional players from the region could join her through qualifying.

The strength of the Latin American contingent gives fans throughout the region several players to follow beyond the tournament’s established global stars.

Why Cincinnati Matters Before the US Open

The Cincinnati Open is more than another stop on the summer tennis calendar. Its position immediately before the US Open makes it an important measure of player form. The conditions in Ohio can be hot and humid, and the hard courts reward players who can control points quickly while remaining physically strong through long matches.

A strong week in Cincinnati can change expectations entering New York. It can also expose injury concerns, fatigue or tactical weaknesses at the most important stage of the season. The expanded men’s and women’s singles draws provide additional opportunities for emerging players, qualifiers and lower-ranked entrants to face the sport’s biggest names.

For established contenders, however, Cincinnati is about more than preparation. An ATP or WTA 1000 title carries considerable ranking value and is one of the most prestigious trophies available outside the Grand Slams.

A Transformed Tournament Venue

The Lindner Family Tennis Center completed a $260 million redevelopment before the 2025 tournament. The project expanded and modernized the grounds, adding new courts, improved stadiums, park-style landscaping, additional shade, upgraded fan areas and a new player clubhouse.

The transformation helped the Cincinnati Open earn both the ATP Masters 1000 and WTA 1000 Tournament of the Year awards following the 2025 event. The venue now has 31 outdoor tennis courts, giving spectators more opportunities to watch matches and practices at close range.

When Will the Draw Be Released?

The qualifying and main draws are expected closer to the beginning of competition. Once the draws are published, fans will know each player’s potential route through the tournament, possible early-round matchups and where the leading Latin American players have been placed.

The daily order of play will then determine match times and court assignments. The Tico Times will provide on-site coverage and photography from the Cincinnati Open beginning August 13, with particular attention to Latin American players, major tournament storylines and the final preparations for the US Open.

World.title: Costa Rica Protest to Defend Judiciary Amid Government Clash
World.content:
Judicial employees, university representatives and civil society groups are preparing demonstrations across Costa Rica today as the dispute between President Laura Fernández’s government and the Judiciary grows increasingly confrontational. The main gathering is scheduled to begin at 4 p.m. at Plaza de la Democracia in downtown San José.

Organizers have described the event as a peaceful demonstration in defense of judicial independence, democratic institutions and Costa Rica’s system of checks and balances. The protest is expected to continue until approximately 8 p.m. and will include speeches, cultural presentations and activities organized by unions and civic groups. Participation is open to the public.

The National Council of University Rectors (Conare), has also called on university communities and the public to participate. Its march will leave the Fuente de la Hispanidad in Montes de Oca at 3:30 p.m. before continuing toward Plaza de la Democracia. Similar gatherings have been announced outside judicial buildings in other areas of the country. Confirmed locations include Nicoya and Liberia, while calls have also circulated for demonstrations in Puntarenas, San Carlos and other judicial districts.

Eight unions and professional organizations representing judicial employees are among the groups supporting the San José protest. They include the Judicial Workers’ Union, or Sitrajud; the Public Defense Union, Sindepu; the National Association of Criminal Investigators, ANIC; and the Costa Rican Judges Association, Acojud.

The National Association of Judicial Employees, Anejud; the National Association of Judicial Professionals, Anprojud; the Association of Accounting and Finance Professionals of the Judiciary, Asprotcofi; and the National Front of Struggle, FNL, are also involved. The demonstrations follow several weeks of escalating tension over government spending cuts and a Constitutional Chamber ruling involving substitute Supreme Court justices.

The dispute intensified after the Constitutional Chamber (Sala IV), issued a ruling on July 30. In a 4-3 decision, the court overturned the Legislative Assembly’s attempt to return a list of candidates for substitute justices to the Supreme Court. The ruling also temporarily extended appointments that had expired on December 16, 2025.

The court said the temporary measure was needed to prevent disruptions in urgent cases while lawmakers complete the appointment process. Substitute justices are required when permanent members of the Constitutional Chamber cannot participate in a case because of conflicts of interest, illness or other legal restrictions.

Fernández responded by accusing part of the Judiciary of carrying out a “coup d’état” against the Legislative Assembly, which has the constitutional authority to appoint Supreme Court justices. The Constitutional Chamber rejected that characterization and said its decision fell within its legal authority to protect access to constitutional justice and prevent the court from becoming unable to handle important cases.

On August 3, Legislative Assembly President Yara Jiménez and ruling-party lawmakers filed a criminal complaint against the four justices who supported the majority decision: Fernando Cruz Castro, Paul Rueda Leal, Ingrid Hess Herrera and Jorge Araya García. Fernández, several Cabinet ministers and supporters of the governing Pueblo Soberano party accompanied the lawmakers to the Supreme Court.

The complaint accuses the justices of suspected prevaricato, a criminal offense involving a judge or public official who knowingly issues a decision contrary to the law or bases it on false facts. The judicial dispute comes alongside growing concern over spending reductions ordered by the Ministry of Finance, which is headed by former president Rodrigo Chaves. Chaves also serves as minister of the Presidency in the Fernández administration.

Judicial authorities say three government budget actions during the past two months have reduced funds available to the courts, the Public Prosecutor’s Office and the Judicial Investigation Police, known as the OIJ. The Judiciary has said one of the measures reduced its operating budget for the second half of 2026 by approximately 42%.

Officials have warned that the reductions could affect fuel, expert reports, criminal investigations, court proceedings and the execution of search warrants. Those warnings come as Costa Rica continues to confront organized crime, drug trafficking and high homicide levels. Fernández and Chaves have rejected allegations that their administration intends to close, control or dismantle the Judiciary.

Both have argued that spending reductions are required because of the government’s fiscal position and that the judicial system needs significant reforms. The government says the changes are intended to reduce spending, eliminate privileges and make the courts more efficient. Judicial leaders and protest organizers argue that the measures could weaken one of the country’s most important democratic institutions.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Route 32 Remains Closed After Overnight Landslide
World.content:
Route 32 remained closed early this morning after a landslide left material on the highway connecting San José with Limón, forcing drivers to use longer alternate routes to reach the Caribbean. The Ministry of Public Works and Transportation closed the road at 5:50 p.m. on Wednesday, August 5, because of debris on the highway and unsafe weather conditions.

As of 6:55 a.m. this morning, Costa Rica time, authorities had not announced an estimated reopening time. Crews were expected to inspect the affected area after sunrise and begin clearing the road once conditions were considered safe. Officials had not identified the exact kilometer where the material fell.

Drivers traveling between the Central Valley and Limón were advised to avoid Route 32 until an official reopening announcement is issued. The available alternate routes are:

Bajos de Chilamate–Vuelta de Kooper, which can be used by all types of vehicles.

Route 10 through Turrialba and Siquirres, which can also accommodate cars, buses and freight vehicles.

The Vara Blanca route, which is recommended only for light vehicles.

Motorists should expect longer travel times and possible congestion along the alternate roads, particularly through Turrialba and the northern route through Sarapiquí. Route 32 is Costa Rica’s main direct connection between the Central Valley and the Caribbean province of Limón. It is heavily used by residents, tourists, buses and trucks traveling to the Caribbean coast and the ports of Moín and Limón.

The mountainous section through Braulio Carrillo National Park is especially vulnerable to falling rocks, trees and landslides during periods of heavy rain. Much of the highway passes between steep slopes where saturated ground can become unstable with little warning. A recent technical assessment identified dozens of sites along the San José–Río Frío section with potential landslide risks. Areas near Zurquí were among the sections with the highest concentration of concerns.

Authorities frequently close the highway overnight or during intense rainfall as a safety measure. Reopening depends on daylight inspections, weather conditions and whether crews can remove the fallen material without further movement from the surrounding slopes. Travelers heading to Puerto Viejo, Cahuita, Tortuguero, Guápiles, Siquirres or Limón should check the latest official road conditions before departing. Drivers already using alternate routes should reduce speed and remain alert for rain, fog and debris.

World.title: Costa Rica Builds One of Central America’s Longest Four-Lane Bridges
World.content:
Construction is continuing on a 308-meter (1,010-foot) bridge that Costa Rican officials say will become one of the longest four-lane bridges in Central America. The Cañuela Bridge will cross the Cañuela River between the areas of Naranjo and San Ramón. It is the largest and most technically demanding structure included in the southern section of the long-delayed highway to San Carlos.

Crews are currently building the bridge’s foundations, which include two abutments and two central piers. The structure will rest on 94 concrete piles driven 25 meters (82 feet) into the ground. Each pile measures 1.2 meters, or nearly 4 feet, in diameter. Once completed, the bridge will carry four lanes of traffic across the steep and mountainous terrain separating Costa Rica’s Central Valley from the Northern Zone.

The bridge forms part of Punta Sur, an 8.2-kilometer (5.1-mile) section of National Route 35 running from the Bernardo Soto Highway near San Miguel de Naranjo to Sifón, in the district of Volio de San Ramón. The entirely new road will have two lanes in each direction, internal and external shoulders, central safety barriers and horizontal and vertical signs. It is being designed for traffic traveling at up to 80 kilometers per hour (50 mph).

Construction is taking place on at least eight work fronts along the route. Current work includes major earthmoving operations, drainage systems, large culverts, excavations and pile-supported retaining walls needed for bridges and viaducts. In addition to the Cañuela Bridge, crews are working on the Guarumal overpass, the San Roquillo Bridge, the Alto Palmas overpass and the Concepción de San Ramón overpass. Punta Sur will eventually contain 13 major structures, including bridges, interchanges, overpasses, underpasses and viaducts.

The project also includes wildlife crossings and design changes intended to improve the road’s ability to withstand extreme rainfall and other effects associated with a changing climate. Costa Rican construction company MECO is carrying out the work. Construction officially began in May 2025 with approximately $196 million in financing from an Inter-American Development Bank loan.

The current completion date for Punta Sur is April 2028. The section is an important piece of the wider plan to complete the highway between the Bernardo Soto Highway and the San Carlos area, a project Costa Rican governments have pursued for decades. Punta Sur will not complete that connection by itself. A separate central section must link Sifón with La Abundancia near Ciudad Quesada before drivers can use the entire new corridor between the Central Valley and the Northern Zone.

Once all sections are finished, the highway is expected to provide a faster and safer route for anyone traveling between San José, San Ramón, Ciudad Quesada and other Northern Zone communities. The government estimates that the wider road project will directly benefit more than 848,000 people and improve transportation for the agricultural, tourism and commercial sectors.

World.title: Department of Environment investigating fish kill in Belize River Valley, public urged to avoid untreated river water
World.content:
Department of Environment investigating fish kill in Belize River Valley, public urged to avoid untreated river water

By Zoila Palma: The Department of the Environment (DOE) is investigating a fish kill reported in the Belize River Valley and has issued a public advisory warning residents not to consume fish or other aquatic resources from affected areas while the investigation continues.

The Ministry of Sustainable Development, Climate Change and Solid Waste Management said the DOE received reports on August 4 of numerous dead fish floating along sections of the Belize River, prompting a multi-agency response.

According to the department, a joint assessment was launched involving Belize Water Services Limited (BWS), the Ministry of Health and Wellness, the National Emergency Management Organization (NEMO), the Fisheries Department, the Ministry of Infrastructure Development and Housing (MIDH), and other relevant agencies.

The release stated that “the Department is actively responding to the ongoing fish kill issue reported in the Belize River Valley area.”

DOE said the exercise included “water quality monitoring and sampling, as well as assessments of land-clearing activities, potential wastewater discharge sources, and other factors that may have contributed to impacts on the aquatic environment.”

As investigations continue, the DOE is advising residents to take precautionary measures.

The department warned the public “not to consume fish or other aquatic resources from the affected areas and not to drink untreated river water or use untreated river water for cooking or food preparation.” It also advised against using untreated river water for livestock or pets until further notice.

The department emphasized that the advisory applies only to untreated water taken directly from the river and does not affect the public water supply.

The release noted that “BWS has confirmed that the water currently being supplied from its Water Treatment Plant remains safe for consumption and meets the required potable water quality standards. There has been no disruption to the continuity of the water supply.”

DOE noted that technical assessments are ongoing to determine the cause of the fish kill and pledged to keep the public informed as new information becomes available.

The DOE also reminded the public that the release of untreated wastewater, or treated effluent that fails to meet environmental standards, is prohibited under Belize’s Environmental Protection Regulations and constitutes an offence.

World.title: The case for Allan Pollard, measured the way a city should measure a mayor
World.content:
The case for Allan Pollard, measured the way a city should measure a mayor

By Horace Palacio:

The People’s United Party will soon ask its Belize City delegates a single question. Who should carry its banner for mayor in 2027, Councillor Allan Pollard Jr. or Deputy Mayor Eluide Miller?

Today I am going to answer that question openly, and make the case for Pollard. But I will make it the way this column has always insisted arguments be made, on the record, with respect for both men, and by a standard bigger than either of them.

Because before we compare two candidates, remember what the prize actually is. Belize City is not a title. It is the largest, hardest job in municipal government in this country. Flooding that swallows streets. Drains that fail. Garbage that piles. Traffic that strangles. Crime that shadows whole neighborhoods. Whoever wins this convention inherits all of it. So the question for delegates is not who do you like. It is who is readiest, this March, for that load.

Measure the two men by that standard, and the case builds itself on four pillars.

Pillar one. The record. Allan Pollard has served the people of Belize City as an elected councillor for eight years, across three terms, including service as deputy mayor. Eluide Miller, a capable young man, has served two. That is not an insult to Miller. It is arithmetic. Pollard has sat through four times the budgets, four times the floods, four times the hard seasons of that council. He has already held the deputy’s chair Miller holds now, and then kept serving. The city’s problems are too old and too heavy for the top job to double as a classroom. Experience is not everything, but in a crisis city, it is not nothing either. It is the difference between learning the machine and driving it.

Pillar two. Character, tested in the dark. Here is the part of Pollard’s story that tells you more than any manifesto. In 2023, he wanted this same candidacy. The party asked him to step aside for unity’s sake. He swallowed his ambition and did it. Reports say the Prime Minister personally assured him his patience would be honored this cycle. Now, let me be precise about why this matters, because it is not the reason some think. I have written before that no seat in Belize should be awarded by turn, only by merit, and I stand by every word. Pollard does not deserve the candidacy because he waited. He deserves consideration because of what the waiting revealed. A man who can put the team above his own ambition, keep working for three more years without sulking, and return stronger, has shown you his character under the hardest test politics offers, the test of being told no. Most politicians fail that test loudly. Pollard passed it quietly. That is the temperament you want holding a city’s purse and pressure.

Pillar three. Whose hands hold him. Look carefully at the two campaign launches, because launches are confessions. Miller announced flanked by seven fellow councillors, the establishment closing ranks, with the outgoing mayor reportedly grooming him as successor. Pollard arrived with no councillors at all, just a crowd of ordinary city people, family, friends, supporters he did not have to summon. One candidacy was born in the council chamber. The other was born on the street. And a mayor, understand, does not answer to the chamber. He answers to the street. Give me the candidate the people carry over the candidate the machine crowns, every single time. It is also worth noting what Pollard said about that machine, that he wants the door open to new faces, talented people, older, younger, business people, and that whoever the delegates elect to the slate gets his full backing. That is a builder’s posture, not a boss’s.

Pillar four. The money question. There is a figure floating around this race, two hundred dollars per delegate, the whispered price of convention support. I wrote months ago that free is the most expensive thing in Belize, that every bought vote is a purchase the politician later recoups from the public. So hear what Pollard put on the record when the figure was raised. He does not pay for delegates. His relationships with them were built over years of showing up, and, in his words, that is something money cannot buy. A candidate who refuses to buy his way in owes nothing on his way up. That single stance, publicly planted, is worth more to this city than any promise on any flyer. And let me be crystal clear in fairness, no evidence before me says Miller pays for delegates, and I make no such claim. I simply issue the challenge this column must issue. Mr. Miller, plant the same flag, publicly, and let this be the first convention in memory where both camps swear off the wallet and compete on the work.

Now, the fairness Miller is owed, because this endorsement will not be built on his burial.

Eluide Miller has done something in this race that deserves genuine applause. When party heavyweights reportedly leaned on him to step aside and clear the path, he refused, and insisted the delegates decide. That is democratic spine, and it is exactly what I have preached in these pages, conventions over coronations, always. Both camps, let us be honest, have maneuvered behind the scenes in this contest, which is precisely why the convention itself is the clean answer. Miller is young, described even by neutrals in the party as energetic and creative, and if he loses this race well, his future in city politics is real. The party leader himself says both men have talent, and he is right.

But talent is the entry fee, not the verdict. The verdict comes from the standard we set at the start. Which man, this March, is readiest for the hardest municipal job in Belize?

Eight years against two. A deputy mayor’s chair already held, then exceeded. Ambition tested by sacrifice and passed. A campaign carried by the street rather than crowned by the chamber. And a public refusal to purchase what should only be earned. On the record before the delegates, that is Allan Pollard’s case, and it is a strong one.

So to the delegates who will file into that convention, I close with this. You hold a privilege thousands of city residents wish they held. Do not sell it, to anyone. Do not lend it to pressure, from anyone. Weigh the records, question both men hard, and choose the readiest hands.

Weighed that way, honestly and without malice, my case is made.

The city’s next chapter should be written by the man who spent eight years learning to hold the pen.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author, Horace Palacio, and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.

World.title: Prime Minister meets with stakeholders in sugar industry to discuss mealbug infestation
World.content:
Prime Minister meets with stakeholders in sugar industry to discuss mealbug infestation

By Zoila Palma: Today, Prime Minister John Briceno met with stakeholders in the sugar industry to discuss the mealbug infestation.

In addition, the PM also received updates on two important initiatives —CRESAP and the Building the Adaptive Capacity of Sugarcane Farmers in Northern Belize (BAC-SuF) Project.

The PM explained that financed by the Green Climate Fund and implemented by the Caribbean Community Climate Change Centre (5Cs), BAC-SuF is helping to strengthen the resilience of our sugarcane farmers and safeguard the future of this vital industry.

World.title: Cabinet Approves Amendments to Cybercrime Bill to safeguard freedom of expression
World.content:
Cabinet Approves Amendments to Cybercrime Bill to safeguard freedom of expression

By Zoila Palma: Cabinet has approved amendments to the Cybercrime Bill aimed at clarifying the scope of offences while ensuring the legislation aligns with constitutional protections for freedom of expression.

According to the Cabinet statement, the changes are intended to preserve the Government’s ability to prosecute serious forms of technology-facilitated abuse, including malicious deepfakes, online impersonation, extortion, threats, and targeted harassment.

At the same time, the amendments seek to safeguard freedom of expression, political debate, journalism, satire, and public accountability.

As part of this safeguard, the cabinet release notes that the DPP’s written consent will be required before the prosecution of an offence can occur.

This latest revision comes after concerns were raised by media organizations, civil society groups, and members of the public that earlier provisions of the Cybercrime Bill could have had unintended consequences for free speech and press freedom.

World.title: Cabinet approves US $8 million loan from Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) for efficiency of wage bill
World.content:
Cabinet approves US $8 million loan from Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) for efficiency of wage bill

By Zoila Palma: During Cabinet’s meeting on July 28th and August 4th, 2026, the Government of Belize approved entering into a loan agreement with the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) for US$8 million.

According to the cabinet release, the loan will be used to “improve the efficiency of the Central Government’s wage bill and to increase the efficacy of strategic public employment”.

The funding is expected to help improve the allocation of public resources, promote more efficient staffing across government ministries and departments, and support efforts to modernize public sector management.

The project carries a total value of US$9 million, or roughly BZ$18 million, made up of the US$8 million in IDB financing and US$1 million in local counterpart funding, and is to be implemented over a five-year disbursement period.

World.title: Cabinet approves 20.9 million dollar investment in electric buses and charging infrastructure
World.content:
Cabinet approves 20.9 million dollar investment in electric buses and charging infrastructure

By Zoila Palma: During Cabinet’s session on July 28th and August 4th, 2026, the Government of Belize approved the change of its planned investment in the National Bus Company (NBC) from “terminals to electric buses and related charging infrastructure with a value of approximately BZ$20.9 million”.

The decision will require a revised Public Transportation Investment Bill to reflect this change.

The revision will include a proposed long-term lease agreement under which the Government would lease the bus terminals to the NBC.

The move forms part of the Government’s efforts to modernize Belize’s public transportation system through the introduction of electric buses and supporting infrastructure.

World.title: Youth Shadow Mayor Begins Leadership Journey at Belize City Hall
World.content:
Youth Shadow Mayor Begins Leadership Journey at Belize City Hall

By Zoila Palma: Youth Shadow Mayor Caitlin Aragon officially began her leadership experience with the Belize City Council after being welcomed by Mayor Bernard Wagner during an introductory visit to City Hall.

As part of the visit, Aragon toured the Office of the Mayor and learned about the daily responsibilities of the Mayor’s Office and the Belize City Council’s role in serving residents and guiding the city’s development.

The initiative provides mentorship and hands-on exposure to local government, giving the Youth Shadow Mayor valuable insight into leadership and public service

World.title: Blue Teddy Bear Campaign launches teacher training to strengthen Child Protection in Belize
World.content:
Blue Teddy Bear Campaign launches teacher training to strengthen Child Protection in Belize

By Zoila Palma: The Blue Teddy Bear Campaign has launched Phase II of its national child protection initiative, expanding its efforts to equip teachers, parents, and students with the knowledge and skills needed to create safer environments for children across Belize. The new phase officially began today with teacher training sessions aimed at strengthening child safeguarding practices in schools.

The latest training brought together 22 educators from Wesley College, Excelsior High School, and Gwen Lizarraga High School. It followed an earlier session involving 60 teachers from Maud Williams High School, Anglican Cathedral College, and Sadie Vernon Technical High School. With the support of the Ministry of Education, Culture, Science and Technology, a total of 82 teachers will receive training during this phase of the campaign.

Teachers are among the most influential adults in a child’s life and often serve as the first line of defense for vulnerable children. As mandatory reporters under Belize’s child protection framework, educators play a vital role in identifying signs of abuse, taking appropriate action, and ensuring children receive the protection and support they need.

The training focuses on child protection principles, safeguarding measures, recognizing indicators of abuse, reporting obligations, and practical approaches to supporting children who may be at risk. Organizers said strengthening educators’ understanding of these areas will help ensure schools remain safe spaces where children can learn, grow, and thrive.

The Blue Teddy Bear Campaign is a partnership between the National Commission for Families and Children (NCFC), UNICEF Belize, the Ministry of Human Development, Family Support and Gender Affairs, and the Office of the Special Envoy for the Development of Families and Children. Since its launch, the campaign has promoted awareness and action to eliminate violence, abuse, and exploitation of children. Phase II builds on those efforts by focusing on adults and institutions that play a central role in children’s daily lives, reinforcing the message that protecting children is a shared national responsibility.

World.title: Card, Douglas win silver in 100m at World U20 Championships
World.content:
Jamaica's Shanoya Douglas parades with the Jamaican flag after winning the silver medal in the women's 100m on Thursday's second day of the 2026 World Athletics Under 20 championships at Hayward Field in Eugene, Oregon. Douglas, the world leader was beaten by American Maria Maxwell. (Photos: Paul Reid)

OREGON, USA — Jamaica’s Gary Card and Shanoya Douglas won silver medals in the men and women’s 100m on Thursday night at the World Athletics Under-20 Championships at Hayward Field in Eugene, Oregon.

It was the first medals for Jamaica at the championships, putting them in ninth position on the medals tables.

Americans Tate Taylor and Mia Maxwell delighted the home fans by winning the double, only the second time athletes from the same country had taken both gold medals at the same under-20 championships after Americans Noah Lyles and Candace Hill achieved the feat in 2016 in Bydgoszcz, Poland.

Card got off to a fast start but was chased and caught by Tate who passed him to win in a personal best 9.94 seconds (0.1m/s), the Jamaican second in 10.05 seconds. South Africa’s Marko Ferreira took the bronze with 10.16 seconds.

Maxwell got the edge over Douglas at the start and held off the Jamaican to the tape, running 11.14 seconds (-0.1m/s). Douglas finished second in 11.17 seconds with Italy’s Kelly Ann Maevane Doualla Edimo third in 11.27 seconds. Theianna-Lee Terrelonge was sixth in 11.37 seconds

It was the first time in 10 years an American won the women’s 100m and snapped the four-championships winning streak by the Jamaicans – Briana Williams in 2018, Tina Clayton in 2021 and 2022 and Alana Reid in 2024.

Also on Thursday, thrower Able Mills failed to record a legal throw in both the women’s discus and shot put finals that were held within two hours of each other.

Mills had thrown distances close to her lifetime bests to qualify for both finals but failed to make a legal mark in either.

Jamaica also failed to qualify any runner in the 400m finals set for Friday afternoon, all four failing to get past their semifinals.

Jabari Matheson who was running his fourth 400m race in two days, placed sixth in his semi-final in 47.29 seconds, the first time he failed to go under the 47.00 second mark at the championships.

Jason Pitter failed to get up to his high standards, and was sixth in his semi-final in 46.50 seconds after he advanced on time from the first round.

Daniellia Dixon was fifth in her semi-final in 53.77 seconds and Shameika McLean, who had run three times since the start of the championships, just failed to get into the final after placing fourth in her semis in 54.24 seconds.

-Paul A Reid

World.title: Celebrating 64!
World.content:
Thousands of Jamaicans packed the National Stadium in St Andrew on Thursday as the country marked 64 years of Independence with the signature Grand Gala event celebrated under the theme ‘United in Celebrating Resilience’. The Grand Gala, held annually by the Ministry of Culture, Gender, Entertainment, and Sport through the Jamaica Cultural Development Commission, is the grand finale of Jamaica’s Emancipation and Independence season. Portfolio minister Olivia Grange said that the event, which had more than 1,800 participants, would present Jamaica’s story, diversity, achievements, and creative power on the nation’s largest cultural stage. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

World.title: Fingers crossed for ganja
World.content:
Walter Melbourne, director of licensing and applications at the Cannabis Licensing Authority, speaking at this week’s Jamaica Observer Monday Exchange. (Photo: Joseph Wellington)

THERE is no indication when Jamaica could see its first cannabis company registered on the local stock market, but key players in the sector are hopeful it will happen soon.

As global powers equivocate with the classification of the weed, leaders at Jamaica’s Cannabis Licensing Authority (CLA) are keeping their fingers crossed that the tight hold on the plant will be relaxed to allow the medical and commercial industry to grow.

During this week’s Jamaica Observer Monday Exchange the top brass of the CLA pointed to the recent indication by the United States (US) that cannabis could be moved from a Schedule I drug to Schedule III.

That announcement earlier this year was welcomed by players in the industry; however, months later it is not clear where cannabis will sit on the US drug scheduling list as US lawmakers continue debate on the matter.

According to CLA Chief Executive Officer Farrah Blake, “rescheduling of ganja would answer a lot of questions” in relation to access to the banking system and eligibility for grants for farmers and businesses in the industry.

As it relates to Jamaica possibly seeing its first regulated marijuana company hit the stock market, chair of the CLA Dr Nadeen Spence said, “We have to keep our fingers crossed” that marijuana will in fact be reclassified to reflect a Schedule III status.

It would, she argued, “translate into something that reassures the banking sector that ganja is not as risky as it currently is”.

Although uncertainty looms over ganja’s position on the list, Walter Melbourne, director of licensing and applications at the CLA, said there nevertheless needs to be an appreciation for the progress being achieved by the entity.

“Wherever we are now, it is a metamorphosis, a giant leap. In the 1970s, if you were caught with even a small amount it was a mandatory prison sentence. Some of our prominent people in society have had trouble. There was a lot of persecution and prosecution. Where we are now is really a massive step. I am making the point to say, who knows. Let’s keep going and we might very well see it there one day,” said Melbourne.

The US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) describes Schedule I drugs as substances or chemicals with no currently accepted medical use and have a high potential for abuse, such as heroin and ecstasy.

Schedule III drugs are substances or chemicals with a moderate to low potential for physical and psychological dependence. The DEA states that drugs listed under Schedule III are considered to have less potential to be abused than Schedule I and II drugs.

The US Department of Justice has already officially reclassified cannabis as less dangerous, marking a major shift in that country’s drug policy.

Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche changed the classifications of products containing marijuana that are covered by the Food and Drug Administration or that have received a state medical marijuana licence.

They will move cannabis from a Schedule I narcotic like heroin to a Schedule III drug — on par with Tylenol with codeine.

Marijuana remains illegal at the federal level. Despite the federal ban, most US states have legalised the medical or recreational use of marijuana, and many have shops where it can be purchased legally.

World.title: Come Alive delivers!
World.content:
H.U.M.B.L.E (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

The East Lawns of King’s House became more than a venue on Saturday night. For several hours it was transformed by a sea of worshippers into a space of praise.

It was the perfect start to the month in which Jamaica celebrates its 64th year of Independence as hundreds gathered for the second staging of the Come Alive Gospel concert.

Dubbed a national call to worship, it became evident from the very first note that this was no ordinary musical showcase. It was an invitation — one that patrons answered with lifted hands, tear-filled eyes, and hearts fully surrendered to praise.

Christian worship, often confined to church walls, spilled freely across the grounds as saints gave their whole beings to the moment, proving that praise can command the same passion and intensity as any secular spectacle.

Yet, unlike the fleeting excitement of entertainment, what unfolded at King’s House was rooted in something deeper — an encounter with the divine.

The group H.U.M.B.L.E opened the main event with a spirited rendition of the Jamaican National Anthem, their harmonies echoing across the venue before they returned with a medley of old-time gospel favourites that ignited a revival spirit which lingered for the remainder of the programme.

That spirit only intensified when Petra Kaye took the stage. With a commanding voice that carried effortlessly across the lawns, the singer brought a fervency reminiscent of the “old-time religion” of generations past. Songs such as Crown Him, I Can Recommend My God, and the beloved Sovereign God Medley became more than performances. Attendees sang along with conviction, their praises rising heavenward like incense.

Johnmark Wiggan followed with a deeply personal set, sharing snippets of a testimony marked by trials that, by his own admission, should have destroyed him had it not been for the hand of God. As he delivered songs including Still Deh Yah, Because You Are Good, Run Me Dung, and Testimony, an intimate atmosphere settled over the audience. Eyes closed, hands lifted, and voices trembling with emotion, patrons appeared to journey back to defining moments in their Christian walk, as if remembering prayers answered, valleys crossed, and the faithfulness of God through every season.

The praise continued with Jermaine Edwards, whose set list included Peace In My Soul, Not Forget, Naa Bow, and Make You Smile. By the time he closed with his hit single Beautiful Day, the East Lawns had erupted into celebration.

Joy radiated from faces of attendance across the venue and, for a while, worries seemed to dissolve beneath the weight of worship.

Then came the evening’s international headliner, Michael W Smith.

Making a grand entrance, the singer’s band set the tone with a dramatic prelude before the legendary worship leader greeted the crowd.

“Jamaica, it’s so good to be here,” he said to great applause.

“We have a set list, but we might not stick to it,” he added, signalling that while plans had been made, the direction of the evening ultimately belonged to God.

Without hesitation, Smith launched into crowd favourites Open The Eyes of My Heart and Draw Me Close To You. The response was immediate. Worshippers surrendered themselves to the music.

Pausing between songs, Smith reflected on the immeasurable love of God; a love, he reminded the audience, that surpasses human understanding despite the Creator’s infinite power. He then transitioned into

Arms Around the Sun, a moving reminder of God’s unwavering affection for humanity.

Reflecting on his time in Jamaica, the singer shared that beyond the island’s beauty, it was the warmth and spirit of its people that had touched him most.

“Honestly, I love the people. I love your country, and I bless your country with all the promises of God,” he said before delivering favourites such as The Air I Breathe, Lord, I Give You My Heart, Above All, and There Is None Like You.

“Here is my prayer for Jamaica — at least one of them,” he said before leading the audience into

Let It Rain.

His set also included stirring renditions of Waymaker, Agnus Dei (Worthy Is The Lamb), Goodness of God, and Awesome God.

Had the curtains closed at that very moment, patrons would likely have left fulfilled, their faces glowing from an evening already overflowing with worship. But Come Alive still had one final offering.

Papa San emerged to deafening cheers, lifting the energy to even greater heights.

From the opening notes of Glory God, the veteran deejay had the audience captivated.

Songs like Hell Bruk Loose and Step Pan Di Enemy transformed the East Lawns into a grand dance floor as patrons abandoned their seats, dancing and rejoicing with uninhibited praise.

“I haven’t been here in a while ennu, so mek we go down memory lane likkle bit,” he told the crowd before launching into a nostalgic rendition of

Pop Style.

But amid the excitement, his message remained clear: “Worship should be a part of your life. Sing about what Jesus did for you,” he encouraged before performing Smile Again, a testimony of redemption and restoration.

Long after the final song faded, the message of the evening remained.

According to Eric Hosin, chairman of the Come Alive Collective, the success of the event was possible only because of God’s grace.

“We’re happy and giving God thanks and all the praises because this was only because of his goodness and his mercy,” he told the Jamaica Observer.

“People seemed to have enjoyed themselves. Papa San closing was just something else, and we’re giving God thanks. We saw worship taking place with Michael W Smith, Jermaine Edwards, Johnmark Wiggan, Petra Kaye, and H.U.M.B.L.E, who started out with that lovely rendition of the national anthem. It was an amazing night.”

He added: “It was a national call to worship. We answered a call from the Lord, where He said He was seeking true worshippers. Persons even came with their tambourines for worship and we thank the Lord.”

World.title: FLOW’S US$25-M REBUILD
World.content:
Flow Jamaica has spent more than US$25 million on the Hurricane Melissa rebuild efforts. .

FLOW Jamaica has spent more than US$25 million ($3.90 billion) restoring its network after Hurricane Melissa, including US$12 million ($1.87 billion) during the second quarter as it continued reconnecting fixed-line customers in western Jamaica.

Balan Nair, chief executive officer of Liberty Latin America Limited (LILA), disclosed the expenditure during the company’s earnings call on Thursday, while discussing recovery work in Jamaica.

“The actual business operations itself is improving, and we are getting very close to getting back to full strength. As a matter of fact, our mobile business has improved coming out of this, and our market share has improved coming out of this. Our ARPU (average revenue per user) has improved coming out of this,” Nair said of the recovery effort.

Liberty’s Caribbean segment added 11,000 postpaid subscribers during the second quarter ended June 30, with 6,000 subscribers coming from the Jamaican market. Revenue from Jamaica was down US$3.1 million or three per cent to US$101.6 million ($15.86 billion) for the second quarter. Liberty’s quarterly filing with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission noted that Hurricane Melissa had a negative impact of US$8 million on revenue.

“We continue to see negative headwinds from Hurricane Melissa in Jamaica, the effect is clearly diminishing,” Nair said.

However, the recovery in Jamaica continues to be impacted by the pace of infrastructure restoration in western Jamaica. LILA noted that approximately 38,000 RGUs (revenue generating units) in the Jamaican market remained offline at the end of the quarter. This comprised 19,000 broadband internet units, 15,000 fixed-line telephony and 4,000 video subscribers.

“I think there are some homes that we will not rebuild back to, and it’s just gone. For the most part, we think we can get back to a pretty high level of penetration,” Nair noted as the company brought 48,000 RGUs back online during the first six months of 2026.

Liberty’s Jamaican operation, led by Flow Jamaica, reported a US$5.2 million or two per cent reduction in six-month revenue to US$204.8 million.

The hurricane had a US$20 million negative impact to Liberty’s revenue and a US$22 million impact on its operating income before depreciation and amortisation.

Nair credited the recovery trajectory to the work of the company’s teams in Jamaica and Miami, including the managers overseeing its Jamaica operations.

Despite the headwinds it experienced from Hurricane Melissa, Flow Jamaica continues to expand its offerings to the Jamaican market. Flow launched the 5G network on June 11 providing coverage to approximately 70 per cent of Jamaica’s population. This service is available to residential and enterprise postpaid subscribers.

Flow also launched the ‘Unbeatable’ Network campaign as it pushes fixed mobile convergence which bundles fixed and mobile services. The fixed broadband service is backed by the ability to switch from home Wi-Fi to the mobile network during power outages. Mobile connectivity is, in turn, supported by satellite through Flow’s Starlink DTC partnership.

“The Unbeatable campaign is now live in Jamaica and Cayman and coming soon to other Liberty Caribbean markets, as well as being deployed across the broader LLA group. In the Caribbean, it encompasses the unique concept of an always-on network, both in fixed and mobile,” Nair said during his presentation.

The Category 5 hurricane and the recent El Niño phenomenon prompted analyst Matthew Harrigan to ask about the availability of parametric insurance in the Caribbean.

LILA Chief Financial Officer Chris Noyes said the company had parametric insurance coverage for the hurricane season.

Parametric insurance has helped Jamaica rebuild and recover from the last two major hurricanes, with a US$81-million payment from weather derivatives received in 2025.

“I think we are one of the key global issuers of the parametric. We were able to do it even with the event we had in Jamaica, with a very cost-effective cover similar to prior years,” Noyes told Harrigan.

Nair said the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) website has become a permanent monitoring tool for his team since July.

He added that LILA’s leadership team would visit NOAA’s headquarters in Boulder, Colorado, to meet climatologists and hurricane experts.

LILA’s consolidated revenue increased one per cent to US$1.10 billion for the second quarter, US$10 million above analysts’ estimates.

Due to lower impairment and restructuring charges, LILA reported an operating profit of US$181.2 million compared to an operating loss of US$333 million. LILA’s adjusted OIBDA grew five per cent to US$436 million.

With a 34 per cent reduction in non-operating expenses to US$157.2 million, LILA reported a profit before tax of US$24 million versus a loss before tax of US$570.8 million.

However, higher taxes resulted in LILA reporting a consolidated net loss of US$10.6 million, with a US$24-million loss attributable to shareholders.

LILA’s consolidated revenue for the six-month period edged up to US$2.19 billion, while the company reported an operating profit of US$326.4 million, compared with an operating loss of US$204.9 million.

The net loss attributable to shareholders improved to US$46.7 million from US$559.7 million.

LILA’s asset base stood at US$12.23 billion, including US$3.78 billion in property and equipment and US$714.1 million in cash. Total liabilities stood at US$11.23 billion, while equity attributable to shareholders was US$528.1 million.

LILA’s Class C shares traded at US$8.54 on Thursday, while its Class A shares traded at US$8.66. The company has repurchased US$60 million of its common shares and has US$140 million remaining under its share-repurchase programme.

“As we look to [the] rest of 2026, we intend to build upon our H1 operational progress and lap the October 2025 Jamaica hurricane, all of which should set us up for a strong fourth quarter and positive momentum leading into 2027,” Nair said.

World.title: Ready to strike
World.content:
Marria Crossfield (left) competes in the first round of the women’s 400m hurdles on Thursday’s second day of the World Athletics Under 20 Championships at Hayward Field in Eugene, Oregon. She ran a personal best 58.22 seconds to qualify for the semi-final. Emily Montaño of Colombia completed the race in 1.01.43. (Photo: Paul Reid)

OREGON, USA ­— Jamaica’s Marria Crossfield and Shevaughn Thomas both ran personal best times to qualify for Saturday’s semi-finals in the women’s 400m hurdles in Thursday’s first round at the World Athletics Under-20 Championships at Hayward Field, Eugene, Oregon.

Both women and Jahvanie Tyrell and Robert Miller in the men’s event all made progress while the mixed 4x100m relay team also advanced to today’s first ever final in the event that was added this year.

Meanwhile, today Gary Card and Shanoya Douglas will start their 200m qualification, while the first two rounds of the sprint hurdles for men and women will also be contested.

Joel Morgan and Kevongaye Fowler will contest the semi-finals of the men’s and women’s 800m, respectively.

Yesterday, Crossfield, who was fourth in her first-round heat in 58.22 seconds, was lowering her lifetime best for the 10th time this season, after starting the year with a 1:01.59 time at the Youngster Goldsmith meet at the National Stadium on the first weekend of February.

She lowered the 58.59 seconds time she ran at the Jamaica Athletics Administrative National Junior Championships in June to get into the semis.

Thomas was second in her semi-final heat in 58.36 seconds, lowering the 58.41 seconds she had run last year at the Carifta Games.

Tyrell was a surprise winner in his first-round heat, getting off to a fast start, and clocked 51.02 seconds, while Miller was second in his heat in 51.27 seconds.

The mixed 4x100m of Justin Stewart, Natrece East, Detarje Morgan and Renecia Edwards established a new national Under-20 of 42.08 seconds finishing third in their semi-final race.

Morgan told the Jamaica Observer they were pleased to be part of Jamaica’s track and field history, being the first to contest the event.

“It’s an extraordinary feeling. Jamaica have a great legacy, and we continue to fulfil that during our time running for Jamaica in Under-20s,” Morgan said. “We furthermore will be representing Jamaica sooner or later in the senior level so this is a good start for us.”

For the final he admitted they would have some work to do to get on the podium as they were sixth-best on the day. “We just have to fix it going into the finals and hope for a medal that we can take back home,” he said.

Also today, Sashana Johnson will accompany Shanoya Douglas in the first round of the women’s 200m, while Nathaniel Martin joins Card in the first round of the men’s race.

Tianna Marshall and Akeelah Bell are down to contest the 100m hurdles, while Marquies Page and Taj-Oneil Gordon will run in the 110m hurdles.

World.title: Geely EX5: New EV horizons
World.content:
The Geely EX5 brings some never-yet-seen features to the market. (Photo: Rory Daley)

The electric vehicle (EV) market has blossomed into maturity, with a wide range of options to suit the needs of the masses. With that variety comes competition, and then the need to stand out from the crowd. The Geely EX5 embraces its electric architecture to bring a brand new sense of what is considered premium to the everyday SUV.

EXTERIOR

Like most modern SUVs, the EX5 doesn’t try to reinvent the wheel. This is a very conservative end of the automotive market, and anything too outlandish may scare prospects. LED lighting all around, check. Flush door handles, check. Aero-efficient wheels, check. Black plastic trim over the wheel arches, all there. The EX5 has the EV and SUV design cues to ensure a visual connection to what the buyers expect these days.

That said, the EX5 is a clean modern design, as dictated by its all-electric needs. There’s a hint of sci-fi to it, as if someone ran a current SUV through a time machine — this time forward, not retro.

INTERIOR

This is where things get interesting. Without a traditional internal combustion engine layout, EVs are able to take full advantage of this relatively free engineering direction. For the EX5, it’s space. The Geely feels expansive inside as it maximises the area between its wheelbase for occupant comfort, storage, and features. This can be best experienced in the passenger seat, which can be electronically folded near flat for total relaxation. Just a button press will stretch the lower section of the passenger seat to that of lounge chair proportions. And if that isn’t enough for the passenger prince or princess, then the headrest can be removed to fold completely flat against the base of the rear seat, extending the first-class experience. Look up into the panoramic sunroof and things approach heavenly. At night, standard ambient lighting retains the relaxed vibe of the EX5.

For the rest of the cabin, fit and finish, plus material quality is up to par as soft-touch materials cover every contact surface. The convenience technology is abundant. Most major functions are automatic or powered, accessed from the 15.4-inch touchscreen running Geely’s Flyme Auto infotainment system, or via the voice assistant. Interior noise is low, allowing the 12-speaker surround system to reach its full potential. Wireless charging and smartphone connectivity add even more functionality to the EX5.

Families will appreciate the number of storage solutions and their size.

ON THE ROAD

The front wheels of the EX5 are motivated by a single 215bhp electric motor fed by a 60.22kWh battery. Torque is rated at 236lb/ft. It can fast-charge up to 160kWh. It can be fully charged from 10 per cent using AC power in just over six hours, whereas DC fast-charging can restore up to 80 per cent of the battery in 20 minutes. Maximum range is 267 miles. The Geely EX5 delivers its power in a very linear fashion, rather than outright speed. This makes it handle the urban slog with ease, never really upsetting occupants, but having that instant torque to exploit holes in the city traffic.

From the 10.2-inch instrument cluster, drivers have a plethora of driving assist systems that ease vehicle operation and aid in safety. The suspension matches the overall theme of the vehicle — comfort, absorbing road imperfections without transferring them to passengers. This also helps on longer journeys that may take the EX5 on to the less than perfect country roads.

VERDICT

The Geely EX5 is aimed directly at the family looking for an EV SUV as it’s bursting at the frame with the essentials buyers in this segment are looking for — space, technology, and safety, further adding premium features not usually found in many class rivals, including the unique first-class front seating arrangement. That said, comfort and ease of use are the primary characteristics of the EX5, with enough range to eliminate operational anxiety.

World.title: Market Bag: ‘Auntie Bev’ shares old-time market wisdom as prices fluctuate
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — As Jamaica celebrates Independence Day, this week’s episode of Market Bag takes a nostalgic trip through Coronation Market, where veteran shopper Beverley Thomas Edwards shares decades of experience and the tricks and trades she uses to get the best value for her money.

From choosing produce with brighter colours and firmer textures to selecting clean, quality items, “Auntie Bev” shares tips on comparing prices and shopping wisely to make the most of every dollar.

Meanwhile, prices at Coronation Market continue to fluctuate, with sweet peppers selling for $400 per pound; ginger at $450 per pound; onions at $200 per pound; tomatoes at $200 per pound; Scotch bonnet peppers at $400 per pound; lettuce at $600 per pound; carrots at $300 per pound; and yam at $500 per pound.

Ripe bananas remain one of the more expensive commodities at the market, selling for $1,000 per hand, while plantains are priced at $900 for three.

In the latest feature, Auntie Bev and host Carlysia Ramdeen explore how market culture has evolved over the years, from informal setups of the past to the more organised stalls shoppers see today.
