World.title: Musk says French Greens’ presidential candidate should be ‘shut down’
World.content:
“I’d rather be accused of defending democracy than of trying to buy it.”

Musk, who is a former adviser to U.S. President Donald Trump, has regularly weighed in on European politics and thrown his support behind far-right candidates and parties — and France is no exception.

In July, Musk said far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen was “France’s last hope,” but her National Rally party was quick to downplay his backing to avoid being associated with the controversial owner of Tesla and SpaceX.

Hard-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon also slammed Musk’s attacks against Tondelier on Thursday, before accusing the French government of not doing enough to fight foreign interference.

“The French presidential election is an open bar for all the manipulators in the world,” he wrote — a criticism Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot promptly rejected.

Earlier this week, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the government was boosting efforts to detect and punish foreign interference in the upcoming 2027 election, while presidential candidates Gabriel Attal and Édouard Philippe, as well as likely candidate Raphaël Glucksmann shared they had been victims of Russian disinformation campaigns.

World.title: L’Europe veut sortir de sa dépendance à Palantir
World.content:
"Soyons honnêtes, le produit de Palantir est très bon et addictif, c’est un peu comme le sucre dans le Coca", reconnaît le député MoDem Philippe Latombe, défenseur français de la souveraineté numérique. "Palantir est capable de traiter d’énormes quantités de données avec une grande précision et, grâce à son expérience, l’entreprise a eu le temps d’améliorer ses algorithmes auprès de nombreux clients et de les adapter à de nombreux cas d’utilisation."

Pourtant, la volonté de se libérer de Palantir gagne tout le continent : de Madrid, où le gouvernement de Pedro Sánchez a ordonné aux entreprises publiques d’exclure Palantir des futurs marchés publics, jusqu’aux services de renseignement intérieurs français (DGSI), qui ont préféré l’entreprise française ChapsVision à Palantir. Au Royaume-Uni, le prochain test pourrait avoir lieu en février 2027, lorsque le nouveau gouvernement travailliste d’Andy Burnham devra décider s’il met fin au contrat de 330 millions de livres sterling conclu avec Palantir pour la plateforme fédérée de données de la Sécurité sociale (NHS).

La décision prise le mois dernier par les services de renseignement français et allemands d’opter pour ChapsVision a porté un double coup dur à la direction de Palantir. Le PDG du géant américain, Alex Karp, est toutefois resté sûr de lui après ce revirement soudain, affirmant qu’il ne s’inquiétait pas de la concurrence européenne. "Nous avons un exemple de ce qui ne fonctionne pas", a-t-il ironisé la semaine dernière sur Fox Business. "Ça s'appelle l'Europe."

Alex Karp, PDG de Palantir, est l'invité de l'émission « The Claman Countdown » aux studios de Fox Business Network. | John Lamparski/Getty Images

Olivier Dellenbach, fondateur et PDG de ChapsVision, concède à POLITICO que son entreprise avait tiré profit de ce qu’il qualifie de "rejet viscéral de Palantir" en Europe.

Il refuse toutefois que ChapsVision soit réduit à une simple alternative anti-Palantir. La souveraineté numérique, affirme-t-il, restera une formule creuse si les gouvernements ne la transforment pas en politique industrielle. "Il faut plus de commandes publiques", estime Olivier Dellenbach.

La Belgique, l'Allemagne, le Luxembourg, la Roumanie, les Pays-Bas et le Canada ont déjà manifesté leur intérêt pour le système d'IA "Artemis" de l'armée française, selon Patrick Moreau, l'un des architectes de cette solution développée par l'entreprise française d'aérospatiale et de défense Thales.

World.title: France will test crisis response with 2027 blackout drill
World.content:
Its purpose will be to determine how the country would respond to a paralyzing electricity outage of the kind that hit Spain and Portugal in April 2025, or a major cyberattack targeting the power grid as Poland experienced last year — an act of sabotage Brussels has attributed to Russian intelligence services.

The simulation will test “the country's ability to respond," said one person familiar with preparations for the exercise, adding that it is intended to assess the time needed to restore power and the country’s ability to ensure the continuity of essential services.

The exercise was formally confirmed during an interministerial committee on national resilience on July 8. A detailed announcement should come before the end of the year.

The meeting notes outline other priorities, such as making sure the French state maintains access to goods considered "essential to ensuring the continuity of the state and the protection of the population."

These include “emergency blankets, generators, medicines, telecommunications equipment, equipment for law enforcement, as well as rare and critical raw materials.”

Stress test

Crisis preparedness has turned into a political issue in France as record-breaking heat and wildfires are forcing the country to reckon with its ability to respond to emergencies.

World.title: 31 days of solitude: Welcome to Brussels in August
World.content:
Older readers may remember when in 2017 — back when the EU was entirely in black and white — then-European Parliament President Antonio Tajani wrote to Commission chief Jean-Claude Juncker to point out that the Parliament was taking its summer break, and that no work should be sent over before early September. Tajani’s note was dated July 13.

A note from our Irony Department: This column is off next week as I’m on vacation. Although, as Tuscany is out of my price range, I’ll be vacationing at the Schuman roundabout instead.

But if major events happening while you’re on a beach or halfway up an Alp is a bad look, the alternative — working all through the summer just in case something happens — isn’t much better.

In the hot summer of 2009, when Tajani — yes, him again — was merely the European transport commissioner, he drew the short straw of running the good ship Berlaymont while the other commissioners took a break. He then used the time to remind Europeans not to lose their luggage, describing the “phenomenon” of lost luggage as “very important” and “extremely worrying.” Tajani, of course, was a close ally of the late Italian leader Silvio Berlusconi, who had an awful lot of baggage (maybe even 10,000 suitcases full a day).

The summer before Tajani’s plea to keep a closer eye on your suitcases, the EU had launched a bloc-wide labeling scheme for sunscreen. Günter Verheugen, the commissioner for industry at the time, called the scheme an example of “responsible business behavior.” And Verheugen had perhaps more of a need for sunscreen than most, as in 2006, photographs had emerged of him relaxing on a nudist beach in Lithuania wearing nothing but a baseball cap — oh, and he was with his chief of staff.

World.title: Germany’s hot topic this summer: A chancellor swap
World.content:
Ahead of crucial regional elections in September — in which the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has a realistic chance of taking power in a German state for the first time — there is increasingly open discussion of a Kanzlertausch, or chancellor swap, in the fall.

Public criticism has mainly come from those ousted from government in the reshuffle. But behind the scenes, a growing number of politicians from Merz’s center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) are discussing what would, by German standards, be a remarkable scenario: replacing the leader after little more than a year in the job.

Europe’s biggest economy has long been one of its most stable democracies, with no history of rattling through leaders like postwar Italy or post-Brexit Britain.

But the expected success of the AfD, in elections in which the CDU is expected to lose ground, is upending the country’s conventional political dynamics.

The theory behind a Kanzlertausch is that the conservatives will need to stem the fallout from the eastern elections and give themselves a boost by replacing a leader unable to shake his rock-bottom ratings.

But the stakes are high. The AfD — now the most popular party in national polls — would seek to capitalize on further coalition unrest. Replacing a chancellor years before the end of his term would mean venturing into largely uncharted political territory.

World.title: UK Labour membership plummeted under Keir Starmer
World.content:
Starmer faced a tricky 2025 after winning a landslide victory the previous year, which brought the center-left party back into power after 14 years.

He was forced into a series of policy U-turns by his party, and sacked Peter Mandelson as U.K. ambassador to the U.S. after fresh details on the closeness of his friendship with convicted sex-trafficker Jeffrey Epstein emerged.

Membership swelled under Starmer’s predecessor Jeremy Corbyn, with the party recording more than half a million Labour members at the peak of his popularity.

But under Starmer and his Chancellor Rachel Reeves, the party moved rightwards economically and on issues such as immigration and benefit payments, and expelled left-leaning party stalwarts such as Corbyn and Diane Abbott.

Such changes put the leadership at odds with its members, sections of whom are notably more left wing than the British public at large. The removal of the whip from several Labour MPs for voting against government welfare policies in 2024, and again in 2025, were watershed moments.

In 2023, Starmer told members: “If you don’t like the changes that we’ve made, I say the door is open, and you can leave.”

World.title: Spain gives Italy two days to lift border checks on Spanish travellers after Ceuta migrant rush
World.content:
The Spanish government has issued an ultimatum to Italy, demanding that it lift border controls imposed on travellers coming from Spain by Sunday, arguing that the measure is "unjust, contrary to the interests of the European Union and discriminatory towards the Spanish population."

 

If the measures remain in place, the administration of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez warned that it will adopt "proportionate measures" to defend the interests of Spanish citizens, but gave no details about what those measures might be.

In a statement released on Friday, the Spanish government argues that the decision taken by Rome on 1 August "is based on spurious arguments incompatible with the Schengen Borders Code and with the facts."

Italy justified the temporary reintroduction of checks after the mass arrival of migrants in Ceuta, although the inspections mainly affect air and sea traffic between the two countries.

Migrants who crossed from Morocco into Spain line up for food distribution on a beach in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, 3 August, 2026 AP Photo

The Spanish government points out that none of the migrants who entered Ceuta irregularly last week were allowed to move freely within the Schengen area, as the autonomous city has a special status.

It also stressed that the vast majority have already returned to Morocco and rejected the idea that this migrant crisis poses any risk to the other EU member states.

Spain also noted that, according to Frontex data, Italy has recorded in recent years the highest number of irregular crossings of the European Union's external borders, in some periods double Spain's figures.

It also criticised the Italian government for breaching the Dublin Regulation since 2022, shifting greater migratory pressure onto the rest of its European partners.

The government further underlined that Spain never responded with border controls despite that situation and recalled that it showed solidarity with Italy by taking in some of the migrants who arrived in Lampedusa in 2023 and by repeatedly opening its ports to people rescued on the Central Mediterranean route.

The government expressed confidence that "commitment to the European project, common sense and good faith" will prevail and accuses the Italian government of stoking "divisions and pointless conflicts driven by domestic electoral motives."

World.title: Scientists create first AI-designed viruses to fight drug-resistant superbugs
World.content:
Scientists are using a new form of generative artificial intelligence to design specialised viruses that can hunt and kill harmful bacteria. This breakthrough could lead to a new generation of antibiotics designed to defeat drug-resistant "superbugs".

 

Using the AI model Evo 2, which can create new DNA, scientists at Stanford University created a series of viruses known as bacteriophages – microorganisms able to kill bacteria.

In lab tests, a mixture of 16 “exceptionally good” viruses designed by Evo 2 was able to rapidly kill E. coli bacteria that were already immune to natural phages.

E.coli is a group of bacteria that can cause gut infections and is increasingly resistant to available antibiotics.

Antibiotic resistance is rising worldwide, driven mainly by the mis- and overuse of these kinds of antibiotics, which cause bacteria to develop ways to survive them, making current medicines useless.

“If the bacteria gain resistance to a single phage, it’s game over for the medication,” said Brian Hie, chemical engineer at Stanford and co-author of the study.

“But if you have multiple genetically distinct phages in a mixture, it would be harder for the bacteria to develop resistance to the entire cocktail.”

The researchers noted that this technology could be used in the future to target other harmful bacteria, such as those that cause tuberculosis, or a common hospital-acquired infection (MRSA).

Model available for everyone

The researchers have made the Evo 2 AI model openly and freely available for everyone to download and use, which has raised safety concerns.

The study authors acknowledged that making the tool open source has raised discussions about safety and that one primary concern is that "bad actors" could potentially use modified versions of the tool to design harmful biological agents.

“As the authors highlight, this raises some serious regulatory and safety concerns, to say the very least,” said Simon Clarke, associate professor in cellular microbiology at the University of Reading in the United Kingdom, who did not participate in the study.

“While work of this nature is normally tightly regulated, it is reassuring that these scientists have shown further restraint in providing important guardrails, but there is no guarantee that every other scientist attempting to do something similar will be so careful,” he added.

He argued that naturally occurring pathogens currently pose a greater risk than AI-designed ones, as they are already easier to access and produce than to create new ones from scratch.

According to the authors, an advantage of AI-designed biology over natural evolution is the ability to build safety checks directly into the process.

The future of biology AI models

The model, Evo 2, was trained on millions of natural genomes from all across the world, allowing it to learn the complex "grammar" and rules that make a DNA sequence functional.

As with other biology AI models, this dataset includes biological data such as genetic sequences and pathogen characteristics.

Currently, no universal framework regulates these datasets, and while some developers voluntarily exclude high-risk data, researchers argue that clear and consistent rules should apply to all.

In February 2025, Evo 2’s team announced that they had excluded pathogens infecting humans and other complex organisms from their datasets due to ethical and safety risks, and to “preempt the use of Evo for the development of bioweapons”.

Earlier this year, more than 100 researchers across the world wrote an open letter arguing that while open access to scientific data has accelerated discovery, a small subset of new biological data poses biosecurity risks if misused.

“The stakes of biological data governance are high, as AI models could help create severe biological threats,” the authors wrote.

The researchers said that striking the right balance between openness and necessary security restrictions on high-risk data will be essential as AI systems become more powerful and widely available.

World.title: 'Disney need to sue': White House blasted over Spider-Man ICE campaign post
World.content:
The White House has made an enemy out of Marvel fans.

 

A recent post on its official Instagram account sees Spider-Man imagery being used as part of media campaign to promote Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Accompanied by the caption "Your friendly neighbourhood ICE agents", the four-part post shows Spider-Man firing a web which ends up in the final image, showing a group of men caught in the web.

The final caption reads: "Criminal illegal aliens will be caught and deported."

This sort of thing is not usual for Donald Trump and his administration, who love to co-opt popular culture, specifically movies, as part of his “memetic warfare”.

Several cultural touchstones used by Trump on Truth Social or the White House have included Superman, Hannibal Lecter and Jedis, and the references have backfired every time – not only by sparking the ire of the original creators and fans, but also for how these hijacked cultural winks displaya lack of appreciation or understanding when it comes to the references themselves.

This Spider-Man post clearly shows that the White House couldn't resist the cultural moment the latest Spidey film is having, with Spider-Man: Brand New Day smashing all box office records and becoming the second fastest film in history to cross the $1 billion box office milestone.

However, the desperate attempt to be a part of the cultural moment has massively backfired...

The controversial Spider-Man post - Parts 1 & 2 White House Instagram screenshot

The post has sparked controversy online, with people calling for the account to take the post down and Marvel fans outraged that their favourite hero has been used to promote ICE.

Many are calling for Marvel and Sony to sue, with fans rallying behind comments like "This is the worse misrepresentation of Spider-Man to the highest order. Marvel/Sony need to get off their damn knees and take legal action immediately.”

The comments section for the White House post includes: "Stan Lee would never approve"; "I am so ashamed of this administration"; and "Our government is a freaking joke posting unprofessional things like this".

One post added "spiderman would NEVER", while another user stated: “Coming from the official communications arm of the United States government, this is embarrassing.”

"It would be the opposite actually. Spider-Man would take down ICE and that shit fascist president in one night," another chimed in.

The controversial Spider-Man posts Parts 3 & 4 White House Instagram screenshot

Today's post follows several high-profile artists who have previously condemned the White House for using their music in ICE or military videos.

The likes of Ariana Grande, Olivia Rodrigo, Sabrina Carpenter, SZA and Katy Perry have all slammed the use of their songs to promote Trump’s controversial political agenda.

Perry recently added her name to the long list of musicians who have called out the Trump administration for unauthorised use of their songs.

She took to X last month to express her anger at a video showing footage of military strikes, writing: "I am deeply appalled and angry to see 'Firework' used on the @WhiteHouse TikTok account as a backing track for video footage of military strikes. I did not approve this, I was not asked, and I absolutely do not condone it."

She added: "I wrote this song to be an anthem of hope, healing, and inner strength for people going through their darkest personal moments. To see a message of self-worth and upliftment weaponized to soundtrack destruction and violence is a complete violation of everything my song stands for. My music is for bringing people together, not celebrating warfare."

World.title: Forget the ferry: Hop aboard a high-speed sailing boat from England to France this September
World.content:
The English Channel is one of the busiest stretches of water in the world, and one of the most carbon-heavy. But one company is pioneering passenger ferry crossings between the UK and France that are much kinder on the environment – powered almost exclusively by wind.

 

SailLink currently runs one sail-powered ferry between Dover and Boulogne-sur-Mer. Now, it is launching a one-week pilot route between Shoreham-by-Sea in West Sussex and Fécamp in Normandy. If the trial crossings go well, a permanent second route could follow.

The crossing is a far cry from the usual car ferry services. Instead of duty-free shops and soulless cabins, passengers can sit on deck feeling the wind and salt spray with views of the White Cliffs of Dover. Here’s how to book your experience on board.

A greener ferry link across the Channel

SailLink’s vessel is an 18-metre sailing catamaran skippered by Michel Desjoyeaux, a two-time winner of the Vendée Globe, one of sailing's toughest solo races, with SailLink's founder, Andrew Simons, alongside him.

The catamaran is built from recycled ocean-racing parts, including the mast and rudders from Desjoyeaux's former IMOCA 60 race boat.

The catamaran has the capacity for up to 12 passengers and eight bikes per sailing. Toby Savage

It’s purpose-made for speed, with a 23-metre mast and 165 square metres of sail, while its cockpit is spacious enough to comfortably carry foot passengers.

Last year, SailLink, which is self-funded, carried 465 passengers and 135 bikes across the Dover-Boulogne route. Nearly 70% of those crossings were completed by sail alone, with the engines kicking in only when the wind drops or in harbours.

How to book your space on board

The trial crossings link Shoreham-by-Sea and Fécamp, two town centre marinas as opposed to big ferry terminals. They will run from 8-13 September 2026, with crossings alternating direction.

The catamaran has the capacity for up to 12 passengers and eight bikes per sailing.

Cycling tourists are particularly encouraged as the route connects directly to the National Cycle Route 2 and the Downs Link path in England and La Vélomaritime (EuroVelo 4) and the GR21 coastal path along the Alabaster Coast in France.

While the timetable is still to be finalised, the crossing time will be roughly eight hours, weather permitting, and passport control is handled dockside at both ports.

Fares are £220 (€256) one-way and £440 (€513) return. It will cost £10 (€12) to bring a bike. Tickets can be purchased from the SailLink website.

World.title: EU sanctions five people linked to Russia’s military industry after Ukraine strikes
World.content:
The European Union has imposed sanctions on five individuals involved in Russia’s military-industrial complex following recent Russian air strikes on Ukraine, the bloc’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Friday.

 

“Each new attack on Ukraine is another reason for Europe to tighten the screws on Russia,” Kallas wrote on X.

The new sanctions were adopted on 7 August in response to the strikes, Kallas said, but she did not identify the individuals targeted or provide further details about the measures.

Kallas said Moscow was escalating its attacks on civilians as Russian forces remained stalled on the battlefield.

“With its army stalled on the battlefield, Moscow is further escalating its campaign of terror against civilians,” she said. “The EU must continue to intensify pressure on Russia until Moscow ends its war.”

The five listings come just over two weeks after EU governments adopted the bloc’s 21st sanctions package against Russia.

Approved on 23 July, the package added 48 individuals and 170 entities to the EU sanctions list, the largest round of listings since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The measures target Russia’s financial, energy and military-industrial sectors, as well as cryptocurrency networks, the shadow fleet used to circumvent oil restrictions and companies involved in supplying Moscow’s war economy.

The package includes 56 listings targeting Russia’s military-industrial complex, including 37 individuals and entities directly linked to the production and supply chain of long-range drones.

The agreement was reached after Greece secured an annually renewable exemption allowing companies to continue shipping Russian liquefied natural gas to non-EU customers.

World.title: Trojan horse alert: Pirated online versions of 'The Odyssey' could contain hidden viruses
World.content:
Pirated digital copies of the blockbuster film The Odyssey are being used to hack into viewers' computers, according to new research by cybersecurity company Bitdefender.

 

"Internal Bitdefender insights show that users have already tried to download malicious executables disguised as the movie," the multinational cybersecurity firm said in a statement.

The Odyssey has not yet been released online, while IMAX screenings remain sold out widely for weeks ahead in many locations.

"Only days after The Odyssey became one of the biggest movie launches of the year, cybersecurity researchers have already observed fake pirated copies distributing the Lumma Stealer malware," the statement continued.

This raises significant cybersecurity concerns, as it could allow online attackers to gain access to thousands of consumers' laptops, particularly as several illegal sites present files posing as legitimate video downloads of the film.

In many cases, however, these files are actually concealed versions of malware known as "Lumma Stealer," which infects viewers' devices when opened.

Developed in Russia, Lumma Stealer is believed to be capable of stealing sensitive information, including saved login and payment credentials, session cookies, browsing history, remote access tools and communication apps, as well as any other documents or files saved locally on the device.

By accessing such a vast range of data and tools, attackers can gain significant entry and control not only over a user's device, but also their finances and wider relationships.

Illegal movie copies being used for hacking

While this latest campaign involving The Odyssey may be alarming, it is only the latest in a long trend of popular films being used to spread hacking tools and malware.

Hackers typically exploit the window between a film's cinema release and its arrival on legal streaming platforms such as Netflix and Amazon Prime.

Bitdefender identified several lure file names circulating online, including:

the odyssey 2160phd (2026) engsubs eztv.exe

the odyssey 2026 1080p h264-djt.exe

the odyssey 2026 1080p webrip-lama.exe

Despite promising a film download, these are in fact Windows executables designed to infect a victim's device rather than play any video.

Bitdefender cautioned that this list is not exhaustive, and that criminals are likely using many other file names, too.

This is not a new technique. In 2025, researchers documented an almost identical campaign abusing fake downloads of Mission: Impossible – The Final Reckoning, in which attackers distributed Lumma Stealer through torrent websites using files disguised as movie releases.

"The latest campaign simply replaces one blockbuster with another. Rather than inventing new attacks, criminals continually recycle successful delivery methods around whatever film is dominating search engines and torrent sites," the report said.

Torrent trackers are chock-full of this type of malware. Popular movies are not the only target for Lumma and other stealers — the same goes for TV shows, cracked games and software.

This trend is made worse by the fact that people may be less vigilant about checking file types and names on these kinds of websites, since they already know the content is illegal and may expect to see unusual file names.

To avoid these threats, Bitdefender emphasised the importance of watching films only through recognised and legitimate streaming services, while also keeping cybersecurity software and computer systems up-to-date.

World.title: Euronews Culture's Film of the Week: 'Her Private Hell' - Nicolas Winding Refn's horny bore
World.content:
It takes a unique mind to make a psychosexual fairytale featuring a leather-clad serial killer, futuristic vistas, and Tom of Finland levels of homoeroticism and make it boring. But Nicolas Winding Refn has achieved just that.

 

Ten years since his last feature (The Neon Demon), the director of Drive and Only God Forgives has indulged in some of his worst tendencies by making Her Private Hell a very public one.

You've been warned.

It opens promisingly enough, with mist engulfing a neon-soaked metropolis. A young woman, Elle (Sophie Thatcher), meets blushing ingénue Hunter (Kristine Froseth) in the lobby of the hotel she's staying in. The two are meant to collaborate on a film adaptation of a sci-fi comic book called "Candy Floss", set to be directed by Elle's father, Johnny Thunders (Dougray Scott).

Little does Hunter realize that she's entering into a world of pain... Elle is having to grapple with the reality of her greasy pops (who's constantly surrounded by a hareem of models who call him "daddy") shacking up with her former friend / lover Dominique (Havana Rose Liu), who is now her stepmother.

Meanwhile, the mist has brought along an urban legend: the dreaded figure known as The Leather Man. He's a BDSM gimp with razor sharp diamond gloves and superhuman strength who likes to kill women and leave a gory mess behind. He's being chased by Private K (Charles Melton), a military man who failed to protect his daughter and believes that stopping The Leather Man will reunite them.

Her Private Hell Neon

If there’s one thing you can’t take away from Her Private Hell is that it's visually striking. There is a lot to admire about the look and sound of this futuristic Giallo which initially feels like Suspiria set inside Tron: NWR's cinematographer Magnus Nordenhof Jønck creates some moody visual compositions, while composer Pino Donaggio’s score gives Her Private Hell an appropriately melodramatic quality. Without their efforts, admiration would have faded far quicker.

When it does vanish for good, what remains is the definition of style over substance - a posturing and deeply banal mess of a film teeming with frustrating storytelling and faux Lynchian élans. It often feels like a series of erotically charged fashion commercials featuring all the clichéd non-sequiturs you'd expect from posing models who have downed fistfuls of Benzos.

Speaking of which, my brain activity slowed down as the runtime progressed, so much so that I abandoned taking notes during the film and started jotting down some of the stilted dialogue that populates NWR and Esti Giordani's dire script.

"Aren't you the poor little match girl – Hans Christian Andersen."

Self-consciously name-checking one's reference is embarrassing. It also isn't metatextual. It's barely textual.

"Daddy is fascinating."

Using "Daddy" in a sexually loaded way needed to end yesterday.

"Stop" / "No you stop, this means something."

No, it most demonstrably doesn't.

"I am a wholly unique consciousness, and I am made of stardust."

I wish I was made of stardust right now so I could blow away and not watch another minute of this preening drivel.

"I like freaky shit."

Don't we all, but chances are that if you have to signpost it, you're a) terminally vanilla in the bedroom; and b) performative edgy to the point of self-deception.

"I am a victim of the mist."

I am a victim of this film.

"This movie's going to be hell."

You took the words right out of my mouth.

Her Private Hell Neon

For anyone who gets swept up in NWR's horny daydream, more power to you. The director's devoted fanbase will defend Her Private Hell as a heightened fairytale, in which the dialogue is purposefully mannered and the disjointed fever dream functions as self-aware provocation. Congratulations, you've found a vibes-over-narrative opera worth championing. And to be fair, the film within a film (a camp cross between Barberella and Star Trek) and the bursts of visceral violence in the Private K segments do liven things up. Kudos to Charles Melton, who temporarily makes you forget Sophie Thatcher's annoying performance and Kristine Froseth's incessant grinning. He's the only one who makes it out of this unscathed.

Minor pull factors aside, discerning viewers will come to the conclusion that while it's wonderful to witness a filmmaker who is content to just do his thing, Her Private Hell can't be excused as the uncompromising vision of an enfant terrible. It's far too vacuous and dull for that.

Her Private Hell premiered Out Of Competition in Cannes in May and is currently out in the US, Canada, Greece, Poland and Portugal. It screens on 16 August at the Edinburgh International Film Festival, and its European rollout continues next month.

World.title: "A shame for Portugal": Israeli ambassador urges cancellation of Kanye West concert in Algarve
World.content:
The Embassy of Israel in Portugal has criticised Kanye West's concert, scheduled for this Friday in the Algarve, and has called for the show to be cancelled, citing the artist's public statements, deemed antisemitic and supportive of Adolf Hitler and Nazism.

 

"Someone who glorified Hitler, promoted antisemitism and claimed that slavery was a choice, a remark that deeply offended millions of descendants of slavery's victims. This is not provocation, it is hate speech," says ambassador Oren Rozenblat in a video posted on social media.

In a statement, the ambassador recalled comments by the musician in which he said he "liked Hitler" and that he was "a Nazi", accusing him of glorifying the Nazi regime, promoting antisemitism and offending communities affected by racism and slavery. The embassy argues that these statements go beyond mere provocation and constitute hate speech.

Rozenblat points out that other countries have already taken measures against the artist performing or entering their territories, arguing that "a democratic society should not give a platform to someone who glorifies Hitler, promotes Nazism and defends antisemitism".

The Embassy of Israel in Portugal also says it has asked the mayor of Faro for the cancellation of the concert and urges citizens not to attend, arguing that going ahead with the show would be "a disgrace for Portugal and for the Portuguese".

Would you buy a ticket for an artist who promoted hatred against Black people, against Muslims, against Christians or against LGBT people? If the answer is no, why should it be any different when the target is Jews? Embaixador de Israel em Portugal, Oren Rozenblat

The Israeli ambassador in Portugal stresses that the issue is not about people's positions on Israel, but about what he considers to be statements of hatred against Jews.

He also questions whether the Portuguese would buy tickets for an artist who encouraged attacks against other communities, such as Black people, Muslims, Christians or LGBT people, insisting that the same principle should apply to antisemitism.

"A non-issue"

Torcato Jorge, CEO and co-founder of Raya Culture, the event organiser, said earlier, in an interview with Euronews, that cancelling Kanye West's concert is "a non-issue", driven by "disinformation".

"It is a music event that is going ahead. It would become an issue if the security services identified a national threat to public order, which is not the case," he reiterates.

The organiser expressed confidence that all the conditions are in place for the concert to go ahead and says that the organisation has complied with the law from day one. "The SIS has not identified the artist, or in this case the US citizen, as a national threat or a terrorist," he notes. "There has to be an internal state security report saying that this citizen cannot enter the country," he adds.

Speaking to Euronews, the CEO acknowledges that the issue is becoming "a political matter". "Each country is free to decide whether or not to allow a citizen to enter, but within the European Union no country has vetoed his entry into its national territory."

Controversial statements and cancelled concerts

In recent years, Kanye West has been at the centre of various international controversies, mainly because of comments considered antisemitic and because of contentious behaviour, including episodes linked to sexist attitudes, such as the case involving his wife, Bianca Censori, at the Grammys.

Although he has apologised for some of his comments, the European tour of the rapper, who also goes by the stage name Ye, has run into difficulties, with concerts cancelled in several countries.

In the United Kingdom, three performances at the Wireless festival, scheduled for July, were cancelled after the country revoked the rapper's permission to enter. In France, the artist himself postponed a concert scheduled for Marseille after criticism from local authorities.

Poland also cancelled a show planned for June, citing legal and formal reasons, after the minister of culture criticised the rapper's antisemitic statements. In Switzerland, FC Basel decided not to go ahead with a concert planned for its stadium, stating that it did not want to give the artist a platform.

In Italy, Kanye West also had a concert cancelled. The show, scheduled for July in Reggio Emilia, was banned by the local authorities because of concerns about security and public order, in particular the potential for protests and unrest. Rapper Travis Scott also had a concert cancelled in the same Italian city.

World.title: Myanmar's Min Aung Hlaing seeks legitimacy in Thailand
World.content:
Bangkok rolled out the red carpet for the Myanmar leader, but experts say the former junta chief still faces major obstacles in his bid for regional acceptance.

Myanmar's junta chief turned president Min Aung Hlaing wrapped up a two-day visit to Thailand on Friday.

His first visit to the neighboring nation as civilian leader was aimed at recasting himself as the leader of a civilian government after years of diplomatic isolation, experts told DW.

His reception on landing in Bangkok on Thursday had all the pomp and circumstance befitting a visiting head of state — red carpet, honor guard, blaring national anthems and smiling photo ops with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul.

"Naypyidaw equates engagement with acceptance," said Moe Thuzar, head of the Myanmar Studies Program at Singapore's ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, referring to Myanmar's capital.

"Min Aung Hlaing is seeking to leverage Naypyidaw's space in bilateral relations with neighbours' specific interests to secure greater acceptance of his administration from external partners."

Min Aung Hlaing has pledged to pursue peace and improve ties with the 11-member ASEAN bloc Image: Athit Perawongmetha/REUTERS

Since the retired general seized power in a 2021 coup that toppled a democratically elected government, a brutal civil war between the military and armed resistance groups has killed an estimated 100,000 people and displaced well over 3 million.

Western countries have imposed several rounds of sanctions on Min Aung Hlaing's regime over alleged war crimes and other human rights abuses, charges the government rejects.

In 2024, the then-chief prosecutor of the International Criminal Court requested an arrest warrant for Min Aung Hlaing himself for crimes against humanity committed against Rohingya Muslims.

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), which traditionally emphasizes non-interference in another member's domestic affairs, has barred him or his foreign minister from attending its leaders' summits.

Hoping to break out of its growing isolation, Myanmar held staggered elections in December and January that were widely criticized by the United Nations and Western governments as a sham designed to legitimize continued military rule.

The military-aligned Union Solidarity and Development Party won more than 80% of seats, paving the way for parliament to elect Min Aung Hlaing president in April.

What is Thailand's role in Myanmar's reengagement?

Myanmar's government rejects criticism of the electoral process, saying the elections were part of a transition to civilian rule and a return of power to the people.

Since becoming president, Hlaing has paid official visits to India, China, Laos and now Thailand, as Bangkok pushed for peace efforts in Myanmar's civil war and its reengagement with ASEAN.

"For Min Aung Hlaing, visiting Thailand is also [about] finding legitimacy in the ASEAN region, because Thailand is a … founder of ASEAN and has [a] big voice in ASEAN," said Wai Yan Phyo Naing, a visiting scholar at Taiwan's Academia Sinica who studies Myanmar.

"He can show the [other] ASEAN members that Thailand is treating me like this, Laos already treated me like this. So, do you want to [act] based on the realistic point of view, or are you still wanting to argue I'm not the legitimate leader of Myanmar?" he said.

Moe Thuzar and Wai Yan Phyo Naing both agree that the bloc, which did not officially endorse Myanmar's last elections, like most countries, was not likely to let Min Aung Hlaing back to its leaders' summits any time soon.

Human Rights Watch's Elaine Pearson on Myanmar election To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

ASEAN still insists that Myanmar first make meaningful progress on a peace plan for the country that they all agreed to a few months after the coup, a plan Hlaing has dismissed repeatedly, most recently last week.

Still, Min Aung Hlaing may be hoping that his official trips abroad as newly installed president

help convince ASEAN to accept his government "on its own terms," Moe Thuzar added.

Either way, she said, Min Aung Hlaing will use his trip to Thailand to build on the bilateral relationship between the neighbors, which share a 2,400 kilometer (1,490-mile) land border.

The visit included a business forum on Thursday for Thai and Myanmar firms.

"The focus on trade and economic deals reflects Naypyidaw's and Bangkok's interest in prioritising economic engagement and addressing concerns related to border trade," said Moe Thuzar.

The economics of legitimacy

Thailand is among Myanmar's top trade partners and foreign investors, including in energy projects vital to both. A Thai firm operates two of Myanmar's main gas fields, which supply much of Thailand's natural gas.

David Mathieson, an independent Myanmar analyst based in Thailand, says convincing those investors to stay, or new ones to come in, helps shore up support for Hlaing among a key constituency.

Regardless of the ex-general's official title, he said, "he's a military dictator, and to be a dictator you need a certain level of cooperation, and cooperation comes from economic elites."

"He's appealing to an incredibly cynical international system that's like, hey, you did this. None of us buy it, but it's good enough for us. You dressed up for the party, well done, and [it's] business as usual," Mathieson said.

"Does that help the 54 million people of Myanmar? No, it doesn't. It helps him and it helps the system that props him up."

Rohingya caught in the middle of Myanmar's civil war To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: Germany: Far-right AfD extends its lead in nationwide polls
World.content:
In the latest Sunday poll, the AfD continues to pull ahead. And more and more people are against excluding the right-wing populists from decision-making, at least on a case-by-case basis.

For the time being, there is still widespread agreement among all democratic parties in Germany: Cooperating with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) remains out of the question. However, whether this will remain the case is becoming increasingly uncertain. The established parties have so far been unable to halt the AfD's surge in the polls over recent months.

This has also been confirmed by the latest ARD-Deutschlandtrend survey conducted by the polling firm infratest-dimap. 1,300 eligible voters were asked what party they would vote for if a federal election were held next Sunday, and 28% said they would vote for the AfD. This represents a one-percentage-point increase and a new record high for the AfD in the monthly polly.

In contrast, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's party, the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), and its sister party, Bavaria's Christian Social Union (CSU), have seen a slight decline compared to the last poll in early July while all other parties have maintained their previous levels.

A clear majority supports reaching out to the AfD

In September, state elections will take place in two important eastern German states: Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. In both states, the AfD leads in the polls. In Saxony-Anhalt, they are polling at 41% and might be able to govern alone, if the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) fails to cross the 5% threshhold for representation in parliament.

However, only 37% of voters across Germany are opposed to any form of cooperation with the right-wing populists while 32% believe such decisions should be made on a case-by-case basis.

A total of 27% are generally in favor of cooperating with the AfD, most of whom are AfD supporters.

What is especially interesting in the poll, however, is the contrast between East and West Germany. The AfD has its strongholds in the East, where more people than in the West are willing to fully embrace the party: 38% want to treat the party — of which several regional chapters have been categorized as far-right extremist by the domestic intelligence agency — just like any other political group. That figure roughly corresponds to the level of support for right-wing populists in the formerly socialist East Germany (GDR).

Many AfD supporters feel marginalized

This figure also reflects the continuing shift away from "mainstream" parties. A good half of those surveyed — more than ever before in the Deutschlandtrend — support a fundamental change in German politics while only four in ten prefer isolated policy adjustments.

In other words, confidence and trust in the political system continue to wane. Forty-three percent of all respondents say they constantly feel marginalized. When this question is put to AfD supporters, that figure jumps to 70%.

The past few weeks in German politics have been marked by heated debates over proposed reforms and by a rather chaotic reshuffling of the cabinet. Even before this, approval ratings for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's policies were not high; now, only 12% believe that the new cabinet appointments will lead to better policies.

One-third are afraid of terrorism

And the latest terrorist attack in Germany has also had a significant impact on people's views. On July 25, a young Islamist from Berlin drove a rental car into a crowd during the Berlin Pride celebrations, killing one woman and seriously injuring 31 people. The following day, police shot and killed the man, who had fled after carrying out the attack. This horrific event has once again drawn attention to how vulnerable Germany is to terrorist attacks.

One-third of all respondents said they are very concerned they might become victims of terrorism themselves. Now, 70% see Islamist terrorism as the greatest threat. At the end of the last decade, on the other hand, right-wing extremist terrorism was still seen by German citizens as the greatest threat.

For the ARD-Deutschlandtrend survey in August, infratest-dimap interviewed approximately 1,300 representative German citizens between August 3 and 5.

This article was translated from German.

World.title: Testosterone and fertility: the trade-off men aren't told about
World.content:
Testosterone is trending in gyms, on social online and in politics. US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth even wants troops screened for low testosterone. But taking supplements can shut down the body's natural production.

Making sperm is, in large part, what testosterone is for. Which is why it is ironic when a man who doesn't need it starts taking it anyway: His brain registers an unusually high level of the hormone in his blood, concludes his body has made too much, and sends the order to stop. The testes go silent and sperm production declines.

Testosterone is having a moment. It is all over social media, gym culture and wellness forums, sold by online labs, gym contacts and telehealth services. The information surrounding it ranges from oversimplified to outright dangerous. Men are taking more of it than ever, in pursuit of feeling more like men. In doing so, they may be telling their bodies to stop producing it themselves.

Here is what the science says — what testosterone does, who genuinely needs treatment, and what it can cost the men who take it without needing it.

How does taking testosterone stop sperm production?

Your body regulates testosterone the way a thermostat regulates heat. When the brain detects abnormally high levels of the hormone in the bloodstream, it sends a signal to the testes to stop producing it naturally. The testes effectively go offline, and because sperm production depends on what happens inside them, that shuts down too.

Some men who self-medicate with testosterone push their levels to more than four times the clinical lower threshold. The consequences include blood clotting disorders, cardiovascular stress, mood instability and, in some cases, irreversible fertility damage. What's sold as a shortcut to strength and libido can, unsupervised, cost a man his fertility.

What are normal testosterone levels by age?

Testosterone peaks during puberty, typically between 13 and 15. After that, it declines slowly for the rest of a man's life. A lower level at 40 than at 15 isn't a disorder — its aging.

What counts as low testosterone?

The threshold that doctors use is 300 nanograms per deciliter of blood.

But this threshold comes with a condition: It must be confirmed by at least two blood tests taken at different times of the day, because levels fluctuate.

Below that number, a doctor may begin to consider treatment. Above 300, there is no clinical basis for intervention.

How can you increase testosterone naturally?

Before any medical treatment is considered, four key lifestyle factors should be examined: sleep, alcohol consumption, smoking and drug use, and chronic stress. Each of these has a measurable impact on testosterone levels. Addressing them may be all that's needed and carries none of the risks of hormonal therapy.

What is testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) and who actually needs it?

Testosterone replacement therapy, or TRT, treats a diagnosed hormonal deficiency. It's a legitimate medical procedure — involving injections, pills, creams — that works for men who need it.

But plenty of men taking it don't have that deficiency. Men with normal testosterone levels are increasingly seeking TRT out anyway, not as a treatment but as a performance enhancer. They're getting it from unregulated online labs, gym contacts and telehealth services that write prescriptions without adequate medical assessment.

Can testosterone therapy cause permanent infertility?

In some cases, yes.

Men who stop taking testosterone are likely to recover their own production within months. But not all of them. Depending on the dose and how long a man has been using, research puts the share who never recover at somewhere between one in ten and one in five.

Low testosterone: What it does to men's health To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Does testosterone therapy actually work – or is it a placebo?

Many men who self-administer testosterone report feeling stronger, sharper and more energetic. Some of that may reflect genuine physiological change.

A significant portion is likely the placebo effect — a well-documented human tendency to feel better when we believe we are being treated. That does not make the feeling less real. It does mean that unsupervised hormonal intervention is a high-risk gamble for a benefit that may exist entirely in one's mind.

The bottom line

Doctors' advice is unambiguous: Get tested, know the number, and treat everything else — the websites, the influencers, the gym contacts — as anecdote, not medicine.

A lot of men aren't waiting. Chasing peak masculinity online, they're reaching for the one substance that could tell their own bodies to stop making it.

Edited by: Kaukab Shairani

World.title: Is it really the hottest day ever?
World.content:
Every time a new heat record is broken, skepticism follows. How do scientists know a day or a summer was really the hottest on record or that a heat wave was historic? DW has the answers.

Another summer, another wave of headlines about record-breaking heat. From Northeast Asia to Europe to the United States, extreme temperatures are contributing to thousands of deaths, fueling wildfires and straining water, food and energy supplies.

But what do the words behind the headlines mean? How do scientists know if temperatures are record-breaking? Why do cities warm up more than rural areas? And does humidity really make everything feel hotter?

DW spoke to climatologists to answer some common questions about how heat is measured, and why understanding heat terminology matters for everyone.

What does 'record-breaking heat' mean anyway?

It depends on what's being compared. Thousands of weather stations around the world track temperatures. A location can set a record if its temperature exceeds the previous high recorded at the station for a specific day, month or season.

Scientists also calculate regional and global temperature records by combining data from weather stations, ships and ocean buoys and determining the average across larger areas.

How far back that comparison goes depends on the dataset. The oldest continuous record of temperatures in the world is the Central England Temperature Data Series, which started in 1659.

The 10 warmest years in modern global record-keeping have all occurred within the past decade Image: Thorsten Wagner/W2Art/picture alliance

But the three most complete datasets — maintained by the United States' Goddard Institute for Space Studies and National Centers for Environmental Information, plus the United Kingdom's Met Office Hadley Centre — began recording comprehensively in 1880.

These are the datasets behind statements such as "the past decade was the warmest on record." When media outlets use the shorthand "hottest day ever," they are talking about recording temperatures.

While Earth has experienced hotter climates and extreme temperatures over its 4.5-billion-year history, today's warming is exceptional in the context of the 12,000 years of human civilization.

But how do scientists know about Earth's climate before humans and thermometers were around?

To understand Earth's earlier climate, scientists rely on natural records known as "climate archives" that help them recreate long-term patterns in temperature. Those include ice cores, tree rings, ocean sediments and fossils.

"These preserve information about past temperatures, rainfall and atmospheric conditions going back thousands to millions of years," Friedrike Otto, a climatologist and founder of research group World Weather Attribution (WWA), told DW in an email.

The most complete continuous ice core record, drilled in Antarctica, stretches back more than a million years, for example. It contains ancient air bubbles that allow researchers to measure past atmospheric carbon dioxide levels. But other "climate archives" stretch back much further.

"As we know the equations that govern the physics of the climate, we can also use climate models to see how changes in different drivers produce different climate and weather conditions," said Otto.

That's helped scientists discern that higher greenhouse gases are closely linked with warmer global temperatures throughout Earth's history. For instance, about 56 million years ago, large amounts of carbon entered the atmosphere, likely from volcanic activity and methane released from ocean sediments, triggering a major period of global heating.

The difference today is climate change is primarily caused by humans burning fossil fuels and is happening at a much faster rate than over the last million years or so, says NASA.

But how do scientists know if heat waves are a trend or an anomaly?

Climate scientists analyze decades of data to distinguish long-term climatic changes from normal weather fluctuations. A single hot year doesn't prove a trend. But as records grow longer, statistical analyses and climate models make it easier to identify persistent patterns.



"You're looking for consistency. You're looking for a convergence of all the evidence," said Gerald Mills, a climatologist at University College Dublin.

How to deal with a heatstroke To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Scientific agencies across different continents — including NASA, NOAA and the EU's Copernicus Climate Change Service — track global temperatures, using different methods and data sets. Despite those differences, they've reached the same conclusion: there is a heating trend and that the last decade has produced the hottest years ever recorded.

Researchers also use attribution science to assess the role climate change plays in extreme weather. Using climate models, they compare the likelihood and intensity of an event in today's climate with a simulated world without human-caused warming.

WWA ran exactly that analysis on Europe's June 2026 heat wave. The scientists found it was the most severe on record for the region studied. In 1976, a famously hot year across Europe, those temperatures would have been virtually impossible.

What heat metrics should you pay attention to in a weather forecast?

Air temperature or "actual temperature" don't fully describe how heat affects the human body. That's why weather services also provide "feels like" figures, which account for other factors.

In the US, the National Weather Service's heat index is based on air temperature and humidity. The UK's Met Office's "feels like" temperature also factors in wind chill.

Why does high humidity make it feel hotter and why is a high wet bulb temperature dangerous?

High humidity means more moisture in the air, which makes it harder for sweat evaporate. That reduces the body's ability to cool down, so the air temperature feels hotter in humid conditions.

Scientists also use the wet bulb temperature as a measure for heat stress. It is recorded by wrapping the bulb of a thermometer in a damp cloth. As water evaporates from the cloth, the bulb cools and the temperature reading drops, similar to how evaporation of sweat cools the human body.

As the wet bulb temperature approaches the actual air temperature, the air becomes increasingly saturated, and the body struggles to cool itself, increasing the risk of dangerous heat stress.

At sustained wet bulb temperatures of around 35 degrees Celsius (95 degrees Fahrenheit), the body can overheat even if people are resting in the shade or staying hydrated. But dry heat can be dangerous too, considering the risk of dehydration.

Why are cities hotter than rural areas?

That's because of the urban heat island effect, which makes cities warmer than surrounding areas for a few reasons.

Cities often replace vegetation and trees with roads, buildings and other hard surfaces that absorb and store heat. Greenery, on the other hand, cools an area through shade and evaporation. Dense buildings and narrow streets in urban areas also reduce air ventilation.

"All those things together, depending on where you are in relation to the city, can make it quite uncomfortable," Mills said.

Planting more trees, adding parks and green roofs, unsealing paved areas where possible and using lighter-colored, more reflective building materials can all help reduce the urban heat island effect by increasing shade, evaporation and the reflection of sunlight.

Edited by: Jennifer Collins

World.title: Thailand: Several killed in school shooting north of Bangkok
World.content:
The shooting incident took place at the Debsirin Nonthaburi School in ​the ‌Bang Kruai district of Nonthaburi, just north of the capital city of Bangkok. Several people were killed in the attack.

Several people were killed and others injured in a shooting at a high school in Thailand's Nonthaburi province, north of the capital city of Bangkok, local authorities said.

Students, teachers and other workers were evacuated from school as authorities deployed police officers, rescue workers and emergency doctors to the scene.

Boy accused of killing grandparents before school shooting

According to the police, the suspected gunman, who is a 14-year-old student at the school, first fatally shot his grandparents with his grandfather's handgun. Then, he went to his school and killed three teachers and three students before killing himself.

Earlier, Thai national police spokesperson Trairong Phiwphan said that 15 people were wounded.

In a statement, police said the gunman fired 26 rounds, and an additional 34 rounds of ammunition were found at the scene.

Students, teachers and other staff members were evacuated from the school Image: Chalinee Thirasupa/REUTERS

Meanwhile, Thailand's Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul expressed his condolences and stated that he had instructed relevant officials to assist those affected.

"It's such a terrible incident. It should never have happened. How could this happen in our country?" he told reporters.

Later, Anutin said that the teenage suspect in the deadly school shooting was "under stress" and had planned the attack. The prime minister also told reporters that he would discuss gun control with the country's police chief.

Students express shock

The incident took place at the Debsirin Nonthaburi School in ​the ‌Bang Kruai district of Nonthaburi.

"I didn't think it was a gun at first," an 18-year-old student told Reuters, adding that he initially thought there were firecrackers. "There were many shots: bang bang bang. Then it went quiet. ​Then it started again."

Belongings left behind by evacuated students at Debsirin Nonthaburi School, following the shooting incident at the school Image: Chalinee Thirasupa/REUTERS

"I was afraid that I would die, and I was scared that I wouldn't be able to pursue my dreams," said Pawarisa Maylissa, a grade 12 student who hopes to attend medical school. "I heard many gunshots very loudly because it seemed the suspect was on the floor directly above us. I could even hear bullets hitting the floor."

According to district authorities, the Debsirin Nonthaburi School had an enrollment of around 3,100 students and 147 teachers in the 2025 academic year.

School shootings in Thailand

Thailand has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in the region. It is estimated that around 10 million firearms are in circulation, or about one for every seven people.

In February, a 17-year-old stole a gun from the police and opened fire at a public high school in southern Thailand. The two-hour attack resulted in one death and two injuries.

In October 2023, a 14-year-old opened fire at Bangkok's popular Siam Paragon shopping mall, killing two people and wounding five others. Police said the shooter used a modified pistol, originally designed to fire blanks, that had likely been bought online.
