Poland’s top administrative court has upheld a decision by the finance ministry to withhold state subsidies from the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party due to campaign finance irregularities. The decision was welcomed by the government, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying that there will be “no money for grifters”. PiS, however, argues that the money is being withheld for political reasons and accuses the authorities of “Russian standards”. Naczelny Sąd Administracyjny oddalił w środę kasacje ws. dotacji i subwencji dla PiS. – Miażdżący dla PiS wyrok podtrzymany! – stwierdził szef MF Andrzej Domański https://t.co/bcL18WbiYf — OKO.press (@oko_press) August 6, 2026 The dispute dates back to August 2024, when the National Electoral Commission (PKW) rejected PiS’s financial report for the previous year’s parliamentary election campaign after identifying around 3.6 million zloty (€838,000) in unauthorised expenditure. As a result, the PKW ordered that PiS should lose 10.8 million zloty from the state subsidies that political parties in Poland receive based on their level of electoral support. The party would normally have received 25.9 million zloty based on its 2023 election result. The decision triggered months of legal wrangling, with PiS arguing that the funding should be restored after the Supreme Court upheld its complaint against the PKW’s decision. However, finance minister Andrzej Domański refused to release the money, saying there were unresolved legal doubts over the ruling. The finance minister has refused to comply with the electoral commission's decision to pay out subsidies to the opposition PiS party He says there are "legal doubts" over the issue. But PiS says he is obliged to pay and will be held criminally responsible https://t.co/ZwIZRqn5tp — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 9, 2025 Those doubts stem from a broader dispute over the controversial and contested judicial reforms implemented by PiS when it ruled Poland from 2015 to 2023. The chamber of the Supreme Court that ruled in PiS’s favour was created as part of those reforms. It has previously been found to not be a legitimate body by both the European Court of Justice and European Court of Human Rights because it contains improperly appointed judges. After the Supreme Court chamber’s ruling, the PKW initially said it would not recognise the decision until the chamber’s legal status was clarified. Two weeks later, however, it reversed that decision and approved PiS’s financial report. Domański still declined to restore the subsidy, arguing that the PKW’s resolution was internally contradictory. While it approved the payments, it also stated that the chamber’s ruling should come from a body recognised as a court and that it was not determining whether the chamber met that standard. PiS challenged Domański’s decision. However, its case was initially rejected by a lower court in June last year, and that decision has now been upheld by the Supreme Administrative Court (NSA), which is the final court of appeal for administrative issues. The NSA found the minister had acted lawfully in withholding the funding. It also said the Supreme Court chamber’s ruling had no legal effect because it had been issued by a body that was not a properly constituted court, reports news website OKO.press. The ruling was welcomed by Domański, who called it a “crushing blow to PiS” and said that “yet another PiS lie has been exposed”. Prime Minister Donald Tusk, meanwhile, wrote on social media: “Just as we said, there is and will be no money for grifters.” Tak jak mówiliśmy, dla przekręciarzy pieniędzy nie ma i nie będzie. https://t.co/4Kqexj6NoC — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) August 5, 2026 The PKW’s decision to cut PiS’s funds was made after it found that government resources – including from the justice ministry, Government Legislation Centre (RCL) and Research and Academic Computer Network (NASK) – had been used to support the party’s election campaign. However, PiS has always argued that the decision was a political one, implemented at the behest of the new Tusk government in order to undermine the main opposition party. Radosław Fogiel, a senior PiS lawmaker and former party spokesman, said that the new NSA ruling “does not change the essence of the matter: it unlawfully deprives the main opposition party of the subsidy to which it is entitled. After a ten-year-long investigation, prosecutors have concluded that Poland’s government in 2010 – which was led by current Prime Minister Donald Tusk – was not guilty of “diplomatic treason” in its response to the plane crash in Russia that killed President Lech Kaczyński. The national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party – which ruled Poland from 2015 to 2023 and is led by Lech’s twin brother, Jarosław – has always rejected the findings of official Polish and Russian investigations into the crash, which found it to have been an accident. Instead, PiS claims that the disaster, which claimed the lives of 96 people, many of them senior Polish state officials, was caused deliberately by Russia and then covered up with the help of Tusk’s government. However, while PiS launched various investigations during its time in power, it has never substantiated its claims. And prosecutors now say that there is no evidence that diplomatic treason, a crime that carries a potential prison sentence of up to ten years, took place. Uprzednio wygrałem sprawę cywilną z posłem @OficjalnyJK, który w efekcie musiał wpłacić 50,000zł na siły zbrojne broniącej się Ukrainy. Teraz potwierdzenie @PK_GOV_PL: nie było żadnej zdrady dyplomatycznej ani żadnej intencji jej popełnienia. Oczywiście żaden z kłamców… https://t.co/VKZHlF5xkX — Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) August 5, 2026 Wednesday’s announcement by the National Prosecutor’s Office was welcomed by Radosław Sikorski, the current foreign minister, who held the same role in 2010. He condemned the “Smolensk liars”, such as Jarosław Kaczyński, who he suggested had exploited the tragedy for their own benefit. “They brainwashed millions of people, divided families, stirred up hatred within the nation,” he wrote. “They’ll burn in hell for it. But the power, money and satisfaction they gained from spitting on their rivals – that’s theirs.” The idea that Smolensk was an assassination of Lech Kaczyński has been a core part of PiS rhetoric. In 2022, for example, Jarosław Kaczyński said that the decision was made “at the highest level of the Kremlin” and Tusk’s government then “covered up” the incident as part of a “macabre reconciliation with Russia”. Smolensk was an “attack decided at the highest level of the Kremlin”, says Jarosław Kaczyński ahead of the 12th anniversary of the crash. Donald Tusk's government then “covered up” the incident as part of a “macabre reconciliation with Russia”, he adds https://t.co/5ae0gHJj3B — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 4, 2022 The investigation into diplomatic treason – a crime consisting of acting to the detriment of Poland while authorised to represent the country in relations with foreign states or organisations – was launched in August 2016, less than a year after PiS had come to power. Among the individuals who had formally notified prosecutors of a potential crime was PiS deputy leader Antoni Macierewicz, who from 2015 to 2018 served as defence minister. He has been the foremost proponent of conspiracy theories around the Smolensk air disaster. In their notifications to prosecutors, Macierewicz and the others accused Tusk and other officials of, in their relations with Russia, deliberately choosing a legal basis for an investigation into the crash that was unfavourable to Poland by giving it no real influence over how it was run. However, prosecutors now say that, after ten years in which they questioned 488 witnesses, gathered extensive documentation and requested legal assistance from several countries, they have “concluded that no crime of diplomatic treason was committed”. In a statement explaining the decision, the National Prosecutor’s Office said that the legal basis chosen for cooperating with Russia on an investigation – Annex 13 of the Convention on International Civil Aviation – was, in fact, “the most advantageous solution” for Poland. It ensured the participation of Polish representatives in the Russian-led investigation, including access to the wreckage and crash site. Other legal options would have offered no greater benefits and involved significant risks, concluded the Polish prosecutors. They acknowledged that Russia “subsequently failed to fulfil some of its obligations arising from the adopted procedure”, but said this should have no bearing on assessing the decisions that were previously made on setting up the investigation. The defence ministry will notify prosecutors of 41 suspected crimes linked to a commission established by the former PiS government to investigate the 2010 plane crash in Russia that killed President Lech Kaczyński https://t.co/aEAlmk9lDM — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 24, 2024 The prosecutors also found that, not only did Polish officials choose the best legal solution, but there was also “no evidence indicating that individuals authorised to act on behalf of Poland, including the prime minister and members of the Council of Ministers, acted with the intent to harm Poland”. Given that the crime of diplomatic treason requires intent, this finding further reinforced the decision to drop the investigation. However, the prosecutors note that their decision can still be appealed. At the time of writing, neither Kaczyński, Macierewicz, nor other senior PiS figures had commented on the prosecutors’ announcement. However, it is likely they will point to the fact that the current national prosecutor was appointed by Tusk’s government after it had removed the previous PiS-era incumbent in a legally questionable move. The Supreme Court has issued a ruling that effectively found that the government unlawfully replaced a senior prosecutor earlier this year However, the justice minister says the ruling has no legal force as it was issued by illegitimately appointed judges https://t.co/9fCE6d18uy — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 27, 2024 In 2020, in a separate civil case, a court ordered Jarosław Kaczyński to apologise for accusing Sikorski of “diplomatic treason” in relation to the Smolensk crash. Two years later, after Kaczyński had refused to comply with the ruling and Sikorski published the apology himself, Kaczyński was ordered to pay the costs. In 2024, an investigation by Tusk’s government found that the PiS administration had wasted tens of millions of zloty on a commission, headed by Macierewicz, that was tasked with re-investigating the Smolensk disaster. It notified prosecutors of dozens of suspected crimes relating to the functioning of the commission. Macierewicz, however, accused the government of spreading “lies and disinformation” designed to “protect Putin”. Jarosław Kaczyński has been ordered to pay 700,000 zl (€150,000) to publish an apology to ex-foreign minister @sikorskiradek. Poland has urged the European Union to adopt tougher measures in response to the recent migration crisis in Spain’s African exclave of Ceuta, including making migrants who enter the bloc illegally ineligible for obtaining residence rights. During a special meeting of EU interior ministers on Tuesday, Poland shared its own experience of dealing with “weaponised” migration from Belarus, which prompted the Polish government last year to restrict the right to asylum for people who cross irregularly. 🔵 KOMUNIKAT | Polska przedstawiła swoje stanowisko ws. migracji na nadzwyczajnym posiedzeniu Rady JHA w sprawie ostatnich wydarzeń w Ceucie 🇵🇱🇪🇺 Wiceminister spraw wewnętrznych i administracji @MaciekDuszczyk wziął udział w odbywającym się we wtorek (4 sierpnia br.)… pic.twitter.com/glfyiu5ZW3 — MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) August 4, 2026 Last week, tens of thousands of migrants entered Ceuta, most of them by swimming there from neighbouring Morocco. Dozens died while trying to cross. Among those who managed to enter Ceuta, Spain says that the vast majority have been returned to Morocco. The incident prompted expressions of concern from many European leaders, including calls to restrict Spain’s participation in the Schengen free movement zone (despite the fact that anyone leaving Ceuta for the European mainland is subject to identity checks). Among those to speak out was Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who on Friday called on Spain to “follow our example if Schengen is to survive”. Poland has tightened asylum laws, border procedures, and has built effective barriers on its border with Belarus, which is the eastern border of the EU. We have invested billions of euros and engaged thousands of soldiers, police officers and border guards. Spain must follow our… — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 31, 2026 That was a reference to Poland’s response to a crisis on its eastern border, where since 2021 Belarus has encouraged and assisted tens of thousands of migrants – mainly from Asia and Africa – to try to cross irregularly into the EU. Both Poland and the EU have accused Belarus and its ally Russia of deliberately “weaponising” migration in an attempt to destabilise European societies as part of Moscow and Minsk’s broader “hybrid threats” against the EU. Tusk noted that, in response, Poland has restricted the right to asylum, invested billions in strengthening physical and electronic barriers along the border, and has deployed thousands of soldiers, police officers and border guards there (who have also been given expanded rights to use firearms). A court has ruled that Poland's recently introduced partial suspension of the right to asylum is justified and lawful. It rejected a complaint by a Sudanese man who had been denied the right to claim asylum after crossing irregularly from Belarus https://t.co/jx3s1AxRgG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 10, 2025 On Saturday, Tusk and 21 other EU leaders jointly signed a letter expressing “serious concern” at the situation in Ceuta and warning that the EU “cannot allow uncontrolled mass border crossings, the instrumentalisation of migration, or other hybrid threats to create the impression that illegal entry…is possible”. While they welcomed Spain’s cooperation with Morocco to send most of the migrants back, they also called for an extraordinary meeting of EU interior ministers to “agree on a coordinated European response, including the rapid mobilisation of available EU instruments and the necessary support to Spain”. At that meeting, which took place on Tuesday, Poland’s interior ministry said that it had expressed the view that “illegal entry into the European Union should automatically exclude the possibility of obtaining residence permits, and therefore the possibility of permanent stay in the future”. While Poland’s statement did not mention it directly, earlier this year Spain’s government launched an amnesty that allowed undocumented migrants to apply to legalise their stay in the country. Over one million people had signed up for the scheme by the time it closed at the end of June. In its statement, Poland’s interior ministry warned that “migration must be fully controlled”, as otherwise it can “be used against the values that guide the EU”. It also called for the “official recognition of migration as a challenge directly linked to security”. It added that during Tuesday’s meeting it had “presented its own experiences with border protection in the context of the instrumentalisation and weaponisation of migration and adapting law to migration challenges”, including restrictions on asylum claims. “The example of Ceuta clearly demonstrates that absolute access to asylum is impossible to maintain in the face of such real threats,” wrote the interior ministry, which said that it “welcomed the shared perspective on migration among a growing number of member states”. In a statement of its own, the European Council noted that there had been a “common understanding of the need to continue relentlessly fighting migrant smuggling networks, to reinforce returns, to strengthen EU borders, to build deep partnerships with third countries, and to improve foresight.” It added that member states “were united in expressing strong solidarity with Spain”, appreciated its “swift and effective efforts” to deal with the crisis, and had also expressed their condolences for the people who died while attempting to cross from Morocco to Ceuta. ESPAÑA: CEUTA PIDE CERRAR LA FRONTERA POR LA LLEGADA MASIVA DE MIGRANTES DE MARRUECOS Más de mil jóvenes marroquíes se congregaron en la frontera con Ceuta para intentar ingresar al enclave español, y cientos lograron superar las barreras de protección, que en ese momento no… pic.twitter.com/Mx0LuQwMW2 — Clarín (@clarincom) July 30, 2026 When the migration crisis on its border with Belarus broke out in 2021, Poland recorded almost 40,000 attempted illegal crossings that year. Despite efforts to discourage and prevent crossings, the figures remained high, with just under 30,000 attempted crossings recorded in each of 2024 and 2025. However, those figures have fallen dramatically this year, with only 235 attempted crossings recorded in the first half of 2026. Meanwhile, the estimated number of successful crossings has been falling, from 12,000 in 2023, to 5,000 in 2024, 1,700 in 2025, and zero in the first half of this year, according to the Polish interior ministry. Last August, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen visited Poland’s border with Belarus, where she thanked the Polish authorities for defending Europe from “cynical hybrid attacks” orchestrated by Belarus and Russia. The number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants from Belarus to Poland fell from 15,500 in the first half of 2025 to 235 this year – a drop of over 98% Poland also now claims a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally https://t.co/RFZkd7CeIk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 20, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Unexploded WWII ordnance discovered under busy Warsaw street
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Part of central Warsaw was shut down today after unexploded ordnance from World War Two was found buried under a major road during construction work. The discovery, which came just days after the city commemorated the anniversary of its wartime uprising against Nazi-German occupation, led to traffic being diverted and residents being warned to stay away from their windows and avoid going outside while bomb disposal experts worked to safely remove the item. W Al. Solidarności znaleziono niewybuch, najprawdopodobniej z czasów II wojny światowej. ℹ️ Czytaj więcej: https://t.co/Fv6oe84XiM pic.twitter.com/BfjQPZveYZ — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) August 4, 2026 The object, reportedly around 70 centimetres long, was found early on Tuesday morning on Solidarity Avenue, a major thoroughfare, during modernisation work on tram lines. “We were digging a trench and I literally just touched it with the tip [of my digger],” the operator of the excavator who found it told broadcaster TVN. Staff working at the site were immediately evacuated to a safe distance. Police later confirmed that the item is unexploded ordnance, and that initial findings indicate it dates from World War Two. Bomb disposal experts arrived at the scene in the afternoon. However, they have not confirmed precisely what type of ordnance was discovered or its origin, reports Polsat News. Warsaw was the site of major fighting during World War Two, beginning in 1939, when Nazi Germany invaded and occupied Poland. In 1943, the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, the largest single act of Jewish resistance during the war, took place. On 1 August 1944, the Polish underground Home Army launched the Warsaw Uprising, which was the largest single act of armed resistance anywhere in German-occupied Europe during the war. In response, the Germans destroyed much of the city, around 85% of which lay in ruins by 1945. Warsaw’s historic Old Town was meticulously rebuilt after the war. But many other parts of the city were redeveloped by the newly installed communist authorities, including Solidarity Avenue (which during the communist era was named after Polish-Soviet Red Army General Karol Świerczewski). Thousands of vehicles drove over the unexploded ordnance every day for decades. “Warsaw is marked by history, and there are many such surprises,” Witold Urbanowicz, spokesman for the city’s tram operator, told news website Interia. After the fall of the Warsaw Uprising – which began 80 years ago today – the German occupiers expelled the city's entire population. However, some survivors decided to remain among the ruins. They became known as "Robinson Crusoes" and this is their story https://t.co/UuVbfbcpQ4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 1, 2024 Unexploded ordnance is regularly found in Poland. In May this year, around 200 anti-personnel mines dating from World War Two were discovered at the construction site of a student dormitory at Kraków’s Jagiellonian University. In October last year, two men were hospitalised after an artillery shell that one of them had brought home from a forest exploded in his apartment while the pair were under the influence of alcohol. Earlier that year, wild boars unearthed 21 mortar shells buried in a forest since the war. In 2023, 72 unexploded artillery shells were discovered during renovation work at a primary school and four pieces of World War Two ordnance were found in the walls of a church undergoing renovation. Wild boars dug up 21 mortar shells from World War Two that had been buried in a Polish forest. The unexploded ordnance has now been safely removed without harm to either the animals or humans https://t.co/W9kaPr1BNw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Russia condemns Poland’s “sacrilegious” demolition of Soviet monument
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Russia has criticised the demolition of a Soviet-era monument in Poland, calling the decision “sacrilegious” and a “flagrant violation” of an agreement between the two countries on respecting places of remembrance. However, Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), which financed the demolition, says that the monument was a “Soviet propaganda object” that was removed under a law requiring the “decommunisation” of public spaces. On Friday, around 150 residents in Pyrzyce, a town of 12,000 in northwestern Poland, gathered to watch the demolition of a monument to the Red Army that had stood there for decades. Initially, a memorial had been established in the town alongside a cemetery for Red Army soldiers in the immediate aftermath of World War Two, when the Soviets had driven the Nazi German occupiers out of Poland but then introduced a new communist government of their own. However, the soldiers’ remains were later moved to a military cemetery elsewhere in the region and the monument itself was redesigned and moved to another location within Pyrzyce. Its final form, created in 1984, was a huge rectangular concrete structure weighing several hundred tons and featuring a relief depicting the head of a Soviet soldier. A plaque said “Eternal glory to the fallen heroes 1941-1945” (a timeline that ignores the Soviet invasion and occupation of parts of Poland in 1939). Such Soviet monuments remained in many Polish towns and cities long after the fall of communism in 1989. In 2016, the then-ruling national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government introduced a law requiring local authorities to “decommunise” public spaces by removing objects and names that “propagate communism”. However, only in 2022, after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, did the removal of Soviet-era monuments gather pace, with dozens demolished since then. Those efforts were led by the IPN, in particular during the time that the institute was headed by Karol Nawrocki between 2021 and last year, when he was elected president of Poland. Another Soviet memorial has been demolished in Poland – the 43rd since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. "We say ‘no’ to Russians who believe these lands somehow belong to their sphere of influence,” declared the Institute of National Remembrance https://t.co/aG9VQVlUQI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 12, 2025 At the start of this year, the local authorities in Pyrzyce began public consultations on removing their Soviet memorial, finding that a majority were in favour of the move, according to the IPN. In February, the town council voted to remove the monument. It will now be replaced with a new one commemorating Polish independence. “We are aware that this change evokes various, often very strong, emotions among residents,” wrote the local authorities on social media. “We respect both the voices of those supporting the actions taken and those who differ in their assessment of the current monument and its place in the history of Pyrzyce.” “We hope that independence – as a paramount value for all Poles – will unite residents beyond differences of opinion and assessment of the past. We want the emerging space to be a space of shared remembrance, reflection, and a dignified celebration of the most important national ceremonies.” The removal of the monument drew condemnation from the Russian embassy in Warsaw, which announced on Monday that it had lodged a formal protest. It called the decision the “latest sacrilegious step by the Polish authorities” and said that it “constitutes a direct and flagrant violation” of a 1994 agreement between Poland and Russia on respect for graves and other places of memory. “The illegal dismantling of monuments is an overt attempt to falsify history, to erase from the consciousness of the Polish nation the memory of the heroism of Soviet soldiers,” added the embassy. ⚡️Komentarz Ambasady Rosji w Polsce 31 lipca 2026 r. w Pyrzycach (województwo zachodniopomorskie) na podstawie decyzji władz polskich został przeprowadzony demontaż pomnika ku czci poległych w latach 1941–1945 bohaterów – żołnierzy radzieckich. ❗️Ten kolejny świętokradczy krok… pic.twitter.com/cKhfFxIL9s — Russian Embassy, PL (@rusemb_pl) August 3, 2026 In response to such complaints from Russia, Poland has regularly pointed out that the 1994 agreement relates to graves and war cemeteries, not separate monuments and symbols, which can be legally removed. The IPN notes that such monuments were “Soviet propaganda objects”, designed to support the Moscow-backed communist regime, rather than genuine places of commemoration. Attending the demolition ceremony in Pyrzyce on Friday, IPN deputy president Karol Polejowski pointed out that the final version of the monument had been established in 1984 shortly after the period of martial law in Poland, when the authorities brutally clamped down on the democratic opposition. “Local communist activists, eager to curry favour with their Soviet masters, erected a monument honouring the Soviet army. This is not a symbol of liberation – it is a symbol of enslavement!” he declared, as the monument was torn down. 💪 Sowiecki obiekt propagandowy zostanie zastąpiony przez Pomnik Niepodległości, a przestrzeń wokół nowego monumentu stanie się godną sceną dla uroczystości patriotycznych. pic.twitter.com/5x4KEzG3Vb — Instytut Pamięci Narodowej (@ipngovpl) July 31, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland’s WIG20 stock market index hits record high
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s blue-chip WIG20 stock market index hit its highest ever level on Monday, surpassing a record that had stood for almost 19 years. The WIG20 has been Europe’s best-performing major blue-chip index so far this year. According to market monitoring website MarketScreener, the index has gained just under 25% since the start of 2026, ahead of the Dutch AEX (16.9%) and Sweden’s OMX Stockholm (14.9%). The WIG20, which tracks the 20 largest and most liquid companies on the Warsaw Stock Exchange (GPW), climbed to 3,963.21 points on Monday, breaking its previous record of 3,940.53 points set in October 2007. It continues a rally that began in October 2022, since when the index has almost tripled in value. “The market continues to be supported by solid economic growth, rising consumer spending, and the prospect of further EU investment,” commented analysts from BNP Paribas, a bank, quoted by business daily Parkiet. “However, after such strong gains, we do not expect the pace of appreciation to remain as high as in recent years,” they added. On Monday, the biggest boosts to the WIG20 index were provided by PGE, Poland’s biggest power producer, and KGHM, a Polish multinational mining company, with their shares rising 3.3% and 1.6%, respectively. The surge was also supported by improving risk appetite across global markets following signs of a de-escalation in tensions in the Middle East. This has pushed WIG20 above the levels last seen 19 years ago, just before the index plunged almost 70% during the 2008 global financial crisis, and then suffered another sell-off during the euro zone debt crisis in 2011. Reform of one of the pillars of Poland’s pension system in 2014, which reduced the role of open pension funds, ushered in years of market stagnation and left the index struggling to meaningfully rebound in the following years. Another decline came during the COVID-19 pandemic and then in the aftermath of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. In October 2022, however, the WIG20 started its rebound, rising by 195% since then. More than 30 Polish-listed companies have doubled in value over the past three years, including large-cap stocks such as Orlen, PKO BP, Bank Pekao, KGHM and Tauron, according to an analysis by economic journalist Rafał Hirsch published by news service WNP. Polish state energy firm Orlen has seen its market valuation rise to its highest ever level, and surpass Russia’s Gazprom for the first time https://t.co/w3po4izshJ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 12, 2026 BNP Paribas’s analysts, however, note that, “despite a long-term upward trend and reaching record highs”, the Polish stock market “is still valued below many other European markets”. “Our stock market…remains significantly cheaper than the US market and most European markets, but at the same time, when viewed against its own historical performance, it is now relatively highly valued,” they said. Poland’s main stock index, the broader WIG, also closed on Monday at a record high of 148,428 points, having hit several records in recent months. Poland’s benchmark WIG stock index has passed the 100,000-point mark for the first time. Meanwhile, the Warsaw Stock Exchange has been the world’s best performing so far this year "It is a clear signal of the strength of our economy," says the PM's office https://t.co/fIgGWOLLn8 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 25, 2025 Analysts warn, however, that unlike in the case of WIG, the WIG20’s record may prove short-lived because the benchmark is a price index, which excludes dividends. When companies in the index pay dividends, their share prices usually fall by about the same amount, which automatically pulls the index down even if nothing has changed in the companies themselves. Monday was the last day investors could buy shares in PKO BP and qualify for this year’s dividend. From Tuesday, the bank’s shares will trade ex-dividend, a move expected to reduce the WIG20 by about 0.8% because of PKO BP’s large weighting in the index. World.title: Prague to Restore Tram Service Between Holešovice and City Center
World.content:
Residents of Prague 7 will regain a tram connection between Holešovice and the city center from September, with tram line 5 set to operate through the district and continue toward Wenceslas Square.

The change follows months of pressure from Prague 7 officials and local residents, who have called for better tram connections since the cancellation of line 14.

The district had previously requested either the return of line 14 or the introduction of an equivalent service and organized a petition supporting the demand.



The new arrangement will initially be temporary. According to the Prague Integrated Transport (PID) system, two trams will operate on the route at least through December 2026.

Line 5 to replace temporary route

The new service is linked to planned transport changes in Žižkov. Because of a traffic closure there, tram line 34 will be replaced by line 5 in Holešovice.

At Holešovice train station, line 5 will connect with line 6, effectively creating a continuous service between the two routes. Trams will run from the station through the Holešovice area, past the market and across Vltavská Street before continuing toward Wenceslas Square and other parts of central Prague.

For passengers in Holešovice, the move restores a connection that was lost when line 14 was discontinued.

Service could change again next year

The situation between January and June 2027 has not yet been fully settled. According to PID, the final arrangement will depend in part on discussions between the incoming leaderships of Prague 3 and Prague 7.

Maintaining the additional tram service in Holešovice during that period could require limited reductions elsewhere in Prague 3. Another option would be to temporarily return to the existing arrangement using combined tram lines 6 and 34.

PID has warned that permanently combining lines 5 and 6 could also create delays at both ends of the route. Such a change could affect passengers travelling through Prague 2 and Prague 5, even though it would provide the direct connection sought by Prague 7.

World.title: “Ivan, Go Home!” Rally to Take Place Outside Russian Embassy in Prague
World.content:
A Czech-Ukrainian rally will take place outside the Russian Embassy in Prague on August 20 to mark the 58th anniversary of the Soviet-led invasion of Czechoslovakia.

The event, titled “Ivan, Go Home!”, is scheduled to begin at 6 p.m. on Thursday, August 20, at Boris Němcova Square in Prague 6.

The rally comes one day before the anniversary of the night of August 20-21, 1968, when troops from five Warsaw Pact countries entered Czechoslovakia to crush the Prague Spring reform movement.



The invasion brought an end to the country’s attempt to pursue a more liberal form of socialism and was followed by two decades of political repression and Soviet military presence.

The event is being organized jointly by People in Need (Člověk v tísni), Memory of the People (Paměť národa), Million Moments for Democracy (Milion chvilek pro demokracii), and the European Congress of Ukrainians.

Organizers say the rally will connect the historical experience of the Soviet occupation with Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine.

Participants will gather to remember those killed or persecuted following the 1968 invasion and the people who lived under the communist regime that followed. The organizers also plan to express support for Ukraine and draw attention to what they describe as the continuing use of imperial violence by Russia.

The choice of the rally’s name refers to one of the best-known slogans associated with the 1968 invasion. “Ivan, go home!” appeared on posters, walls, buildings and military vehicles as Czechoslovaks protested against the foreign troops occupying the country.

The invasion halted those reforms. Soviet troops remained in Czechoslovakia until the end of the communist era, while the subsequent period of “normalization” brought censorship, political purges and restrictions on civil liberties.

World.title: World of Warcraft Film Ibelin to Shoot in Prague
World.content:
Production of Ibelin, a new film based on the life of Norwegian World of Warcraft player Mats Steen, is moving to Prague this summer.

Filming is expected to take place at Barrandov Studios from early August through early October, following the production’s spring shoot in Norway.

The film is not connected to the 2016 Hollywood movie Warcraft. Instead, it tells the real-life story of Steen, who lived with Duchenne muscular dystrophy and built friendships, relationships and a social life inside the online world of World of Warcraft.



The Prague production is reportedly seeking extras for roles including blacksmiths, guards and innkeepers. The casting suggests that parts of the film set in the game’s fictional world could be filmed in the Czech Republic. The producers have not yet officially confirmed which scenes will be shot in Prague.

Charlie Plummer leads the cast

American actor Charlie Plummer will portray Mats Steen. Toni Collette and Stephen Graham will play his parents, while the supporting cast includes Bill Nighy, Isabela Merced, Maisy Stella, John Bradley and Ivanna Sakhno.

The film will be directed by Norwegian filmmaker Morten Tyldum, whose credits include The Imitation Game and the science-fiction film Passengers.

At the center of the story is the difference between Steen’s increasingly restricted physical existence and the freedom he experienced online. His character, known in World of Warcraft as Ibelin, became an important figure to people he met through the game.

One of Norway’s largest film projects

The Prague shoot is part of an international production with a reported budget of CZK 1 billion.

According to the Norwegian Film Institute, the project received 20 million Norwegian kroner in production support.

Ibelin is being produced by Vendôme Pictures, Pathé and Neby-Tyldum as an international co-production. The Norwegian Film Institute describes it as an English-language drama with a planned running time of around two hours.

The film is being developed for theatrical release, with its premiere currently expected in the third quarter of 2027.

World.title: GALLERY: Time Capsule Buried Beneath Prague’s Wenceslas Square Tramline
World.content:
A time capsule containing different items, newspapers and messages documenting life in 2026 has been buried beneath Prague’s reconstructed Wenceslas Square.

The capsule was placed on Wednesday, August 5, near the statue of St. Wenceslas as work continues on the upper section of the square.

The Prague New Town Association, which is involved in activities around the statue and the surrounding area, organised the ceremony.

The date was not originally chosen for its historical significance. Construction work ultimately determined both the day and the location of the burial. But the association later discovered that August 5 also marks the 60th anniversary of the release of the Beatles’ Revolver album.

“We were wondering what made August 5 go down in history. Then we found out that it was 60 years ago that the Beatles released their famous album Revolver. So now we are leaving a message here for future generations,” said Monika Vlková, the association’s executive director.



The box, measuring 60 by 40 by 23.5 centimetres and weighing about eight kilograms, was then taken to a prepared pit beside the statue. Workers had excavated the hole to a depth of around 1.7 metres, where the capsule was placed before the site was covered.

The container had been wrapped in transparent protective film, as had its contents.

The collection includes coins, newspapers published during the first week of August 2026, T-shirts, badges and written messages. It also contains proposals submitted by architects during the competition for the redesign of Wenceslas Square.

The box reportedly also holds a hammer and a beer glass.

The objects are accompanied by a 20-page report describing everyday life in the Czech capital in 2026. The capsule also contains USB drives with digital material documenting the period of the Covid-19 pandemic and its effects on life in central Prague.

The capsule is intended to remain underground for decades. The association estimates that Wenceslas Square could undergo another major reconstruction in roughly 50 years, although nobody can predict when the next intervention will actually take place.

World.title: Czechia Tightens Temporary Protection Rules for Ukrainian Men Aged 23 to 60
World.content:
New rules affecting Ukrainian men seeking temporary protection in the Czech Republic will take effect on August 5, 2026.

Under the changes, men aged 23 to 60 applying for temporary protection will have to demonstrate that they are exempt from military service in Ukraine.

The requirement will apply to new applications and certain other applications for protection, but not to people who already hold valid temporary protection.



The Czech Interior Ministry says the new rules follow an EU Council decision published in the Official Journal of the European Union on August 4. The decision also extends temporary protection for people fleeing Russia’s war in Ukraine until March 31, 2028.

For applicants aged 23 to 60, military registration documents will be checked as part of the application process. Applicants will use Ukraine’s Reserv+ system to demonstrate their military status, with the electronic military registration document showing whether they are exempt from military service.

The rules are different for younger applicants. People aged 18 to 22 will only need to demonstrate that they are registered in the Reserv+ system.

The new requirement concerns people applying for temporary protection for the first time, as well as repeat applications and applications connected with family reunification. It does not apply to people who already have valid temporary protection.

The military-service requirement will also not be introduced as part of the regular extension process. Ukrainians whose temporary protection is already valid will therefore not have to provide this additional documentation when extending their status through March 2028.

Interior Minister Lubomír Metnar said the Czech government had pushed for stricter conditions for new applicants. According to the ministry, the change is expected to reduce the number of new arrivals and ease pressure on public services, including health care and social security.

World.title: Filming of American Spy Series to Bring Restrictions to Prague 7
World.content:
Filming for the American series Birdwatcher will take place at the Prague 7 tax office on Kapitána Jaroše Embankment from August 8 to 24, bringing temporary restrictions to the area.

The production will use the tax office building at Kapitána Jaroše Embankment 1000/7, while part of the sidewalk outside the building will be closed to accommodate filming equipment.

The restrictions will not affect the normal operation of the tax office.



Drivers should also expect temporary parking restrictions on nearby Na Ovčinách Street. Vehicles will still be allowed to pass through the street, but parking will be prohibited during the designated filming periods.

The restrictions will not be in force continuously throughout the filming period. They will apply only on specific dates, with Prague 7 publishing a map showing the affected areas and individual dates on its website.

Prague has become a major filming location

Birdwatcher is an American spy fantasy series set during the Cold War. The production is being led by Legendary and Apple TV, with Andy Goddard directing. Wyatt Russell plays the lead role.

The story follows Colonel Lee Shaw as he embarks on a covert mission behind enemy lines to prevent the Soviet Union from unleashing a new Titan capable of devastating the United States and altering the balance of the Cold War.

The series is set in the 20th century against the backdrop of the Cold War, and parts of the production are being filmed in Prague.

Czech production company Stillking Films is handling the local production. The company has previously worked on major international productions filmed in the Czech capital, including The Gray Man.

World.title: Seven Prague Rooftops to Visit Before Summer Ends
World.content:
Summer is already moving on, and Prague’s rooftop season won’t last much longer.

August is the time to make the most of the city’s terraces, sunset views and outdoor events before they disappear for another year.

Here are seven rooftops and terraces worth visiting before autumn arrives.



1. REASON at Masaryčka

Eleven floors above Masaryk Station, REASON offers one of Prague’s newest rooftop dining spots, with views over the city and the Zaha Hadid-designed Masaryčka development.

This summer, its terrace is also home to the seasonal Frerejean Frères Champagne Bar, serving champagne by the glass, cocktails, oysters and light bites. The menu includes THE REASON KIR, made with herbs grown on the rooftop.

This summer: Champagne, oysters and cocktails above Masaryčka.

2. W Prague – ABOVE Rooftop

ABOVE Rooftop at W Prague brings a Mediterranean feel to the top of Wenceslas Square.

The daily Mediterranean Hour runs from 5 to 6 PM, with two spritzes and a Taste of the Mediterranean platter for CZK 990. Oysters are also served from Thursday to Saturday, alongside a programme of summer events and pop-ups.

This summer: Mediterranean Hour, sunset drinks and oysters in the centre.

3. MINUTY Rooftop Terrace

The rooftop at Fairmont Golden Prague offers views across Pařížská, Letná and the city centre from nine floors up.

MINUTY Rooftop Terrace by Golden Eye focuses on champagne, oysters, caviar and cocktails. The terrace is seasonal and is expected to remain open until September, weather permitting.

This summer: Champagne, oysters and caviar with a view.

4. Sky Lounge 360°

For the view alone, Sky Lounge 360° is hard to beat. The rooftop looks across Prague’s historic centre and becomes livelier during the summer months, with DJs, sunset events and Prague Rooftop Festival activities.

It is more about drinks and atmosphere than a long dinner — a good option for an evening that starts at sunset and continues after dark.

This summer: Sunset events, DJs and panoramic views.

5. The Cloud One Rooftop

The Cloud One Prague on Hybernská has its own rooftop cocktail bar overlooking the Masaryčka area.

The relaxed terrace works well for an after-work drink, while summer events bring DJs and a livelier atmosphere at sunset. It has also joined the Prague Rooftop Festival programme.

And if you want to make a night of it, REASON is just a short walk away.

This summer: Cocktails, sunset events and views of Masaryčka.

6. Casablanca Sky Bar

On the sixth floor of The President Hotel, Casablanca Sky Bar looks out over the Vltava and Prague skyline.

With DJs, cocktails and regular sunset events, it has more of a party atmosphere than a traditional hotel rooftop. It is also one of the venues taking part in the Prague Rooftop Festival.

This summer: DJs, cocktails and sunset parties above the Vltava.

7. Monkey Bar

Monkey Bar at Falkensteiner Hotel Prague is a quieter alternative, with a green, jungle-style terrace close to the main railway station.

Every Thursday until the end of August, the terrace hosts BBQ & Beats, combining barbecue, live music and summer drinks. Frozen margaritas are also on the menu.

For daytime plans, there is Jungle Brunch, including a bottomless mimosa option.

This summer: BBQ & Beats every Thursday through August.

World.title: Prague Kettlebell Brand Železná Koule Opens 600-Square-Metre Gym in Karlín
World.content:
Czech kettlebell training brand Železná koule has opened its largest location yet at Danube House in Prague’s Karlín district.

The new 600-square-metre gym expands the brand’s presence in Prague and comes ahead of the next edition of its flagship Amazing 12 fitness programme.

Železná koule has built a community around kettlebell training and coached workouts rather than the traditional self-service gym model. The company says more than 20,000 people have trained through its programmes since its launch.

At its Karlín location, members train under the guidance of coaches in small groups. The approach is designed to provide more personal instruction and a structured training environment, rather than simply giving members access to gym equipment.



The new location is also the latest venue for the company’s Amazing 12 programme, a 12-week fitness and body transformation course that combines regular training with nutrition guidance and ongoing support.

What is the Amazing 12 programme?

The programme is aimed at both people who are new to structured strength training and more experienced gym-goers looking for a more organised approach to their workouts.

Although the programme itself lasts 12 weeks, participants first complete a preparation week, making 13 weeks in total. During the programme, they take part in 64 training sessions, with one-hour workouts held every weekday under the supervision of a coach.

Groups are limited to a maximum of five participants, allowing coaches to work closely with each person throughout the programme.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Železná koule (@zelezna_koule)

The programme is designed to provide a structured routine covering exercise, nutrition and recovery, with progress tracked throughout the 12 weeks.

The next Amazing 12 programme starts on August 31, 2026, with places available at the new Karlín location as well as Železná koule gyms in Smíchov and Strašnice.

The Karlín opening is part of the continued expansion of a Czech fitness brand that has developed a following around kettlebell-based training and small-group coaching. For people unfamiliar with the name, Železná kloule roughly translates from Czech as “iron ball,” referring to the kettlebell at the centre of its training approach.

More information about the Amazing 12 programme, including registration, is available at amazing12.cz.

World.title: Soviet shell, cannonball and German Panzerfaust warheads found near Budapest university
World.content:
Hungarian Army bomb-disposal experts removed explosives from the Danube embankments near the Raoul Wallenberg Holocaust Memorial Park and the Budapest University of Technology early on Friday, the armed forces’ bomb-disposal unit said.

Earlier reports said a Soviet 203mm concrete-piercing shell from the Second World War and a cannonball believed to date from the 19th century had been found near the Raoul Wallenberg embankment. A German Second World War ammunition container discovered near the university held eight Panzerfaust launching tubes, their Faustpatrone warheads and detonators, MTI wrote.

The unit said the Soviet shell was too corroded to be defused on site. It was therefore taken under police escort to a designated demolition area, where it will be destroyed along with the other explosives.For the operation, Szabadság Bridge and the embankments, university buildings and a petrol station on the Buda side were temporarily closed early on Friday. Police lifted the restrictions and reopened the roads once the operation had been completed.

World.title: Plunging inflation in Hungary: analysts surprised, but how long can the favourable trend last?
World.content:
In recent years, we had grown used to inflation figures bringing unpleasant news: rising prices, soaring food bills or ever more expensive fuel. For the first time in a long while, however, Hungary’s inflation rate can be discussed in a positive context, having fallen to a ten-year low. Experts explain what lies behind the plunge – and what may be in store over the coming months and year.

Even experts surprised by low inflation

The public’s experience of prices in recent years could be summed up as follows: although everyone was earning more in nominal terms – something Orbán’s governments were only too keen to boast about – our money somehow bought less and less. High wage growth was accompanied by even higher price rises, with some sectors becoming prohibitively expensive. The property market alone is enough to illustrate the point.

Property prices in Hungary rose between 235-240% between 2016 and 2026. The growth is even bigger in Budapest. Photo: depositphotos.com

For the first time in many years, shoppers may now be finding that their money goes further in certain cases. One reason is that Hungary’s inflation rate has fallen to a ten-year low – a development that also caught Hungarian experts by surprise. Annual inflation stood at just 1.2 per cent in July, well below the 1.5 per cent previously forecast. According to portfolio.hu, Hungary has not seen inflation this low since 2016. Analysts had expected annual inflation of 1.5 per cent in July, following figures of 1.7 per cent in June, 1.8 per cent in May and 2.1 per cent in April.

Photo: MTI

The economic news website attributed the sharp slowdown in inflation to three factors:

favourable trends in food prices; calmer conditions in fuel markets; a strong forint.

Reasons for concern remain

The newspaper also pointed out that core inflation rose by 0.3 per cent, which is not low. Moreover, inflation plunged because of factors beyond the authorities’ control – external forces that could change in the future.

Services have also become significantly more expensive. Major telecommunications and financial-services providers have now raised their prices after exercising “restraint” before the election, at the request of the previous government. According to portfolio.hu, this caused a “smaller price shock” across the services sector.

The central bank could cut interest rates further in the future, the outlet said. The only reasons for caution, at most, would be turbulent geopolitical developments and volatility in energy markets.

What experts expect next

Gábor Regős, chief economist at Gránit Fund Management, said that the strong forint, low inflation expectations and rising business confidence had combined to create an environment of subdued inflation, MTI reports. The National Bank of Hungary could therefore cut its base rate to 5 per cent in September, even if the forint continues to weaken.

Orsolya Nyeste, Erste Bank’s chief macroeconomic analyst, said July’s figure could prove to be the annual low. Inflation may edge up from August onwards, but is expected to remain below the central bank’s 3 per cent target.

Photo: Daily News Hungary

Dávid Németh, chief analyst at K&H Bank, emphasised that rising gross wages had pushed up the cost of services. He expects inflation to remain below 2 per cent for the rest of the year, with the annual average likely to come in at around 1.8 per cent.

If you missed: Hungary’s central bank governor sends a strong message about the country’s financial position

Dániel Molnár, chief analyst at the GFÜ Centre for Economic Analysis, said the poor harvest caused by drought could feed through into food prices. The current energy crisis, meanwhile, is forcing companies to reassess how they calculate their energy costs. Inflation is likely to accelerate next year, he predicted, reaching around 3 per cent.

Record fall in food prices

The National Trade Association highlighted a 4.4 per cent fall in food prices, which is almost certainly a record. It said the decline was not the result of the margin cap, but of the favourable exchange rate of the forint and positive domestic and international market trends. These had more than offset the increase resulting from rising energy costs.

World.title: MÁV railway group preparing with extra services for the Sziget Festival – details

After a short walk from Filatorigát, the island can be reached via the K Bridge, it added.

World.title: What could he have found? Georgian authorities send home Hungarian journalist who criticised Orbán-friendly government
World.content:
The Hungarian journalist who has reported extensively on the Georgian Dream government’s excesses – and its ever-closer ties to the Orbán administration and Moscow – has been effectively expelled from the Caucasian country. Local authorities cite irregularities in his residence permit; back home, newspapers suggest he may have stumbled upon something awkward in the nexus between the Orbán system and the Georgian ruling party, which is cultivating increasingly warm relations with Russia.

Detained, then sent home

László Róbert Mézes, a Hungarian journalist who has lived in the country for years and regularly filed reports for Magyar Hang on the country’s political crisis, anti-government protests and Georgian Dream’s grip on power, was taken into custody in Tbilisi before being deported. The Georgian Interior Ministry said Mézes was in the country “without legal grounds” and had exceeded the permitted period of stay, invoking a provision of the aliens’ law that allows detention where there is a risk of absconding. His lawyer maintained that his client’s stay was lawful. Mézes ultimately left the country at his own expense, escorted to the airport by migration officials.

Mézes leaves Georgia – at his own expense:

The case is notable not least because Mézes is no ordinary Hungarian correspondent based in Georgia: he has been an outspoken critic of Georgian Dream. For Magyar Hang, reporting from Tbilisi, he wrote repeatedly on the so-called “foreign agents” law – a near word‑for‑word translation of the Russian model – and on the suffocation of civil society and independent media, the blocking of voting rights for the diaspora (some one million of Georgia’s five million citizens, whose remittances underpin the economy), the imprisonment of opposition politicians and critical journalists, and the near‑constant street protests. He also reported for Magyar Hang that Prime Ministers Orbán and Fico were obstructing EU moves towards targeted sanctions against Georgian political leaders.

On the 612th day of protests following the 2024 election, he published these photographs last Saturday:

Beaten in Tbilisi – and he told Orbán what he thought

In October 2024, during Viktor Orbán’s visit to Tbilisi, Mézes shouted at the Hungarian Prime Minister in Hungarian that he had come to legitimise “stolen elections”, and asked whether he was proud that Georgian Dream was copying Fidesz. Orbán, alone among EU leaders, congratulated the victors almost immediately after the poll, while the rest of the EU (save Slovakia), the European Parliament, the Georgian President and the opposition all rejected the result. Mézes’s situation deteriorated further in September 2025: while working as a journalist at an anti-government demonstration, he was attacked by Georgian Dream activists outside the party headquarters. He was beaten, required stitches to his face and sustained hand injuries; Georgian authorities later formally recognised him as a victim.

In this post, featuring a photograph with Péter Magyar, he informed his Georgian followers that Péter Magyar would be the next Prime Minister:

A pro‑Russian turn

Although the Caucasian country was at war with Russia in 2008 over South Ossetia and Abkhazia – territories occupied by Moscow and subsequently recognised as independent states – the Georgian Dream party has lately been cultivating conspicuously pragmatic relations with Putin’s Russia. The “foreign agents” law, passed in 2024 on the Russian model, targeted critical NGOs and media outlets; in November 2024 the government announced it would not commence EU accession talks until 2028. Tbilisi has not joined sanctions against Russia and continues to trade with Moscow, even though diplomatic relations have never been restored since the 2008 war.

If you missed: Georgian-Israeli businessman linked to former propaganda minister Rogán allegedly sought to gain access to key aide of PM Péter Magyar

Good relations to be maintained, PM Péter Magyar pledges

Péter Magyar, Hungary’s prime minister-elect, said at a press conference shortly after the 12 April election that he would maintain good relations with Georgia. Asked by a reporter from the pro-government Georgian broadcaster Rustavi 2, Magyar said that the fact Viktor Orbán’s government had forged strong ties with a country in the Balkans – or anywhere else – did not mean Hungary would have a less close relationship with that country.

“But if Hungary has bad relations with a country, we will improve them, because it is in our shared interest to work together, to co-operate and to prosper together,” he added, according to civil.ge. Magyar also said he was open to visiting Tbilisi and looked forward to working with the Georgian government.

“But we are not going to interfere in the internal affairs of other countries. We will not try to influence elections in your country, North Macedonia or anywhere else. That’s not our style, and it is not the job of any European government. Everyone is elected to support and represent the electorate of their own country,” he said.

The media outlet noted that Irakli Kobakhidze, Georgia’s prime minister, had visited Hungary on 21 March to address CPAC Budapest and express his support for Mr Orbán. On 13 April, following the Tisza party’s victory in Hungary’s general election, the Georgian Government congratulated Mr Magyar and his party, while thanking Orbán for his “outstanding and steadfast support for Georgia’s national interests and the Georgian people over the years”.

World.title: PM Magyar shared good news about voluntary consumption cuts as heat records were broken again
World.content:
There will be no need for voluntary consumption cuts from Friday, PM Péter Magyar announced on his Facebook page on Thursday evening.

Magyar said: “Together, we did it, and we protected our country’s energy security. Thank you, Hungary!” He added that the Defence Council’s decisions will be announced on Friday morning.

Multiple heat records, along with a wind-speed record, were broken on Thursday, the weather service HungaroMet said on Facebook, citing preliminary data. The new national daytime heat record was recorded in Kiskunfélegyháza, where the temperature reached 41.8 degrees Celsius, surpassing the previous record of 40.2 C set in Orosháza in 1905.

Budapest also saw a new daytime and all-time heat record of 41.6 C, recorded at the Ujpest station. The previous daily record for the capital was 37.8 C in 2012 at the Budapest city centre station, while the previous absolute record was set on Wednesday at the Újpest station.

Meanwhile, a thunderstorm also led to a new daily wind-speed record in Szolnok, where a gust of 113kmh was recorded. The previous daily wind record was 107kmh in Körösladány in 2010.

World.title: PM Magyar: Orbán knew that Hungary’s energy system was on the brink of collapse, but failed to act
World.content:
Prime Minister Péter Magyar on Thursday accused the former prime minister, Viktor Orbán, of knowing that Hungary’s energy system was on the brink of collapse but failing to act.

Hungary could not provide as much electricity as Orbán promised

In a video posted on Facebook, Magyar quoted a 2022 bill submitted by the previous government, which stated that Hungary’s energy supply was on the edge of a precipice because the government had burdened the system with a “full Paks-worth” of electricity demand to benefit major investors, MTI wrote.

“In other words, they promised more electricity to major industrial players, often battery investment projects, than the domestic energy system could safely provide,” the prime minister said. Magyar said Hungary needed “an energy and water revolution”, including “unprecedented development” of energy storage capacities and the electricity grid.

Negative prices for solar energy

Magyar noted that while Hungary has over 8,800MW of solar capacity, its energy storage capacity is only 980MW, meaning the country can produce roughly nine times more energy from the sun than its storage facilities can absorb at any given moment. As a result, Hungary often produces surplus energy during sunny periods, which it can only sell at minimal or even negative prices, yet it struggles to store enough for night-time or cloudier conditions, he explained.

Despite this, he said, the Orbán government had consistently removed requirements for storage capacity development from regulations and subsidy programmes for industrial and residential solar projects. He vowed that the current government would develop energy storage capacity to reduce Hungary’s import dependence.

Magyar also blamed the previous government for the underdevelopment of the electricity grid. He said that on Friday, the government will announce the results of a nearly 600 billion forint (EUR 1.7bn) EU-funded tender to develop the electricity grid, enabling the construction of new power lines, substations and higher-capacity transformers. “Hungary’s energy will be safer, cheaper and increasingly domestic,” he said.

If you missed – Danube water crisis: hotel ships and cargo vessels stranded in Hungary

Water and energy crises almost over

Referring to the current heatwave and drought, which has led to a reduction in output of the Paks plant, the prime minister noted that major industrial consumers are still expected to voluntarily reduce energy consumption, and he thanked the public for avoiding or rescheduling electricity use between 5pm and 10pm.

Photo: Anadolu/Robert Nemeti

Magyar added that the Danube’s water level at Paks has risen by 11cm since Sunday, and rain is currently falling in the Austrian catchment areas. However, this will likely not be enough to fully restore Hungary’s nuclear power plant, and a new period of dry, hot weather is expected next week, meaning “we will have to count every centimetre again,” he said.

World.title: Budapest city centre roads to be closed this morning after explosives found in the Danube
World.content:
Szabadság Bridge and the Buda embankments near the Budapest University of Technology and Economics (BME) will be temporarily closed early Friday morning due to the removal of explosive devices from the Danube, the Hungarian Armed Forces’ bomb disposal unit said on Thursday.

Last weekend, the unit received two reports of unexploded devices found near the Danube’s Raoul Wallenberg embankment and near the Valdemar and Nina Langlet embankment.

On Tuesday, a bomb disposal patrol identified the devices near the Raoul Wallenberg embankment as a Soviet-era 203mm concrete-piercing shell from the Second World War and a suspected 19th-century cannonball. Near BME, they identified a German Second World War-era supply container holding eight Panzerfaust launch tubes, their warheads and detonators.

Budapest, Szabadság Bridge. Source: John Woods/DNH

At 4 AM on Friday, Szabadság Bridge and the entire length of the Raoul Wallenberg embankment will be closed to remove the devices.

World.title: Danube water crisis: hotel ships and cargo vessels stranded in Hungary
World.content:
Eleven river cruise ships are currently waiting on the Hungarian stretch of the Danube because of exceptionally low water levels, while most cargo vessels have also been forced to halt operations, Hungary’s Ministry of Transport and Investment (KBM) told the Hungarian News Agency (MTI) on Wednesday.

10 cm needed between riverbed and hull

The ministry said low water levels were currently hampering the movement of deeper-draught vessels not only in Hungary but along the entire 2,412-kilometre navigable stretch of the river. For safety reasons, vessels must maintain a clearance of at least 10 centimetres between their hulls and the riverbed.

As a result, some cargo vessels can operate only after drastically reducing their loads, in some cases to just 10 to 20 per cent of their normal carrying capacity, the ministry said.

The authorities stressed that water-management agencies regularly survey the river, while the navigation authority issues official notices warning vessels about shoals where the standard navigable depth of 270 centimetres is no longer available.

A German cargo ship in Budapest. Photo: Creative Commons CC BY-SA 3.0

Several stretches of the Hungarian Danube too shallow

The water level determines the maximum draught that can safely be accommodated on each section of the river. At the current levels, several stretches of the Hungarian Danube have become too shallow for normal commercial navigation.

If you missed: Did the Danube run dry in Budapest and Paks because the Slovaks diverted it?

The navigation authority is not imposing a blanket restriction on shipping because of the low water levels. Instead, the master of each vessel is responsible for deciding whether it is safe to proceed, taking into account the latest published water levels and information on shoals, as well as the vessel’s own draught, the ministry said.

The number of stranded river cruise ships has nevertheless fallen in recent days. According to an earlier statement from the ministry, 15 cruise ships were still waiting on the Hungarian section of the Danube last Tuesday.

World.title: Romania’s eMAG to come under sole control of Naspers after EU approval
World.content:
The European Commission has approved, under the EU Merger Regulation, the acquisition of sole control over Dante International of Romania by South African investment fund Naspers Limited.

"The Commission concluded that the notified operation does not raise competition concerns, as the companies are not active on the same markets or on markets that are in a vertical relationship, and the impact on the market structure is limited. The transaction was examined under the simplified merger control procedure," the EC stated in a press release.

Last month, businessman Iulian Stanciu announced the sale of his stake in the eMAG Group to global consumer internet and technology investment group Prosus, 17 years after taking over the company and 14 years after signing the partnership with Naspers, the owner of Prosus.

After the sale, eMAG will continue its development and extensive investment plans, with RON 1.2 billion budgeted in this fiscal year alone for technology, logistics and financial services, with the support of Prosus and an experienced management team, company representatives stated. They also noted the regional growth potential of e-commerce, which remains significant, with growth rates of up to three times in the coming years, compared to the current penetration rate of 11-12% of total retail.

"The investments will be directed predominantly toward logistics and delivery infrastructure, AI and financial services, consolidating the foundation for a strong digital economy in the region. I want to thank Iulian for his dedication, vision, and for keeping us focused on the customer and on continuous personal development," said at that time Tudor Manea, CEO of eMAG Group, cited by News.ro.

At group level, eMAG recorded in fiscal year 2025 a turnover of RON 11.4 billion (USD 2.64 billion), up 11% compared with the previous financial year. The eMAG Group portfolio includes the eMAG brand, the Fashion Days online store, Romania’s 100% online hypermarket Freshful, the IT and electronics specialist store PC Garage, the Romanian national and international express courier company Sameday, the Depanero repair workshop, the most relevant recommerce platform in South-Eastern Europe Flip, as well as the financial services company HeyBlu.

World.title: Eurostat: Romania allocated only EUR 18.8 per inhabitant to R&D in 2025, lower than in 2015
World.content:
European governments allocated an estimated EUR 130.2 billion, or 0.69% of their combined GDP, to research and development in 2025, according to a Eurostat analysis published on Friday, August 7.

The sum represents an increase of 2.4% compared to 2024 (EUR 127.14 billion) and an increase of 60.5% compared to 2015 (EUR 81.13 billion).

In 2025, on average, government budget allocations for research and development at EU level amounted to EUR 288.9 per inhabitant, an increase of 57.7% compared to 2015 (EUR 183.2 per inhabitant). Luxembourg (EUR 917.2 per inhabitant) recorded the highest budget allocations for research and development per capita among the EU member countries. It was followed by Denmark (EUR 627.1) and Germany (EUR 553.5).

At the opposite end, the lowest values were recorded in Romania (EUR 18.8), Hungary (EUR 57.4) and Malta (EUR 73.7). Moreover, compared to 2015, Romania (-9.6%) was the only EU country that recorded a decrease in budget allocations for research and development expressed in euros per inhabitant, from EUR 20.8 in 2015 to EUR 18.8 in 2025.

The other EU countries recorded increases ranging from +14.7% in Sweden (from EUR 363.4 per inhabitant in 2015 to EUR 416.7 in 2025) to +495.5% in Bulgaria (from EUR 15.5 to EUR 92.3).

As regards the distribution according to socio-economic objectives, 37.3% of the amount was allocated to the general advancement of knowledge, financed mainly through a global public grant known as public general university funds, used by public higher education institutions to support their activities. In addition, 18.4% of R&D funds were allocated to the general advancement of knowledge from sources other than the general university funds, 9.5% to industrial production and technology, 6.7% to health, and 5.8% to defense.

World.title: EIB lends EUR 100 million to BRD Sogelease to increase financing for businesses in Romania
World.content:
The European Investment Bank (EIB) is lending EUR 100 million to the leasing subsidiary of BRD Groupe Société Générale to expand financing for businesses in Romania.

The goal is to facilitate financing for Romanian SMEs and Mid-Caps, which face greater hurdles in accessing long-term funding than their counterparts in many other European Union countries, EIB said.

The operation will enable BRD Sogelease to provide funding to Romanian companies seeking business expansion, productivity improvements and sustainable development.

Of the total loan, 15% is earmarked for green projects such as energy efficiency, renewable energy and sustainable transport.

Around 80% of the EIB loan is projected to be deployed in less-developed areas known in the EU as “cohesion regions.”

The new operation builds on previous EIB loans to BRD Sogelease IFN that total EUR 305 million over the past decade.

“In today’s rapidly changing economy, access to finance is a key enabler of competitiveness,” said EIB Vice-President Ioannis Tsakiris. “By partnering with BRD Sogelease, we are mobilizing investment where it matters most: among Romanian entrepreneurs. This financing will help businesses become more resilient, more innovative and better prepared for the opportunities of tomorrow.”

“Our long-standing partnership with the European Investment Bank reflects a shared commitment to supporting the growth and resilience of the Romanian economy. This new financing facility will enable us to provide SMEs and Mid-Caps with enhanced access to long-term funding on attractive terms, helping them invest in expansion, innovation, productivity and sustainable development,” said BRD Sogelease GM Gabriel Mihai.

BRD Sogelease IFN SA is the leasing subsidiary of BRD Groupe Société Générale, one of the leading banks in Romania with total assets of RON 96.3 billion as of June 2026. Established in 2001, BRD Sogelease IFN provides financial lease and other asset-based financial solutions to over 10,000 SME and Small-Cap clients in Romania.
