World.title: Careless waste handling attracts rodents to the city
World.content:
The Põhja‑Tallinn district government is collecting tips about rat and mouse activity through mid‑August to direct pest control efforts to the most affected areas. Experts say careless waste handling encourages rodent spread.

Kadri Karnau, communications specialist at the Tallinn Environment and Public Works Department, said the city does not gather centralized statistics on rodent numbers because they cannot be reliably assessed. Still, residents' observations are welcome because they help identify larger colonies.

Rodent control in the capital is divided by areas of responsibility, meaning homeowners' associations play an important role. "When a colony is discovered, the first step is to speak with the private property owner or the homeowners' association, which is responsible for rodent control. The city and district government can only carry out control on areas they manage," Karnau said.

The Environment and Public Works Department uses rat poison placed in special plastic boxes. Karnau said districts do not conduct large‑scale preventive poisoning because it would pose a danger to pets, birds and people. Control is always targeted and based on specific nesting sites and movement paths.

Ettevõtmise eesmärk on leida üles kõige probleemsemad ja pahategelikud rotid. Autor/allikas: slyfox photography/Unsplash

Joosep Sarapuu, a zoologist at the Estonian Museum of Natural History, said local control will not eliminate rodents from the city. "It is not possible in practice to achieve 100‑percent eradication of rats. When one colony disappears, the area becomes freely accessible to newcomers again," he said.

Rat control is complicated by their biological behavior. They exhibit neophobia, meaning fear of new objects. When a plastic box with poison or a trap appears, rodents need time before they dare to approach it.

A common belief that colonies send their weakest members to test poison is not entirely accurate, Sarapuu said. "Dominant individuals do not check new things because they have established routes and a stable food supply. Lower‑ranking members are forced to look for new feeding sites and movement paths. That is why they are the first to encounter poison and traps," he said.

Joosep Sarapuu. Source: ERR

How can people keep rodents away from their homes? Sarapuu said summer is a good time to check a home's rodent‑proofing because pests try to enter houses when the weather gets cold. "You should find small gaps and openings where rats and mice can get inside and seal them carefully. Second, you must check food waste to make sure it is not easily accessible. In that case, rodents are likely to be fewer or not present at all," he said.

Karnau also said a tidy neighborhood is the best way to keep rodents away. "Trash rooms and waste containers must be kept in good condition and closed to prevent food waste from spreading into the surroundings. It is also wise to avoid feeding birds and squirrels and to keep the areas under bird feeders clean because fallen food attracts rodents," she said.

World.title: Expert: Talk of a direct Russian attack is extremely foolish
World.content:
Claims by anonymous American intelligence sources that a possible limited Russian attack against NATO may happen in the coming years are exaggerated speculation, said security expert Rainer Saks, former secretary general of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (2015-2020) and the Foreign Intellegence Service (2011-2015).

ERR: A U.S. intelligence assessment has been published by The Wall Street Journal, stating that Russian leader Vladimir Putin, whose invasion of Ukraine has stalled, could test NATO in the coming years by attacking one of the alliance's member states. The report mentions both cyberattacks and a limited ground incursion. What should we make of all this?

Rainer Saks: First of all, this is another classic case where anonymous sources have said something, fragments have been written down, but official comments are either unavailable or refused. It is a very broad and diffuse text.

As for these general assessments that Russia "could do something," there is no significant indication behind them that Russia is actually planning to do so. It is a hypothetical assessment that Russia could do this, that or the other. As long as Russia is not planning such actions, publishing assessments like this in the current context actually works very much in Russia's favor. Even the suggested time frame, from this autumn until 2029, is completely absurd.

Russia is certainly not making plans like that.

It is difficult to judge whether this was leaked by the U.S. government or is the initiative of an individual intelligence official. We will not speculate about that, but this is speculation rather than a report based on a concrete intelligence assessment.

The proposed actions — from cyberattacks to a limited military incursion — essentially cover the entire range of scenarios that could theoretically be considered. Therefore, I would not take this at present as a serious warning requiring the rapid implementation of countermeasures.

For example, Russia has been carrying out cyberattacks against NATO member states continuously since at least 2005–2006.

At the same time, NATO countries' responses have so far not been appropriate, because before the invasion of Ukraine, several European countries sought to engage Russia and develop energy cooperation instead. Examples of the kind of situation described in the intelligence report can also be found 15 to 20 years ago, so there is nothing new in it.

At the moment, publishing such a report works more to Russia's advantage, because Russia itself has not directly threatened NATO countries with any military action. Instead, a context is now being created that allows it to manipulate information even more than it has done so far.

In that sense, I think the text published by The Wall Street Journal is extremely foolish.

The article also points to indications that Russia is already testing NATO's response, for example, drones and missiles have fallen on the territory of Romania and Poland. This is presented as one indication that perhaps something is underway.

At the same time, those very countries have themselves said that they do not regard this as deliberate Russian action, but rather as accidental or technical incidents. I cannot say whether the official comments differ drastically from what is actually happening.

This is, of course, a problem because while active warfare is taking place in Ukraine, the possibility of, for example, Ukrainian drones ending up in allied territory or being shot down there is indeed an elevated risk.

There are only two main scenarios under which Russia would begin testing NATO's unity.

The first is that NATO has completely fallen apart internally. Although NATO's unity has suffered in several respects recently, there is no full political unity and there are sharp disagreements between different member states, it cannot be said that there is no unity at all. I would not yet go so far as to claim that NATO's collective defense has therefore been called into question.

The domestic political problems of member states and NATO's internal weakening are, in fact, the most likely scenario that could lead to a military confrontation between Russia and a NATO member state. At the moment, however, that process is clearly not advancing rapidly.

The second theoretical possibility is that if Russia truly decides to attack NATO militarily, it would first have to reorganize its forces. For such an attack — or even a test — to be genuinely supported, Russia would most likely have to carry out a mobilization. To some extent, that is theoretically possible after the State Duma elections, because the forces fighting against Ukraine have been unable to achieve success, and according to the Russian General Staff's calculations, there are too few troops.

In a situation where a full-scale war is still being fought in Ukraine, launching a new war against an even stronger opponent would, in my view, require Russia to declare martial law and carry out full-scale mobilization. That is something without which I do not believe Russia would proceed with very aggressive plans.

The article repeatedly refers to the fact that the Americans are running low on missile stockpiles because of operations in the Middle East and donations to Ukraine. Could it instead be that this article and the intelligence assessment are aimed at a domestic U.S. audience, to remind people of the need to replenish weapons stockpiles quickly?

That may indeed be the case. However, there is one important nuance here: the issue is not that the United States lacks certain types of missiles in its stockpiles, primarily air defense missiles and Tomahawk-type long-range strike weapons, of which too many have been expended against Iran. It is natural for stockpiles to decline during active military operations, but production is reportedly not keeping pace with what is needed. That is an embarrassing situation — what is the point of launching military operations if you cannot simultaneously replenish your stocks?

What is being overlooked, however, is that Russia has exactly the same problem, only even more severe. It also lacks sufficient air defense capabilities, as demonstrated by the success of Ukraine's long-range strikes. For example, this morning yet another large Wildberries warehouse, deep in the Urals some 1,800 kilometers from Ukraine, was set on fire.

Russia is in exactly the same position of weakness. Its entire missile capability is focused on Ukraine, and it is unable to carry out large-scale missile strikes on a daily basis. The war has lasted four years and has significantly exhausted Russia.

Of course, we can talk about hybrid attacks, but the conditions for Russia to launch a military incursion into NATO territory or start a military conflict with NATO are in no way favorable for Russia at present.

Why do you think intelligence assessments claiming that Russia is about to start testing NATO keep being published, when in reality they do not correspond to the facts?

I cannot answer that question. It is probably influenced by many different factors, ranging from incompetence and foolishness to domestic political objectives.

There is, of course, genuine reason to be concerned about the overall situation. There is nothing good about it. A major war is underway, and the governments of Europe and the United States have been unable to bring it to an end. That is indeed a very serious problem. Supporting Ukraine has also not been as successful as it should have been — a great deal has been done, but not enough.

A separate question is why European leaders have been unable to pull themselves together. Four years after the start of the full-scale war, they are still unable to produce enough of the military equipment that is needed. That is a very bad sign. In that sense, it is understandable that many people are seriously concerned about the situation and are trying to warn of possible negative developments.

World.title: Ministry review to map gaps in children's mental healthcare
World.content:
Estonia is reviewing how children move through mental health services to identify gaps, shorten waits and improve coordination across health, education and social care.

The Ministry of Social Affairs says children's access to mental health care is uneven, with long wait times, regional differences in access and little understanding of how young patients move between healthcare, schools and social services.

Now the ministry is seeking a clearer picture of the system to improve how kids receive mental healthcare.

The review follows a 2024 study that found Estonian schoolchildren's mental health has steadily worsened since 2010, with the sharpest decline among girls.

"Specialists' roles and responsibilities are not always clear, access to services varies by region, and long wait times delay care," said Krista Järv, a project manager in the ministry's Department of Children and Families.

She added that support can also break down during key transitions, such as starting school, moving between grade levels or aging out of children's services.

The Social Affairs Ministry is commissioning an 11-month study to map those gaps and design a future care pathway for children needing mental health support.

"The goal is to ensure kids receive timely, continuous care that meets their needs," Järv said.

Budget option, ideal option

The study will also propose ways to improve coordination between professionals, case management, information sharing and referrals between services, as well as examine whether legislative changes are needed and produce an implementation plan outlining responsibilities, timelines and recommended reforms.

To improve the chances that recommendations are adopted, the ministry has asked researchers to develop two options: one that could be implemented with existing resources and another, optimal solution requiring additional funding.

"The study may find that some recommendations can be implemented with existing resources, while others will require more funding," the ministry official noted.

The study is slated to cost up to €100,000, with results expected by mid-2027, after which any reforms would still require political decisions, cross-sector agreements and, where needed, additional funding.

World.title: Rescue Board official: I would not let children go to sea on a SUP board
World.content:
Children should never set out onto the water on a SUP board without an adult, while proper safety measures must be used when using them, a Rescue Board official said.

Stand up paddle (SUP) boards resemble surfboards but are considerably larger and thicker and, as their name suggests, are mainly propelled by paddling.

A recent rescue reported by Eesti Ekspress highlighted how changing conditions and missing safety equipment can quickly turn a normal SUP outing into a dangerous situation.

"People underestimate the risks. A SUP board seems like something very safe on the water, and people do not deploy enough safety equipment. A life jacket must be worn properly, otherwise it is no use, while the leash attached to the SUP board must be fastened to your leg," Rebecca Charlotte Rebane from the Rescue Board's (Päästeamet) Northern Rescue Center told Vikerraadio.

Rescuers also get callouts to cases where various other types of flotation devices, such as inflatable mattresses, sometimes called lilos, or even powered vessels, have drifted beyond what might be considered a safe distance from the shore. "Inflatable mattresses and pink flamingos, which people use to take fun pictures, are also popular. People do not realize the risks. Engine failures on boats and jet skis are also common," Rebane said.

The recent incident, which involved children, has highlighted the responsibility of parents, particularly in today's world, where people tend to have their heads buried in their phones. In fact, on this latter point, Rebane said, it seems to be more the case of children having to be responsible for their parents.

A person SUP boarding. Source: Pixabay / pasja1000

"Unfortunately, what I have noticed at the beach is that people go there with their children and then think, 'Now I can relax for a moment,' then pick up their phones. A minute or two is enough for the situation to become very dangerous. I have told my children that when we go to the beach together, they should make sure Mom is not on her phone. They are very good about that," Rebane added.

In the incident reported by Eesti Ekspress, three children drifted up to 400 meters offshore on a SUP board at Vainupea beach in Lääne-Viru County after strong winds carried them away. The children's mother and another woman were unable to reach them after swimming into the sea and had to call emergency services. The board later capsized, pitching everyone into the water before nearby kayakers, while a motorboat rescued the children and one of the adults. While the episode did not end in tragedy or even injury, rescue officials said the lack of life jackets, a safety leash, and a fin increased the danger and made the case a time-critical rescue.

If you witness people getting into difficulty on SUP boards or similar, and drifting offshore, the Rescue Board says you should:

• Call the emergency number, 112, immediately.

• Keep the individual(s) in sight at all times while waiting for rescuers to arrive.

• If possible, get another person to meet emergency responders and direct them to the location.

• Only attempt your own rescue if it is safe to do so, preferably wearing a life jacket, and avoid swimming long distances, particularly if you do not have a flotation device.

If you find yourself getting into difficulty on a SUP board, stay on or with the board and do not attempt to swim for shore. Sitting or kneeling on the board to keep your center of gravity low will improve stability.

When going SUP boarding, always use appropriate safety equipment, including life jackets and a safety leash. Remember, rescuers often also put themselves at risk when responding to callouts.

World.title: Birk Rohelend: History does not fit into a single simplified narrative
World.content:
Estonia has reached a time when we could talk about the past in all its contradictions, not only through one permitted story, writes Birk Rohelend.

Over the past two years, I have found myself in a new role — as the volunteer producer of the summer production "Now I Study" in Mustamäe. It all began when Andra Teede had the idea to tell the history of the technical university. Two summers ago, I fortunately had no idea that this meant a mega‑project involving a total of 123 people, most of them volunteers.

Andra's idea was delightfully crazy, because who would even be interested in the past, Mustamäe, and a university whose wonderful inner courtyard is known only to its members and alumni? Dance and song are of course lovely, but why should today's digital youth want to come outdoors with their grandmothers and grandfathers to share a common experience? Yet I immediately felt that something in this idea spoke to me deeply: in its DNA were questions I had pondered privately for many years.

"Mom, you don't understand anything"

My teenage daughters have used that sentence from time to time. The last time, I replied: "Why do you think that? In fact, it's exactly the opposite — I have been fifteen, I remember that time, and I know what you feel. You are the one who has never been forty‑five. It would be much more accurate to say that you don't understand me."

But I also remember that same feeling — that my mother didn't understand me. She was born in 1941, and at exactly the same time the summer production takes place, she too was studying at the university. Although my mother has been in the ground for seventeen years, I still remember how confused she was by a simple word like fashion. She wasn't a city girl; she grew up on a farm deep in the forest. "What difference does it make what you wear?" she often said when I begged for another piece of clothing from the store. "In our time, everything was sewn at home; everyone made things as they could and wanted." She never truly understood my longing for toys either: she had the forest and the meadow, birds and butterflies, horses and dogs. She never understood the phenomenon of plastic Barbie dolls.

I have often felt that same lack of shared background in Estonia. The feeling is so deep: in the bone marrow, beneath all experience and wisdom. As a child of 1981, I remember the Soviet Union well — red stars, parades, street names written in Cyrillic. The patronymic Antoevna given by the state, awkward because my father's name resisted Russian grammar.

"'What difference does it make what you wear?' she often said when I begged for another piece of clothing from the store."

And of course it is also true that I do not understand today's youth, cannot imagine growing up on the internet, constantly watched and commented on, in a world of endlessly altered images where no one is as they appear in their virtual form. In this almost schizophrenically two‑faced world, where everyone looks happy in pictures but more and more people secretly suffer from depression — a daily normality for many and a social stigma at the same time — because everyone must be equally successful, wealthy and famous.

May we even talk about history — and when?

As a child of the early 1980s, I did not grow up only in Estonia, but at least half mentally in Germany, ever since satellite television arrived. So although I lived in the Soviet Union, I do not truly know what that time meant. No one bothered to explain to a child where we came from or where we were going. I remember hearing warnings about tanks on the radio and standing in the Baltic Way, but I had no deeper understanding of why I was there.

Because even for us, children of the 80s, not everything was spoken aloud. I knew one grandfather was a kulak and the other died in a concentration camp, but what those life paths meant and why things happened that way — no one discussed it. Perhaps even at home, around kitchen tables, people feared trusting a child with the whole truth, just as the protagonist in Andra Teede's play asks her mother: "But why have you never told me about my father?"

More than that, I have sensed all my life a strange social pressure that we should think about everything that happened in one particular way. That one may always sing Estonian songs and wear folk costumes, but asking why the neighbor denounced my grandfather still seems almost forbidden. Or what was the name of the German whom my other grandfather hid in the forest for fifteen years? That this history — which my generation will one day also become part of — may be remembered only partially: only the chosen, clear side of it, heroic survivors or even more heroic fallen ones, without all the complexity of individuals, society, identity and relationships that actually existed.

"I have sensed all my life a strange social pressure that we should think about everything that happened in one particular way."

Perhaps it is my birth year: that we are the generation with enough comfort and too little fear to no longer understand why the past should be told through only one simplified narrative. That we, accustomed to freedom, can no longer fully grasp why we should not dive into all those parallel and deeply contradictory worlds where everyone is right and no one is right. Even if the societal picture served to us through old photos and books seemed monotonous, real life must have been extraordinarily rich. I am glad Andra dared to reveal those layers; one can only hope the time is ripe for speaking about the past.

To strive harder than necessary

On stage before us is an even bigger question than the nature of one era. It is the question of life choices, a true Heracles dilemma: whether to choose the easy and comfortable path, or the path over stones and stumps for a greater goal. Whether to choose one's own comfort or dare to take responsibility for something larger. In this play, no one has easy choices; only hard and even harder struggles.

Why should anyone, in any era, choose a life in science? I remember my father talking about defending his candidate degree. "Imagine — the day before the defense, my supervisor said I had to make changes to my written work. My thesis was over a hundred pages, typed on a typewriter; rewriting it would have taken more than a whole night, and I had already retyped it several times. What he demanded was impossible! So I simply told him: 'Go to hell!'" My father defended his degree nonetheless.

About twenty years later, I stood as a student in a gene technology lab, marveling at the patience of people who conduct experiments day after day, year after year, where perhaps the ten‑year work of a hundred people leads to one breakthrough, one news item. I did not have that patience, which is why I think with reverence of all scientists. Yes, everyone has everyday worries — families, children, mortgages — but many of us are free from responsibility for the future. No one expects an ordinary person to solve climate problems, the energy crisis or society's governance model. Scientists carry all those heavy expectations. Can people who are not scientists ever truly understand what it feels like to live with such responsibility?

Art is easy — it has no clear direction, it does not have to arrive anywhere. Art may endlessly ask questions without offering answers. Science cannot do that; science must provide solutions: discover cancer treatments, create more sustainable materials, faster and smaller technology.

But art can do something for science: lift scientists onto a pedestal in all their humanity and struggle, facing difficult choices in any era. Art can bow to science: express gratitude to all those people thanks to whom we have reached this world of possibilities. Because it is the work of scientists that is not only on the stage, but above it, beside it and beneath it: all those powerful stage constructions, sound and lighting technology, video footage. It is a special experience to see that art can be part of science and science part of art — both can inspire, advance, interpret and empower each other.

World.title: US dollar exchange rate continues to rise in Iraq
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The exchange rate for the US dollar compared to the Iraqi dinar rose on Thursday in the Iraqi capital, Baghdad, and the capital of the Kurdistan region of Iraq, Erbil.

The US dollar exchange rate slightly rose in Baghdad’s al-Kifah and al-Harithiya stock exchanges, reaching 1,523.5 Iraqi dinars compared to 1,520.5 Iraqi dinars on Thursday morning.

The exchange rate in currency exchange shops in Baghdad ranged between 1,530 Iraqi dinars and 1,520 Iraqi dinars, Shafaq News reported.

In Erbil, the US dollar exchange rate also rose, fluctuating between 1,525.5 and 1,525 Iraqi dinars.

The Central Bank of Iraq (CBI) said in February 2023 that it has begun using the new US dollar exchange rate of 1,300 dinars to every US dollar.

The previous official exchange rate was 1,450 dinars to one US dollar, which was being exchanged in the parallel market at a rate of 1,550 dinars.

While the official exchange rate was 1,450 dinars per dollar in January 2023, the US currency was being exchanged at 1,610 dinars during the same month in the parallel market in Iraq. This variation indicated a difference of over 10 percent in the exchange rates.

World.title: Iraq to increase production from Kirkuk oil fields
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Oil Minister Basim Khudair announced on Thursday plans to increase oil production from the Kirkuk oilfields.

The decision intends to capitalize on a recent agreement with Turkey for exporting oil to the port of Ceyhan.

This move also aims to circumvent the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and increase Iraq’s oil exports via ports on the Mediterranean.

The instruction utilizes the recently expanded Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline deal, with the goal of increasing exports from 180,000 barrels per day to approximately 750,000 barrels per day.

Khudair stated that increasing production lays the groundwork for boosting export volumes through Turkey to 1.5 million barrels per day.

Turkish Petroleum Corporation (TPAO) has officially partnered with British Petroleum (BP) to bolster cooperation in oil and natural gas projects in Kirkuk oilfields.

In 2025, BP reached a deal with Iraq’s North Oil Company (NOC) to develop oil fields in the northern Iraqi province of Kirkuk, with investments projected to reach $25 billion.

The step is part of the Iraqi government’s attempts to optimize energy sector investments, increase oil output, and minimize gas flaring.

The enhanced output directly addresses the Iraqi government’s growing deficit as a result of continued maritime restrictions in the Strait of Hormuz.

By producing more petroleum from Kirkuk, Baghdad reduces internal shipping expenses from southern fields while increasing supplies to global markets via outlets on the Mediterranean.

World.title: Iraqi Prime Minister orders higher military readiness as security tensions rise
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister and Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces Ali Al-Zaidi has directed all security and military formations to raise their operational readiness and combat preparedness, according to the Security Media Cell.

The directive aims to maintain a high state of preparedness across Iraq’s security forces through intensified training exercises and operational movements designed to strengthen national security and protect public interests.

In a statement, the Security Media Cell said the Commander-in-Chief instructed security and military forces to increase their level of readiness while conducting training exercises and field movements.

The measures are intended to ensure that all security formations remain fully prepared to carry out their assigned duties and respond to potential security developments.

According to the statement, the directive is part of ongoing efforts to maintain continuous operational readiness across Iraq’s armed forces.

The Security Media Cell said the enhanced readiness program is designed to reinforce Iraq’s security framework and improve the capabilities of military and security units.

Officials stated that maintaining high readiness contributes to:

Strengthening national security.

Preserving public stability.

Protecting Iraqi citizens.

Safeguarding public institutions and national interests.

The government has increasingly emphasized preparedness amid evolving regional security challenges.

The announcement comes during a period of elevated security concerns in Iraq following recent regional developments and heightened tensions involving armed groups.

The official statement, however, does not specify any particular threat or military operation linked to the readiness order.

Some media reports and political analysts have suggested the move may be connected to broader security developments or precautionary planning ahead of upcoming government deadlines. These assessments are analytical interpretations and were not included in the official Security Media Cell statement.

The latest directive reflects Baghdad’s continued focus on ensuring the operational effectiveness of Iraq’s security institutions.

By ordering additional training activities and maintaining high alert levels, the government aims to preserve stability while ensuring security forces remain prepared to respond to any developments affecting the country’s security environment.

World.title: Iraqi Drilling Company completes well rehabilitation at West Qurna 1 oil field
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Iraqi Drilling Company (IDC) has successfully completed the rehabilitation of oil well WQ1-132 at the West Qurna 1 oil field, marking another step in Iraq’s efforts to enhance oil production efficiency and support the long-term development of its energy sector.

The project was carried out as part of the company’s operational program to improve well performance and maintain sustainable crude oil production.

According to a statement issued by the Iraqi Drilling Company, the rehabilitation work was completed in line with directives from Oil Minister Bassem Mohammed Khudair Al-Abadi and under the supervision of the company’s Director General, Mohammed Hantoosh Asad Al-Azirjawi.

Technical and engineering teams carried out the operation using the company’s specialized expertise and equipment.

The company said the rehabilitation project forms part of its broader strategy to improve the efficiency of existing oil wells while supporting sustainable production across Iraq’s major oil fields.

Restoration work on producing wells helps maximize output, extend operational life, and improve field performance without the need for entirely new drilling operations.

The Iraqi Drilling Company emphasized that the successful completion of the project reflects the capabilities of its engineering and technical staff, who continue to execute specialized rehabilitation operations according to approved operational plans.

The company noted that relying on local expertise strengthens operational efficiency while supporting the continued development of Iraq’s oil infrastructure.

West Qurna 1 is one of Iraq’s largest producing oil fields and plays a significant role in the country’s crude oil output.

Ongoing rehabilitation and maintenance projects are designed to ensure production stability, improve operational reliability, and meet the technical requirements of field development programs.

The completion of well WQ1-132 is expected to contribute to maintaining efficient production operations within the field as Iraq continues investing in the modernization of its energy sector.

World.title: Iraqi PM, Kurdistan president discuss Erbil-Baghdad cooperation
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and the president of the Kurdistan region of Iraq, Nechirvan Barzani, discussed on Wednesday the country’s political, economic, and security situation.

During their meeting in Baghdad, the two leaders indicated that it is important to boost cooperation between the federal government and the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) to enhance stability, address challenges, and serve the interests of the Iraqi people, according to a statement released by the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO).

Al-Zaidi affirmed the government’s commitment to resolving outstanding issues in line with the constitution, preserving Iraq’s unity, and strengthening national partnership.

Barzani stated that it is important to continue dialogue between national parties. He added that the KRG supports the federal government’s efforts to enhance stability and promote national development.

The discussions focused on approaches to secure the success of the government’s national agenda.

This high-level meeting comes after al-Zaidi’s trips to Turkey and Iran, where he met top officials, and Barzani’s visit to Damascus, where he met with Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa.

World.title: Iraq wins legal case in Jordan for Samarra Pharmaceutical Company
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s Ministry of Justice has announced a legal victory before the Jordanian judiciary after securing a final court ruling in favor of the State Company for Drug Industries and Medical Appliances in Samarra, a subsidiary of the Ministry of Industry and Minerals.

The ruling requires a Jordanian company to pay financial compensation following a dispute over the supply of medical materials that failed to meet agreed specifications.

According to a statement from the Ministry of Justice, the ministry’s Legal Department successfully represented the Iraqi pharmaceutical company throughout all stages of the legal proceedings before Jordanian courts.

The case involved a supply contract under which the Jordanian company was expected to provide metal covers for medical supplies. However, the supplier allegedly delivered products that did not comply with the contractual specifications.

Director of the Legal Department, Haitham Mohi Radi, said the final judgment issued by the Jordanian Court of Cassation, and upheld by both the Court of Appeal and the Court of First Instance, ordered the Jordanian company to pay financial amounts to the Samarra-based pharmaceutical company.

The ruling concludes a lengthy legal process aimed at protecting the contractual rights of the Iraqi state-owned enterprise.

The Ministry of Justice described the outcome as an important achievement in safeguarding Iraq’s financial interests abroad.

Officials said the successful litigation reflects the ministry’s continued efforts to defend state institutions before international courts and judicial authorities while protecting public funds from contractual violations.

The ministry added that the case demonstrates the expertise and professionalism of Iraq’s legal teams in handling international commercial disputes.

By successfully pursuing the claim through multiple judicial levels in Jordan, the Legal Department reinforced Iraq’s commitment to enforcing contractual rights and ensuring accountability in cross-border commercial agreements.

The decision is expected to strengthen confidence in the government’s ability to defend the interests of Iraqi public institutions through legal channels.

World.title: Ammar Al-Hakim and Iranian Science Minister discuss academic cooperation
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The head of Iraq’s National State Forces Alliance, Ammar Al-Hakim, met with Iranian Minister of Science, Research and Technology Hossein Simaei Sarraf in Baghdad to discuss expanding academic cooperation between Iraq and Iran through university partnerships, knowledge exchange, and joint educational initiatives.

The meeting focused on strengthening higher education ties while emphasizing the role of universities in addressing labor market needs and societal challenges.

According to a statement released by Al-Hakim’s office, the two sides reviewed opportunities to deepen cooperation between Iraqi and Iranian universities by promoting twinning agreements, expanding academic collaboration, and exchanging expertise.

The discussions highlighted the importance of strengthening institutional relationships to support scientific research and educational development in both countries.

During the meeting, Al-Hakim stressed that university graduates should possess skills that match the demands of today’s job market.

He also urged academic institutions to prioritize scientific research that offers practical solutions to national challenges and contributes to sustainable development.

Al-Hakim emphasized the importance of equipping university students with strong scientific knowledge to prepare them for future professional opportunities.

The Iraqi political leader underscored the role of research institutions in supporting innovation and policymaking.

He noted that universities should focus on producing research capable of addressing economic, social, and developmental issues while enhancing academic excellence.

The discussion reflected a shared interest in strengthening educational cooperation as part of broader bilateral relations.

The meeting also touched on the annual Arbaeen pilgrimage, with Al-Hakim praising the hospitality shown by Iraqis toward visitors traveling to commemorate Imam Hussein.

He said the event demonstrates positive values of solidarity and cooperation, while calling for stronger ties between societies based on shared humanitarian and religious principles.

The visit concluded with discussions on enhancing educational cooperation alongside broader people-to-people engagement between Iraq and Iran.

World.title: Iraq’s State Administration Coalition warns armed groups after September 30
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s State Administration Coalition has reaffirmed its support for restricting all weapons to state control, warning that any armed activity outside the authority of the government after September 30, 2026, will be treated under the country’s Anti-Terrorism Law.

The position was announced following the coalition’s 37th regular meeting, hosted by Prime Minister Ali Falih Al-Zaidi, with the participation of Iraq’s senior political and constitutional leaders.

According to a statement issued by the Prime Minister’s Office, the meeting brought together the President of the Republic, the Speaker of Parliament, the President of the Supreme Judicial Council, the President of the Kurdistan Region, and leaders of the State Administration Coalition.

Participants reviewed Iraq’s political, security, economic, and public service developments, as well as regional events and their impact on the country.

The coalition reiterated its backing for the government’s efforts to ensure that all weapons remain under state authority, in line with the government program approved by the Iraqi Parliament.

The coalition stressed that Iraqi territory must not be used as a launchpad for attacks against neighboring countries or for actions that could draw Iraq into regional conflicts.

It warned that individuals or groups engaging in such activities would be committing crimes that threaten national security.

According to the statement, after September 30, 2026, any armed activity conducted outside the state’s legal framework will be dealt with under Iraq’s Anti-Terrorism Law.

Officials also cited constitutional provisions prohibiting the formation of armed organizations outside the official security forces.

Prime Minister Al-Zaidi briefed coalition members on government efforts to strengthen security, improve public services, implement the ministerial program, and address Iraq’s financial and economic challenges.

The coalition emphasized the need to:

Maintain national security and stability.

Protect essential public services.

Diversify Iraq’s oil export routes.

Increase non-oil revenues.

Combat corruption, smuggling, and financial waste.

The meeting highlighted the government’s commitment to protecting citizens’ interests while strengthening economic resilience.

On regional affairs, coalition leaders expressed support for diplomatic efforts aimed at reducing tensions across the Middle East.

The meeting reaffirmed Iraq’s rejection of resolving disputes through military force and emphasized Baghdad’s willingness to play a constructive role in promoting dialogue between regional parties.

Participants also discussed border security, counterterrorism cooperation, combating drug trafficking and organized crime, and strengthening relations with neighboring and international partners based on mutual respect and national sovereignty.

At the conclusion of the meeting, the State Administration Coalition called for accelerating the completion of the government formation process and submitting the government’s official program to the Council of Representatives for discussion and approval.

The coalition said completing these constitutional steps remains essential for advancing Iraq’s political stability and governance agenda.

World.title: 'Internal matter for us': MEA dismisses US lawmaker's criticism of FCRA Bill
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Ministry of external affairs on Friday rejected criticism of India's foreign funding law, saying the issue is an internal matter on which Parliament will take a decision.

During a bi-weekly media briefing, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said several countries, including the United States, regulate foreign funds and foreign financing.

"Regarding the issue you are referring to, we have seen it, and several comments have been made on it. As far as legislative matters are concerned, and particularly matters relating to India's own legislation, this is an internal matter for us, on which our Parliament takes the decision," Jaiswal said.

"I would also like to tell you that there are several countries in the world, including the United States, that regulate foreign funds and foreign financing," he added.

The remarks came days after a US lawmaker criticised the proposed amendments to India's foreign funding law, alleging they could allow the government to take over churches and religious charities and warning that the issue could affect India-US ties.





US Congressman Riley Moore said the proposed changes to the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act (FCRA) amounted to "a clear attack against Christians" and urged India not to proceed with the legislation in its current form.

In a post on X, the Republican Congressman from West Virginia said Christianity had a long history in India dating back to the arrival of St Thomas the Apostle on the Malabar Coast.

"But despite this long Christian history, India's Parliament is considering amending the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act to permit government takeovers of churches and religious charities," Moore wrote.

"This is a clear attack against Christians. If this bill proceeds in this way, it would be a point of major concern in our bilateral relationship with India," he added.

The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026 proposes the creation of a Designated Authority to take over the management of foreign contributions and assets created using such funds if an organisation's FCRA registration is cancelled, surrendered or lapses after not being renewed.

The Bill specifies that where such assets include a place of worship, the Designated Authority must ensure its religious character is preserved.

It also proposes reducing the maximum punishment for violations of the Act from five years' imprisonment to one year.

The FCRA regulates the receipt and utilisation of foreign contributions by NGOs, charitable trusts, educational institutions, religious bodies and other associations. According to the Ministry of Home Affairs, 13,520 organisations received foreign contributions worth Rs 55,741 crore between 2019 and 2022.

Government data shows that as of July 15, 2026, there were 14,449 active FCRA registrations, while 22,498 had been cancelled and another 15,212 had expired.

World.title: Former Nestle CMD Suresh Narayanan says India Inc needs to shed the ‘elite’ tag
World.content:
Former Nestle CMD Suresh Narayanan in his new book, 'Courage Under Fire', writes that in a crisis people follow those they trust.

For over four decades,

Suresh Narayanan

has navigated boardrooms, brand battles and one of

India Inc

's defining crises. In â

Courage Under Fire

â (

Penguin Random House India

), the former NestlÃ© India chairman and managing director looks beyond business strategy to explore what truly shapes

leadership

.

In an exclusive chat with Lopamudra Ghatak, he argues that clarity matters more than charisma, challenges India's obsession with pedigree thatâs causing companies to overlook leadership potential, and reflects candidly on the lessons of the

Maggi

crisis. He also explains why

Gen Z

's approach to work-life balance deserves respect rather than ridicule, and recalls how a woman boss taught him that empathy is one of the key traits to being a good leader.

Congratulations on your book. How did the idea to write 'Courage Under Fire' come to you?

In 'Courage Under Fire' you write that "great leadership is not about position; itâs about responsibility, authenticity, and the ability to inspire trust, when it matters". In an increasingly trust-deficit and information-surplus world, how does a leader earn trust? And how does an organisation make trust a part of its DNA?

'Performative' is the word that's often used today ...

mukhota

Trust is the real currency of leadership.(Image generated by AI)

This bring me to my next question: Can leadership be taught, or is it something people are simply born with?

Nestle India CMD Suresh Narayanan (File photo)

That's an interesting point about the 'charisma myth' that surrounds

leadership. You mention in the book about visiting Tier-2 and Tier3- colleges, and how students there are often more grateful, hungry and eager to learn. Do you think they make better leaders?

The 'tag' matters?

Why great leaders don't need charisma(Image generated by AI)

You have spent over four decades across big brands. Do you think India Inc has begun to move beyond that elitism?

The modern workplace has become very volatile, with geopolitics and global uncertainty adding new layers of complexity. What's your advice for leaders navigating crises?

What should I say? How should I behave? What tone should I set?

In hindsight, do you feel that your response to the Maggi crisis was appropriate? Looking back, is there anything you would have done differently?

In 'Courage Under Fire', you write about the emotional effect the loss of colleagues during the pandemic had on you. Do you think business leaders, particularly men, are becoming more comfortable showing their vulnerable side?

You also had a woman boss during your career. Did her leadership style differ from your male mentors?

Gen Z and the emerging Gen Alpha are reshaping workplace expectations as they place a premium on work-life balance, purpose and flexibility. How do you see that influencing India's workforce in the years ahead?

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

After a 40-year career in corporate India, I wanted to leave behind a few lessons that had served me well. They're not prescriptions, but perspectives shaped by the crises and difficult moments I have experienced.'Courage Under Fire' is more of a personal journey through those defining moments - that focuses on people, purpose, partnerships, values, behaviour and outcomes. I thought it would be of some use to a younger generation entering the workforce.I think you've hit the nail on the head! Trust is the most valuable currency - for an individual as much as for an organisation. It emerges when three streams converge at one point in time.The first is purpose. Every organisation, and every individual, needs a clear sense of purpose, something that guides decisions and actions.The second is values. What do you want to be known for? What principles define how you conduct yourself, especially in adverse situations?Purpose and values, in turn, lead to the third element: authenticity. Unfortunately, in today's digital world, authenticity often gives way to performance.We spend too much time embellishing, instead of being genuine.Correct. Leadership isn't about saying what you'll do, it's about doing what you say. That's the dilemma many leaders face. Do they wear a(mask) that projects one image while concealing another?In order to establish trust among people, there has to be a convergence between purpose, values and authenticity, and that leads to outcomes. Over time, those actions create credibility, and credibility becomes trust.Trust is built when purpose, values and authenticity consistently translate into action. Over time, those actions create credibility, and credibility becomes trust.I've also come to see vulnerability as a strength, not a weakness. When people know you're human, that you have strengths as well as limitations, they know what to expect from you. Predictability in values and behaviour is reassuring. What people fear most is unpredictability.Ultimately, trust isn't about being the most liked person in the room. In a crisis, organisations don't rely on the most loved people; they rely on the most trusted ones. If I'm liked but not trusted, I won't be asked to lead when it matters. Trust, more than popularity, is what carries an organisation through difficult times.Leadership, for long, has suffered from some myths. The first is the myth of charisma - that great leaders must have magnetic personalities. The second is that complex communication (by leadership) is somehow superior. The third is executive presence: the belief that a leader must be a larger-than-life figure at any gathering and dominate every room they enter. And the fourth is the idea that leaders should only display their strengths while hiding every flaw, angularities.I don't subscribe to any of those myths. Leadership can absolutely be taught because, at its core, leadership is an act of being human.You don't have to be charismatic; you have to be clear. You don't have to be complex; you have to be transparent in your communication. You don't need the loudest voice or the most commanding presence. Some of history's greatest political and business leaders inspired people far beyond the reach of their voices.But leadership doesn't develop in isolation. It blooms through the right mentors, timely nudges and experiences. Looking back, I benefited from teachers, parents, colleagues, relatives and even competitors who pushed me to exceed my own expectations. Those influences gradually built confidence, not just the confidence to lead others, but the confidence to manage myself first.One thing we need to do as a society is demystify elitism. We place far too much value on where someone studied, where they work, the company they built or the organisation they belong to â as though those labels alone define success and achievement.Exactly, the tag culture. I believe those days should be behind us. Look at ISRO. They might have their own travails but the fact is that most of the talent that comes there are not from the premier institutions in the country and yet they do premier and outstanding work and make us proud as a nation.The same is true of organisations that consciously recruit from Tier-2 cities and smaller towns. I often find students there to be remarkably humble, eager and determined. They are trying to prove themselves against a system that has long suggested only the elite succeed.As leaders, we have to move away from that entitlement mindset and create space for talent to flourish. India has extraordinary talent. Some young people may not be the most articulate when speaking in English but they are capable of hard work and possess grit, discipline and can deliver on their promise each and every time.That's what the country needsânot people who merely preach from the pulpit, but people who consistently deliver.I think as a country now we are mature enough to realise that we cannot be a developing country or hope to become a wealthy country one day on the crutches of elitism. I think elitism is a crutch that we have to get out of as quickly as possible.I think the kind of companies that I worked in - Unilever, Colgate-Palmolive and Nestle - they always prided themselves in a middle-class culture. Their leaders weren't chosen because they came from privileged backgrounds; they rose through competence, commitment, energy and hard workI use the term middle class in a positive sense because it symbolises humility, integrity, transparency, trust and a strong work ethic. This is what middle-class India is, and these are the values we strive to teach our children. When those values enter an organisation, they become a source of strength.I do think the growing recognition of talent from Tier-2 institutions and smaller towns is slowly weakening elitism. But there's still work to be done. Our education system and employers must create more opportunities for capable graduates from less celebrated institutions.Too many people still believe admission to a top college guarantees success. Life doesn't work that way. Success is usually about moving two steps forward, one step back, and repeating that journey with resilience and consistency.There are two principles that have guided me throughout my career.The first is simple: a crisis never arrives with a calling card. You have to remain alert at all times. Don't be caught sleeping at the wheel. Anticipate risks before they balloon into crises.The second is to manage yourself before you manage others. That's often overlooked. When a crisis hits, we immediately focus on facts, meetings and firefighting. But we spend far less time asking:In a crisis, everyone's anxiety levels are elevated. The leader's role is to remain calm, anchored in the organisation's purpose and values, and provide stability.That's often the difference between a crisis handled well and one handled badly. The outcome rarely depends only on strategy. More often, it depends on leadershipâhow clearly you communicate, how consistently you act and how much confidence you inspire.The first lesson, that a crisis doesn't come with a calling card, certainly applies in this case. In hindsight, we could have done better in terms of sensing the environment and knowing that something was brewing in parts of the country. If we had been able to address it more comprehensively, maybe we would have been able to manage the outcome a lot better.Secondly, one of the important issues in managing a crisis is to have a single point of contact communicating to the environment. One criticism we faced was that we were slow in communicating. Looking back, I believe we could have responded faster.I don't know whether the dial has shifted enough in India to say that with confidence. But I do believe people follow leaders who are authentic, humane and emotionally present â not those who remain distant and issue instructions from above.Professor George Kohlrieser at IMD Business School describes a leader as a "secure base." I find that idea deeply meaningful. Just as we turn to a parent in moments of uncertainty, employees should feel they have someone they can approach with their fears, concerns and aspirations, someone who will provide anchorage in a crisis.Vulnerability, to me, is a source of strength. It acknowledges that you're still learning and growing. That's not weakness, it's humanity.We've long been told that men don't cry. But they do. Suppressing emotion doesn't make you stronger; it makes it harder to empathise. And empathy is one of the most powerful qualities a leader can possess.Wan Ling, who headed Nestle Asia-Oceania-Africa, was one of the toughest leaders I worked with. She could be incredibly demanding, yet deeply compassionate.What struck me most was that every conversation with her began with family. With many of my male bosses, business came first and family last. With her it was always, âHow is your family doing?â. Only then would we move on to tackle the toughest business crisis moments.One of her greatest strengths was her ability to read a room. She sensed what people were feeling before anyone uttered a word. Just as importantly, she had the ability to step back, consider various perspectives and avoid rushing into decisions. That balance of empathy and judgement made her an exceptional leader.I see it as a positive shift. The old belief that success demanded 80-hour work weeks came at a huge personal cost. You may have earned more, but you often missed out on family, friendships and life's important moments. There's little value in reaching 80 and regretting that you never spent enough time with your parents or your children. So I welcome this change.These youngsters are not work-shy. They simply want work to coexist with life, and I think that's a healthy aspiration. I only wish my generation had the courage to tell our bosses at seven in the evening that we were leaving to meet family or friends. Instead, we stayed back until the boss switched off the lights, as though commitment was measured by the last person to leave the office.That said, balance has to be calibrated. Every generation has something to learn from the other.What also strikes me about young professionals is that they're driven by experiences. They move from one challenge to another in search of learning and fulfillment. I would encourage them to embrace the challenge itself rather than becoming overly anxious about the outcome. Careers are rarely linear. If you focus on learning, growth and doing meaningful work, the outcomes usually take care of themselves.

World.title: 'News, Spice Rani, He Ram': Names on police merit list triggers row in Chhattisgarh
World.content:
The unusual names prompted the opposition Congress to question the credibility of the selection process. (Representative image)

What really happened

What the board said

Several candidates clarify

NEW DELHI: What began as a routine police recruitment result in Chhattisgarh quickly turned into an internet sensation after candidates with names such as 'News', 'Space Rani', 'He Ram', 'Bhakt Prahlad' and 'Tufail' appeared on the list of successful applicants, sparking disbelief, political allegations and eventually, a defence from the candidates themselves.The unusual names, which surfaced in the results of the Chhattisgarh Public Service Commission's (CGPSC) preliminary examination for police recruitment, prompted the opposition Congress to question the credibility of the selection process.The commission, however, dismissed the allegations, insisting that the names were genuine and matched the details submitted by candidates during registration.The controversy erupted after the results of the preliminary examination for 341 posts of subedar, sub-inspector and platoon commander were declared on August 4. A total of 7,301 candidates qualified for the mains examination.According to the CGPSC, the candidates had appeared for document verification, physical tests and the preliminary examination under the same names, which were also printed on their admit cards.Former chief minister Bhupesh Baghel mocked the list after sharing it on X."The Public Relations Department should spend Rs 1 crore daily on s to display this achievement at public intersections so that, in the coming days, 'Radio' and 'Space Raja' might also succeed in some examination."State Congress communication wing chief Sushil Anand Shukla accused the BJP government of failing to deliver transparent recruitment despite promising PSC examinations on the lines of the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC).He alleged that the names reflected the alleged "negligence" of the CGPSC and the state government and claimed that several recruitment and promotion examinations held over the past two-and-a-half years had come under suspicion.Rejecting the allegations, the CGPSC described the claims circulating on social media as "misleading and baseless" and said they unfairly ridiculed candidates over their names."The names of the candidates displayed in the examination result are the same as those entered by them in their online application forms, which they finally submitted. The candidates appeared for document and physical tests as well as the preliminary examination under these names, and their names were also displayed accordingly on their admit cards," it stated.The commission urged candidates and the public not to believe misinformation and rely only on information published on its official website.As the debate gathered pace online, several candidates clarified that the names attracting attention were the same as those recorded in their official documents."My name is News Kumar Pradhan. My surname was not added to my Class 10 marksheet. My marksheets of Classes 10 and 12 and Aadhaar card carry the name News, without the surname. People think that the name is incorrect," said News Kumar Pradhan, who qualified in the preliminary examination. He added that he is from Bhatanpali village in Raigarh district.Tufail, a 29-year-old candidate from Nayapara in Raipur district, said his name appeared the same in all official records."After the result was released, rumours are being spread about names such as Spacerani, News and Tufail without any information or facts. These are the names of students who have prepared for the examination for years," he said.He appealed against spreading rumours and said such claims were hurting the morale of candidates from ordinary families.Another successful candidate, He Ram, said there was nothing unusual about the way his name was recorded."My name is He Ram, and I have qualified the PSC preliminary examination. Some people are raising objections over my name. My surname is Kashyap, but it is not mentioned in any of my documents. Hence, I entered only my name while filling the form," he told PTI.Bhakt Prahlad also clarified that his name was correctly recorded in all official documents."My surname is not mentioned. Please do not spread confusion regarding my name," he said.

World.title: Monsoon Session: Congress issues whip to MPs ahead of FCRA Bill discussion in Parliament
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Congress on Friday issued a whip to its MPs, directing them to be present in both the Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha as the government is set to take up the contentious FCRA Amendment Bill for discussion.

Congress has asked its parliamentarians to remain present in their respective Houses on August 10, 11 and 12.

"Very important issues will be taken up for discussion in the Rajya Sabha on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, i.e. August 10, 11 and 12, 2026," Congress chief whip in the Rajya Sabha said in the whip.

World.title: Sukhbir Singh Badal meets PM Modi, fuels BJP-SAD alliance buzz ahead of Punjab polls next year
World.content:
NEW DELHI:

(SAD) chief

met Prime Minister Narendra Modi in Parliament on Friday. The meeting has sparked buzz over whether the BJP and the SAD are preparing to turn the page on years of political estrangement ahead of the

due early next year.

For both the BJP and the SAD, the timing is significant. Once the state's dominant political combine, the two parties have spent the past several years on the margins of Punjab politics, watching their traditional support base shrink while Kejriwal-led

Aam Aadmi Party

gradually emerged as the state's principal political force.

The BJP-SAD who were allies for over two decades, parted ways in September 2020 after the Akali Dal walked out of the

NDA

, with much credits to Centre's three farm laws. The legislation triggered massive protests across Punjab and countrywide and became a political flashpoint.

However, even after PM Modi-led government repealed the laws in 2021, relations between the two allies remained strained.

In the 2022 Punjab assembly elections, voters not only rejected the Congress, which was crippled by the Amarinder Singh-Navjot Singh Sidhu power struggle, but also delivered a crushing verdict against both the BJP and the SAD.

Contesting separately, the BJP won just two seats while the Akali Dal managed only three in the 117-member assembly.





Instead, Punjab handed Kejriwal's AAP a historic mandate. The party stormed to power for the first time in its second attempt, with Bhagwant Mann becoming chief minister, recording a dramatic shift in the Sikh-majority state.

Against this backdrop, the Modi-Badal meeting in Parliament assumes greater political significance. While neither side has officially indicated that an alliance is on the cards, the interaction is likely to intensify discussions over whether the estranged partners can rebuild their relationship before Punjab votes next year.

World.title: 'Avoid Lutyens web': PM Modi's advice to 45 NDA MPs at breakfast meet
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi Friday met 45 National Democratic Alliance (NDA) MPs at a breakfast meeting amid the stormy Parliament monsoon session, advising the parliamentarians to "not carry the anxiety from inside the House to outside" and avoid the "web of Lutyens' Delhi".

In the meeting, which also included the rebel factions from the Uddhav Sena and Mamata Banerjee's

, PM Modi said: "No one should say anything trashy on TV. Maintain full dignity at all times. Engage actively in social media through Facebook, Instagram and X; interact with youth, inform government welfare work, encourage youth for sports activities."

Modi advised the MPs to follow the party line and calmly present their views on every issue and that there was "no need to speak angrily or shout (in House) in anger".

"Do not carry the anxiety from inside the House to outside. Because sometimes there is such an atmosphere in the House that it causes anxiety, you should not carry it with you. There is also no need to speak angrily or shout in anger. You all know the party line, and you should calmly present your views on every issue," said PM Modi as per the sources who informed news agency ANI.

NDA a 'collective identity'

Jagdish Basunia, a leader of the Nationalist Citizens Party of India (NCPI), which was formed after breaking away from the TMC, described his meeting with Modi as a "great interaction," noting that the Prime Minister emphasised the collective identity of the National Democratic Alliance (NDA) as a "family."





Speaking to ANI after the session, Basunia characterised the meeting as highly cordial and focused on the shared goal of national development.

"It was a great interaction with PM Modi over breakfast today, a very cordial meeting. PM told us we are all part of the NDA family. Let's work together for public welfare, the way NDA works," Basunia said.

Uttarakhand Forward 2.0 is the second edition of The Times of India's flagship video series spotlighting the state's journey of growth, innovation and transformative governance. Through exclusive conversations with policymakers, administrators, industry leaders, educationists and experts, the series explores the ideas, initiatives and vision shaping Uttarakhand's future across infrastructure, clean energy, education, tourism, sustainability and more. The campaign highlights the policies driving progress, the challenges and opportunities ahead, and the roadmap for the state's next phase of development.In this episode of Uttarakhand 2.0, Richa Jain Kalra is in conversation with Dr Manoj Kumar Pant, Director, Department of Planning, Government of Uttarakhand, about the state's long-term vision. World.title: KGMOA demands an end to overreach by Kerala Health Minister’s private secretary
World.content:
The Kerala Government Medical Officers’ Association (KGMOA) has reacted sharply to what it termed was an “overreach” by a private secretary of Health Minister K. Muraleedharan, who, they said was consistently discourteous and arrogant to doctors and other health workers.

The Thiruvananthapuram district committee of the KGMOA has now come out in the open to condemn the Health Minister’s private secretary, who, they said had behaved disrespectfully towards a senior woman colleague and civil surgeon at a community health centre (CHC) while he was on a visit to the CHC on Thursday.

Registers protest

The KGMOA has formally registered a strong protest against the Minister’s private secretary over the incident.

Though primary and community health centres (PHCs/CHCs) are officially required to begin functioning at 9 a.m., the Health Minister’s private secretary publicly rebuked the senior medical officer for not having started work at 8 a.m. Such arrogant behaviour towards a woman doctor with years of experience is not justifiable and cannot be condoned, the KGMOA said.

Such unnecessary interference and attempts to demoralise and undermine the dignity of doctors who have been working sincerely to improve the State’s public health is not acceptable, the KGMOA said.

The KGMOA pointed out that the Health Minister’s private secretary has no official authority to conduct official inspections of government health institutions or to directly intervene in its administrative affairs.

Yet, such “inspections” by the private secretary in health-care institutions seems to continue and there have been multiple occasions when the private secretary chose to behave discourteously towards doctors and other health workers, the association alleged.

Such overreach by the Minister’s private secretary, exceeding his jurisdiction, will affect the smooth and efficient functioning of the State’s health system and adversely affect the morale of health workers.

‘Will resist interference’

The KGMOA said that it will continue to extend its support to all constructive measures taken by the Health Minister to strengthen the State’s public health system and improve the quality of government health institutions. However, the organisation will strongly resist unnecessary interference from the Minister’s office that goes beyond its authority and is demeaning to health workers.

The KGMOA pointed out that it was essential to protect the dignity of doctors and other health workers as well as the administrative autonomy of government health institutions. It demanded that the government take immediate measures to prevent the recurrence of incidents such as the one on Thursday or that the organisation will be forced to launch a strong protest to safeguard the dignity of health workers.

World.title: Conflict of interest in startup funding panel “unavoidable”, says Technology Development Board secretary
World.content:
Conflict of interest in selecting expert panels to disburse public funds for technology startups is “unavoidable” and a matter “to be managed,” Technology Development Board (TDB) secretary Rajesh Pathak said on Friday.

His remarks came after the government disclosure in Parliament on July 30, followed by media reports, that members of an expert panel constituted by the TDB had financial links to companies that they adjudicated as eligible for public funds.

The TDB, affiliated to the Department of Science and Technology (DST), is among the agencies selected to channel money under the Centre’s ₹1 lakh crore Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund. As of July, the TDB has approved support for 22 projects—a company can be part of multiple projects—involving ₹2,192 crore of RDI financing.

In response to questions from Congress MP Praveen Chakravarthy in the Rajya Sabha on July 30, the DST identified the members of TDB’s Investment Committee. The committee is chaired by Dr. Saurabh Srivastava and includes K.R.S. Jamwal (Tata Industries), Lalithesh Katragadda, Sudhir Mehta, Sanjay Nayak, Anand Deshpande, Gopal Srinivasan, Debashish Bhattacharjee, Bala C. Deshpande, Jaswinder Ahuja and Sudhir Sethi, with the TDB secretary serving as member-secretary without voting rights.

The same parliamentary disclosure stated that several companies approved for TDB funding had received funding from organisations represented on the Investment Committee or TDB’s Governing Board. These include Noccarc Robotics, EndureAir Systems, e-TRNL Energy, Dhruva Space, BigEndian Semiconductors, Astrome Technologies, Peptris Technologies and Serigen Mediproducts in relation to Dr. Saurabh Srivastava; Noccarc Robotics, EndureAir Systems, Tejas Networks, BigEndian Semiconductors, Peptris Technologies, ThinkMetal and Manastu Space Technologies in relation to K.R.S. Jamwal; Ather Energy and Tejas Networks in relation to Sanjay Nayak; Serigen Mediproducts in relation to Anand Deshpande; Agnikul Cosmos in relation to Gopal Srinivasan; Neo Seekermetals in relation to Debashish Bhattacharjee; and Replus Engitech in relation to Sudhir Mehta.

“When we were formulating guidelines, it was clear that conflict of interest was unavoidable because experts (in identifying technology start-ups) will almost certainly have direct or indirect financial connections to the innovation ecosystem. However, such conflicts of interest can be managed, and we have clear guidelines,” said Mr. Pathak.

These include members disclosing any financial interest in the companies being evaluated, leaving the room when any of their companies are being discussed. “There are 11 voting members in the committee. Following a recusal, a selected committee has to be voted on not by a simple majority but a super majority,” said Mr. Pathak. He explained that in a scenario involving 11 members, one needs at least eight to approve funding. “Moreover, companies where the expert committee members are promoters or board directors are straightaway not considered – irrespective of merit. However, if they have indirect stakes through funds, it may be permissible.”

The RDI Fund, conceived to increase private-sector investment in research and development, is intended to support startups and companies developing technologies at Technology Readiness Level (TRL)-4 and above—a stage at which a technology has moved beyond laboratory proof-of-concept and its components have been validated in a laboratory environment, making it ready for further development towards commercialisation. The scheme aims to bridge the shortage of long-term capital for high-risk technologies in sectors such as deep technology, biotechnology, artificial intelligence and energy transition.

Unlike conventional government grant programmes, the RDI Fund does not finance companies directly. Instead, the Department of Science and Technology acts as the nodal ministry, with approved Second-Level Fund Managers (SLFMs) evaluating and financing eligible technology entities through long-term, low-interest loans, equity and equity-linked instruments. The Technology Development Board (TDB) and Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council (BIRAC) were the first organisations designated as SLFMs, while additional entities are being selected.

World.title: Maharashtra govt. bans 114 radical literature items associated with terrorist outfits
World.content:
The Maharashtra government has banned the literature of terrorist organisations, including the Islamic State, Al Qaeda, Hizb-ul-Mujahideen, and Islamic State in Khorasan Province, for glorifying violent extremism and providing ideological indoctrination.

In a gazette notification on August 6, 2026, the Home Department stated that the literature which glorifies violent extremism and jihad, besides promoting radicalisation will be banned.

“The State Anti-Terrorism Squad (ATS)’s investigation and their cyber surveillance reports suggest that there has been continued circulation, possession and transmission of radical and extremist literature, publications, and propagandist material linked to terrorist organisations,” the gazette stated.

In the gazette, the government has instructed respective authorities to “forfeit 114 items of radical literature, including magazines and books”. The 114 banned literature material, includes 44 issues of Voice of Khurasan magazine, Are you still sitting, Why Should You Join the Islamic State and Nida-e-Khurasan-Urdu, that are all linked to the Islamic State and all its manifestations, along with issues of The Revolutionary Resurgence linked to Hizb-ul-Mujahideen/ Hizb-ul-Mujahideen Pir Panjal Regiment, Nawai Gazawa-e-Hind, School Of Yusuf and Modern Warfare linked to the Al Qaeda/Al Qaeda in Indian Subcontinent (AQIS).

Citing reasons for the decision, the authorities in the gazette highlighted that the particular literature poses a threat to public law and order and internal security as it consists of material that glorifies violent extremism and provides ideological indoctrination. It also becomes a way of recruitment and incites or encourages acts prejudicial to the sovereignty and integrity of India.

ATS raids

Over the last few months, the ATS conducted several raids across Maharashtra. For instance, in February, it launched a search operation across 21 locations in Yavatmal and Ahilyanagar districts over extremist activities, questioning 14 suspects. During the raid, the ATS seized documents, laptops, books, and mobile phones over objectionable content. Last year, in November, the ATS arrested 37-year-old software engineer Zubair Hangargekar from Pune for allegedly preaching youngsters that “democracy is against shariat” and created content on topics, including jihad and ‘Ghazwa-e-Hind’, the takeover of the Indian subcontinent by a caliphate.

In March, the ATS informed the State government of several literature that were associated with activities prejudicial to the sovereignty and integrity of India and that this literature needs to be banned.
