World.title: Perth business claims $250k loss over Metronet works disruption
World.content:
A Perth business owner says years of railway construction work have cost him hundreds of thousands of dollars.

Joe Mahon says the removal of the Oats Street Metronet level crossing and subsequent works to elevate the rail line and build a new train station have caused road closures and parking issues that have seriously affected his bottom line.

He told 102.5 ABC Perth he did not object to the public transport upgrades at East Victoria Park from late 2023 to mid-2025, but has asked the Public Transport Authority (PTA) for compensation.

The corner of Bank Street and Forward Street was chosen as the location for Reid's Remotes because of the visibility from the street, customer parking and ease of access.

When Oats Street was subject to closure, it forced prospective customers to access more complicated detours that were subject to frequent change.

"At the start it was gradual because it was issues like their workers taking up all the parking onsite so our customers couldn't actually park," Mr Mahon said.

"Then, once they introduced a road closure, it was like falling off the edge of a cliff. Basically, people couldn't access us.

"The one street that they were supposed to access us through, Forward Street, was full of trucks and cranes and concrete trucks. We even struggled to get there ourselves just to get to work."

The shop was extremely difficult to access at times, Joe Mahon said. (Supplied: Joe Mahon)

Mr Mahon said the sometimes roads were closed during certain times of the day and online maps and GPS services could not keep up.

"Customers would actually give up in frustration and just cancel their booking," he said.

Mr Mahon said in the four years before the level crossing removal works his turnover had been growing by 25 and 30 per cent per annum.

But in the 2024 and 2025 accounting years his turnover fell by 7.45 per cent and 8.75 per cent.

Mr Mahon attributes that decline to the loss of passing trade caused by the Metronet works.

"In 2018 we started documenting every customer who came to us how they found us. One of the main ones is that they're passing trade, so they just saw the signage on the building and came in," he said.

"At the point where the [Metronet] project started that started to decline.

" By about April in 2024 it had gone to zero, and so we had no passing trade for the next 18 months. "

The Metronet worksite on Bank Street, opposite Joe Mahon's business. (Supplied: Joe Mahon)

Mr Mahon said he did not learn that Oats Street would be closed for 18 months until after it was shut.

After the works finished he submitted a compensation claim for $250,000, which he believes his business would have made had it continued to grow at the rate measured before the works began.

The PTA recently denied his claim, saying the changes to traffic conditions were reasonable in the circumstances and undertaken for the benefit of the entire community.

Its legal representatives also said access to the property was continuously maintained and that there was no reasonable alternative way the works could have been carried out.

The PTA also said reasonable steps to mitigate the impact on the community were taken.

But Mr Mahon said he intended to continue his fight for compensation.

"I can't see any other option. I can't afford not to. My business almost closed last year," he said.

"I've sunk the last 19 years into that business.

"I have no problem with the works and the fact that they're essential. I think public transport is essential.

"But when a government department does work that knowingly will impact people and has no consideration for that impact, then that's a problem."

In a statement, a spokesperson for the PTA said: "All claims are assessed on an individual basis. As some claims are still being assessed, details of compensation payments will not be provided."

World.title: Artwork riffing on Renaissance painting and George Orwell wins $100k
World.content:
Ryan Presley, a Marri Ngarr artist from Alice Springs, has taken out the $100,000 top prize at the National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Art Awards (NATSIAAs), the longest-running and most prestigious award for Indigenous artists.

Presley — who also has Scandinavian ancestry — won the Telstra Art Award for his oil painting, Our lifestyle of tranquillity undisturbed, a painting of a reclining Indigenous man between his dog and a hunting rifle, which riffs on Renaissance artworks.

Full list of winners Telstra Art Award

Ryan Presley General Painting Award

Vanessa Inkamala Work on Paper Award

Jenna Mayilema Lee Bark Painting Award

Barayuwa Munuŋgurr Wandjuk Marika Memorial 3D Award

Napuwarri Marawili Emerging Artist Award

Guruwuy Murrinyina Multimedia Award

Colin Heenan-Puruntatameri

Measuring 1.8 by 1.5 metres, the painting also speaks to a quote from British author George Orwell's dystopian novel 1984: "Who controls the past controls the future: who controls the present controls the past."

Talking to ABC Radio National's Awaye! at the Museum and Art Gallery of the Northern Territory in Darwin, Presley described his win as both "daunting" and a "great honour" with which he is still coming to terms.

"It's taken me a while to soak it in," he says.

He says the painting channels representation of sacred spaces and chamber architecture — which can be either a sanctuary or a kind of prison or tomb.

"I want these ideas woven together," he says.

"These are a part of our lives that we negotiate. In Queensland and the Northern Territory, both places I've lived and grown up in, our young people are jailed at alarming rates and at very low ages. That's part of the idea of the work."

Currently based in Logan in south-east Queensland, Presley has worked as an artist for about 20 years, having graduated from Griffith University's contemporary Australian Indigenous art program in 2009.

He has exhibited at Adelaide's Samstag Museum of Art, Melbourne's Gertrude Contemporary and the Institute of Modern Art in Brisbane.

"Basically, I hope [winning] means I'll be able to keep making work," he says.

"I've been working for 17 to 20 years and trying to be consistent and build my work and improve my work, so I'm hoping this helps me continue another 20 years."

2026 NATSIAA finalists on display There's a range of artworks among the finalists vying for this year's National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Art Awards.

This year's NATSIAAs were judged by Kokatha and Nukunu artist Yhonnie Scarce, Trawlwoolway artist Julie Gough and Kamilaroi artist Warraba Weatherall.

"What caught my attention about Ryan's work is the multi-layered iconography and that story of past, present and, for me, future as well," Scarce says.

"And I think the precision of the painting, the technique of his work, is just next-level amazing."

Presley is one of seven winners, from 64 finalists and 221 entries, at this year's NATSIAAs, including $15,000 awards for general painting, work on paper, bark painting and more.

Blending artistic traditions

In Our lifestyle of tranquillity undisturbed, Presley draws on styles and iconography from throughout art history, including Italian Baroque artist Caravaggio, 16th-century Italian painter Domenico Beccafumi's The Annunciation, and Spanish artist Francisco Goya and his late 18th-century print The Sleep of Reason Produces Monsters.

"I'm threading together several well-known works," Presley explains.

Presley created Our lifestyle of tranquillity undisturbed over a period of about six months. (Supplied: MAGNT/Katherine Travis)

He wanted to imitate how those artworks use light, shade, and strong contrasts between the two — a technique known as chiaroscuro.

"The work pushed the boundaries of my skills," he says.

But the painting is more than an act of mimicry.

Presley says he wanted to "reinterpret" those classic works for modern Australia, including by incorporating a bushfire that blazes in the distance.

In his version, Presley affords the Indigenous figure and Australian landscape the "importance, reverence or magnificence" of the subjects of Renaissance paintings, while also drawing a link between the "flourishing" art scene of that period and Aboriginal artists working today.

Presley is also heavily influenced by other First Nations artists, including Clifford Possum Tjapaltjarri, Albert Namatjira, Gordon Bennett, Fiona Foley, Judy Watson, Gordon Hookey and Richard Bell.

That broad range of influences reaches back to his childhood growing up in Alice Springs and the artists he's worked beside since moving to south-east Queensland.

"[Alice Springs and Brisbane] both definitely shaped me and my world view and what I hold dear and treasure," he says.

"You get a real sense of spirit, cultural survival and transmission to the next generations [from this exhibition]," NATSIAA judge Julie Gough says. (Supplied: MAGNT/Charlie Bliss)

A three-time NATSIAA finalist, after being exhibited in 2016 and 2020, Presley is following in the footsteps of his uncle and fellow artist Laurie Presley, who was a finalist in 2007.

"That was really inspirational to me," he says. "[I thought] if he can do it, maybe I can do it too."

Now, Presley is proud to join the ranks of past winners, with their work over decades demonstrating the vitality of Aboriginal art and artists.

"Aboriginal people make the most important work in Australia, in my opinion," he says.

'A little act of defiance'

Larrakia, KarraJarri and Wardaman artist Jenna Mayilema Lee won the $15,000 Work on Paper Award for her work Taking back taken, in which she weaved dilly bags from paper maps stolen from the British Museum in London.

Lee attended the NATSIAAs as a child, growing up in a family of artists, including her uncle, former NATSIAA winner Gary Lee. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

The project grew from the time Canberra-born Lee — who also has Chinese, Japanese, Filipino, Irish, and Scottish ancestry — spent living in London in 2019, where she would visit museums and ask to see their collections of stolen Aboriginal artefacts.

Visting the British Museum one day, she noticed the museum's map of its galleries and facilities cost a suggested donation of 2 British pounds.

"I thought that was really cheeky: to suggest that the world can access their culture here, but in order to find out where it is, please give us 2 pounds," she says.

" So, I just decided to take one without paying as a little act of defiance. "

When she got home that evening, she realised the map could become material for her art.

Over the next year, she returned to the museum to nick more maps to turn into Taking back taken, before she moved back to Australia during the pandemic.

From Australia, she recruited family and friends visiting London to steal maps for her.

"I ended up with this network of people who were pinching maps from the British Museum on my behalf, which is not dissimilar to the way that Empire sent people out to collect world culture," Lee says.

"The act of taking it was the work."

Lee has exhibited at Setouchi Trienniale in Japan, the TarraWarra Biennial and as part of Melbourne Now at the NGV. (Supplied: MAGNT/Katherine Travis)

It took about five years for Lee to work up the skill to turn the maps into dilly bags — which she created in the style of the traditional objects she would visit in both local and international museum collections.

"[Taking back taken] is the culmination of a number of years, and of that singular moment of realising that I'd just taken material from the British Museum and that there the opportunity to turn it into something," she says.

It also seemingly builds on work Lee created for the 2020 NATSIAAs, titled HIStory Vessels, which landed her that year's Wandjuk Marika Memorial 3D Award.

Responding to the 250th anniversary of James Cook landing in Australia, Lee used the pages of a Ladybird history book titled The Story of Captain Cook to make a series of objects, including woven bags.

Turning paper into string for weaving is a difficult process — one Lee ascribes to her "sheer stubbornness" as well as to her urge to make work from plant fibres.

But, as an artist working in Melbourne, not on Country, she doesn't have access to the traditional materials used for weaving.

"If I wanted to be a weaver, I had to really think about what I was weaving," she says.

"But if I took a step back and looked around my own home and my own environment, it was just covered in books and paper.

"If I'm following the ways of my ancestors, it's being an expert in the resources around you — these are just the resources around me."

The NATSIAA exhibition is at Museum and Art Gallery of the Northern Territory, Darwin, until January 24.

World.title: Nicole Kidman delivers message to former school on 150th anniversary
World.content:
Lane Cove Public School on Sydney's Lower North Shore has been celebrating its 150th anniversary, and among the former students invited to participate was Academy Award-winner Nicole Kidman.

Birthday celebrations culminated in an open day on Friday during which former students and teachers were welcomed back to the school grounds to mark the occasion.

Hundreds gathered including former teachers and alumni. (Supplied: In the Cove, Jack Kelly)

Kidman responded with a message from her location in Santorini, Greece.

ABC News was on the ground to hear her congratulate the school on 150 years in a recording played out in the hall.

"I wish I could be with you," Kidman said.

"I remember running around that playground.

" I made friends that I'm still friends with now … and I'm so grateful that I went to such a great school. "

Kidman had previously told Network 10 she was going to try to make it to the celebrations after being invited there by students who posted a video encouraging her to turn up.

"It's the sweetest thing ever," Kidman told Angela Bishop.

Former teachers and alumni gather

The event attracted hundreds of people including former teachers and alumni, among them Channel Nine presenter Peter Overton who was a school captain in 1977.

Lane Cove Public School alumnus Peter Overton was quizzed by current students. (Supplied: In the Cove, Jack Kelly)

"You know when I first came here? 55 years ago," Overton said.

"I have so many happy memories of this school."

Overton reeled off the names of teachers he remembered, saying he was lucky to have attended the primary school.

Overton told the audience his good friend Kidman wanted to be there.

"Happy birthday from Nicole," he said.

Meredith Lucas, who was one of Kidman's classmates, returned to the school for the celebrations.

Nicole Kidman (front row, sixth from left) with fellow students including Meredith Lucas (first from left in front row). (Supplied: Lane Cove Public School)

Ms Lucas attended Lane Cove Public School from 1973–1979, from kindergarten to year six, alongside Kidman.

"It was a very close knit school and community and we sang in the choir together," Ms Lucas said.

"I applaud her for all her successes.

"She's a natural talent, she's a hard worker, she came from a good family and a good community.

"And I have watched her career from afar and I feel like she's done amazingly well in a very tough environment, being film and media."

Lane Cove Public School principal Terry McKinnon said he was proud of current and former students, including Kidman.

He said the birthday message she sent arrived just in time.

"It came in very late today and we were very happy to play it," Mr McKinnon said.

"It's great to hear from all our alumni, but particularly Nicole after we invited her to this event.

"We're extremely proud of her, as we are of all our alumni."

The school's official birthday fell on January 14.

It has been around since 1876 and prides itself on its creative arts and music programs.

A woman accused of running over a man while stealing his car will face court on Saturday, after a dramatic arrest where police officers were allegedly forced to jump out of the way of a moving car while conducting a search warrant.

The 51-year-old woman was one of three arrested at Narvick Crescent, Heidelberg West on Friday, almost a week after an incident in nearby Blackwood Parade that left a 68-year-old man fighting for life.

Earlier this week, police urged a woman to hand herself in after she allegedly ran over a man who was trying to stop her from stealing his car in Heidelberg West. Victoria Police

In Friday’s incident, officers were conducting a search warrant at Narvick Crescent, when a vehicle parked in the driveway allegedly drove at them, forcing them to jump out of its path.

World.title: AFL LIVE: Lions rip the Hawks apart in prime time; Hawkins takes aim at Cats over scandal

Geelong great Tom Hawkins has called out the Cats hierarchy for not speaking to the public on Thursday and explaining their actions regarding the secret concussion waiver with premiership defender Jake Kolodjashnij.

“It’s hard to formulate an opinion when there has been so little information given,” Hawkins said on Kayo Sports on Friday night.

Geelong’s games record holder Tom Hawkins and 355-gamer Joel Selwood with their former teammate Mark Blicavs ahead of his 300th game. AFL Photos

“As a football spectator now, I was frustrated with the process, that it has taken so long to hear from the Geelong Football Club. We heard from Steve Hocking. It was a misstep.

World.title: Roosters pip Bulldogs to draw level with league leaders
World.content:
Sydney Roosters have edged past Canterbury in a 20-18 win that has blown the race for the NRL’s minor premiership wide open.

On a pivotal night in the make-up of the top four, the Roosters moved up to second with a late win at Allianz Stadium that puts Trent Robinson’s men level on 36 points with ladder-leading Penrith.

Loading

The Panthers, who sit first as a result of their superior for and against, host the Roosters next Thursday and look set to be without captain Isaah Yeo.

Even without facing Yeo, the Roosters will have to turn things up a notch against the Panthers as the race for the minor premiership looks set to go to the wire.

Robinson’s side led 8-2 at half-time on Friday but were stunned when a try from Lachlan Galvin and a Jacob Kiraz double in a 12-minute second-half spell catapulted the Bulldogs into an unlikely lead.

But a miscommunication at the back by Bulldogs fullback Connor Tracey allowed Salesi Foketi to dive on a loose kick and claim the match-winning try in the 69th minute.

Loading

The victory gave the Roosters a seventh-straight win but also puts a major dent in Canterbury’s top-eight aspirations after they threatened to upset the home side.

Stephen Crichton kicked a penalty to get the Bulldogs on the board after sixth minutes before Sam Walker and Hugo Savala combined down the left to send Billy Smith in at the corner.

Then after Matt Burton failed to gather a Daly Cherry-Evans bomb, Siua Wong touched down for the Roosters who led 8-2 at half-time after Walker failed to convert both kicks.

The Bulldogs had struggled for spark in the first half but they came back after half-time with a bang as hooker Bailey Hayward burst up the middle of the field and found a supporting Kiraz.

The Canterbury winger scored under the posts as Crichton converted to tie the game up.

Galvin then put the Bulldogs ahead for the first time when the five-eighth drifted across field and darted through a Reece Robson tackle to score.

Galvin set up Kiraz for his side’s third but Canterbury were unable to find a knockout blow and the Roosters clawed their way back into the game.

Smith added a second with 15 minutes left before Foketi was in the right place at the right time, touching down a Walker bomb that Tracey failed to take to score the decisive try.

AAP

World.title: ‘Doesn’t look great’: Fears Penrith co-captain Isaah Yeo’s season could be over
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 ‘Doesn’t look great’: Fears Penrith co-captain Isaah Yeo’s season could be over Christian Nicolussi Updated August 7, 2026 — 9:25pm ,first published 8:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Isaah Yeo suffered a suspected pectoral injury on Friday evening, with Penrith coach Ivan Cleary conceding: “It doesn’t look great.” And to make matters worse, their opponents next Thursday night, the Sydney Roosters, plucked a come-from-behind win over Canterbury – and now have the chance to move to the top of the ladder should they triumph at CommBank Stadium. Loading Panthers supporters will be hoping scans clear their co-captain of any serious damage after he came from the field late in the first half during the 28-12 loss to the New Zealand Warriors. Yeo reeled out of a tackle and immediately looked in pain. He is expected to have scans back in Sydney, which is most likely to be Sunday.



The competition leaders scored two tries in three minutes late in the game, and were rightfully denied a third when Liam Martin was ruled offside during a kick chase. But the immediate focus will be on inspirational leader Yeo, whose importance to the premiership favourites is the equal of Nathan Cleary. Panthers captain Isaah Yeo. Getty Images A ruptured pec would mean Yeo misses the rest of the season for Penrith, and also require Kevin Walters to find a new captain for Australia ahead of the World Cup. At the very least, Yeo is next to no chance to be available for the heavyweight showdown with the Roosters.



Lindsay Smith and Billy Phillips are early contenders to replace Yeo at lock forward. “Obviously ‘Yeoy’ is a big loss and hard to replace, but that’s how it goes; if that’s the case we’ll have to [move forward without him],” Cleary said. “You can’t win the game at the start, but you can sort of lose it. We missed the start tonight.” Luke Metcalf scores for the Warriors against Penrith. Getty Images The Panthers could also lose centre Paul Alamoti who was binned and placed on report for up-ending opposite centre Leka Halasima in the first half.



Penrith (shoulder) are likely to welcome back Dylan Edwards, but Casey McLean (hand) and Mitch Kenny (foot/ankle) will not be available until the eve of the finals. The Roosters trailed 18-8 with 15 minutes remaining against the Bulldogs before their halves Sam Walker and Daly Cherry-Evans built pressure through their kicking games. Billy Smith bagged a double, then Salesi Foketi won the race to a Walker kick that was bizarrely allowed to bounce by the Dogs. The 20-18 loss for the Bulldogs means they will finish the weekend outside the top eight, and potentially as low as 10th should Manly beat Melbourne in Perth. Back-rower Sitili Tupouniua returned for the first time since round 16, but lasted five minutes before succumbing to a hamstring injury.



The Warriors, meanwhile, also kept themselves in the minor premiership race, with coach Andrew Webster admitting the win would serve as a wonderful confidence boost, and timely reminder “we belong” at the pointy end of the year. Related Article Live

Sydney Roosters 20 Canterbury 18

NRL 2026 Roosters pip Bulldogs to draw level with league leaders They take on the Broncos and Rabbitohs in the next fortnight, and round out the regular season at home to Newcastle and Manly. Penrith take on the Roosters, followed by Melbourne, then the Bulldogs and Tigers. In his first game since April, out-of-favour Warriors half Luke Metcalf scored in the first half, then stepped inside to score his second try to seal the result inside a rocking Go Media Stadium. A top-two finish for the Warriors would be a huge bonus, with the intimidating atmosphere sure to help when hosting a qualifying final and potentially preliminary final.

All but one westbound lane on the M5 motorway in Sydney’s south-west have reopened following a garbage truck fire that led to a traffic jam stretching about 10 kilometres, causing hours of delays for drivers during peak hour.

The fire broke out on the truck, which was travelling on the motorway at Milperra in Sydney’s south-west just before 4pm.

One westbound lane reopened about 6pm, before a second lane reopened about 9pm, with one lane remaining closed.

The truck was fully alight when crews arrived, Fire and Rescue NSW acting Superintendent Peter Murray said.

A woman accused of running over a man while stealing his car will face court on Saturday, after a dramatic arrest where police officers were allegedly forced to jump out of the way of a moving car while conducting a search warrant.

The 51-year-old woman was one of three arrested at Narvick Crescent, Heidelberg West on Friday, almost a week after an incident in nearby Blackwood Parade that left a 68-year-old man fighting for life.

Earlier this week, police urged a woman to hand herself in after she allegedly ran over a man who was trying to stop her from stealing his car in Heidelberg West. Victoria Police

In Friday’s incident, officers were conducting a search warrant at Narvick Crescent, when a vehicle parked in the driveway allegedly drove at them, forcing them to jump out of its path.

“The vehicle lost control, crashing into a wall before allegedly ramming an unmarked police vehicle,” police said in a statement on Friday night.

World.title: AFL LIVE: Lions rip the Hawks apart in prime time; Hawkins takes aim at Cats over scandal
World.content:
Geelong great Tom Hawkins has called out the Cats hierarchy for not speaking to the public on Thursday and explaining their actions regarding the secret concussion waiver with premiership defender Jake Kolodjashnij.

“It’s hard to formulate an opinion when there has been so little information given,” Hawkins said on Kayo Sports on Friday night.

Geelong’s games record holder Tom Hawkins and 355-gamer Joel Selwood with their former teammate Mark Blicavs ahead of his 300th game. AFL Photos

“As a football spectator now, I was frustrated with the process, that it has taken so long to hear from the Geelong Football Club. We heard from Steve Hocking. It was a misstep.

“I don’t know – I think there is still more to be played out. I just find it staggering that yesterday [Thursday], they [Geelong] didn’t front the media and talk us through the process of what has actually happened.”

World.title: Roosters pip Bulldogs to draw level with league leaders
World.content:
Sydney Roosters have edged past Canterbury in a 20-18 win that has blown the race for the NRL’s minor premiership wide open.

On a pivotal night in the make-up of the top four, the Roosters moved up to second with a late win at Allianz Stadium that puts Trent Robinson’s men level on 36 points with ladder-leading Penrith.

Loading

The Panthers, who sit first as a result of their superior for and against, host the Roosters next Thursday and look set to be without captain Isaah Yeo.

Even without facing Yeo, the Roosters will have to turn things up a notch against the Panthers as the race for the minor premiership looks set to go to the wire.

Robinson’s side led 8-2 at half-time on Friday but were stunned when a try from Lachlan Galvin and a Jacob Kiraz double in a 12-minute second-half spell catapulted the Bulldogs into an unlikely lead.

But a miscommunication at the back by Bulldogs fullback Connor Tracey allowed Salesi Foketi to dive on a loose kick and claim the match-winning try in the 69th minute.

Loading

The victory gave the Roosters a seventh-straight win but also puts a major dent in Canterbury’s top-eight aspirations after they threatened to upset the home side.

Stephen Crichton kicked a penalty to get the Bulldogs on the board after sixth minutes before Sam Walker and Hugo Savala combined down the left to send Billy Smith in at the corner.

Then after Matt Burton failed to gather a Daly Cherry-Evans bomb, Siua Wong touched down for the Roosters who led 8-2 at half-time after Walker failed to convert both kicks.

The Bulldogs had struggled for spark in the first half but they came back after half-time with a bang as hooker Bailey Hayward burst up the middle of the field and found a supporting Kiraz.

The Canterbury winger scored under the posts as Crichton converted to tie the game up.

Galvin then put the Bulldogs ahead for the first time when the five-eighth drifted across field and darted through a Reece Robson tackle to score.

Galvin set up Kiraz for his side’s third but Canterbury were unable to find a knockout blow and the Roosters clawed their way back into the game.

Smith added a second with 15 minutes left before Foketi was in the right place at the right time, touching down a Walker bomb that Tracey failed to take to score the decisive try.

AAP

World.title: ‘Doesn’t look great’: Fears Penrith co-captain Isaah Yeo’s season could be over
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 ‘Doesn’t look great’: Fears Penrith co-captain Isaah Yeo’s season could be over Christian Nicolussi Updated August 7, 2026 — 9:25pm ,first published 8:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Isaah Yeo suffered a suspected pectoral injury on Friday evening, with Penrith coach Ivan Cleary conceding: “It doesn’t look great.” And to make matters worse, their opponents next Thursday night, the Sydney Roosters, plucked a come-from-behind win over Canterbury – and now have the chance to move to the top of the ladder should they triumph at CommBank Stadium. Loading Panthers supporters will be hoping scans clear their co-captain of any serious damage after he came from the field late in the first half during the 28-12 loss to the New Zealand Warriors. Yeo reeled out of a tackle and immediately looked in pain. He is expected to have scans back in Sydney, which is most likely to be Sunday.



The competition leaders scored two tries in three minutes late in the game, and were rightfully denied a third when Liam Martin was ruled offside during a kick chase. But the immediate focus will be on inspirational leader Yeo, whose importance to the premiership favourites is the equal of Nathan Cleary. Panthers captain Isaah Yeo. Getty Images A ruptured pec would mean Yeo misses the rest of the season for Penrith, and also require Kevin Walters to find a new captain for Australia ahead of the World Cup. At the very least, Yeo is next to no chance to be available for the heavyweight showdown with the Roosters.



Lindsay Smith and Billy Phillips are early contenders to replace Yeo at lock forward. “Obviously ‘Yeoy’ is a big loss and hard to replace, but that’s how it goes; if that’s the case we’ll have to [move forward without him],” Cleary said. “You can’t win the game at the start, but you can sort of lose it. We missed the start tonight.” Luke Metcalf scores for the Warriors against Penrith. Getty Images The Panthers could also lose centre Paul Alamoti who was binned and placed on report for up-ending opposite centre Leka Halasima in the first half.



Penrith (shoulder) are likely to welcome back Dylan Edwards, but Casey McLean (hand) and Mitch Kenny (foot/ankle) will not be available until the eve of the finals. The Roosters trailed 18-8 with 15 minutes remaining against the Bulldogs before their halves Sam Walker and Daly Cherry-Evans built pressure through their kicking games. Billy Smith bagged a double, then Salesi Foketi won the race to a Walker kick that was bizarrely allowed to bounce by the Dogs. The 20-18 loss for the Bulldogs means they will finish the weekend outside the top eight, and potentially as low as 10th should Manly beat Melbourne in Perth. Back-rower Sitili Tupouniua returned for the first time since round 16, but lasted five minutes before succumbing to a hamstring injury.



The Warriors, meanwhile, also kept themselves in the minor premiership race, with coach Andrew Webster admitting the win would serve as a wonderful confidence boost, and timely reminder “we belong” at the pointy end of the year. Related Article Live

Sydney Roosters 20 Canterbury 18

NRL 2026 Roosters pip Bulldogs to draw level with league leaders They take on the Broncos and Rabbitohs in the next fortnight, and round out the regular season at home to Newcastle and Manly. Penrith take on the Roosters, followed by Melbourne, then the Bulldogs and Tigers. In his first game since April, out-of-favour Warriors half Luke Metcalf scored in the first half, then stepped inside to score his second try to seal the result inside a rocking Go Media Stadium. A top-two finish for the Warriors would be a huge bonus, with the intimidating atmosphere sure to help when hosting a qualifying final and potentially preliminary final.

World.content:

All but one westbound lane on the M5 motorway in Sydney’s south-west have reopened following a garbage truck fire that led to a traffic jam stretching about 10 kilometres, causing hours of delays for drivers during peak hour.

The fire broke out on the truck, which was travelling on the motorway at Milperra in Sydney’s south-west just before 4pm.

One westbound lane reopened about 6pm, before a second lane reopened about 9pm, with one lane remaining closed.

The truck was fully alight when crews arrived, Fire and Rescue NSW acting Superintendent Peter Murray said.

World.title: Pacific Islands Forum fails to reach consensus on anti-missile statement against China
World.content:
Disagreement from some China-aligned Pacific Islands countries has prevented regional countries within the Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) issuing a joint statement against missile testing in the Pacific.

At their meeting in Suva on Friday, PIF foreign ministers failed to agree on a unified statement against China after it fired a nuclear-capable missile into Pacific waters last month, despite deep concern among most countries about Beijing's actions.

It is understood there was a majority of countries represented at the meeting who wanted a clear joint regional statement condemning such missile testing in the nuclear-free Pacific.

However, the Forum's usual Pacific decision-making by consensus could not be met because Kiribati and Nauru were opposed to a strong statement condemning the testing.

New Zealand's Foreign Minister Winston Peters told media some Pacific nations were using the consensus system because they were more concerned with external partners' wishes than those that belong to the Pacific Islands Forum, something he described as an "unusual view".

"They didn't actually lay out any reasons, apart from their disagreement, and not wishing for us to make the clear statement such as 'we are opposed to missiles being fired into the Pacific'.

"That's what the statement should have said, and we're still waiting for that to get laid out."

Foreign Minister Winston Peters speaking to reporters in Fiji ahead of the Pacific Islands Forum Foreign Ministers' meeting on Friday. Supplied / screenshot

Some governments have pointed out that China is not the only country testing nuclear-capable missiles in the Pacific. The US regularly conducts tests into the Marshall Islands.

Peters said that testing in the Marshall Islands was done with the country's consent.

Security agenda

The PIF Foreign Ministers Meeting was held to set the agenda for the annual Leaders' Meeting in Palau later this month.

A Solomon Islands proposal for a regional security treaty was one of the discussion points, although it's clear more consultation is required on the matter.

The Solomon Islands' Foreign Affairs and External Trade permanent secretary George Hoa'au told RNZ Pacific that there was already a range of regional security mechanisms in the Forum fale.

"The missing part is to have a common thatched roof over them," he said.

"The proposal for this single security treaty by Solomons is to provide an umbrella on top of what is already regional MOUs which are non-binding."

World.title: Warriors shock NRL table-topping Panthers in Metcalf comeback
World.content:
Halfback Luke Metcalf made a triumphant return to the NZ Warriors, leading his current team to a stunning 28-12 victory the NRL table-topping Penrith Panthers at Auckland's Go Media Stadium.

Metcalf was summoned into the Warriors line-up, after Te Maire Martin pulled out with a hamstring injury, and celebrated his comeback with two tries and 16 points, as the home side never really let their rivals into the game.

They pounced early with a try to lock Erin Clark, before Metcalf grabbed his first, looming in support of break by second-rower Kurt Capewell.

Five-eighth Chanel Harris-Tavita added another try before halftime, as the Warriors took an 18-0 lead into the sheds.

They had not lost a game that they led at the break this season and they took another step towards victory, when fullback Charnze Nicoll-Klokstad - another forced to wait his turn this season - was first to score after the restart.

Penrith threatened to spoil the party, when they scored back-to-back tries to halfback Nathan Cleary and fullback Jaxen Edgar, both masterminded by Cleary.

They crossed for a third to wing Paul Alamoti, but it was overruled for offside in a kick chase.

Moments later, Metcalf sealed the win with his second try.

The result consolidates the Warriors' position in the top three - it puts them second on points difference, with Sydney Roosters yet to play this weekend - now two points behind Penrith.

World.title: Dargaville man faces multiple firearms charges after shooting into a garage
World.content:
A Dargaville man faces multiple firearms charges after firing a shot into a garage and sparking a major police operation on Thursday night.

The 37-year-old appeared in the Whangārei District Court on Friday charged with discharging a firearm in a house, discharging a firearm to intimidate, presenting a firearm at a person, unlawful possession of a firearm, and unlawful possession of ammunition.

The drama began on Ranfurly Street in Dargaville, close to Selwyn Park Primary School, just after 6.30pm.

Local residents reported seeing the police Eagle helicopter circling over the town, as many as 10 police cars, and spikes being laid to stop any fleeing vehicle.

Other residents attending a public meeting in town were told not to leave the building.

Inspector Maria Nordstrom, Whangārei-Kaipara Area Commander, said police responded to reports of a man pointing a firearm at a person during a family harm incident.

He then allegedly fired a shot into an unoccupied garage on the property.

"Our staff responded into the area, and took this man into custody," she said.

"Police would like to reassure the community that this was an isolated incident, involving parties known to each other."

Police enquiries were continuing.

World.title: Firefighters battle house fire in Auckland's Milford
World.content:
Emergency crews have battled a house fire on Auckland's North Shore.

Fire and Emergency (FENZ) says it was called to the house in Milford about 3.30pm.

At 6.30pm, FENZ told RNZ the fire had been contained to the upper floor.

Two crews were still at the scene, alongside a fire investigator to determine the cause.

At its height, six fire trucks were at the scene.

World.title: Winston Peters says Pacific missed chance to issue statement after Chinese missile test
World.content:
Foreign Minister Winston Peters says the Pacific missed an opportunity not to issue a joint statement soon after China launched a nuclear-capable missile into waters near Tuvalu.

He spoke before Friday's Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) Foreign Ministers' Meeting where the ministers failed to agree on a unified statement against China. Peters had earlier labelled it a "delicate issue".

Peters is in Fiji for the meeting along with counterparts from 17 other Pacific countries, in preparation for the leaders' meeting in Palau, in early September.

It's been a month since China test-launched a nuclear-capable ballistic missile with a dummy warhead into the Pacific Ocean - a nuclear free zone.

It was met with condemnation from some Pacific leaders, and Christopher Luxon said the New Zealand government made clear to China that the move was unacceptable - but there has not been a unanimous statement from Pacific nations.

Peters said New Zealand had been pushing for one.

Peters - who did not name the countries - said they were granting outside partners' wishes rather than those of the Pacific Islands Forum.

"So we made it very clear that we do not think that outsiders should be telling the insiders - that's us [who] have been here for thousands of years - what our position should be, and it's an ongoing piece of work at this piece of time."

"It's a very delicate issue," he said, suggesting some countries would come to the meeting with their minds made up.

"The roadblock is that if you've had a predetermined position, any discussion here and any logic and reasoning will not land," he said.

"We'll see whether logic prevails in this debate, or whether the debate has already been settled by people having a predetermined position from which they will not move."

The PIF Foreign Leaders' Meeting group photo in Fiji on 7 August 2026. RNZ / Lauren Crimp

He said it was not too late to take a joint position however it should have been done sooner: "the sooner the better."

The countries should not be in a position where they could not reach consensus on the matter, said Peters.

"At this point in time, we've got one third of the world's surface, there's a desperation for serious funds when it comes to resilience building in this part of the world," he said.

"The economic situation is not good, so we need each other more than ever, and we need international recognition as well more than ever."

Peters had a brief discussion with Australia's foreign minister Penny Wong on Friday morning ahead of the meeting, but would not say whether the two countries were on the same page.

He said there would also be discussion about how partner countries work with PIF following the controversial decision to ban them - including heavy hitters like China and the US - from last year's meeting in the Solomon Islands.

Peters has spoken out repeatedly about "outsiders" influencing the Solomon Islands Prime Minister Jeremiah Manele to implement the ban, which Manele denied, arguing the block made sense while PIF leaders considered how best to respond to the increasing interest from partners wanting a seat at the regional decision-making table.

"We need their help," Peters said.

"This idea of tiering people and all sorts of this part of the discussion, if it means that you actually lose the chance for buy-in by serious countries, then that'll be a big mistake."

Fiji's foreign minister Sakiasi Ditoka opened the meeting with a call for unity.

"Even as our strategic environment becomes more complex, the Pacific response should not be fragmentation or division," he said, as the Pacific Islands Forum Foreign Minister's meeting kicked off.

"It should be greater regional solidarity, stronger consensus and continued confidence in our own regional institutions and processes."

He said the foreign ministers had a "unique responsibility," helping to shape how the Pacific "engages the world, manages these partnerships, and protects the integrity of our regional institutions".

Ditoka said the matters before the forum reflect that responsibility, from "strengthening our peace and security architecture", to advancing the 2050 "international engagement strategy" and "deepening regional integration".

He also stated it was about "ensuring our partnerships continue to serve Pacific priorities".

"Together they represent practical steps towards implementing the vision set out in the 2050 strategy for the blue Pacific continent."

The secretary general Baron Waqa followed, saying guidance from the foreign ministers would continue to shape the evolution of regionalism and the "trajectory of regional institutions".

For his part, he said, "allow me to reaffirm that the secretariat remains committed to supporting a forum that is increasingly strategic" and responsible.

"One that is able to anticipate emerging challenges, coordinate regional action, and deliver effectively on the priorities set by leaders."

Meanwhile, Tuvalu's foreign secretary Pasuna Tuaga said his country had asked for help searching for the dummy warhead, which landed in nearby waters.

World.title: Bad week? Try being a Chris
World.content:
Analysis: It's been a rough week in politics and if it's not one Chris having a bad day, it's the other.

That was the case on Friday when four shocker days for the prime minister swung to the left following a woeful poll result for Labour's Chris Hipkins.

Christopher Luxon's foot-in-mouth moments would have been enough on their own without adding in his foreign minister telling a Chinese-Kiwi Parliamentary colleague to "go back to where you've come from", and unemployment at an 11-year high, with just 92 days until the election.

A sympathetic observer would look to Luxon's time at the helm and say he's had bad luck with being handed a complicated coalition, an economy on its knees, and an unpredictable US president.

Yet, Luxon is the first to ignore the complexities of Covid - a worldwide pandemic never seen in our time - and the problems that created for Labour and Jacinda Ardern.

So, on that basis his starting point for all prime ministers is that regardless of the crisis - health or economic or both - it's not an excuse for the government of the day's performance, or lack thereof.

That's a problematic baseline for a governing party that sold itself as the economic fixer.

While there are plenty of improvements to be celebrated - turning points in some (not all) business confidence, inflation at times getting closer to the target bracket - there are also some nightmare numbers Luxon cannot ignore.

Christopher Luxon. Pool/AFP/Michael Bradley

The biggest one came this week in the form of an unemployment rise to an 11-year high of 5.6 percent.

There are now 171,000 people unemployed and around 8000 more people are experiencing long term unemployment - those out of work for a year or more - this June quarter than in the same quarter last year.

Couple that with Luxon's brainfart moment last weekend where he decided to attack provincial New Zealand small and medium sized businesses (SMEs) telling them they had a "parent-child mentality" and needed to be more "adult" and the prime minister's grip on the economy doesn't look so tight.

Former National Party leader turned Auckland Business Chamber chief executive Simon Bridges summed it up best in a NZ Herald column on Friday morning.

"And to state what I hope is blindingly obvious, but clearly isn't, SMEs are very different from a business with thousands of employees and hundreds of millions or billions in turnover. They didn't, as the Prime Minister says he did, "sit in Illinois for six years" as an executive of consumer goods company Unilever, and they don't think that much about "commercially superior returns, great customer experience and awesome internal culture". Not explicitly anyway. The owner very often is the internal culture, the HR manager, accounts, marketing and everything else, rolled into one. They are busy just surviving. They do their best every day without huge analysis or much if any support.

"Yet, such lowly businesspeople do worry about what the Government does, because the Government in this small nation controls so much in terms of spending, sentiment, policies and programmes. Its taxes, costs and red tape make all the difference, as do its statements and initiatives," Bridges wrote.

It's a scathing reality check for the prime minister who prides himself on getting out of the Wellington bubble and connecting with everyday Kiwis living in the region to find himself managing to offend, and later having to apologise to, what was considered a friendly business audience.

NZ First leader Winston Peters and Green MP Lawrence Xu-Nan. RNZ

Supporters have commended Luxon for acknowledging he got it wrong and saying sorry, but there are others who have asked how he stuffed it up in the first place.

The point Luxon was trying to make about him wanting government to get out of the way so that business can thrive is valid, but despite making this point on so many occasions in the past two-and-a-half years to various business audiences he still hasn't nailed the delivery of it.

The other notable gaffe this week was turning a day of celebration in Auckland that the long-awaited CRL finally had an opening date into a confused mess about whether National was going to hold a referendum on MMP.

It was an own goal when instead of concentrating on an infrastructure success, or taking a whack at Labour's plan to ditch National's much-loved Investment Boost policy, Luxon loose-lipped his way into an election promise that even his caucus doubted was real.

National would have breathed a deep sigh of relief when the Taxpayers' Union-Curia poll landed on Friday with some good news for the party.

Not only was it up on 31 percent and ahead of Labour, but the coalition was also in a position to form a government and Luxon was up in the preferred prime minister numbers.

Chris Hipkins. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Labour has plummeted to 27.8 percent - a dire result that on first glance looks to have come from Luxon ruling out working with Opportunity after the election.

Opportunity has soared to 6 percent in the poll at the expense of Labour.

Labour has been operating on a small-target strategy with policy announcements this election year after learning the lesson of flooding voters in 2023, and losing sight of what the party stood for and was trying to sell.

But the new approach appears to be having its own problems with National getting centrist policy like solar panel loans for households and KiwiSaver policy out ahead of Labour, and leaving the Opposition unable to criticise something it broadly agrees with.

Hipkins also has his own popularity issues to deal with. He's a known quantity having been prime minister before, which he was handed and then had ripped off him when voters went to the polls and chose the other Chris.

He has a difficult job explaining to voters why he'd do a better job second time round.

World.title: Concern Wellington ratepayers will refuse to ration water
World.content:
An advocate for ratepayers says there is a risk Wellington residents will refuse to follow water restrictions, with growing frustration over pricey bills.

Tiaki Wai's first quarterly bills were sent out over the past few weeks, leaving residents shocked at the pricetag, some over $1000.

Come September, Wellington region will be asked to only use sprinklers every second day, and just between the hours of 6-8am and 7-9pm. The Upper Hutt area was already under those restrictions.

James Ross from the Wellington Rates Payers Alliance said the rationing had been unfair for a long time, but had been hidden away in rates bills.

Now, with water charges under a spotlight in a separate Tiaki Wai bill, he said restrictions would likely not be taken well.

"There's a very real concern that people won't be motivated to follow those water restrictions, because frankly I think a lot of people will see them as unfair.

"You've now got these huge water bills ... and yet we're still being told the assests are in such a bad way that you can't use your sprinklers when you need to."

For Ross, this would be solved with water meters, which he said would motivate residents to ration water.

Tiaki Wai planned to roll out water meters so bills reflected actual water use, rather than a fixed rate based on capital value.

However, its draft strategy said installing meters could take between five and seven years, and may cost upwards of $500 million.

Ross said the entity needed to begin this roll out sooner - and cheaper.

He said restrictions were a reality of mismanaged water systems, but meters would allow people to pay for what they actually use.

Tiaki Wai said there was no correlation between water conservation and the amount Wellington property owners have paid for water as part of their rates or will pay as part of their water services bill.

Upper Hutt was always on level one restrictions, following a decision made by the council years ago, a spokeperson said.

Wellington, Porirua and Hutt City were on the restriction during daylight saving months.

The restrictions were to conserve the region's finite water supply, the spokesperson said.

World.title: Wellington, Wairarapa mayors agree to put two amalgamation proposals to ministers
World.content:
Wellington and Wairarapa mayors have agreed to put two amalgamation proposals to ministers by Sunday.

Mayors from the eight councils in the region met this afternoon to discuss plans for a super-merger for local government reforms.

One proposal supported by Wellington, Lower Hutt, Porirua and South Wairarapa District Councils calls for a region-wide merger of all eight councils,

Caterton and Masterton District Councils are proposing a separate Wairarapa-only authority.

Some mayors opposed these ideas but proposals can be submitted against other councils' wishes.

Upper Hutt and Kapiti District Councils have opposed amalgamation.

Kapiti District wanted to submit their own proposal to be a singular unitary authority.

But individual councils cannot submit a proposal to become singular authorities without being part of a larger submission to the ministers.

And other councils disagreed on the grounds that the proposal did not meet the rules of the Head Start programme for local government overhaul.

World.title: New jumper revealed as NRL grants Perth Bears salary concessions
World.content:
The NRL's newest side, the Perth Bears, have unveiled their inaugural playing jersey on the same day they were granted salary cap concessions ahead of their entry to the competition in 2027.

In an event coordinated between Perth and North Sydney, where the unveiling was live-streamed, the Bears revealed the jersey by dropping the design from the famous WACA Ground light towers.

The design, which features red hoops on a black background, pays homage the North Sydney Bears, which left the NRL at the end of the 1999 season and currently play in the NSW Cup competition.

Peter V'landys (second from left) announced the concessions alongside WA Premier Roger Cook (speaking), Bears CEO Anthony De Ceglie, and Perth coach Mal Meninga (left). (ABC News: Tom Wildie)

The unveiling of the jersey marks a major step towards the Bears' entry into the NRL, which club chief executive Anthony De Ceglie said was on track to have 35,000 members by the beginning of the 2027 season.

Salary boost

In a big boost to the club, Australian Rugby League Commission chair Peter V'landys announced the Bears would be granted a concession for signing a marquee player.

"They will be given a 20 per cent dispensation for any player above a million dollars [salary]," V'landys said.

"If the player is worth $1.5 million, they can pay another 20 per cent from a sponsor and that won't be counted in the salary cap.

" So that gives them the opportunity to get somebody because they've got a 20 per cent bonus for that player from the sponsor. "

The Perth Bears will play in the 2027 NRL season. (ABC News: Tom Wildie)

Additionally, the Bears will have first rights to any player who wants to leave their club but is under contract for 2027.

"You may have a marquee player that's not happy in a particular club and the club and the player want to separate. That player can only go to Perth in the first instance," V'landys said.

"There will be some good players that will come up and be given the opportunity to play in Perth."

The concessions will help the Bears land a high-profile player, which has so far being lacking in their signings.

Meninga happy with progress

Bears inaugural coach Mal Meninga says he is "really happy" with the club's progress to date and talked down the need for a marquee player.

"We've worked within the conditions of obviously our entry into the NRL and you know … let me be frank with this … I'm really excited about the roster we've built," he said.

"You look through the team, we've got some high-profile players already.

"We've certainly got players of the future, there's no doubt.

"I really appreciate Peter and the club's great concessions, but I'm really happy with where we are at the moment."

Bellamy excited

Veteran Melbourne Storm coach Craig Bellamy said the arrival of the Bears was exciting for the league.

And he said the club was in good hands with coach Mal Meninga steering the ship.

"I worked with Mal, I played with Mal and I know the amount of work that he puts in and the amount of work he will put into the coaching," he said.

"I'm sure it will be a very successful venture."

The Storm has already seen two of their players, Nick Meaney and Tyran Wishart, sign on with the Bears, but the coach was magnanimous about their departure.

Tyran Wishart of the Storm will line up for the Bears next season. (AAP: Morgan Hancock)

"They're very excited to be coming over here," he said.

"They're obviously doing what they think's best for them and best for their families.

"They're still doing a great job for us.

"That's just the way the game is."

World.title: Live: 'Doesn't look great': Fears Penrith captain could miss rest of NRL season
World.content:
Penrith captain Isaah Yeo may miss the rest of the NRL season after injuring his pectoral muscle, while the Sydney Roosters joined the Panthers on top of the table after defeating the Canterbury Bulldogs.

Yeo came off in the first half of Penrith's 28-12 loss to the New Zealand Warriors in Auckland on Friday night, with the Auckland-based side solidifying their status as a genuine premiership threat in 2026.

Yeo was clutching his pectoral muscle after reeling out of a tackle, with scans needed to confirm if he has sustained a tear.

Should scans confirm a pectoral tear, he could be out for the rest of the season.

"It doesn't look great," Panthers coach Ivan Cleary said during his press conference.

"Obviously Yeoy's a big loss and hard to replace, but that's how it goes.

"If that's the case, we'll have to (replace him)."

Meanwhile, the Roosters have joined the Panthers on 36 points at the top of the NRL ladder, surviving a scare to pip the Bulldogs 20-18.

The Roosters held an 8-2 lead at half-time, but the Bulldogs scored three tries in 11 minutes to take an 18-8 lead with 25 minutes to play.

But two quick tries in the final 15 minutes for the Roosters earned them a hard-fought win.

Meanwhile, Craig Bellamy says he will be coach of the Melbourne Storm in 2027, despite recent health issues.

Follow the live blog below, keep up to date with all the latest stats in our ScoreCentre, and tune in to our live radio coverage.

World.title: De Minaur haunted by Montreal Masters double-fault drama
World.content:
A double fault has proved costly for Alex de Minaur with the Australian star blowing a match point before falling to Briton Cameron Norrie at the Montreal Masters.

Third-seeded De Minaur was up 5-2 and 40-30 in the second set, but stumbled to allow Norrie back into their third-round match.

He had another chance when serving for the match at 5-4, but again double-faulted to surrender the game on Norrie's fourth break point.

World number 37 Norrie then dug deep to record a 5-7, 7-6 (5), 6-1 victory after two hours and 52 minutes in difficult, humid conditions.

Norrie said he had to weather de Minaur's early onslaught with the newly married Aussie starting with a bang.

"From the beginning, Alex came out firing and I was like, 'Woah, this is a crazy level', and I had to match it," Norrie said in his on-court interview.

"I managed to go up a break [in the first set], but he stayed really tough and I know he's so tough as a competitor and stole that first set.

"He was looking good in the second set, and I think he took the foot off the gas very slightly and I managed to free up, steal the tie-break and then it was just a battle.

"It was a great match to win, and to test my level and I can take so much confidence from this one."

Australians through in Montreal Alex de Minaur and fellow Australians Alexei Popyrin and Tahlia Gibson all record encouraging wins three weeks out from the US Open in New York.

Entering Thursday's (Friday AEST) match, de Minaur was the highest seed remaining at the hard court tournament, also known as the Canadian Open, with defending champion and fifth seed Ben Shelton taking over that title.

In some good news for de Minaur, because American Taylor Fritz and Italian Flavio Cobolli have also exited the event early, he can only possibly drop from seven to eight in the rankings, and that's only if Shelton wins the title.

That means the Australian, who broke through for a career-high number five ranking in July, will keep his top-eight US Open seeding intact for now.

De Minaur is looking to improve on quarter-final finishes at Flushing Meadows in the past two years.

Norrie will next take on 18th seed Arthur Fils, who earlier cruised past Mariano Navone 6-3, 6-2 to maintain his impressive record at Masters 1000 events this year.

AAP

World.title: Ex-AFLPA boss calls for independent tribunal over Cats concussion waiver
World.content:
Former Richmond player and AFL Players Association (AFLPA) chief Joel Bowden has criticised the AFL, Geelong and the AFLPA for their handling of the secret concussion waiver signed by an unknown Cats player, calling for a Senate committee hearing to investigate.

The Cats have avoided any sanction from the AFL for making a deal with a player who had a history of concussions that required him to assume all legal responsibility for future brain trauma.

Geelong had a secret arrangement in 2024, which was revealed on Thursday, with an undisclosed player who signed the agreement in a bid to exonerate the club and its medical staff from future court action.

Speaking to ABC Radio Melbourne on Friday, Bowden said he found it "absolutely outrageous that a young person's been taken advantage of", calling it "gambling with a young [player's] health and safety".

Dogs coach on concussion controversy Western Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge gives his view on concussion in the AFL following revelations of Geelong putting a waiver into a player's contract.

Bowden — who is also a former trade unionist and member of the Northern Territory parliament — pointed to the close ties between the club and the AFL, with former Geelong president Craig Drummond the chairman of the AFL Commission and Geelong chief executive Steven Hocking being the former general manager of football at the AFL.

"How this has got through, how people have thought that this is possibly OK is now ever more outrageous with the facts that have been put on the table," Bowden said.

Loading...

"It's conduct unbecoming. The AFL will fine players, they will fine people who are involved in the community sport — if you breach the code of conduct anywhere in the AFL at a game of community football you can be brought in front of a tribunal.

"And this AFL club, Geelong, have gone and signed a contract outside the standard playing contract and I would say outside of WorkSafe Victoria's legislative framework to provide a duty of care and a safe workplace.

"And now they're going to say: 'Nothing to see here, let's move on and watch the footy.'"

Bowden took aim at his former organisation the AFLPA for putting out a joint statement with the AFL over the issue and saying that the association had to "act more like a union, the union they are."

"They [the AFLPA] are too close [to the AFL] and this example says to me that the industry has got control of the Players Association," Bowden said, citing the AFL's funding of the AFLPA "to the tune of millions of dollars per year".

He called for Geelong to be brought in front of an independent tribunal to get to the bottom of the issue.

"I don't think there's been a press conference where anyone from the AFL or Geelong has stood there and taken questions," he said.

"Concussion is the nmber one issue in the AFL at this point of time. It's going to be huge in years to come, the CTE research and understanding now, the history that we know.

"They're all too close and the industry is too close at times so maybe it needs to go to a Senate estimates committee hearing or something and get David Pocock to ask some questions and get independent senators and Sarah Hanson-Young to level these to the AFL.

"A young man has been put at risk and been asked to sign a secret waiver that says he'll exonerate the club from any future issues with his health. That needs to be investigated and that's not OK."

Asked if he thought Geelong would end up being sanctioned over the waiver, he replied:

"Yes I do. I think the court of public opinion will demand that they be sanctioned because this type of behaviour in modern AFL but also in workplace safety laws is not acceptable. Independent separate contracts are unacceptable."

A Victorian government spokesperson responded on Friday.

"Players safety must never be compromised," the spokesperson said.

"The AFL must have evidence-based policies and procedures in place to protect their players.

"The AFL, as the governing body for Australian rules football, has responsibility for managing concussion within the code."

World.title: Athletes go missing after Commonwealth Games
World.content:
Several athletes, including four members of the Ugandan boxing team, have reportedly failed to return home after competing in the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

Ugandan sports website NBS Sport said four members of the nation's boxing squad had gone missing in Scotland and had not rejoined the rest of the delegation before the team's scheduled return to Uganda.

The Pakistan Today newspaper also reported boxer Qudrat Ullah did not return home with the Pakistani team.

Scottish police are investigating the reports after the games finished last Sunday, local time.

"Police Scotland has received reports of several athletes who are unaccounted for," a spokesperson said.

"Enquiries are ongoing to assess the circumstances, and early engagement is taking place with the Home Office."

'No idea what type of asylum'

Uganda's chef de mission, Godwin Kayangwe, said he hoped the missing athletes would return before their visas expire in October.

"I don't know anything about why they decided not to fly home, but I know they communicated with their team manager and said they would be coming back," Mr Kayangwe said in an interview with BBC Scotland.

"But after that their phones went off, so they have definitely broken the camp rules because no athlete is supposed to leave without permission.

"I have totally no idea, absolutely no idea what type of asylum they would be seeking. It's nothing political, it's nothing to do with gender or something [like that]. I have absolutely no idea why they would be doing that."

NBS Sport identified the missing Ugandan athletes as two men and two women: Angel Katushabe, Nuhu Batte, Ibrahim Khemis and Emily Nakalema.

Team Uganda during the athletes parade at the Commonwealth Games opening ceremony. (Reuters: Hannah Mckay)

There have been numerous cases of athletes seeking asylum following previous Commonwealth Games, including 2018 on the Gold Coast and 2014, also in Glasgow.

Former Iranian footballers granted citizenship Fatemeh Pasandideh and Atefeh Ramezanisadeh sought asylum after the Asian Cup in March this year, due to fears of reprisal from the Iranian government.

In March, five Iranian football players were granted asylum in Australia after competing in the 2026 AFC Women's Asian Cup, after they escaped from their handlers.

Three of the players returned to Iran, while two remained and were eventually granted Australian citizenship.

Glasgow 2026 chief executive Phil Batty said the games were working with the police.

"We want to deliver a safe and secure games, so we work really closely with Police Scotland, the Border Force, and UK visas and immigration to make sure everyone arrives and departs in line with regulation," Mr Batty said.

Some 3,000 athletes from 74 nations attended the 11 days of the Glasgow Games.

World.title: Dogs coach says he would have signed concussion waiver to keep playing
World.content:
As the AFL and Geelong continue to face questions about their handling of a concussion issue, Western Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge believes players are looked after better than ever.

The Cats avoided any sanction from the AFL for making a deal with a player who had a history of concussions that required him to assume all legal responsibility for future brain trauma.

Geelong had a secret arrangement in 2024, which was revealed on Thursday, with an undisclosed player who signed the agreement in a bid to exonerate the club and its medical staff from future court action.

Calling it a "complex and unique case", the AFL insisted it was "satisfied that the letter was not used by Geelong to allow a medically unfit player to return to play".

The Cats also issued a statement, saying they would remove the waiver from the contract.

Geelong avoided punishment and said it would remove the waiver in the unnamed player's contract. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Michael Willson)

"The club was not attempting to vary the terms of the AFL standard playing contract, or attempting to avoid its responsibilities under health and safety laws," the Geelong statement read.

When asked about the bombshell revelation out of Geelong, Beveridge spoke generally about concussion rather than commenting directly on the Cats' case.

"I think every player wants to keep playing until your boots fall off," Beveridge said after the Bulldogs' shock loss to North Melbourne.

"All I know that when I was playing, we all had concussions, and if I had to sign a waiver to keep playing, I would have.

"We're so careful with our players now.

"The way we train, as far as the duty of care goes, we really look after them."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Kangaroos coach Alastair Clarkson, who earlier this year sprayed insurance company Zurich for rejecting concussion insurance claims, insisted he knew nothing about Geelong's case.

New AFL Commission chair Craig Drummond was the president of the Geelong board at the time the deal was struck.

Drummond was not mentioned in the statement from the AFL.

Deciding not to front the media to explain the situation, Drummond issued a three-line statement on Thursday night calling concussion a "challenging medical and legal issue for all contact sports globally".

Multiple AFL players, including former Melbourne star Angus Brayshaw, champion West Coast defender Jeremy McGovern, premiership Magpie Nathan Murphy and former number one pick Paddy McCartin, were forced into retirement due to repeated concussions.

Several deceased players, including Danny Frawley, Shane Tuck and Graham "Polly" Farmer, were posthumously diagnosed with degenerative brain disease chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE).

There is also a multi-million-dollar concussion class action case against the AFL, led by former Geelong defender Max Rooke, in the Supreme Court of Victoria that is set to go to trial next year.
