World.title: Some of rugby league's truest believers await the NRL in Perth
World.content:
Most of the time when we talk about an expansion team it's all about firsts.

It starts with the first signing, then it's the first look at the jersey, then on to the first match, first win and first loss as they settle into their new place in an older world.

The Perth Bears are midway through that process right now. With 27 players on their books, their roster has well and truly come together and on Friday afternoon they'll reveal their playing strip to the world ahead of their NRL debut next year.

But amid all the firsts there will also be a last. The jersey unveiling will be held in conjunction with Melbourne's game against Manly this weekend, which is the final NRL game that will be played in Perth before the city has a team of its own.

The next NRL game Perth Oval hosts will be the local side's home debut. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre )

As the old world dies, plenty expect the new one to struggle in birth.

Much has been written and said about the new franchise's lack of star power and whether they can be competitive as they fight against the tyranny of distance and the money monster of their fellow expansion team in Papua New Guinea.

But their entry goes both ways as the beginning looms. It's not just about what awaits Perth in the NRL, but what awaits the NRL in Perth.

With the elite level of the sport about to finally put real roots down, how fertile is the soil? The spark of the game has been flickering for decades, but can it catch fire? Ahead of the last game before the start of forever for the Bears, what is rugby league in Perth really like?

A player's life at the outpost

Samisoni Langi is used to life on rugby league's frontiers. It's where he spent his finest playing days and where he helped make history.

The 33-year old got his start with the Sydney Roosters back in 2013, playing a handful of NRL matches before a long career in Europe, highlighted by five years with Catalans Dragons in France.

Langi played five-eighth for the Super League club when they won the Challenge Cup in 2018 to become the only non-English side in the competition's 125-year history to win the trophy.

He also represented Tonga while he was in the NRL and played for France at the last World Cup after qualifying through residency.

After finishing at the top level at the end of the 2023 season, Langi resettled in Perth to be closer to his wife's family and before long rugby league came calling.

Langi spent five years playing with Catalans Dragons in France. (Getty Images: Tim Clayton )

"It wasn't anything to do with footy, just for family. But a few clubs reached out when they found out I was here," Langi says.

"The players and the clubs here, they live and breathe rugby league. The people in the background are so passionate, they love their club and they love the sport.

"When I first came over there was only five teams in the first grade competition, that's up to nine now. It's a tough competition with lots of pride that's growing each year.

"There's so many volunteers who are at the fields setting up from 6am on Saturday for seniors and they all back up for the juniors on Sunday.

"They love it so much, and they're looking forward so much to the Bears."

Langi linked up with South Perth Lions, a local powerhouse with 20 premierships to their name since their formation in 1948, and got into the world of West Australian rugby league.

Langi played the 2025 season with South Perth Lions and was named the competition's player of the year. (NRLWA)

As Langi got about in that first season, which ended with him being named the competition's player of the year and the Lions making the grand final, the Bears slowly came to life.

In the 18 months since, they've put together their roster and now their first pre-season is well and truly on the horizon.

The discerning football fan might notice a lack of big names, but according to Langi that won't matter to most in Perth.

Australian Rules remains the biggest game in town by an indomitably huge margin and rugby union is firmly in second with the Western Force celebrating its 21st season this year.

For league to carve out a niche the key isn't in brand name players, as much as they'd help the on-field prospects, but in the name of the team itself.

There's a core of league fans that can provide a base for the club — crowds for NRL matches in the west have held steadily over 30,000 for the double headers at Perth Stadium and over 10,000 for one-off matches at the Bears' future home, Perth Oval.

Attendances and interest at NRL matches in Perth have held steady. (Getty Images: Paul Kane )

But for the Bears to become part of the fabric of the city they need to tap into the general sports population and the way to do that is strengthen the links to the community as much as possible.

In terms of sustainability, local pride beats imported star power every time and parochialism is a way of life in rugby league which should serve the city well, given Perth fans would show up to a letter-opening, so long as it's a letter about Perth.

"Everyone's excited to have a team of their own. A lot of footy people still have their teams from back east, the Roosters have come over and the Sharks and Raiders were here a few months ago, but having the Perth Bears will be different," Langi says.

"Nobody's too fussed about the players, they're just excited a team will be here.

"The biggest thing is being visible and accessible. Spend time in schools, visit junior clubs, support local competitions, build genuine relationships in the communities across Perth. Young players need to see the club as something they can be a part of.

"Whenever there's an NRL game coming here it's always big. The entire comp either has the week off or we push our game to Friday night or Sunday afternoon so everyone can get along to the NRL.

Why Luai's move to PNG has changed everything Jarome Luai's decision to sign with Papua New Guinea is a showcase of the economic power behind the Chiefs and marks the start of the greatest rugby league gold rush since Super League.

"You can feel the buzz around the city. It also inspires young players and they can see what's possible and dream to be out there playing professionally. Even the captain's run is big — I teach at a high school and nobody comes the day before the game, all the kids go to the open training session."

Langi doesn't just teach at Baldivis College to the city's south, he also runs the school's girls rugby league program, the first of its kind anywhere in Western Australia.

Finding a game for his charges isn't always easy but their enthusiasm is inspiring to Langi and while it could take the better part of a generation for work like his to bear fruit, the fact that the Bears are coming into a world where that work is already being done bodes well for their future.

"At the start I didn't know what I was getting myself into — the first thing they want to do every session is tackle, they're always asking when we're going to start tackling and I have to say 'we have to go through technique first, we have to catch and pass' and all these other things. But they love it," Langi says.

"The girls so look forward to games and sometimes they get cancelled and that can be disheartening.

"But we're trying to grow the game and with the Bears coming it should get a really good push, I'm looking forward to that."

Langi will be on the frontlines to see it as well. This year he transferred from the Lions to the newly promoted Kalamanda Bulldogs and he is keen to run around again in 2027.

"I'm just trying to help some of the young guys find their way. The club has come into first grade from reserve grade this year, so it's been a big step up," Langi says.

"We're pushing for the finals right now but next year and past that they'll be able to give it a real crack.

"I'll play for another year or two, then it'll be into coaching. I don't think I'll ever give up footy."

The age of the Bear begins

Perth's rugby league future might be more upscale than its past but it'll be nowhere near as colourful.

South Perth Lions, Langi's old club, have enough yarns alone to fill many a front bar session.

There was the time in the 1950s when a local dairy owner auctioned off one of his milk cart horses to raise money for the club but neglected to mention the horse in question had passed on after being hit by a car the day before.

This was around the same time the Lions home ground was next door to Perth Zoo and due to a lack of facilities players would wash in the zoo's artesian hot pools after matches.

A few decades later the team had managed to build its own clubhouse but were having trouble getting a liquor license because it required permission from the nearest publican.

After much resistance from the proprietor of said boozer, two enterprising club officials managed to win him over by approaching him on a Sunday morning in a moment of weakness as he battled a hangover that could kill a brown dog and a nasty bout of gout.

Perth hasn't had a team in the NRL since the Western Reds folded at the end of 1997. (Getty Images)

The club's end of season parties were always a highlight, particularly the year when, in an effort to keep the players out of the local watering hole, each pub donated an 18-gallon keg. It took them four days to get through all 15 of them.

Then there was the time the club had a partnership with a local company to unload produce trucks, which was put in jeopardy when the players unloaded watermelons by forming a makeshift backline and spiral passing them along.

Or the day a plane crashed on Como Reserve during an off-season game of cricket and the boys sprang into action to save the passengers, who fortunately survived the crash, with one man freeing them while still wearing his wicket-keeping gloves.

Some of these stories might be truer than others, but what's certainly true is they're all stories.

What's more iron-clad is South Perth's brilliant record on the field. Amid producing NRL talent like former Newcastle forward Cory Paterson, brothers Bronx and Bryson Goodwin and former Manly prop Kurt de Luis, they have 20 premierships to their name since 1948, the most of any team in the competition.

Other sides, like Joondalup Giants, Fremantle Roosters and North Beach Sea Eagles, had their glory days over the years but those same days never seemed to come around for the Willagee Bears, competition stalwarts since 1966.

When current coach Nelson Davis, who has lived in Perth for more than two decades, first took more than ten years ago the club had played for half a century without ever winning a first grade premiership.

Davis has lived in Perth for over 20 years and been involved with Willagee Bears for a decade. (NRLWA)

Davis, who had been coaching since he was 16 back home in Auckland, was initially daunted when his best mate and current assistant coach, Conrad Ramea, asked him to lend a hand.

"I said 'I'm only a juniors coach, I wouldn't know what to do with seniors.' But I've been at the Bears ever since," Davis says.

"We started from rock bottom. We had a really good base of players and at the time we were one of the strongest junior clubs, we had nearly one team in every grade.

"A lot of our players would come through the 16s and 17s but going to other clubs because we didn't have a first grade team.

"We did go up for two years in 2018 and 2019 and we lost every game. We learnt a lesson then."

After a few years away from the sidelines as the club's coaching co-ordinater, Davis took the reigns of the first grade side again in 2023 and was determined to learn from the pain of the past.

Willagee's trip to the grand final last year was years in the making. (NRLWA)

"I was ambitious. I gave the club a list of things we'd need to go up to first grade because I knew we had to learn those hard times," Davis says.

"I talked about paying players, upskilling staff, getting more support in terms of strength and conditioning and assistant coaches and my president, the man he was, came back to me a few months later and made it happen."

The Bears got to work, signing enough players to give their kids a team they could aspire to and setting new standards.

The results were remarkable. Just a few years after they could barely win a game, Willagee won the club's inaugural first grade premiership by downing Langi's Lions in the 2025 grand final.

It was a triumph of vision, development and self-belief, amid a transformation that would have made any club proud.

Nine of the players in the grand final side had played in the club's reserve grade team the year before and the club's entire spine and front row were local boys.

Willagee scored their breakthrough premiership in 2025 after a lifetime of waiting. (NRLWA)

"Just talking about it now makes me a bit teary. It was one of the greatest days and nights of our lives, to do it with my family and my best mate, it's what rugby league is about — those memories, the people, the bonds and the friendships you make," Davis says.

"That's what matters more than anything, more than any trophy.

"I look back at us getting belted 80-0 five or six years earlier and I never thought I'd be there for a Willagee first grade premiership.

"I thought I might have an influence on it if it happened a long way in the future but for it to happen so quickly was surreal.

"There were so many people who put in so much hard to work to get us there."

When Davis said it was a win for the many he's not kidding — Willagee has 411 people registered at the club and nearly a quarter are volunteers.

Loading Instagram content

Davis doesn't take a salary and several of his players now say they'll play for the club for free.

"That's the passion the guys have for the club and that's what drives a lot of clubs over here — the passion, the loyalty, the community feel and the family environment," Davis says.

"We aren't the biggest club, but we pack a punch and we have high aspirations for where we want to be."

Said aspirations are quickly being realised. Willagee have backed up their breakthrough premiership with a season for the ages and are undefeated at the time of writing just a few weeks out from the finals.

Their reserve grade side is set for the minor premiership as well and a clean sweep could be in the offing given their under-17s team is top of the table.

The family feel is already coming through with their links to their NRL big brother. Davis pinpoints Kaino Gudgeon, man of the match in last year's grand final win, as the club's key signing for their turnaround and his brother Ammaron, a local product, will take up a train and trial deal with Perth over the summer after a standout season with North Sydney in NSW Cup.

Plus none other than Mal Meninga himself, living Immortal and the NRL's sides foundation coach has been along to several Willagee matches and for Davis, those efforts to forge a link with the local league scene will be crucial.

Meninga's role in strengthening the Bears ties with the community will be vital. (Getty Images: Paul Kane )

"Mal's been to a few of our games already and that means a lot to the players and the coaches," Davis says.

"There's a lot of kids I coach who have dreams to play in the NRL and you have to be straight up with them about how hard it is and what the pathways are like — I just hope the Perth Bears can create that for them.

"I do believe there's some real talent here and some kids who could be knocking on the door.

"I know the Bears have big plans with the Tracks Academy and there's some very, very good 16 and 17-year olds, even in our club.

"I've got one player and I'd have had him in first grade the day he turned 17 but his mum won't let him."

Few would dispute that Perth Bears have a huge task ahead of them, but Willagee Bears are proof of what's possible.

People like Davis and the army of volunteers across the clubs that have kept the flame of rugby league alive so far from the game's strongholds have not just given the NRL side an example to aspire to, they've given them a community to serve, a rock on which the elite level of the game can build its church.

For decades, love of the sport was all that kept the lights on and now those lights are about to be so bright as to be dazzling.

Their game has come to them at last and it is a reward they never expected for a passion that never waned.

"People walk around with the Bears shirts on around the streets. When I'm wearing Willagee Bears gear everyone thinks it's for Perth," Davis says.

"There's a strong core community here, it's not the biggest, but it'll only grow with them coming. Even if we have teams already - I'm still a Warrior because I have been since day dot - we're all foundation members, I can guarantee you that.

"I just hope they can be semi-competitive those first few years and give the locals something to turn up for.

"It's been a positive impact already and we're so excited. Every club has seen an increase in numbers already. The banners are up, the billboards are up. I can't wait."

World.title: Le Court wins Tour de France Femmes stage as Reusser keeps overall lead
World.content:
Kimberley Le Court of Mauritius overcame earlier difficulties to emerge victorious in a reduced sprint and win stage six of the Tour de France Femmes, as Swiss rider Marlen Reusser held on to the overall lead with three stages remaining.

Le Court joined a small breakaway group 10 kilometres from the finish, launched her sprint with 300 metres to go and held off French rider Cedrine Kerbaol on the line, with Puck Pieterse of the Netherlands coming in third.

The 30-year-old Le Court suffered a mechanical before the final climb and had to change bikes, but, thanks to her teammates, made it back in time to launch her telling move.

"They brought me back slowly but surely to the bunch, and I got back on top of the last climb, which was a really big effort," Le Court said.

"Then I just tried to stay patient, try to recover from this big effort. Riejanne Markus and I bridged to the breakaway, and we got to the front."

There was no change at the top of the standings after the 153.4km ride from Montbrison to Tournon-sur-Rhone, with Reusser holding a 12-second lead over Dutch rider Demi Vollering. Poland's Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney is third, 1:17 off the leader.

A group of three riders built an early lead of over two minutes but were brought back with 54km remaining.

World champion Magdeleine Vallieres set a blistering pace at the front on the penultimate climb of Col de Lalouvesc, which split the peloton, leaving a reduced bunch of about 30 riders to go for the stage win.

A group of six then got away, before they were joined by Le Court and Markus. The breakaway managed to hold off the chasing pack, and Markus made a move with one kilometre left.

The Dutch rider was unable to make her attack count, and it was left to Le Court to claim an almost carbon copy victory of her stage win last year when she outfought Vollering and Niewiadoma-Phinney in a seven-rider sprint to the line.

Tech.title: The best classic slasher movie you’ll never watch
Tech.content:
Starting with the original in Camp Miasma in 1980, the horror franchise went on to have a long life. There were multiple sequels, spinoffs in the form of arcade cabinets and board games, and just about every kind of merchandise you can think of, from alarm clocks and lunch boxes to Halloween costumes and action figures. It got so popular there were even knockoff costumes at party stores. For several decades the franchise exerted a powerful, albeit dwindling, impact on the world of horror. But if you haven’t heard of Camp Miasma, that’s okay, because it doesn’t really exist. It’s a fictional franchise at the heart of Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma, the latest film from I Saw the TV Glow director Jane Schoenbrun.

In order to convince audiences that Camp Miasma — an ongoing saga about a character called Little Death who terrorizes a summer camp — could be real, the production designers had to create a whole lot of objects that detailed the movie franchise’s fake history. “We probably could’ve spent three years only making stuff for Camp Miasma if those were the marching orders,” says production designer Matt Hyland.

Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma tells the story of a budding director named Kris (Hannah Einbinder) who has been given the green light to reboot the long-dormant Camp Miasma franchise. Before doing so, she decides to meet up with Billy (Gillian Anderson), the final girl from the first film in the series, who has spent decades isolated in the woods. Kris tries to convince Billy to join the project, and from there the two go on an intimate journey, where they connect over sex, slasher movies, and KFC.

Image: Mubi

But before that, there’s Camp Miasma. The film — the real one — wastes no time in quickly telling the history of the franchise during the title sequence. Through old movie posters, VHS tapes, toys, photographs, and even film reviews and news articles, you learn how the series started off strong before steadily dwindling, going from box office success to direct-to-video dreck over the span of around 30 years. Those objects become a powerful and efficient tool — though the process of creating them wasn’t quite so quick and efficient.

First, the designers spent a long time doing research, looking at existing slasher series like Friday the 13th, Sleepaway Camp, A Nightmare on Elm Street, and Halloween in order to get a sense of how those films looked and how they permeated culture at large. From there, they made a kind of historical document, informed by Schoenbrun’s script, which outlined the entire existence of Camp Miasma: when each movie came out, who directed it, how it was received, and what kind of merchandise was released. Then they sat down with the director in order to figure out what items they actually needed to tell this story. “We locked ourselves in a room with Jane and the cinematographer and mapped out the sequence beat by beat, and every beat was an object we needed to fabricate,” explains Brandon Tonner-Connolly, the film’s other production designer.

Image: Mubi

Most of the items only appear on screen for a brief moment, but the work that went into them was extensive regardless. The Camp Miasma board game, for instance, is fully playable, with a complete set of instructions. Even something seemingly simple, like VHS boxes or movie posters, took a lot of effort: The team had to not only determine how they should look, but also make sure to include information like the production and distribution companies and the film’s tagline. That work was necessary to create a level of believability, even if the object in question only had a fleeting moment on camera.

“You can’t make decisions based on screentime,” says Hyland. “If it’s a board game, we’re making a board game, even if it’s on camera for half a second. That’s a resource challenge. It’s part of our process to assign priorities to things. But the truth is that Jane is so full of ideas and very excited, and gets us very excited, so that unlike other movies, this felt like a pencils-down moment. We just wanted to keep making stuff and coming up with ideas, and we only stopped because the camera was ready and we simply ran out of time.”

Image: Mubi

The attention to detail was also in part a nod to fans. “Jane has such an incredible following that you know that people will pause the movie and read the review, or read the instructions for the board game,” adds Tonner-Connolly. That meant ensuring everything was consistent; the team made multiple tie-in lunch boxes, for instance, and made sure the designs were different to reflect if they would’ve been released in 1983 versus 1997.

Nailing the details was important, but the duo also say that their goal wasn’t to 100 percent re-create existing designs and slap the Camp Miasma name on them. Instead, the objects “needed to look and feel like the memory of watching” those movies. According to Tonner-Connolly, it’s the same approach that was used on I Saw the TV Glow, which similarly had a story revolving around a Buffy the Vampire Slayer-style ’90s drama. “We know that we’re technically proficient enough to exactly replicate these [classic slasher movies], but what we’re actually interested in is relying on these fragmented memories of childhood, and how things are remembered and misremembered,” he explains. “We wanted to play with those emotions and create this new thing.”

It’s that combination of detail and emotional resonance that allows the film to tell Camp Miasma’s multi-decade history with just a handful of snapshots. And that helps make everything in the rest of Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma — which includes a long sequence pulled straight out of the film that started it all — feel grounded in something that seems real before taking more fantastical turns. “It’s hard to convince an audience that for the last 30 years this thing has been in the cultural conversation,” says Hyland. “People can smell a phony pretty quickly.”

Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma is in theaters on August 7th.

Tech.title: Why does Apple keep banning Telegram, but never X?
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

For roughly an hour this week, Telegram vanished from Apple’s App Store. Even during that blip, it was a stunning absence for such a major app: an avenue of communication for more than 1 billion users around the world, used widely as a secure platform for people who live in countries under censorship. Apple later revealed that it had removed the app due to the presence of child sexual abuse material (CSAM) and restored it once that content was removed.

But the decision once again stirred up questions and confusion about Apple’s moderation policies and how it treats different companies. And one company in particular sprang to many people’s minds: X, the Elon Musk-owned platform that stayed on the App Store even as sexualized Grok-generated images of children flooded the platform. What led to Telegram’s removal but X’s ability to stay online?

The answer may be more political than technical. “When you are enforcing your content moderation policy against an entire platform, you are subjecting yourself to the blowback that will happen,” Anupam Chander, a professor of law and technology at Georgetown, tells The Verge.

Both Telegram and X have had their fair share of controversies. Telegram, which is headquartered in Dubai, garnered a reputation for having a laid-back approach to content moderation.

“Removing X would have likely caused a firestorm of political response against Apple.”

That’s all to say that, while large and important, Telegram is also seen as a nuisance politically and a problematic platform in its own right. “X has a far stronger base of political support in the United States than Telegram does,” Chander said. That means “removing X would have likely caused a firestorm of political response against Apple” to a degree it wouldn’t receive for taking down Telegram. It was not a first for Apple, either; the company previously removed Telegram due to a CSAM violation in 2018, for a similarly brief period of time.

One instance of illegal content can be enough to get an app removed from app stores, but Apple appears to have taken a very different approach when it came to X’s latest controversy. Late last year, X rolled out an update giving users the ability to edit images on the platform using X’s Grok AI chatbot. Soon after, AI-generated deepfakes that undressed adults and children began spreading across the platform.

Despite all of the pressure on Apple, the company kept X in its store. Instead, it began communicating with X behind the scenes to request changes.

Apple reached out to the teams behind the X and Grok apps “after it received complaints and saw news coverage of the scandal,” according to a letter Apple wrote to US senators seen by NBC News. Apple asked the developers to “create a plan to improve content moderation,” NBC News reports. While Apple later found that X “substantially resolved its violations,” Apple reportedly told Grok’s team that they needed to make additional changes “or the app could be removed from the App Store.”

Musk issued a statement in January, saying: “Anyone using Grok to make illegal content will suffer the same consequences as if they upload illegal content.” xAI later sued a man for allegedly using Grok to generate and distribute CSAM. During this period, Apple removed neither X nor Grok and never has, even though the AI chatbot within both apps generated undressed images of minors.

”Removing X would have had to be a decision made at the very top, a decision that you’re willing to suffer the political consequences, including a very irate Elon Musk,” Chander said. Apple is certainly aware of what can happen. In 2022, shortly after he bought Twitter, Musk began publicly complaining that Apple was trying to restrict the app; the dispute ended with Tim Cook giving Musk a tour of Apple’s campus and resolving the apparent “misunderstanding.”

Meanwhile, Durov claims that Apple removed Telegram before ever contacting the company. Apple declined to comment on the moderation differences between the two apps.

Apple closely guards the process behind its moderation decisions, so it’s hard to tell exactly how the company works with developers behind closed doors. But Apple’s recent actions suggest the rules have some flexibility — at least when the world’s first trillionaire is involved.

Tech.title: Trying to explain One Night Only’s tech-enforced sex dystopia
Tech.content:
is a news and reports editor with more than a decade of experience. She was previously an editor at Vox.com and Racked.

From the omnipresent One Night Only trailer, you’d be forgiven for thinking that the movie glosses over its terrifying and absurd premise — in otherwise normal modern New York, single people can only have sex one night a year — to deliver an entirely traditional romantic comedy.

I’m here to report that it does not do that.

No, the film is very much about life under Sex Purge Law, but where you might expect questions of politics or religion or fear or humanity, there are instead questions of boning. Questions like “Who should I do sex to and why?” are explored in an episodic format that sees two special hot people (Monica Barbaro and Callum Turner) run into each other over and over but not immediately get busy. That obviously raises more questions! (“WHY NOT?”) Questions are really the joy of this movie, if you find joy in it, as I did. It tries to answer some, but it creates so, so many more.

The one you’re probably asking: How is this law possibly enforced?

Editor’s note: This post contains One Night Only spoilers.

When “the mandate” was passed, three years prior to the events of the movie, all adults of legal age were issued subcutaneous tracking chips with attendant, color-changing tattoos. When you’re unmarried, the tattoos — a little lighthouse for our heroine, the Batman symbol for our hero — are red. You know, for “stop” (having sex). When you wed, they go green. But on “The One Night,” as people and brands alike shorthand Sex Purge Day, reds turn green and pent-up singles barely stop themselves from boinking in the street. Largely they do stop themselves, though, because somehow despite its R rating, this movie isn’t like that.

In fact, the movie is somewhat desexed, even though sex is the explicit topic. It is surprisingly amusing, though, if you can quiet your disbelief to only one to two cries of “Really?? This??” per minute. The movie has sort of misfired David Wain energy, with some truly unexpected gags and pleasantly silly set pieces. It helps immensely that Barbaro and Turner are extremely appealing, both individually and as a pair. They have the all-important chemistry that makes romcom heads forgive wild, bizarre sins of plot and conception.

One of these sins is arguably the way the chips monitor sexual activity, which is basically “science???” Dopamine and other erotic neurochemicals are measured, and if they’re discovered to be spiking in two people close in proximity, that’s a violation. You can be arrested — although it’s unclear how many violations this takes, as we only see repeat offenders — and banned from sex even on The One Night. While I can tell you there are no special sex cops, only an exhausted-seeming regular NYPD, this law enforcement technology does engender many more questions. As Verge senior copy editor Kallie Plagge asks, what if you both see a puppy at the same time? What if you do drugs together, asks senior social media editor Tristan Cooper — or if you self-pleasure in the presence of another, how far apart do you have to be? What if you have roommates? I don’t know!!

On the one night a year single people are legally allowed to have sex, hijinks ensue. Universal Pictures

It’s purposefully hand-wavy and a little vague, but maybe not as completely out there as we’d like. Wearables have been proposed that could monitor your sexual fidelity via heart rate, skin temperature, and movement-detecting sensors.

Information about how exactly this became a political reality is not the particular interest of screenwriter Travis Braun or director Will Gluck, but it is allowed to dribble out in the background as Barbaro and Turner separately scheme to get some.

(Sorry, let’s pause here. Actual question No. 1: Why do these two absurdly attractive, totally charming people even have to try, especially on a night such as this? We learn early on that Turner’s handsome pizzamaker had a mishap with his intended, but Barbaro’s character was apparently too busy with her career singing lyrically tweaked pop ballads for pharmaceutical commercials to meet a decent guy in the previous 364 days. That might be even more outlandish than the government decree they’re living under, but the movie makes it clear she’s a romantic — in classic romcom logic that’s a practically insurmountable flaw, until you find the perfect person to mount.)

We learn that Congress passed the measure at the urging of a Christian-coded technomegacorp that makes the chips and also employs Nicholas Braun. We do not learn where the Durex and EPT lobbies were during this vote. We learn that the party line, from the company’s smarmy CEO — distinctly more JD Vance-like than Elon Musk-esque — is that people wanted a return to innocence, and apparently that’s all we’re getting. It’s also implied by a single queer character that queer people have been “getting around” the straights’ sex laws for time immemorial, so this is NBD to them, but this is less a commentary on queer ingenuity or resistance than it is a reason to make that character sit this one out for a babysitting gig. We don’t get a good answer on the divorce or birth rate in SexPurgelandia — although teen pregnancy is down, which… aren’t the kids not chipped? — and it’s unclear if married people can swing (I’m guessing yes).

Where’s the pushback? Where are the people digging the chips out of their skin, refusing to get tagged, storming the Capitol and doing it doggy-style on alternate-universe Nancy Pelosi’s desk? That might be the film’s one kind of neat trick, if you’re feeling very generous. This law is widely unpopular but only lacklusterly protested by a complacent public. We see plenty of graffiti, “Resist” signs in brownstone windows, a well-funded benefit concert. But we see a lot more corporate buy-in with cutesy “One Night”-themed advertising. A society too busy buying and selling things to fight back against religiously inflected fascistic oppression and sex weirdness? I can’t say I have questions about where the creators got that idea.

Tech.title: Meta ordered to pay an additional $567 million in public nuisance ruling
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Meta has been ordered to pay $567 million in the second phase of New Mexico’s landmark child safety case, bringing total charges to nearly $1 billion for being a “public nuisance.” In a ruling published on Thursday, the Santa Fe district court found that Meta’s platforms are a “significant contributing cause” of a teen mental health crisis affecting public health and safety throughout New Mexico.

“This case has always been about protecting children, standing up for families, and making sure that one of the world’s largest technology companies cannot profit from practices that endanger young people without consequence,” New Mexico Attorney General Raul Torrez said in a statement. “Today’s decision is a victory for every parent who has worried about what social media is doing to their child and every child who deserves to grow up safer online.”

The $567 million will be put into an abatement fund that will go towards funding awareness and prevention measures, screening services, and treatment for people harmed by the company’s platforms. The abatement fund order is in addition to the $375 million in civil penalties that Meta was ordered to pay in the first phase of the New Mexico case, bringing Meta’s total charges to $942 million.

In a statement published by Meta spokesperson Andy Stone, Meta says it disagrees with the ruling and plans to appeal:

“We work hard to keep people safe on our platforms and have been transparent about the challenges of identifying and removing bad actors and harmful content. We remain confident in our record of protecting teens online and will continue to defend ourselves against claims that misrepresent the facts.”

Tech.title: Trevor Noah is hosting Google’s Pixel 11 launch event
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google is set to host its next live Made by Google hardware launch event on August 12th, and the company says in a new video that comedian Trevor Noah will be hosting the show.

The video indicates that the event will feature other celebrities and influencers as well, including Call Her Daddy host Alex Cooper (who was at the 2025 event), Indian cricketer Shubman Gill (who has starred in Pixel ads), Japanese actress Ayami Nakajo (who has also starred in Pixel ads), and NBA star / Google Performance Advisor Stephen Curry. (Cooper and Noah are also bringing shows to YouTube.)

Jimmy Fallon hosted the show last year, an event that my colleague Victoria Song described as more like “a live taping of The Tonight Show with Jimmy Fallon” than a traditional tech launch event. Given the celebrity faces set to appear at this year’s event, it seems that Google is once again aiming to reach a more mainstream audience. It’s also airing right at the end of the ET workday: the event, which takes place in New York City, starts at 6PM ET.

As for the gadgets you can expect, Google’s event teaser video features brief glimpses of a new phone and smartwatch, and the company has previously shown teases of the Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro Fold. There are a bunch of leaked images and specs of the upcoming hardware floating around, too. However, if you’re thinking about picking up one of Google’s new gadgets, you should be prepared for a higher price tag.

Tech.title: Jony Ive’s first OpenAI gadget is reportedly a hockey puck-sized smart speaker
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The AI device OpenAI is developing with former Apple designer Jony Ive is “essentially a smart speaker without a display” that’s battery-powered, doughnut-shaped and roughly the size of a hockey puck, according to Bloomberg reporter Mark Gurman. The device, expected to launch in 2027 for a price over $300, reportedly “will have a unique look, complete with moving parts,” including some that will move on their own to show when the device is responding or interacting with the user, along with lights, a camera system, and other sensors.

Gurman’s sources also say the “battery-powered” device is designed to be “easy to carry around the home with one hand,”similar to Amazon’s now-discontinued Tap speaker. Gurman says it will “work similarly to the company’s ChatGPT voice mode on smartphone apps, but with more advanced models for humanlike interactivity” but look and feel nothing like an Apple product — despite their ongoing lawsuit.

The speaker / pocket personal assistant could be the first in a “family of devices” OpenAI has planned, but we’ll probably hear a lot more about all of them before it eventually arrives.

Tech.title: The AirPods Pro are $60 off, their best price since late June
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Best Buy kicked off a sale on Apple products with discounts on its latest smartwatches to phones. Another deal that caught our eye is on the latest AirPods Pro, Apple’s flagship wireless earbuds, which are down to $189.99 ($60 off), with retailers like Amazon and Walmart matching the price. That’s their lowest price since Prime Day in late June, and just $20 shy of their all-time low.

The AirPods Pro are our favorite wireless earbuds to recommend for iPhone owners because they offer better sound quality than Apple’s entry-level AirPods. Our A/V reviewer John Higgins uses them more often than other pairs because of their, praising their excellent audio, best-in-class active noise cancellation, and just how easy they are to use. They also provide a tighter fit, making them more comfortable for some people, especially during workouts.

Beyond how good they sound, they offer a number of perks for Apple users. They can automatically sync with other Apple devices you’re signed in on, so you can move from taking a call on your iPhone to watching a show on your iPad. They also feature a built-in heart rate sensor that works with more than 50 workout types in Apple’s Fitness app, so you can use them as a fitness tracker of sorts.

Tech.title: The Zelda movie’s Ganondorf casting hints at more movies
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Deadline reported Thursday that the upcoming The Legend of Zelda movie will feature Australian actor Uli Latukefu as the villain Ganondorf, and the publication notes that “We hear Latukefu inked a multi-picture deal.”

Nintendo or Sony haven’t formally confirmed that there’s more than one movie in the works, though it’s been rumored that Nintendo and Sony might be planning a trilogy. Still, it’s not exactly unexpected that more Zelda movies might be on the way, especially given the huge success of the recent Super Mario films at the box office.

Nintendo initially announced the live-action Zelda movie, which it’s making with Sony Pictures Entertainment, back in 2023, with Wes Ball directing with Shigeru Miyamoto and Avi Arad producing. Last year, Nintendo announced that Bo Bragason and Benjamin Evan Ainsworth had been cast as Princess Zelda and Link, respectively. The movie is set to release on April 30th, 2027, and filming has officially wrapped.

In a separate report published later on Thursday, Deadline says that Dichen Lachman, Yvonne Strahovski, and the late Sam Neill will be in the Zelda movie as well. Neill’s role is unclear, but the article says Lachman plays Impa while Strahovski has been cast as “a queen character.”

Nintendo is also preparing a big new Zelda game: the company has announced a Switch 2 remake of Ocarina of Time that’s set to launch sometime in 2026.

Update, August 6th: Adds new casting details from another Deadline report.

Tech.title: New Mexico court orders Meta to pay additional $567M in child safety case
Tech.content:
A New Mexico Court judge on Thursday ordered Meta to pay a fine of $567 million, on top of the $375 million levied in March, in a case regarding social media harms and addiction. This brings the total fines the company has to pay to $942 million.

The court also ordered Meta to make changes to how its platforms function in the state: it wants the company to remove Like counts, and only show such metrics to children under 18 with approval from a parent or a guardian. Push notifications to underaged users in the state are also to be paused between 10 p.m. and 7 a.m, and their usage should be limited to 90 hours a month, which amounts to roughly three hours per day.

“Significant numbers of people in New Mexico experience harm from Meta’s products due to risks of sexual exploitation, interference with education, and adverse mental health outcomes,” the order said.

The judge acknowledged that Meta is not the only platform causing a mental health crisis among youth in the state, but maintained that its platforms play a significant part. He said that the company has caused a significant “public nuisance” in New Mexcio, and is required to abate that.

Meta said that it is going to appeal the judgment.

“We work hard to keep people safe on our platforms and have been transparent about the challenges of identifying and removing bad actors and harmful content. We remain confident in our record of protecting teens online and will continue to defend ourselves against claims that misrepresent the facts,” company spokesperson Andy Stone said in an emailed statement.

“For years, Meta knew its platforms were harming New Mexico’s kids, from feeding a youth mental health crisis to connecting predators with children, and it chose engagement and profit over their safety,” state Attorney General Raul Torrez said in a statement.

“Today, Meta is paying for that choice. This judgment holds the company accountable for the damage it caused to our children, our families, and our schools, and it forces real changes to how Meta operates in New Mexico,” he added.

The ruling comes in the wake of another loss in Los Angeles in March, where the court also ruled against the social media company for creating addictive patterns.

Meta is facing several other cases in the country. One of the notable cases is a joint lawsuit by 33 states, which was consolidated in an Oakland, California federal court. Several other states, like Tennessee, have brought their own cases against the company.

Tech.title: OpenAI’s new AI smart speaker will reportedly sell for between $300 and $400
Tech.content:
In Brief

More details continue to trickle out about OpenAI’s mysterious new hardware device — described previously as an AI-fueled smart speaker that will be the “physical manifestation” of ChatGPT.

Bloomberg now reports that the device will be “donut-shaped,” designed thusly to allow users to carry it around their home and place it in different locations, like a bedside table or a kitchen counter.

It will be constructed from “high-quality metal,” have a “premium look,” and (in a detail that mystifies) will have distinct “moving parts,” sources told Bloomberg.

It also could be slightly more expensive than your average smart speaker, perhaps $300 to $400 per unit, according to this report. For comparison, most of Amazon’s smart home speakers range in price from $40 on the low end to $240 on the high end.

So, to sum up: an expensive talking AI donut that has … moving parts? OpenAI releasing a smart home device has a certain logic to it, in that it would further integrate ChatGPT into users’ lives. However, historically speaking, smart speakers have not always been profitable and may prove a difficult market to break into. The potentially high price point also might not help.

The device, which is being developed in partnership with LoveFrom, the design studio founded by famous former Apple developer Jony Ive, will likely be released at some point in 2027, Bloomberg writes.

The company’s attempt to enter the hardware market has not gone off without a hitch. OpenAI is being sued by the current king of hardware, Apple, which has accused the AI lab of stealing trade secrets. OpenAI has denied wrongdoing.

Tech.title: Vogue just gave another nod of approval to the tech world
Tech.content:
Vogue World is coming to San Francisco next year — perhaps another indication that tech billionaires have become leaders in the fashion zeitgeist.

Of course, the announcement of the enormous fashion/art/music event doesn’t say that. Instead, Anna Wintour wrote that Vogue believes in celebrating cities and “San Francisco is a city like none other.”

“It’s a place of diverse communities living side by side, a place that loves the arts, loves creativity, and isn’t afraid of change.” She also noted the city’s history of rebelliousness and innovation.

“I love that San Francisco has always stood up for values and the things it believes in,” Wintour wrote. “Vogue World will support San Francisco’s creative minds and strengthen the entire ecosystem — and it will offer another opportunity to show San Francisco is on the rise.”

There were rumors that Vogue World would head to San Francisco after Winter was seen having meetings with the city’s mayor, Daniel Lurie.

Plus, in the past year, Wintour has cozied up to the most powerful names in tech, culminating in this year’s Met Gala, which saw Jeff Bezos and his wife, Lauren Sanchez, serve as lead sponsors for the event. Google’s Sergey Brin and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg were also spotted at the event (the latter’s first, that is). In fact, OpenAI bought a table, as did Meta and Snap (for $350,000 a pop). It’s true that TikTok, Apple, and Instagram previously sponsored the event, but the presence of the tech crowd was so considerable that the Met Gala this year was dubbed the “tech gala” in some places.

Last year, Vogue put Lauren Sanchez on the cover of the magazine after her wedding to the Amazon founder. To the fashion world, this was Wintour’s stamp of approval — not just for Sanchez’s ascent into the fashion world, but that tech and its leaders were worthy of cultural recognition.

Though Bezos and Sanchez reportedly live in Florida (and Amazon is, of course, headquartered in the Seattle area), there is no city more associated with tech than San Francisco. By locating Vogue World there, this is another indication of Wintour’s approval.

Vogue, as a media publication, is always following the money, and as a cultural bible, is always looking for ways to stay relevant. Turning toward the worldwide headquarters of AI, good or bad, is brilliant for business (and Wintour is nothing if not brilliant).

But Vogue World was previously held in New York, London, Paris, and this year, Milan. Maybe because I live in an East Coast bubble, but I’ve not heard anyone in recent years refer to San Francisco as a beacon of style to rank alongside these other cities.

While the city has a reputation as the land of the free-spirited bohemian, tech and its workers have a reputation for hoodies, Patagonia vests, and expensive athletic shoes, if they even dress up that much.

For instance, billionaire Alexandr Wang, who is now running Meta’s all-important Superintelligence Labs, just did an interview with Y Combinator’s Garry Tan in front of a packed stadium wearing a faded Nintendo T-shirt and what looked like a pair of Crocs. Comfy? Yes. High fashion? Decidedly no.

But maybe that’s changing. Wang’s boss, Mark Zuckerberg, who once always appeared in a plain gray T-shirt and jeans, has made efforts in recent years to become more fashionable. Zuck and his wife Priscilla Chan were spotted front row at a Prada show this season. The new campaign for Meta Glasses has a slew of celeb ambassadors and looks like it could be a Saint Laurent or Balenciaga ad.

OpenAI and Palantir have recently released merch collabs, playing on the minimalist style of tech workers (the merch line of the latter, I would argue, looks inspired by Virgil Abloh’s Off-White).

I concede that creatively there is much to be done with the understated, Northern California style. Surrounded by beautiful nature and cooler temperatures, plenty of fashion designers could be motivated by San Francisco’s tech industry. I look forward to seeing Claude-inspired terra cotta-colored gowns and Vogue-emblazoned quarter-zips soon.

Tech.title: Google says hackers are calling financial firm employees to hack and extort victims
Tech.content:
Even in the age of AI-powered autonomous cyberattacks, the crude, tried and tested hacking techniques of tricking victims into doing things they shouldn’t are still producing great results.

Groups of unknown hackers are targeting and breaking into large financial and investment firms in the United States with the goal of stealing sensitive data to extort the victims with the threat of publishing it, Google’s security researchers wrote in a report on Thursday.

The company did not name the victims, but Reuters reported that among them there are leading private equity firms such as Apollo Global Management, Bain Capital, Blackstone, Bridgewater Associates, CME Group, KKR, Moody’s, and TPG.

The hacking groups, which Google dubbed Falcon, Helix, Pink, and Redact, are using an old-fashioned technique to break into those firms: phone calls to employees’ personal cellphones in which the hackers pretend to be co-workers or IT helpdesk staffers, during which they try to trick targets into entering their credentials and multi-factor codes on spoofed websites, according to Google. In cybersecurity parlance, this technique is known as voice phishing, or vishing.

Some of the groups identified by Google run websites where they publicize their hacks and threaten to leak the stolen data as a way to extort the victims into paying a ransom, a common strategy among cybercriminals.

Image Credits:Google /

“We conduct every negotiation on professional terms. The publication of your data is never our preferred resolution; it is the consequence of refusal to engage, deliberate stalling, or failure to honor an agreement,” read one of the sites. “Respond promptly and in good faith, and the matter is resolved without further incident.”

Google researchers said that the different groups may all be part of a larger umbrella collective the company tracks under the name UNC6671. But it’s unclear if they are affiliates, splinter groups, or they all use the same Phishing-as-a-Service infrastructure.

“We believe that this most likely reflects a coordinated group of threat actors operating multiple public extortion brands possibly in an effort to compartmentalize operations, hide overall breach volumes, and isolate any negotiation fallout,” read the report.

According to Google, the hacking groups have also previously targeted large companies in the manufacturing, real estate, healthcare, and insurance sectors, as well as tech, transportation, and hospitality companies with the goal of stealing “valuable intellectual property, software source code, or sensitive VIP client data.”

More recently, the hackers have targeted legal and financial organizations such as private equity firms. “Concentrating on organizations involved in mergers, acquisitions, capital deployment, and litigation may reflect a strategy to target high-value corporate and confidential data to maximize leverage extortion demands,” wrote Google’s researchers.

Google said that one cryptocurrency wallet associated with one of the hacking groups received around $10 million in bitcoin in the first few months of this year, and that the hackers usually demand from $750,000 to $3 million from victims.

Laurie Bischel, a spokesperson for CME Group, declined to comment.

Apollo Global Management, Bain Capital, Blackstone, Bridgewater Associates, KKR, Moody’s, and TPG did not respond to a request for comment.

Tech.title: China-linked LightSpy spyware caught targeting victims in 13 countries, including the US
Tech.content:
Security researchers say they have evidence that a Chinese-linked spyware has expanded from mainland China to now target victims in over a dozen countries, including across Europe and the United States. The previously identified spyware also has new functionality capable of stealing troves of data and remotely bricking devices.

The researchers at cybersecurity firm Arctic Wolf said that the LightSpy spyware, first discovered in 2018 and previously linked to Chinese state-backed hackers, has since evolved into a commercial spyware platform operated by a single threat actor who caters to governments, enterprises, and militaries.

The platform is said to feature custom branding, billing, and demos for advertising it to prospective customers.

The findings underscore how the use of spyware continues to proliferate beyond governments and nation-backed hackers, and more broadly into the private industry.

LightSpy is a modular spyware platform that allows whoever is controlling it to attack a multitude of different devices, including smartphones, Apple devices, Linux servers, and Windows PCs. By using exploits for each device, the spyware can steal large amounts of sensitive information from its targets, including precise location data, chat messages, screen recordings, and stored passwords. The researchers also said the code is capable of remotely wiping and destroying data on a compromised device.

The researchers said that LightSpy has now been identified infecting routers, which researchers say they had not seen before. By attacking routers, the hackers can gain visibility and access to any other device on the same network.

Some of the compromised routers are associated with NATO member countries, said Arctic Wolf.

According to the company, LightSpy operates a network of at least 117 servers in several countries around the world.

The researchers said they were able to link the latest activity to a Chinese contractor after one of the spyware’s operators used the LightSpy administrator’s panel to place an order with Kentucky Fried Chicken using his real name and office address.

Tech.title: Defense tech Hadrian raises $1.37B at $8B valuation
Tech.content:
In Brief

Defense tech Hadrian announced on Thursday that it had raised a fresh $1.37 billion round at a valuation of $7.87 billion from a mile-long list of well-known investors.

The lead investors in the round include WCM Investment Management, Washington Harbour Partners, Valor Equity Partners, 137 Ventures, and Baillie Gifford. Participating investors include 1789 Capital, Morgan Stanley Wealth Management, funds managed by Apollo and T. Rowe Price, as well as firms like CapitalG, Andreessen Horowitz, Founders Fund, Lux Capital, Altimeter, and others.

Founders Fund and Lux led the company’s $260 million Series C financing about a year ago, bringing the total raised to date to around $2 billion, according to PitchBook estimates.

Hadrian is an interesting defense tech in that it’s not trying to build new AI-powered weapons. The company is building automated manufacturing facilities that will mass-produce parts for the vehicles that the military complex already relies on.

For instance, in March, Hadrian opened a facility in Alabama to mass-produce parts for submarines, making that its fourth facility. The deal for that facility, structured as a public/private partnership, was valued at $2.4 billion, Hadrian said.

Tech.title: Best Webcams (2026): My Honest Take After Testing the Best
Tech.content:
The Insta360 Link 2C Pro magnetizes to its strong aluminum mount, and I never worried about it falling back, even with the weight of the USB-C cable pulling on it. This also makes its panning adjustments super-smooth. It's surprising how many webcams struggle with this very simple motion, but it’s perhaps the result of many mounts being plastic—including the Logitech MX Brio. Because the Insta360 is magnetic, it can also stick to any other metal surface, which can be convenient if you're looking to shoot from a different angle.

In terms of image quality, no webcam at this price delivers lowlight performance on par with the Insta360 2C Pro. Right out of the box, without even tweaking any settings, I was impressed by its ability to handle harsh light. Like all the cameras, I tested it in some poor conditions, including under overhead office lighting and being backlit. The webcam handled these scenarios better than its competitors. It avoided blowing out the highlights and could deliver as much detail in the image as possible, even compared to more expensive webcams, like the Obsbot Tiny 3 ($349).

I also noticed its very natural image-processing contrast compared to options like the Logitech MX Brio, which tended to crush blacks. Under better lighting, the sharpness of the image really stood out. Thanks to that large 1/1.3-inch CMOS sensor, objects in the background fall out of focus in a natural bokeh effect. It mimics the look of a DLSR better than any camera I tested. Other webcams look flat by comparison.

It's not perfect—no webcam is. Sometimes there's a bit too much processing and smoothing for my taste, especially in some of the details around the face. And out of the box, the colors skew a bit cool. The easy-to-use software makes adjusting these issues easy, but it's something to be aware of nonetheless. Hopefully, by now, you'll be convinced that there's little reason to buy the Logitech MX Brio over the Insta360 2C Pro. Logitech has a lot of brand equity in the world of webcams, but considering both models retail for $200, Insta360 definitely has the superior product.

The standard Insta360 Link 2C ($150) is also a strong option. It's $50 cheaper, with a slightly smaller sensor and narrower aperture, resulting in worse low-light performance. I noticed that it introduced more noise, especially in areas of high contrast, such as along my hairline. But let's be real: Though you can hunt down the differences between these two webcams, the standard Link 2C still punches above its weight for the price.

One of the biggest disadvantages of the non-Pro model, though, is in microphone quality. The Insta360 2C is more in line with other webcams I tested. It uses just a single microphone and lacks the ability to pick up the deeper frequencies in my voice, whereas the 2C Pro uses a dual-microphone beam-forming system that does a far better job capturing the fuller spectrum. I still think that the Insta360 Link 2C is one of the best options at around $150, though, handily beating out models like the Razer Kiyo V2 and Logitech Brio 4K.

Cheap Webcams That Get the Job Done

Proceed very carefully with the following recommendations. That's especially true if you are working from a laptop with a built-in camera or already have a decent webcam. In general, I suggest dishing out some extra cash for one of the more premium options listed above, or buying a light to help your existing camera work better. Even a simple lighting accessory, like the $70 Logitech Litra Glow, will dramatically improve the quality of your video calls more effectively than buying a budget webcam.

That said, if you're using an external monitor and need a budget-friendly webcam to pair with it, there are a couple of decent options to consider. The Anker PowerConf C200 ($66) is the best of the bunch that I've tested. It has issues, such as the built-in mount, which can't swivel left or right. It also doesn't grip the monitor as effectively as I'd want. While the 5-megapixel camera can't compare with the larger sensors in the more premium webcams, the image quality is decent enough, especially if your room has nice light and you don't mind tweaking the picture quality in the software.

I'd also hesitantly recommend the Logitech Brio 300 ($60). Like the C200, it has a number of deficiencies. On this model, those drawbacks include an unappealing sticky pad built into the integrated mount and the built-in cable. The microphone also won't be much of an upgrade over the ones built into MacBooks, though it's still better than built-in mics on many of the Windows laptops I've tested. I also don't like that the Brio 300 has a fixed 70-degree field-of-view, which gives it a smaller framing than all the other webcams I’ve tried.

Tech.title: The 5 Best Laptop Power Banks I've Personally Tested (2026)
Tech.content:
Toss the right laptop power bank in your bag, and you'll never need to do that panicked run to the nearest outlet again. A hefty portable charger frees you to sit anywhere with your laptop and keep it running. Power banks with USB-C ports can charge phones and headphones as well, and I’ve tested more than 100 of them over the past few years. These powerful, high-capacity portable batteries are the best ones when laptop charging is a priority. For this guide, I considered power banks that are 20,000 mAh and up, enough to charge most laptops twice.

If you want some smaller portable chargers, check out my guide to the Best Power Banks or Best Qi2 and MagSafe Power Banks, or for more power, the Best Portable Power Stations.

Updated August 2026: I added power banks from ReelCharge and Pisen, removed some older devices, and updated prices.

Best Laptop Power Bank

Power bank manufacturers have made strides in pushing up potential charging rates in their high-capacity portable chargers. EcoFlow’s Rapid Pro X is a prime example, just edging out Anker’s Prime series below. Capable of delivering 300 watts, this power bank is close to the maximum capacity allowed on flights, and can charge a couple of laptops and phones at the same time via the three USB-C ports (140W, 65W, 65W) and a retractable USB-C cable (140W). It has a wee display showing remaining power as a percentage and the charging rate for each connected device. You can also check temperature and battery health, tweak the brightness and screen timeout, and even connect to your phone via the Ecoflow app (though most folks won’t need to).

The Rapid Pro offers a laundry list of charging capabilities (PD3.1, PPS, QC3.0, AFC, Apple2.4A, BC1.2, SCP, FCP, UFCS), but its greatest feature could be its super speedy recharge rate. Charge from a single USB-C input at 140 watts, and it takes an hour or so to fill, but you can plug in both at once to hit 80 percent from dead in under half an hour. Even better, Ecoflow’s dock can charge via the pogo pins on the bottom at 320 watts, enabling you to go from zero to 80 percent in just 20 minutes. You can fully charge it while you pack a bag. The Rapid Pro X comes with the 27,650 mAh model and the charging dock. Ecoflow also offers a 20,000-mAh, 230W Rapid Pro model ($140).

Specs Ports: USB-C x 3, retractable USB-C cable Capacity: 27,650 mAh Charges: Most laptops one to two times Wattage: 300 watts Warranty: 2 years

Best Laptop Power Bank With a Dock

Anker introduced an innovative, high-wattage, high-capacity Prime Power Bank series a few years ago with an optional docking station for faster recharging via pogo pins on the bottom. This model is more compact and powerful than ever, offering 26,250 mAh at 300 watts across two USB-C ports and one USB-A, making it suitable for charging a couple of MacBooks and a smartphone at once. It also boasts a smart display and app control, and it comes with a 3.3-foot USB-C cable. Plug in both USB-C ports, and you can recharge at 250 watts to 80 percent from zero in 20 minutes.

Lenovo LOQ 15 Essential Gen 11 for $1,850: If the version of the LOQ 15 I recommended above isn't available, I would consider this one more seriously. If (and when) that older model goes out of stock, my opinion here will change. While the smaller power brick is nice, it means you can't run intensive games in Turbo mode without draining the battery—even while plugged in. I was told that the updated 2026 model would fix this problem, but it still lists a 135-watt charger. I was fine to overlook that issue when the laptop was selling for less than the competition, sometimes as low as $750. At its current price, though, you're better off with the MSI Cyborg A15.

Tech.title: Ranking the Best Smart Glasses: Meta, Viture, & More (2026)
Tech.content:
Honorable Mentions

Photograph: Simon Hill

RayNeo Air 3s Pro for $299: TCL-owned RayNeo offers many models, and I've tested several. The latest Air 3s Pro glasses boast a 201-inch virtual screen (1080p, 120 Hz, 1200 nits), but the 46-degree field of view lets it down a little. Both color vibrancy and brightness are improved over previous releases like the Air 2s and the older TCL RayNeo Air 2 XR Glasses. You can just about see the whole screen clearly (even after adjusting, I had to slide them down my nose a little to avoid blurring at the bottom). You will also need the lens shade to use them in brighter environments. While they are cheaper than our other virtual-screen picks, I found them inferior in design, fit, and comfort. Rayneo has added some more on-device options, including spatial sound, but it didn't work well for me, though the standard sound is fine. RayNeo’s software, required for 3 DoF, is still buggy and unpolished. This is a good virtual screen for the money, and perfectly suitable for watching movies and light gaming, but if you want more from your smart glasses, I'd pick a different pair. —Simon Hill

Viture Luma Pro for $499: Every time a company comes out with a new pair of smart glasses, the old one instantly looks dated. The same is true here with the older Viture Luma Pro and the newer Viture Beast. The Beat's display is better, and it has the onboard chip, so you don't have to deal with the hassle of the SpaceWalker app. If you're using the glasses for gaming, you're probably going to spend whatever you save buying the older Luma Pro's on accessories anyway. That said, if you exhausted your budget, the Luma Pro is a cheaper way to get a small, portable screen for traveling. —Adrienne So

Photograph: Adrienne So

Engo3 for $400: These sports sunglasses are for high-performance aerobic athletes going at such high speeds that looking down at your wrist might place you in peril. The glasses are a miracle of engineering, weighing only 38.5 grams (half that of the Oakley Meta Vanguard). I tested the version with the photochromic lenses, which have an ambient light sensor to dial the transmittance up or down. You can connect the glasses with a compatible Garmin or Apple Watch and customize the HUD (heads-up display) to show real-time data on a color display as you're working out. It's accurate, and the text is crisp. Unfortunately, the HUD is located right near the bridge of my nose, which means I'm cross-eyed when I check it. Also, it's debatable which is more distracting during a long run: having to look down at my smartwatch or having a giant HUD mirrored display in the middle of my face, falling down my nose when I sweat. —Adrienne So

Chamelo Music Shield for $229: These are the simplest smart glasses on this list. If you're too cool for auto-transition photochromic lenses, you can just slide your finger along the right arm of these electrochromatic sunglasses to dim them anywhere from 17 to 64 percent light transmittance. They also play music. These are comfortable and work well, but the sound is nowhere near as clear or loud as other options. They're also not polarized and are pricey considering their limited functionality. —Adrienne So

Rokid Max 2 Glasses for $429: The Spider-Man–esque lenses give these comfortable smart glasses a bit of character, though they won’t be to everyone’s taste. They project a 215-inch screen (1080p, 120 Hz, 600 nits, 50-degree FoV) and have diopter dials for focus adjustments, but I struggled to eliminate blurring around the edges, and instead of using stylish electrochromic dimming, there’s a clip-on plastic blackout shield. I also tried the Rokid Station 2, which adds an Android TV interface to access entertainment apps, but also a trackpad and an air mouse for easier control. —Simon Hill

Photograph: Simon Hill

Lucyd Reebok Octane for $199: Designed in partnership with Reebok for cyclists and runners, these lightweight Bluetooth sunglasses feature silver polarized lenses, quality speakers, and an eight-hour battery life. I enjoyed listening to music and podcasts on them while hiking. I also like that you can hear the world around you, but the sound leakage isn’t too bad, so you won’t bother the people you pass. They also have physical controls that are much easier to use than touch controls, even when your hands are wet or sweaty (the glasses are water-resistant, too). You can take calls, get directions, and ask your preferred AI assistant questions. Lucyd has been making Bluetooth sunglasses for several years now and offers a wide range of different styles. We also tried the Lucyd 2.0 Bluetooth Sunglasses a couple of years ago, rating them a 7 out of 10. —Simon Hill

Avoid These Smart Glasses

Here's the eyewear that fell short.

Photograph: Simon Hill

Asus AirVision M1 for $699: I was excited to see Asus launch smart glasses, but the lack of fanfare was a red flag. My first impressions of the lightweight design were promising, and the M1 offers up to a 100-inch virtual display and impressive 1100 nits brightness. Designed to plug into your phone, laptop, PC, or handheld gaming device via USB-C, the M1 also features built-in speakers and a microphone. Sadly, the refresh rate maxes out at 72 Hz and is limited to 60 Hz unless you employ the Airvision software, which also enables you to select different modes (working, gaming, infinity), tweak screen position, and set interpupillary distance (IPD). I found the in-focus sweet spot was small, and most of my virtual screen was blurry, no matter how I tweaked the settings. This made the glasses uncomfortable to use, especially for work. There’s also a basic plastic shield to block light, rather than electrochromic dimming, and the speaker quality is decidedly average, leaving me puzzled about why the price is so high. —Simon Hill

Halliday Glasses: While these could almost pass for chunky regular glasses thanks to a clever ring controller and a tiny unobtrusive display, I can confidently say they are not the future of smart glasses. After spending several uncomfortable hours trying to adjust the display to be readable, all I got was a headache. The ring seemed like a smart idea, but it’s big, plastic, and laggy. The eavesdropping AI is slow, and squinting up to try and see the screens of unhelpful text it churns out is painful. The sound quality and battery life are likewise disappointing. —Simon Hill

Solos AirGo Vision for $299: With a built-in AI assistant powered by ChatGPT, the Solos AirGo Vision adds a camera on top of the Bluetooth-connected speakers in the rest of its range. Grant it unfettered access to your location and photo library, and it can describe what you are seeing. The most obvious use cases are translation and navigation, though I’m not convinced about the accuracy of its suggestions. The design is interesting, with chunky temples housing the smarts and interchangeable frames. There’s no virtual screen or HUD, but you can get prescription lenses, and they look relatively normal. Sadly, the photo and audio quality are horrible, and the touch controls are frustratingly finicky. The app is also power-hungry and demands too many permissions. The Ray-Ban Meta glasses do the same things better. —Simon Hill

Frequently Asked Questions What Are Smart Glasses? A Brief History AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron While prototype facial computers date back as far as the late ’60s, it was Google Glass that popularized the idea of smart glasses. First released as a developer kit, Google Glass is more than a decade old. They gave rise to a serious privacy debate but were also beloved by early adopting “Glassholes.” After failing to take off as a consumer product, Google Glass pivoted into factories and warehouses, highlighting the potential of augmented reality in the workplace. The first wave of augmented reality glasses were unappealing and largely unsuccessful. They were chunky and heavy, were light on features, and made wearers look like cyborg extras from a sci-fi B-movie. The first pair I tried from Vuzix made me question the entire category. There was a lot of hype about augmented reality, but most of these chunky glasses offered relatively low-resolution displays superimposed over your field of view. For smart glasses to truly blend the real world in front of you with the virtual world, they would need cameras, processing power, and some very smart software. Many players, big and small, have tried and failed to make an impact in this space. The early excitement generated by companies like Magic Leap evaporated amid clunky hardware at high prices. The trouble with some of the most ambitious examples thus far, like Microsoft HoloLens 2 or Apple’s Vision Pro, is that they are relatively big and heavy and, more importantly, horribly expensive. The most successful smart glasses so far are more focused, less ambitious, and cheaper, though they also fall well short of the original vision. There’s currently a palpable sense that smart glasses are right on the brink of breaking through into the mainstream. Google’s Android XR opens up the space for developers to make the killer apps needed to drive adoption, and it has begun showing off new AI-powered smart glasses and a mixed-reality headset developed with Samsung. Xreal is also working on some new Android XR glasses dubbed Project Aura that are expected to arrive later in 2026. Many other smart glasses are in development, like Meta’s Artemis glasses, new Snap Spectacles, and Emteq’s inward-looking smart glasses. —Simon Hill Are Smart Glasses Worth It? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Smart glasses aren't for everyone, but they can be a worthwhile investment if you value portability and convenience. They’re especially useful if you want texts, notifications, or directions displayed in your line of sight instead of reaching for your phone. And if hands-free features like photo and video capture, open-ear audio, and live translation are important to you, smart glasses are worth it. What Are the Different Types of Smart Glasses? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Smart glasses exist on a continuum of simple to complicated. Like a wearable face computer, they can have a wide variety of price points and specs to accommodate the different types of onboard tech. The most basic smart glasses are electrochromic (automatically darkening) sunglasses . These are for all the people who want control of their glasses’ dimming. They're marketed as smart glasses, but they probably don't have any other tech in them.

XR and AR glasses almost always have a screen component that can show you information like real-time translations of a person you're talking to or arrow overlays to give you directions. There's often an AI component, where you can ask the glasses about the things you see. What Does HUD, DoF, and FoV Mean? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron HUD stands for heads-up display. This refers to the text or screen of information overlaid upon—but not obscuring—view of the world. It usually appears around the periphery of your field of view, like in video games. Simple HUDs might display the time or mirror notifications from your phone, with more advanced versions capable of translating text on signs or identifying places around you.
